reviews.transcript_full: This week I'm in KLM's World Business Class aboard their Boeing 777-200 as I fly their fifth freedom route between Santiago in Chile and Buenos Aires in Argentina. There's plenty of drinks to be had on board, a full three-course meal, a Delft house or two, a fully lie-flat bed with pillow, and legroom that even the husband can't grumble at. Well, bienvenidos a Santiago de Chile and a very warm welcome to this week's video. Warm being the operative word. It is a balmy 28°. I absolutely promise you, and my husband will tilt the camera left and right. This is not a green screen. I absolutely promise you this is not a green screen. I am here in the flesh introducing this week's video. But what a spectacular view of the entirety of Santiago. It really is a beautiful, beautiful city. But of course you're watching the video, so let's tell you where we're off to this week. We're flying over to Buenos Aires in Argentina. Um not with the airline though that most of you would suspect. Most of you would probably say LATAM or Aerolineas Argentinas. But for me and the husband today, we're flying across to Argentina with the Dutch airline KLM on their funky fifth freedom route. So strap yourself in and join us on this pretty unique South American flight. And to get that wonderful view you've just seen, we took the Funicular de Santiago up the side of the San Cristobal Hill, which forms part of the Santiago Metropolitan Park. We really did sample everything the city had to throw at us including numerous pisco sours. You don't ever need to ask me twice. And they were paired with lots of ceviche, wonderful fresh salads, great fish and seafood, and even greater wine. Couple that with beautiful sunsets, and you get a pretty fabulous time. I think Chile might just have become my new favorite place in South America. But sadly, it was time to leave. So, we grabbed a taxi across to Santiago's International Airport in order to catch our flight. Once inside the main terminal building, if you turn to the right and head to zone A, you'll find both the Air France and KLM check-in desks located here. There was a bit of a queue today due to the Air France direct flight departing at a similar time, but our Sky Priority status from the business class ticket meant we sailed through. So, all successfully bag dropped here at Santiago International Airport for our flight over to Buenos Aires, and uh when we got there, we thought, "Oh, the queue does look quite long, but not only is this KLM flight taking off today to Buenos Aires and then onwards to Amsterdam, there's also a direct Paris Charles de Gaulle flight with Air France." And of course, Air France-KLM, uh you know, being partners, uh the queue was quite big, but we got through literally in 2 minutes using that Sky Priority lane. So, bags are all tagged. We're heading through security and off to the SkyTeam Lounge. So, I'll pick up the next shot inside there. You also get access to SCL's priority security lane, a lane that has a real plane just sitting next to the X-ray scanners. How cool. The SkyTeam Lounge is quite easy to find and very well signposted. The lounge is one of three, the others being the Prime Class Lounge and the Banco de Chile Lounge, both of which are located in the same area. Initial impressions were good, and the inner AvGeek in me just loved this SkyTeam artwork of all its member airlines. What a collage. Well, a very warm welcome to the SkyTeam Lounge here at Santiago's International Airport. And of course, if you're flying business class with KLM on their fifth freedom route to Buenos Aires or all the way through to Amsterdam, you will get access if you're flying business class to the SkyTeam Lounge. Also, if you have any related status, you'll get SkyTeam access here as well along with all the other SkyTeam Airlines and there's plenty of them as we saw when we came in the lounge. So, we're just kicking back and relaxing. I'm going to take you on a full lounge tour as always, so you'll see everything you get in this lounge. Husband's out there now scoping it out. So, in a moment I'll take you around. I'll film everything and take you on a full SkyTeam Lounge tour here at Santiago's International Airport. Upon entry, there's an open bar to the right of the lounge with a variety of local beers and spirits, although they're only served between 10:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. due to local licensing laws. I don't think I've ever seen anything like this before in a lounge. There's plenty of different seating areas to take advantage of all with USB A, C, and local sockets, too. There's also an office work desk with printer if you need to get some work done. And the lounge also has great views of the apron and gates. Always a big plus if you're an avgeek. The food and drink are set towards the back of the lounge and on offer today was fresh orange and strawberry juices alongside this chilled orange and lime still water. There was also a selection of meats, cheeses, fresh oatmeal ready for the microwave, a variety of yogurts, and a good fresh fruit selection, too. There were corn flakes if you fancied some cereal alongside a selection of milks. There was also two different types of croissants. There were small sandwiches available as well and also chocolate brownie bites and carrot cake slices, not to mention an array of fruit, too. There was also bread for toasting alongside a variety of jams and preserves, including this local marmalade. There was a fridge full of sodas and mixers, not to mention this touchscreen coffee machine. I couldn't resist a cheeky hot chocolate. There were also teas from Twinings as well, but I also couldn't resist trying the fresh strawberry juice, and it was a sucker punch of flavor. I highly recommend you give it a go. Finally, there was a scan to order menu featuring two types of quiche, scrambled eggs, and also French toast with icing sugar and strawberries. Today's scrambled eggs were the other way, not overdone in any way, shape, or form. In fact, if anything, maybe slightly under. We sat and broke our fast before then heading over down to the gate to await the inbound flight which flies over from Buenos Aires with the same crew that'll be taking us back today. So, all at the gate now, gate E11 for our flight over to Buenos Aires. And of course, that 777-200 with KLM continuing on to Amsterdam. So, of course, there's some people here that have got a very long journey ahead of themselves over to Europe, but um pretty much just kicking back and relaxing, waiting for this zone one boarding, which is the the priority boarding this SkyTeam priority you get when you're flying business class with any of the SkyTeam airlines. And that should commence shortly. But I think we've got a new award for the most friendliest boarding team here at Santiago. So, KLM's representatives down at SCL are probably some of the friendliest I've ever encountered, super helpful, and just really, really polite and pleasant. And as much as most of them are polite and pleasant, it really does shine sometimes when people go above and beyond. I just went and asked a quick question, and they were so helpful and so lovely. So, a big props to KLM staff here at SCL. Today's aircraft is this Boeing 777-200 extended range series, which was delivered to KLM Royal Dutch Airlines in February of 2004, making it a little over 22 years old. The aircraft is also called Epidaurus, named after world heritage sites around the world. We were then called to board and it was a highly efficient process with those in Sky Priority Zone 1 being invited to join the aircraft first. Aboard this 777-200 extended range series aircraft, KLM configures their World Business Class in a 1-2-1 seating layout. And here's my seat for today's journey, 4A, on the left-hand side of the cabin. So, welcome aboard KLM's World Business Class on this Boeing 777-200 aboard this flight over this fifth freedom flight over to Buenos Aires. And then this afternoon it continues over to Amsterdam. And uh we're just taking the first leg so you can completely book the first leg as I explained earlier. Um but I must admit I think we've set a new record for crew friendliness. KLM right at the top of any cabin crew I've ever experienced. So friendly, so helpful, and just really really such a warm welcome on board. So, a big props to KLM for that. That certainly hasn't gone unnoticed. So, let me get settled in the seat and I'll take you on a full seat tour of KLM's World Business Class aboard this Boeing 777-200 across to Buenos Aires. I got my own personal overhead locker as the flight wasn't operating full over to Buenos Aires. The seat also features a comfortable leather headrest, a full-size pillow, and this impressively sized IFE screen. The seat buttons are all touch sensitive on this control panel. And to the left of this is a table with integrated wireless charging too. There's also USB-A, USB-C, and AC power in the seat as well. This cupboard pops open and houses plenty of storage, a mirror, and also a set of noise-canceling headphones. Over your left shoulder is this pop-out reading light. And this is complemented by overhead reading lights, too. There's an IFE remote available alongside this slimline storage area. There's a literature pocket to the right of the seat as well, alongside this raisable lever armrest. And as you can see, an impressive amount of legroom, too. There's also two windows to each seat, and these come with manual window blinds as well. We were then given a menu, which was printed and dated specifically for this flight. I do like detail-driven elements like this. The crew then came round with a welcome drink. There was a selection of champagne, orange juice, or this royal blue legend mocktail made with lemon, ginger, and spirulina. It's absolutely delicious. So much so, the husband wanted seconds. It was then time for us to push back from Santiago and depart. I also caught these two ex-Wizz Air aircraft, which weren't taken up by the airline and were still sat sitting in their liveries. Not something I expected to catch whilst filming in South America. >> So, we're all up in the climb on this KLM flight. It's a bit of a queue for takeoff today out of Santiago. There was four aircraft in front of us and we had to queue. Obviously, that Air France A350-900 going back direct to Paris just slightly ahead of us. But, then the crew just come on over the PA and said that they're going to keep the seatbelt signs on for about 10 minutes because we're climbing up and crossing the Andes and it is known for quite heavy turbulence. So, the crew and all of us passengers are still strapped in still after about 5 to 10 minutes after takeoff. going to be like that for another 5 to 10 minutes. So, beautiful views out of Santiago. If you've never seen out the window or you've never been into Santiago on one of these flights, the views landing and taking off out of here are nothing short of spectacular. So, enjoy the views and when the service starts, I'll show you what happens next. So, of course, for the crew, time is of the essence on this flight because the Andes seatbelt delay, obviously, you know, took about 20 minutes for us remaining in our seats with the seatbelts fastened. And of course, that applied to the crew because the turbulence was quite bumpy coming up through the climb. And of course, from those pesky mountains. And now, just an hour and 1 minute to go, so 61 minutes to go. And my table has been laid for the meal service. So, really looking forward to showing you what KLM offer. They do offer a full service, full alcoholic bar, full hot meal service on this route, which is severely impressive really when you think about it. And considering the time, a sandwich would suffice, but the fact that KLM are pumping out a full hot meal, starter dessert, tea, coffee, and lots of other little services as well, makes me really, really impressed. So, yeah, stay tuned. I'll show you what comes next. Props to KLM for designing a business class tray table that you can actually push out in order to leave your seat. A lot of other carriers can certainly learn a thing or two here. I then thought I'd very quickly check out the IFE, which was very responsive. Time was really of the essence though, as this was a very quick hop over to Buenos Aires, but it's an impressive system, really, really good resolution, and the husband was very happy with Monopoly, which is also controllable from the remote. Well, I tell you what, KLM, I am absolutely blown away. 10 out of 10. That's probably one of the best meals on a flight of this length I think I've ever had. In fact, it beats the Cathay Pacific meal that we had flying from Hong Kong to Taipei on their 777, which was a similar flight of this length. It was sensational. 10 out of 10, guys. Superb work. And that is, you know, I don't mean to sound, you know, full of myself, but I don't always give 10 out of 10, cuz it's not always 10 out of 10, but that was sensational. So, got the menu here, and the appetizer, the starter, was a marinated smoked trout with dill, and that was served with a cream cheese horseradish, a pea hummus, and a courgette roll, and it was just sensational. It was clean, it was really well smoked, and it's a really tasty starter. That was served with a choice of white or whole wheat pumpkin seed topped bread roll, and I went for the pumpkin seed topped roll. It was delicious. Came with butter and a little envelope with salt and pepper in, which was cute. The main course was a tenderloin roll, a tenderloin beef roll filled with dried tomato, cheese, arugula, and And was served with a creamy mushroom sauce, provencal courgettes, and roasted garlic cheesy mashed potatoes. Again, sensational on all counts. And finally, there was an alfajor, a traditional alfajor with chocolate. Apologies if I'm not pronouncing that correctly. You know my Spanish is weak. And that was a wonderful um traditional um biscuit uh sort of sandwich. It is almost and please please I don't want to upset anybody in Chile, but it was like a wagon wheel but a little bit firmer. It was sensationally good. Um it was coated in chocolate and had dulce de leche paste in the middle and it was just really really good. There was an offer of tea or coffee. I have passed. I've kept up with this wonderful blue uh curacao drink this sort of aperitif drink which we had. Um and I've just kept with that. It's a really tasty kind of orange sweet orange drink similar to Cointreau. Um and that's it. We were offered a wonderful chocolate a Delft House chocolate uh milk, white, or plain. The choice was given to us and it was just sensational. Do you know what KLM? I really am happy for you because you've got your in gear and you really know how to deliver a service on a short flight. So props to everyone on this flight. The crew have been sensational and this service offering has been fantastic. 10 out of 10 from me. The husband asked for a glass of milk and he was very impressed that KLM could deliver on that. The in-flight magazine, the Holland Herald, also features a variety of information including a list of KLM's current fleet including its cargo operations, spotlights on various destinations around the world like Batu Caves in Malaysia. We've stood on those very steps. And not to mention the impressive SkyTeam Alliance map. There's certainly enough routes to keep you going here. It was then time for me to turn the seat into a bed to quickly test the fully lie-flat mode out. I mean, I've got to test it, right? So, just kicking back and lying back testing this fully lie flat bed on World Business Class aboard KLM on that 777-200, and this is a really lovely bed. So much space, really, really comfortable. And this pillow behind me is just, you know, super soft and really supportive. So, yeah, I'm a big fan. It really is a nice lie flat bed. And sometimes, like I say, you get those ones where you haven't got much space. But just to prove it to you, there really is so much space. You can really, you know, choose your position where you lie your head. And down below in the footwell, there's even more space to move around. So, yeah, I think on a super long flight, this would be really comfortable. Over to the husband for the toilet review today, and it was full of little surprises, like this real tulip. How awesome. KLM also stocked the toilets with these luxury toiletries from Marie Stella Maris. It was very clean overall, and the left-hand wall is adorned with this lovely little Delft house design. Hope you enjoyed the tour. I've got to make the husband earn his keep after all, haven't I? Much to our surprise, you do get the gin-filled Delft house gift on the short Santiago to Buenos Aires route. I think this really sets KLM apart from its competitors. A small gesture, but one that certainly goes very far. Frank also nabbed one, too. He picked up the Heineken brewery edition, number 95 of 2026, and I got number 97 of 2026, a miniature replica of the Hotel New York in Rotterdam. >> That was excellent. Perfect. No notes. So, the note is KLM are consistently really good. >> So, that's it for us on this Buenos Aires leg. We are about to touch down into Argentina where we spend the next week here exploring and traveling around a bit more. So, really looking forward to it. But, if you're thinking about booking this fifth freedom route from Santiago to Argentina, I absolutely say go for it because if you experience anything like we've experienced today, you're in for a real treat. The crew on this flight have been probably the best You know, you know what? I'll stick my neck on the line. They have been the best I've ever experienced on any flight, and I've been flying for some many, many years now. Decades, in fact. Um so, yeah. It's been really noticeable and just really nice that the crew have gone the extra mile, um which to be honest with you, I think is the standard for KLM now. They really do put time, effort into their delivery of their onboard service, and it really shows. From the little unique touches like the Delft houses and the Delft chocolates to really good catering and really good offering. Even on a flight of, you know, an hour 20 like this, a full three-course meal with coffee, tea, chocolates, and presents. I don't think anybody can complain. So, a big thanks for watching. A big thanks to the crew today for looking after us. As always, I'll see you next week. >> And with an hour of journey complete, it's hard not to reflect on just how special this flight has been. Because truthfully, this felt like far more than just another business class review. From the moment we stepped on board, there was this unmistakable warmth to the experience. A calm, cozy, uniquely Dutch atmosphere that made the entire journey feel genuinely special. Efficient without ever feeling cold, polished without losing personality, and led by a crew whose level of experience really stood out. It's the little details that stay with you. The iconic Delft blue house filled with Dutch gin, the beautifully presented meals, the comfort, the quiet, the feeling that every part of the experience had been thoughtfully designed to make passengers feel well looked after. And every now and then you have a flight that resonates on a deeper level. One that reminds you why we fell in love with travel and aviation in the first place. For both of us, this was one of those journeys. The kind you'll still be talking about years from now. KLM Royal Dutch Airlines absolutely delivered on every front, and this was without question one of the most memorable business class experiences we've had together. Thanks so much for watching, and as always, I'll see you next week. For us, with Asher being autistic, we absolutely need that extra time to get him on board, familiarize with his seat, comfortable with the seatbelt, and to just adjust before there are too many people on board. Southwest no longer offers family boarding the way they used to. Instead they offer pre-boarding for customers with disabilities or anyone who needs additional boarding assistance. Even though Southwest states only one person will be able to accompany the disabled passenger, I just explained my 5-year-old is autistic and asked if we could pre-board. They offer a great range of movies from classics to new releases like The Housemate, Wicked for Good, and Zootopia 2. To access the in-flight entertainment, just turn on airplane mode on your device, connect to Southwest Wi-Fi, and then open up your Southwest app and click on flight entertainment and it will guide you right through. Our flight attendants were great as they always are. The last one is pretty crucial in India. At airports like Mumbai and Delhi, useful slots are incredibly scarce. You can have all the money, aircraft, staff, and demand in the world, but if you can't get a workable slot at the airport people actually want to use, you can't grow where the market is. So, every collapse created an opening for Indigo. And because they had this constant pipeline of new A320s arriving, they could move into the gaps faster than almost anyone else. And so, their market share marched on from 15% in 2009 to 36% in 2014. And with Jet gone in 2019, it pushed towards a 50% market share of the entire Indian domestic market. Now, before we move on completely, there is one small detail from these collapses that is crucial to the whole Indigo story. In their final days, both Kingfisher and Jet Airways did not run out of money in some abstract accounting sense. Both were literally cut off by fuel companies, who at a certain point just refused to keep filling their planes. In India, airlines quite literally die at the fuel pump. So, how did Indigo keep its costs low enough to survive the exact same fuel pump that killed almost everyone else? >> [music] >> Well, look, Indigo was and still mostly is completely obsessed with [music] having the lowest costs in the sky. For a long time, they operated a single aircraft family, the A320, and this meant one pool of pilots, one pool of spare parts, one set of maintenance procedures. And on board, there's no free meals, there's no ovens for hot food, there's no screens, no in-flight entertainment, nothing that adds weight or complexity. I mean, they also only employ female flight attendants because it's on average they're lighter. Every single decision was about moving one seat, [music] one kilometer for less money than anyone else in India. And look, they do this all with famously on-time punctuality. They turn jets around quickly, they keep utilization high, all of the standard low-cost carrier stuff. But there is one part of the IndiGo model that is quite strange. It's a bit intriguing. They have one of the youngest fleets in the world. The average IndiGo plane as of June 2026 is roughly four and a half years old. That's a bit odd, isn't it? Aircraft are built to fly for 20 or 30 years, and most airlines sweat them for all they're worth because they are incredibly expensive things. So, how is a low-cost airline of all things constantly flying brand new jets? And more importantly, why would they even want to? Old planes fly perfectly well. Well, there's two parts to this. Firstly, those gigantic aircraft orders, 100 planes in 2005, then 180 more, and then 250, and then 300, and then in 2023, there was even an order for 500 jets, the single largest aircraft order in the history of commercial aviation. Ordering at that sort of scale gives you an enormous bulk discount from Airbus. And those discounts also let IndiGo pull a financial move called a sale and leaseback. What What is this? Well, essentially, IndiGo buys all of these planes at a huge bulk discount, but then right when they actually get [music] delivered, they turn around and sell these new jets at market rates to lessors with an agreement to lease the exact same planes back for six years. And well, none of the numbers are really public, but from my readings, they are able to pocket [music] something in the region of four to five million US dollars in profit straight away by using this process. [music] And then I guess after the six odd years, just as these planes are starting to get old enough to need [music] expensive heavy maintenance, and just as their fuel burn starts falling behind the latest models, they hand them back to the leasing [music] company and replace them with brand new jets straight off the production line. Now, to be fair, sale and leaseback is not some secret Indigo invention. Airlines everywhere use it, and critics point out that it can flatter your accounts because you bank the gain today while committing to years of future lease payments. But nobody else has run it at this scale with this much discipline for this long. [music] And while there are some financing complexities in the Indian market that makes this sort of move particularly attractive. But I guess this still leaves us with an unanswered question. Why do they have such new jets? Shiny new jets are often the thing that kills an airline, but in Indigo's case it's actually the thing that keeps them competitive in India. Why? Well, it's the fuel. Jet fuel is the biggest cost for pretty much every airline on Earth. For a typical airline in say America, fuel might be around 20 to 25% of their total costs. In 2025, IATA stated that the global average is 25.8%. But for Indian carriers, it has historically been more like 35 to 45%. What's going on here? Is the fuel particularly special in India? No. The reason is tax. Most of the world barely taxes jet fuel. [music] Across most of Europe, commercial jet fuel isn't taxed at all. In America, the tax works out to a few percent, and I mean in Australia, it's much the same. It's a few cents per liter. But then there's India. The central government puts an 11% excise on jet fuel, and then each individual state piles on its own tax on top of that. And those state taxes have run as high as 29%. So, we've got a system where taxes are stacked [music] on top of taxes. And I guess for the accountants in the crowd, these all sit outside of the GST VAT system. So, the end result is that jet fuel in India has historically cost airlines somewhere around 60% more than the international benchmark price. And this leads to some pretty absurd outcomes. Indian airlines often tank of fuel, they will deliberately fill up extra fuel in low-tax states and then carry that extra weight to a high-tax states just to avoid buying fuel there. So they're burning extra fuel to carry fuel to dodge fuel tax. This is the system every Indian airline operates in. Nobody can negotiate with it and nobody has managed to lobby it away completely. [music] And this is precisely why the young fleet matters so much for IndiGo. New planes burn less fuel than old ones. This is [music] actually a thing. But more importantly, the latest generation of jets like the A320 neo burn significantly less fuel, around 15% less. So IndiGo's eternally young fleet isn't just vanity, it's not just about maintenance. It's pretty much their most powerful cost weapon in Indian aviation. And that pretty much is the IndiGo model. You take the traditional low-cost airline system, run it with total discipline, but then add in one crucial modification for India specifically. You never fly old planes. reviews.transcript_full: Three of the largest airlines in the Americas filed for bankruptcy within 7 weeks of each other. A fourth airline, far smaller than any of them, stopped flying entirely in the same crisis. Not most of its flights, but every single one. Its fleet sat parked for five straight months, and yet it never filed for anything. That same airline now posts operating margins that beat carriers many times its size, year after year, with one of the strongest balance sheets in the industry. And the strangest part of the story is that the decision that saved it was made 40 years before the pandemic ever existed [music] by people who had no idea a pandemic was coming. This is the story of Copa Airlines, the flag carrier of Panama, a country of around 4 and 1/2 million people. So, how exactly did the smallest player turn into the strongest? To answer that, we have to go back to 1944, to a small office in Panama City, where the whole story begins with an American partner that would eventually walk away. On June 21st of 1944, a group of Panamanian investors sat down with executives from Pan American World Airways and signed the documents to create a new company, Compania Panamena de Aviacion, Copa, for short. Pan Am took a 32% stake and brought the technical knowledge. The Panamanians brought the capital and the country. It took three more years before the airline actually flew. On August 15th of 1947, Copa lifted off for the first time, >> [music] >> operating three Douglas C-47 aircraft on domestic routes inside Panama. Three planes, three cities, a flag carrier in name only, working a route map that would fit on a postcard. For almost two decades, that is all that Copa was, a small domestic airline in a small country propped up by an American partner. The first international flight did not happen [music] until the 1960s, when Copa added three weekly services to San Jose in Costa Rica using a tiny mix of Avro 748s and Lockheed Electra 188s. Kingston in Jamaica followed. Then Cartagena and Barranquilla in Colombia. By the end of that decade, Copa had finally crossed the border, but only just. Its world still ended a couple of hours from home. The first turning point came in 1971. [music] Pan Am, dealing with its own problems and pulling capital out of regional partners across Latin America, sold its stake in Copa to a group of Panamanian investors. For the first time, the airline was wholly Panamanian [music] owned. No foreign safety net. No big brother in New York covering the gaps. If Copa was going to survive, the people in Panama City would have to figure it out themselves. And almost immediately, they ran into trouble. By the end of the 1970s, a domestic rival called Air Panama was eating into the routes [music] Copa had spent 30 years building. The math at home was getting worse >> [music] >> every year. Panama is a small country. S2 domestic airlines fighting over the same handful of cities is a slow death for both of them. Copa's leadership sat down to make a choice, shrink and die quietly or do something almost nobody in aviation would advise. [music] They went for the second option. In 1980, Copa walked away from the domestic market entirely. Not reduced, not restructured, gone. The airline that had been founded to fly Panamanians around Panama announced [music] it would no longer fly Panamanians around Panama. Every aircraft, every crew, every dollar of capital would now be aimed outward. The same year, Copa took delivery of its first jet aircraft, a Boeing 737-100. The propeller era ended, the international era began, and the country itself, not the passengers, became the product. At first glance, everybody thought that idea was ridiculous. Panama's population was smaller than many American cities. Nobody looked at a map and thought, "This is where one of the most profitable airlines on Earth should be born." But, Copa's leadership had noticed something the rest of the region [music] had not. Panama sits at one of the most useful pieces of geography anywhere on the planet. North America above, South America below, the Caribbean beside it. A narrow strip of land that connects everything. From Panama City, a single Boeing 737 could reach almost [music] every major city in North, Central, and South America without ever needing a wide-body. That unlocked a kind of math nobody else in the region could do. Two mid-size cities on opposite ends of the Americas might never have enough demand to fill [music] a direct flight between them. Run them both through Panama City, and the passengers from a dozen of those thin routes [music] meet in one place, get sorted, and continue on. A traveler from Guatemala connects to Buenos Aires. A traveler from Quito connects to Orlando. A traveler from San Jose connects to Santiago. All through one airport. But, there was a problem. In 1980, the airport was not [music] ready. Panama City's main field had limited capacity and limited reputation. So, through the '80s, Copa expanded slowly. Flights to Miami, to San Juan, and to Santo Domingo. Building experience, building credibility, building a route book. The real Copa Airlines, the airline that exists today, was born in 1992. That year, the airline moved its operations to Tocumen International Airport on [music] the edge of Panama City. And shortly afterward, branded the entire concept as the Hub of the Americas. >> [music] >> And then the expansion began for real. Between 1992 and 1997, Copa launched flights to Caracas, Mexico City, Santiago, Cali, Bogota, Quito, >> [music] >> Guayaquil, Lima, Buenos Aires, and Havana. 10 major Latin American capitals in 5 years. The route map [music] went from regional to continental. But it was still a small airline operating an aging fleet. And to get to the next level, it needed help. Help arrived in 1998 when Continental Airlines of Houston [music] took a major equity stake in Copa, eventually rising to 49%. The deal changed everything. Copa got access to Continental's operational systems, its scheduling discipline, its training programs, its purchasing power. >> [music] >> The livery was redesigned to look almost identical to Continental's. The fleet was modernized aggressively with new Boeing 737 Next Generation aircraft replacing the old jets. For the first time, the airline start to look and feel like a major international carrier. And here is something that [music] does not get talked about enough, well, at least in my personal humble opinion. The years under Continental's wing were a kind of management apprenticeship. Pedro Heilbron, who had taken over as chief executive in 1988 at the age of just 30, spent [music] the late '90s and early 2000s quietly absorbing how a serious airline runs itself. The discipline that would later astonish the industry was learned in [music] this period. The obsession with on-time performance, the fleet commonality, the refusal to expand without economic logic. None of it was invented by Copa. Most of it was learned from Houston. By 2005, Copa was ready to step out on its own. In April of that year, the airline acquired 99.8% of Aero Republica, a Colombian carrier with a fleet of MD-80s and DC-9s and a domestic network across 12 cities for roughly $23.4 million. It was $23.4 million. It was Copa's first acquisition. The Colombian operation would later be rebranded Copa Airlines Colombia. Eight months later, in December of 2005, Copa Holdings launched its initial public offering on the New York Stock Exchange. The ticker was, and still is, CPA. A small airline from a small country was now a publicly traded company answering to American investors. The discipline that had been learned under Continental was now demanded by the market. The years that followed were a steady climb. New routes, new aircraft. The first Embraer 190 joined the fleet, making Copa the first Latin American operator of the type. The frequent flyer program was rebuilt, and in June 2012, Copa formally joined Star Alliance, the largest global airline alliance alongside United. New service to Las Vegas, Curacao, Recife, and Iquitos followed. The airline had gone from being a regional flag carrier to a fully integrated member of the global aviation network in roughly 30 years. And then in April of 2015, Copa placed [music] a single order that would define the rest of its story. 61 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft plus 10 options that were later exercised. A deal worth more than 6 and 1/2 billion dollars at list [music] prices. The airline was betting its entire future on one airframe family from one manufacturer. No Airbus, no wide bodies, nothing else. The same aircraft type Copa had been flying since 1980 would carry the airline into the next generation. That bet looked ordinary in 2015, but by 2020, it looked like genius. Because in the spring of 2020, Pedro Heilbron found himself sitting in one of the worst positions in aviation. Panama moved fast against the pandemic, very fast. >> [music] >> On March 23rd of 2020, international travel slammed into a wall. And within days, every Copa aircraft was parked on the ramp at Tocumen. The airport went quiet, the schedules disappeared, the passengers vanished. For nearly 5 months, Copa's entire network was effectively frozen. And that should have terrified anyone holding the stock. Because unlike most airlines on Earth, Copa had no safety net. Delta had a huge domestic market fall back on. American had one, United had one. Even most carriers in Latin America could keep a few wheels turning on domestic routes. Copa had no domestic operation at all. It had not had one since 1980. The single decision that built the airline was now the decision that exposed it. Now, look at what was happening around them. On May 10th of 2020, Avianca, one of the oldest airlines in the world, filed for bankruptcy protection in a New York court. 16 days later, LATAM, the biggest airline in South America, did the same thing. Before the end of June, Mexico's flag carrier, Aeroméxico, had joined them. Three of the largest airlines in the Americas went into Chapter 11 within 7 [music] weeks. And the airline that looked the most exposed of all simply stayed out of court. No bankruptcy, no restructuring, no emergency rescue. Heilbron waited. He lived off the cash on his own balance sheet. The cushion Copa had spent years >> [music] >> stacking up. When Panama finally cracked the door open in August of 2020, the airline restarted one route at [music] a time, 11 destinations, then more. By the end of the following year, it had won back [music] roughly 80% of its traffic. So, what did Heilbron know that the chief executives of three giant airlines did not? Simple answer, he knew exactly what was sitting in his own hangar. Walk through a Copa operation and the answer hits you immediately. Almost every aircraft looks the same. The airline built itself around the Boeing 737 [music] family and almost nothing else. The Embraer 190 fleet, the only exception in modern times, was sold off to Australia's Alliance Airlines >> [music] >> starting in 2020. Back to one type, one pilot pipeline, one maintenance system, one spare parts inventory, one set of procedures. That sounds boring, but at the same time it is also incredibly powerful because complexity is expensive [music] in this industry. Every new aircraft type creates additional training requirements, additional maintenance overhead, additional scheduling problems, [music] additional risk. Most airlines accumulate those complications over decades. Copa keeps stripping them out. >> [music] >> The result is that Copa runs some of the lowest unit costs of any full-service airline on the planet. [music] Operating cost for every seat it flies a mile sits at around 8.6 cents. Strip out fuel and that figure drops to roughly 5.8. Those are numbers a budget carrier would brag about with the only major difference being Copa is not a budget carrier. It sells business class. It is a full member of Star Alliance. And it still operates with low-cost economics underneath. Efficiency does something even more valuable than save money though. It creates resilience. Years before the pandemic, Copa was already building one of the strongest balance sheets in aviation. It resisted the trap that catches so many airlines. Cheap debt, expansion for the sake of expansion, growth without discipline. Instead, [music] it piled up cash, lots of it. Set Copa next to the airlines that filed and the picture becomes almost embarrassing. [music] LATAM, Avianca, and Aeromexico all spent years rebuilding themselves inside Chapter 11, shedding debt, shrinking fleets, reorganizing under court [music] supervision. They came out smaller, they came out wounded. In 2025, the supposedly fragile carrier in Panama posted a net profit [music] of $671.6 million on revenue of roughly 3 and 1/2 billion. Its full-year operating margin landed at 22.6%. Its net margin came in at 18.6. Earnings per share climbed almost 12% year-over-year to $16.28. Pause on those numbers for a moment. A strong airline in a great year fights to clear a single-digit operating margin. Many of the most famous brands in the sky would be thrilled with 5 or 6%. Copa earns more than 20 cents of operating profit [music] on every single dollar of revenue, and it has done that year after year for most of the last decade. The proof points stack up behind the headline figures. 11 times now, the aviation data firm Cirium has named Copa the most on-time airline in Latin America. Including in 2025, on-time performance in the fourth quarter ran at 89%. Flight completion came in at 99.8. [music] The board approved a quarterly dividend of $1.71 per share, paid four times a year through 2026. [music] And then came April 28th of 2026. On a stage in Panama City, Heilbron stood next to the president of Panama and the chief executive of Boeing Commercial Airplanes >> [music] >> and signed for 40 new 737 Max aircraft with options for 20 more. The deal is worth roughly 13 and 1/2 billion dollars at list prices. With the existing order book, Copa [music] is on track to operate more than 100 737 Max jets in the years ahead [music] and a fleet of more than 200 aircraft by 2034. Passenger traffic is projected to climb from around 20.9 million in 2026 >> [music] >> to more than 27 million by the end of the decade. A tiny carrier from a country of 4 and 1/2 million people is buying enough new aircraft to keep Airbus uncomfortable. The skeptic would still argue that all of this comes back to geography, that Panama just sits in the perfect spot. But geography alone does not explain decades of performance like this. Bogota sits between North and South America, but so does San Jose in Costa Rica, and so does Mexico City. None of them runs a hub anything like Tocumen. Plenty of airlines operate from favorable maps. Almost none achieve Copa's consistency. The difference is discipline. The willingness to keep saying no. No to complexity. No to unnecessary fleet diversity. No to growth that does not make economic sense. No to the temptation of becoming everything to everyone. That said, no strategy is invincible. In fact, the greatest strengths in Copa's story are also its biggest exposures. Start with the obvious one. Boeing. Copa is one of the most committed Boeing customers anywhere on the [music] planet. Every passenger jet it operates is a 737. And its entire forward order book is locked into the 737 MAX family. If Boeing has another deep production crisis, or another safety event that grounds the MAX again, Copa has no [music] plan B. There is no Airbus side of the house to lean on. No wide-body fleet to redeploy. The bet on a single airframe is total. Then there is Tocumen itself. The Hub of the Americas only works as long as the airport has the runway, the gates, and the terminal capacity to keep growing. Copa's plans assume an airport that can handle well over 100 MAX jets banking through [music] it in waves. If that infrastructure falls behind, every other piece of the strategy slows down with it. The wider region [music] is a constant variable. Latin America has been a graveyard for airlines for a reason. Currencies swing hard. The Brazilian real moved enough in 2025 to push a $6 million foreign currency loss into Copa's fourth quarter accounts. Avianca and Aeromexico are out of bankruptcy and rebuilding. LATAM is bigger than ever, plugging back into long-haul. Low-cost carriers like Volaris and Viva keep pressing on price. The competitive set is heating up. And politics is never far away. Copa is the flag carrier of a country whose hub status depends on staying neutral, open, and friendly >> [music] >> to every other government in the Americas. The day that gets harder, the model gets harder with it. The bet though is still pointing the same way. 40 more MAX jets ordered in 2026, options for 20 more on top, a plan for more than 100 MAX aircraft, a balance sheet built for shocks, the same disciplined playbook run by the same small group of people in the same small country for the next decade. For decades, aviation has operated on a simple assumption. Bigger is safer. More routes, more countries, more aircraft [music] types, more markets, more everything. Copa built one of the most successful airlines on the planet by believing the exact opposite. Fewer moving parts, fewer complications, more focus, >> [music] >> more discipline. And year after year, that approach keeps outperforming carriers that are far larger and far more famous. So, here is the question worth chewing on. Is Copa proof that the rest of the airline industry has spent decades confusing size with strength? Or is it a one-off success story that only works because Panama happens to sit in exactly the right spot on the map, and nobody else can copy it? Drop your answer in the comments. I want to read what you think. And if you enjoyed this video, do me a quick favor and hit the like button and subscribe to explain if you have not already. It is the single biggest thing that helps me and my channel grow, and it is completely free. Thank you for watching this video, and I will see you in the next one. >> [music]

reviews.transcript_full: For many travelers, Emirates and Dubai long seemed like a sure bit.  A global hub, a vast route network and the A380 have the symbol of comfortable flying.  However, recent regional tensions have led to a more critical view of things.  From what is currently apparent, what I saw and based on feedback from my community,  the onboard product has not been downgraded.  The greater risk lies in schedule changes, longer flight times, delays or aircraft swaps.  This report is therefore not a volatile crisis analysis.  Instead we ask a different long term question, what does Emirates actually offer on the A380  in business class right now?  Hello everybody from the upper deck of the Emirates Airbus A380. reviews.transcript_full: Hello friends. We are Wonders in Black. We like to travel and discover unique and unusual places and have fun along the way. Life is short, so let's seize the moment. Join us for a wonder on our next destination. >> [cheering] >> So friends, we're on our way to Europe and after a quick [music] visit to the Qantas Business and First Class lounges, our 36-hour trip was truly on the way. >> [music] >> Yes, that's right. It's a very long journey this [music] time around. We're now bound for Singapore. It has been many years since I've been to this airport and also [music] this leg comes with a welcome perk, access to the First Class lounge, a place we've been hearing about [music] for some time. Safe to say expectations were high. While waiting for our champagne, I thought I'd do a little reconnaissance mission around the lounge. My primary objective, investigating the available alcoholic refreshments, of course. I'm pleased to report that the mission was a complete success. And as you'd expect from a first class lounge, the selection was nothing short of impressive. So, friends, after an 8-hour flight, we are in Singapore at the Qantas first lounge. Had a walk around. Plenty of seating, quite spacious. We only have half an hour before we have to board our next flight, uh which is to Heathrow. We're having some very nice champagne, the La Lière. Mhm, very nice and refreshing as champagne normally is. And we're going to squeeze in a couple of cocktails. Cheers. >> Something we're seeing in the Singapore Sling. >> Ooh, yes, please. >> So, what we have here is a banana milk punch. The party's here. >> That is fine. >> It's a banana rum and some milk and and dehydrated banana. >> It's amazing. >> You can try it. >> Wow, they look beautiful already. Thank you so much. >> [music] >> The cocktails were fantastic, full of flavor, smooth, and incredibly refreshing. >> [music] >> It's a shame we had to leave shortly after because I would have happily sampled a few more from [music] the menu. Before heading off, I decided to do one final check, the bathrooms. Rather than a traditional large restroom with multiple cubicles, each guest [music] had access to their own private bathroom. Everything was spotless and exactly what you'd expect from a first class lounge. It was a premium experience. And now, it was time to settle back into the seat and relax once again. With many hours of flying still ahead, there are only so many ways to pass the time. You can lose yourself in a in-flight entertainment, gaze out the window, or try to catch a few hours of sleep. As for me, I prefer a different approach. A few well-chosen adult refreshments tend to make the journey feel a little shorter and the hours pass a little faster. And before we knew it, we were in Heathrow. [music] It had been quite some time since our last visit, so it was a bit nostalgic to be back at one of the world's busiest airports. Like Singapore, we once again had access to the first-class lounge. Unlike Singapore, however, this wasn't our first visit. I remember it as being an outstanding lounge. I was curious to see whether [music] it had changed much since we were last here. The food selection [music] was every bit as impressive as I remembered. Since it was still morning, the breakfast spread was a [music] very welcome sight. There was plenty to choose from, whether you were looking for something healthy and nutritious or something a little more indulgent. I wasn't particularly hungry after the flight, but if I had been choosing a breakfast, [music] I suspect a less healthy option would have won my attention. Speaking of indulgence, it was time to investigate the [music] drink selection. One of the great perks of [music] a first-class lounge is that whatever your preference, whether it's beer, wine, spirits, >> [music] >> it's never far away. >> [music] >> When we travel, however, our drink of choice tends to be champagne. Perhaps it's something about spending hours above the clouds that creates [music] a craving for a glass of bubbles. This lounge >> [music] >> certainly didn't disappoint. The champagne selection was extensive. There was so choices that I wasn't quite sure where to begin. The obvious solution was to head over to the bar and contemplate my options over a glass of the good stuff. Research, [music] after all, is an important part of any travel review. With a glass of champagne in hand, I continued my journey of discovery around the lounge. This place [music] is enormous. I stumbled upon another pleasant surprise. Even more champagne. Clearly, [music] the lounge designers had ensured that no guest would ever have to venture too far in search of a refill. There was [music] also some interesting red wines on offer, but I remained committed to the bubbles. >> [music] >> What struck [music] me most was how quiet this part of the lounge was. It almost felt like a [music] private function. >> So, friends, here we are in Heathrow. We're at the British Airways First Lounge. It's early morning. It's not even 6:00 yet. The sun is just rising. It's a very beautiful morning out there. Um we're starting off with some champagne. We've got about an hour before our next flight, which is to Frankfurt. And then from there, our true adventure begins. Here's to the next step of the journey. Cheers. >> Leaving that incredible lounge [music] wasn't easy. And I gladly would have lingered, but our schedule beckoned. >> [music] >> Only one short flight to Frankfurt stood between us and the finishing line. After 36 hours of [music] travel, this massive journey was coming to an end. And a brand new one >> [music] >> was about to begin. >> [music] >> Thank you so much for watching, friends. And please join us again for the next episode [music] of our traveling and culinary journey. >> See [music] you soon. Cheers.

And here is where you find your footwear. >> [music] >> One interesting feature is the adjustable privacy divider that was installed on this plane. Now, the elephant in the room is the seats facing away from the windows. I still don't love that. There's something magical about having a window seat and actually being able to enjoy the views without performing yoga. But overall, these suites are much better than actually expected. >> [music] >> Before departure, the safety video was played, pushed back at 8:33 a.m. and took off at [music] 8:49. Slightly behind schedule, but thanks to the favorable winds, we actually arrived in Calgary about 20 minutes early. Air Canada deserves credit for keeping this, for sure. One thing worth a mentioning here is privacy. What surprised me, however, was how private the suite already felt. Once seated, I could barely see other passengers. About 45 minutes after takeoff, I started hearing activities from the galley, more importantly, smelling breakfast. I was hungry this morning, so looking forward to that. The service throughout the flight was a little bit of a mixed bag. There were four flight attendants working on flight, and while two of them were absolutely [music] fantastic, friendly, engaging, and looked really, really happy to be there, the two who were serving in the business class cabin could have been a little warmer. During breakfast, for example, I was asked whether I wanted to eat in a tone that felt somewhat abrupt rather than welcoming. This aircraft is equipped with four bathrooms, three in economy and one in business class. [music] My favorite feature, if you ask me, the touchless trash compartment. In other words, passengers aren't the only one learning about the A321 XLR, The crews are two. So, what's the verdict on Air Canada's new A321 XLR? Before this flight, I generally wasn't sure what to expect. Like many people, I looked at the photos online and wondered whether a single-aisle aircraft could really deliver a premium long-haul experience. And after spending nearly 4 hours here, I think Air Canada has something special here. No, it's not perfect. The suite entrance is a little tight. The seats still face away from the window. The breakfast wasn't incredible. And the service was a little inconsistent. And the lack of pre-departure drink felt like a missed opportunity as well. But those complaints feels minor to me when you look at the bigger picture. The suite is far more spacious than it appears in photos. The bed is genuinely comfortable. The cabin is is nice. The technology is excellent. And perhaps most importantly, it never felt cramped at all. This was my biggest concern coming into this flight. And [music] it's also the concern I hear most often whenever people talk about crossing the Atlantic on a narrow-body aircraft. After flying in myself today, I think those fears are largely overblown. For me, the biggest surprise wasn't the OLED screen. It wasn't the Bluetooth connectivity. reviews.transcript_full:
Welcome back to Travel Expertos. Today we’ll be flying with Emirates in Business Class onboard the Boeing 777-300ER from Tokyo Haneda to Dubai on flight EK313. This flight is scheduled for just over 10 hours and will give us the chance to fully experience Emirates’ newer Boeing 777 Business Class product featuring direct aisle access, fully flat beds, premium dining, pajamas, lounge access, and one of the best entertainment systems in commercial aviation. In this full review, we’ll cover the entire experience from the chauffeur transfer through Tokyo, Haneda Airport Terminal 3, check-in, the Japan Airlines Sakura Lounge, boarding, seat 10A, dinner service, bed comfort, sleep quality, breakfast before arrival, and finally our arrival into Dubai before continuing our trip to Frankfurt onboard Emirates First Class. Let’s see how Emirates Business Class performs on this overnight flight from Japan to the Middle East. Our journey begins in central Tokyo with Emirates’ complimentary chauffeur drive service. One of the major advantages of flying Emirates Business Class is that the premium experience starts before you even reach the airport. Instead of navigating Tokyo’s busy evening transport system with luggage, Emirates provides a direct private transfer to Haneda Airport Terminal 3. Tokyo at night feels incredible from the back seat of the car. Soon enough we've reached Tokyo Haneda international airport. The drive to Haneda was smooth, comfortable, and surprisingly fast considering Tokyo traffic. We have now arrived at Tokyo Haneda Airport Terminal 3. Haneda is widely considered one of the best airports in the world thanks to its cleanliness, efficiency, modern design, and proximity to central Tokyo. Compared to Narita, Haneda is significantly more convenient, especially for premium passengers connecting quickly into the city. Tonight the terminal feels calm, modern, and extremely organized. Even during busy hours, the airport maintains a very quiet and premium atmosphere. Haneda was open in late of October 2010. We now head toward the Emirates check-in area for EK313 to Dubai.  Checkin counters were organized and split into First,Business,Premium Economy and Economy class The whole checkin process was well organized efficient and fast. After check-in, we continued through security and immigration. Haneda’s security process is extremely efficient compared to many major international airports. Even during evening departure waves, the airport moves passengers quickly without feeling chaotic. Once airside, we headed through the terminal toward the lounge area. Emirates Business Class passengers departing Haneda have access to the Japan Airlines Sakura Lounge, which is one of the more interesting partnerships in the Emirates network. As we walk through the airport you may notice how clean and spotless the terminal and airport actually is. Soon enough we reach Jal's Business Class lounge at Haneda. Japan Airlines Sakura lounge is located on the 4th floor (1floor above the terminal.) We are now inside the Japan Airlines Sakura Lounge. Food options included Japanese dishes, light snacks, bakery items, drinks, and self-service beverage stations. The lounge provides showers, changing rooms, and spotless bathrooms. The lounge has a very different atmosphere compared to Emirates’ own lounges in Dubai. Instead of flashy luxury, the focus here is calm design, efficiency, privacy, and Japanese hospitality. Large seating areas overlook the apron, offering excellent nighttime views of aircraft movements around Haneda. The lounge atmosphere is extremely quiet, making it a very good place to relax before an overnight departure. Compared to some overcrowded international lounges, this feels far more peaceful and refined. After spending some time here relaxing before the flight, it is now almost time to head toward Gate 144 for boarding. We are now leaving the lounge and heading toward Gate 144. Haneda’s terminal design is simple to navigate, and even the longer walks remain pleasant thanks to the modern architecture and clean layout. Waiting area is divided into Business and First class cabin together and Premium and Economy class together. Our flight is delayed due to bad weather on way to Tokyo, the plane has not even landed yet. Soon enough our plane arrived to our gate. Delay was unfortunately accumulating due to the late arrival of our aircraft. Our aircraft for today is a 6year old B777-300ER registration A6-EQO Soon enough the boarding started with First and Business class passengers boarding first. And its time to board the bird. First and Business class passengers board via the first jet-bridge and Economy and Premium economy passengers via the second one. Have you already flown Emirates? If yes what was your experience? Leave a comment about it please. First class cabin features 6seats in 1-1-1 layout, with middle seats featuring artificial windows via outdoor cameras. The cabin now features direct aisle access for every passenger in a 1-2-1 layout 10A is our seat for the next 10hours to Dubai.  This flight is configured withe the new 4cabin layout featuring new seats in all cabins.AND THEY ARE STUNNING! All business class feature a huge IFE screen, private minibar and much more. My window seat features two windows. As the boarding continues let's have a short peek of this beautiful seat. Located under your IFE screen there is a small pocket storage for travel documents and other necesities. The seat headrest is the most comfortable one I have ever experienced. A comfy pillow is stored at every seat as well. At your seat headphones together with eye mask and slippers are already waiting for you. The ceiling is full of starts again :) Every seat features an iPad, controls for windows, a mini bar, power sockets, air vent and much more. There is also an enclosed storage bin by your seat. Cabin crew walks by and hands out hot towels. And in no time we pushed back from our gate. We pushed back 40minutes behind schedule unfortunately. So far the seat feels incredible, with leather and comfortable seat and high privacy even though not featuring sliding doors as Qatars Qsuite. As preparation for take off Emirates safety video is played. As we roll towards our run way please enjoy taxi and later on stunning Take Off out of Haneda. Take off 1:07 AM Tokyo Time. And we are in the air. Bye bye Tokyo. Once in the air the cabin lights turn the cabin into a stunning place to relax. Soon after cabin crew hands out pre daparture drinks (as there was no time before the take Off. I went with orange juice this time. Let's have look at today's menu. Cabin Crew also hands out amenity kids to every passenger onboard - in my opinion those are the best ones out there.  The amenity kid is packed with accessories. (Emirates also features men and women kits) The kit includes essentials for overnight travel such as dental products, skincare items, earplugs,  and other comfort accessories designed to make the long flight more comfortable. Emirates also offers Pajamas for their Business class passengers. Alongside with an eye mask and slippers. Slippers are really comfortable and easy to wear. Emirates provides their business class passengers with noise cancelling headphones. Those headphones are really comfortable to use and block outer noise perfectly. You plug them next to other power outlets. Blanket is thick and very comfortable. Overall Emirates really went all out with amenities. Let me know if any other airline does it better in Business Class. Seat controls are located by your seat and have plenty of options and are easy to use. An armrest is located by your seat for more comfort when in lounge position. In front of you there is an huge IFE screen featuring the world's best entertainment system ICE. Overall this is one of the best business class seats out there in my opinion. I really like the way Emirates shifts and the colors of its interior in all four cabins. The seat windows are controlled electronically, you can control both of them at a same time from a separate button. Featuring two level of shades - half shade and completely black. Or you can directly control window by window, with the bottom underneath. This is featured in all cabins except Economy Class. It is really easy and simple to use and makes great visual impact of the cabin. There are 38 business class seats spread across two cabins from row 3 to row 12. As we get more and more comfortable in our seat let's have a peek of business class bathrooms onboard this flight.  The lavatory remains clean and well maintained, featuring premium hand products, towels, and additional amenities. And now it's time to start Emirates famous onboard dining. The late-night meal was served about 40minutes after take off, I decided to try the sushi selection together with a cheese plate. The whole meal presentation looked stunning together with an apple juice and sparkling water.  Emirates provided each passenger with a metal cutlery and also chop sticks. For an overnight Business Class flight, this feels more refined and lighter compared to a heavy full dinner service. Overall, the quality was excellent and presentation remained one of the strongest aspects of the Emirates premium experience. After dinner I made my way to the bathroom and it was time to change into Emirates Pajamas. Emirates provided a male and female option. They felt really comfortable not as a piece of low quality clothes. As I left to change into my pajamas the crew prepared the mattress topper for the seat. This is something only the top tier Arlines do. As we were approaching Shanghai the whole cabin was falling asleep slowly. In the meantime let's have a look what our tablet has to offer. The iPad allows you to control the entertainment system, moving map, lighting, and seat functions without needing to use the main screen. It feels modern, responsive, and genuinely useful during the flight only few airlines actually offer this feature even in First Class. Emirates really went all out with these new seats, and to be honest I find them even better than Qatar Airways Q-suite. It's time to put the tablet back in place and look at different features of this wonderful seat. Next to the seat is Emirates’ signature personal mini bar. Inside, there are 2  bottled water and one Sparkling water and a glass available throughout the flight. Together with some snacks. The snacks featured are, M&Ms, mixed nuts and jelly beans. There is also an additional storage above the bar for glass of drink, headphones to anything else you'd need. The reading light by side features 3stages of brightness.  You can also play with your personal seat light by your seat controller. Now let's have a look at world's best IFE ICE. The whole system is well organized providing countless of entertainment. Now it's time to turn our seat into bed. The provided mattress is big and thick All in all the seat is looks spectacular when in bed mode. The cabin lights make this cabin one of the most beautiful ones out there. In the meantime let's have a look where we are. Before going to bed let's head to the bathroom and brush our teeth. Emirates provides its passengers countless amenities in their clean onboard bathrooms. Now let's head to our seat and sleep. Lets take of our slippers and get comfortable in our bed. The seat converts into a 78.6" long flat bed. There is enough space even for back sleeping people and the footwell is wide and comfortable as well. Let's turn the lights down and use the sleeping mask for even greater comfort. We are somewhere over china at this time of our flight. Let's put the blinds down as well. As you may see the minibar is really helpful as you'll never ran out of water. The cabin lights and stars make it perfect place to sleep in. Good night everyone. Good Morning somewhere above India. Most of the cabin is still asleep but we are going to wake up now. Lets turn the seat lights one letting the crew now you are awake so they can come and offer you snack, drinks and more. This mattress was the reason I slept like a baby on this flight. Now let's head to the bathroom to freshen up. Back to our seat we have enough time to relax in the relax position and enjoy more of the ICE entertainment. Emirates uses Mercedes inspired S-lounge leather seats. The pathways between the seat and alley is not as narrow as it may seem. Let's watch some movies in the meantime. In the meantime outside the sun starts to rise. The service continues with a hot towel prior to breakfast. Emirates offers its IFE in countless of languages. Emirates also provides information for arrival gate baggage collection course and departure gates of other flights if connecting. As a proud airline Emirates has a section only about their history, fleet and much more. As the sun starts to rise we are approaching Dubai. Soon enough the tray table is set for our breakfast. This morning’s meal includes a cheese omelette with sausages and spinach, alongside fresh fruit, yogurt, croissant, butter, and preserves. Doesn't it just look fabulous? Together with a metal cutlery and a glass of orange juice. The breakfast was absolutely delicious. For the meantime just enjoy the stunning morning win view. The table is really good quality and holds well but also easy to move a maneuver with.  I am also served a cup of tea prior to arrival into Dubai As we are approaching our final destination it is time to change into normal clothes. So lets head for our final visit of the bathroom. The safety card is stored in the cubby above footwell.  Together with an inflight magazine. Now it's time to check our connecting gate onward to Frankfurt onboard Emirates a380 in First Class. Well there is our EK045 departing from the C gates so we will use Emirates oldest terminal, terminal C. The whole cabin is now awake and ready for arrival into Dubai. And it's time for pre arrival PA. Take off the slippers and prepare for landing. C19 will be our gate for our connecting flight to Frankfurt. Now it is time to summarize this Wonderfull experience onboard Emirates refurbished Business Class on their B777. Chauffeur Service - 10/10. A fantastic start to the journey. Comfortable, professional, and stress-free transportation to Haneda Airport. It adds genuine value to the premium experience. Haneda Airport Experience - 9/10.
One of the best airports in the world. Clean, efficient, modern, and incredibly easy to navigate. Check-In Process - 9/10. Fast and efficient with dedicated Business Class counters. Exactly what premium passengers expect. Japan Airlines Business Class Lounge - 8.5/10. Very peaceful and comfortable with excellent runway views. Food selection was solid, although it doesn't quite match Emirates' flagship lounges in Dubai. Boarding Process - 9/10
Well organized with priority boarding and plenty of time to settle into the cabin. Boeing 777 Business Class Seat - 9/10. The newer 1-2-1 configuration completely transforms the Emirates 777 experience. Direct aisle access for every passenger is a massive improvement over the old 2-3-2 layout. Seat Privacy - 9/10. Good privacy for a Business Class product, although it doesn't quite reach the level of suites offered by some competitors. Bed Comfort - 9/10. The mattress topper, duvet, pillow, and pajamas created a genuinely comfortable sleeping environment. One of the strongest aspects of the flight. Sleep Quality - 9/10.
A quiet cabin and comfortable bed allowed for several hours of quality sleep before arrival into Dubai. Dinner - 8/10. The sushi and cheese plate were both excellent. Presentation was beautiful and perfectly suited to a departure from Japan. Breakfast - 8.5/10. The omelette, sausage, fruit, yogurt, and croissant created a complete and enjoyable breakfast before arrival. Cabin Crew - 8.5/10. Professional, attentive, and polished throughout the flight without being intrusive. Amenities - 10/10. Amenity kit, pajamas, slippers, eye mask, mattress topper, and quality bedding all contributed to a premium overnight experience. Entertainment System - 10/10. ICE remains one of the best inflight entertainment systems in the world. Massive content selection, responsive interface, and excellent screen quality. Noise-Cancelling Headphones - 9/10. Comfortable and effective.  Cabin Atmosphere - 9.5/10. The warm lighting, modern finishes, and quieter overnight environment created a very relaxing premium experience. Value For Money - 8.5/10. Not cheap, but the newer Emirates 777 Business Class product now feels much more competitive against leading global carriers. Overall it was a fantastic flight and exactly what Emirates needed as a push forward in their Business Class cabins. With an overall grade of 9 Emirates proves that they are one of the best Business class products out there to fly. Emirates is the flag carrier of Dubai and one of the largest international airlines in the world. Founded in 1985 with only two aircraft, Emirates has grown into a global aviation giant serving more than 140 destinations across six continents. The airline is famous for its premium cabins, extensive long-haul network, onboard service, and industry-leading inflight entertainment system known as ICE. Today, Emirates operates one of the world's largest fleets of widebody aircraft, consisting almost entirely of Airbus A380s and Boeing 777s alongside a350s. The Boeing 777 fleet is particularly important because it serves destinations that cannot support the larger Airbus A380 while still offering excellent range and cargo capacity. Emirates has become one of the most recognizable airline brands globally and consistently ranks among the world's leading long-haul carriers. Now please enjoy the stunning landing into Dubai. Welcome to Dubai. Dubai International Airport is the primary hub of Emirates and one of the busiest international airports in the world. More than 90 million passengers travel through DXB annually during normal operating years, making it one of the most important connecting hubs on the planet. The airport's location is one of its greatest strengths. Positioned between Europe, Asia, Africa, and Australia, Dubai allows Emirates to connect hundreds of city pairs through a single hub. DXB is famous for its enormous concentration of widebody aircraft. At peak times, passengers can see dozens of Emirates Boeing 777s and Airbus A380s parked simultaneously across the airport. reviews.transcript_full: Hi there. My name is Earl and welcome back to Biyahe Jimenez. It's been more than 2 years since my last Cathay Pacific flight, so I'm really excited to fly with them again. Cathay Pacific was the first airline I flew with when I started this channel, making this return feel extra special. In this video, join me on this quick hop from Manila to Hong Kong aboard a Boeing 777 in economy class with Cathay Pacific. >> [music] [music] >> I arrived at the airport about 3 hours before my flight and the terminal was actually pretty peaceful. There have been a lot of changes since my last international flight through Terminal 3 back in 2024. The most notable would be the new food and retail areas that were opened by the airport's new operator late last year. Before we check in, let's take a quick tour of the new facilities. The old public area on the fourth level where all the fast food restaurants used to be has been downsized and now hosts only a handful of establishments. These include a Goldilocks branch and the newly opened Watson's store. The McDonald's branch on the opposite end is the only one that has remained in this area. Down at the arrivals area is the newly opened Tambayan Food Hall, an all-Filipino dining hub that can accommodate up to 2,000 guests and showcases a variety of homegrown and regional food concepts. Among them are Via Mare Select, the food court version of the well-loved Filipino restaurant. Aboitiz Cebuana Lechon from my hometown of Pasig City and the soon-to-open branch of Palm Grill, a Michelin Bib Gourmand recognized restaurant serving authentic cuisine from Southern Mindanao. The airport is now operated by San Miguel Corporation. So, the presence of a Ginebra San Miguel bar right in the middle of the food hall comes as no surprise. I checked out the menu, and the cocktails are surprisingly affordable. There's also a branch of Treats, the company's convenience store chain, along with a stall selling products from its well-known house brands. If you're new to the channel, my name is Earl, and welcome to Biyahe Manalo. I do trip reports and airport lounge tours. So, if you love aviation content, please consider subscribing. Meanwhile, the 6,000 square meter mezzanine food hall on level two brings together a wide range of local and international dining brands, giving travelers far more options than before. Familiar names such as Popeyes, Kenny Rogers Roasters, and Chili's have all set up shop here, alongside several other fast food and casual dining concepts. Popular local cafe Mary Grace has retained its spot in the terminal, and it's now joined by international bakery cafe brands such as Paris Baguette and BreadTalk. Self-checking counters are also now up and running at Terminal 3. Multiple kiosks are distributed throughout the terminal, but like at Terminal 1, they're only available to select airlines and eligible passengers. Cathay Pacific's check-in counters have since moved from counter A to counter E at the far end of the terminal. Prior to the change, these counters were occupied by Cebu Pacific. Airport management reorganized the check-in areas, moving Cebu Pacific to the opposite end of the terminal in an effort to ease vehicle congestion at the curbside drop-off area. And of course, Cebu Pacific still occupies a significant portion of the terminal, so some might argue that the congestion has simply shifted indoors. Guards continue to check passengers' travel documents at the entrance, creating a bottleneck that often mixes with families and well-wishers saying their final goodbyes near the OFW lounge. Since I'd already checked in online, I headed straight for the bag drop lane. The entire check-in process took less than 10 minutes. So, with that done, let's head to immigration and security. Not everyone, however, is happy with the recent changes being implemented by the airport's new operator. Among the most significant developments is the closure of the dedicated lounges operated by Cathay Pacific and Singapore Airlines at Terminal 3. Cathay Pacific shut down its lounge at the end of May, while the SilverKris Lounge is set to close in mid-June. Unsurprisingly, the announcement was met with disappointment from Cathay Pacific and Oneworld frequent flyers. Rumors about the closure of the Cathay Pacific Lounge had already surfaced back in January, but those proved to be temporary disruptions caused by utility-related issues. This time, however, Cathay Pacific has confirmed the lounge's permanent closure, citing the ongoing redevelopment of Terminal 3 as the reason. So far, there has been no indication that the airline plans to open a replacement lounge in the near future. Instead, Cathay Pacific, along with several other airlines, is now directing its premium passengers to the First Meridian Lounge, a shared-use facility operated by NNIC. Located in the former home of the PAGS Lounge at Terminal 3, the First Meridian Lounge features quiet zones, workstations, shower facilities, golf simulators, a teppanyaki station, a full-service bar, and even a wine cellar. With the closure of the Marhaba Lounge, the A Lounge is now the only remaining option for many Priority Pass members and select credit card holders. As of this recording, there has been no announcement on what will replace the now closed Cathay Pacific and SilverKris lounges. Should there be any developments, I'll be sure to cover them in a future update on the evolving lounge situation here at NAIA.
