The meal came with generous chunks of chicken, while the vegetables on the side complemented the dish nicely. Although I've had this exact meal before on a previous Cathay Pacific flight, I still appreciate that the airline continues to serve proper hot meal on a tray rather than in a box. The inclusion of metal cutlery is also a nice touch. That said, several Taiwanese airlines managed to offer a more substantial meal service on flights of a similar duration, often including an appetizer and dessert alongside the main course. Hopefully, Cathay Pacific reviews its Manila catering in the future. Even a small dessert would be a nice addition. Here's a closer look at the headphones provided for today's flight. Cathay Pacific's in-flight entertainment library is one of the most extensive in the industry, and honestly one of my favorites to explore. Cathay's selection includes the latest Hollywood blockbusters, critically acclaimed films, a huge catalog of award-winning Asian cinema, and popular Korean dramas. Content from Disney Plus and HBO Max is also available, including selected episodes of the hit series The White Lotus. Personally, I'm glad to see that Cathay Pacific has maintained its partnership with A24 and continues to feature many of the studio's films after all these years. We've started our descent into Hong Kong, so let me conclude this trip report with Cathay Pacific. Our journey began at NAIA Terminal 3, which now features expanded dining options, self-check-in kiosks, and several other improvements throughout the terminal. Check-in, bag drop, security, and immigration were all quick and hassle-free. Once on board, the seat offered above-average legroom, while the in-flight entertainment system provided more than enough content to keep passengers occupied on this short-haul flight. The meal service was decent, although I do hope Cathay Pacific refreshes its Manila catering options in the future. It seems that whenever chicken is offered, it's usually adobo. I'd also like to see a more substantial tray, especially considering that some Taiwanese airlines serve an appetizer and dessert on the flights of similar duration. Overall, this was a pleasant and enjoyable short-haul flight with Cathay Pacific. charging port under the armrest,   you can also find a USB-A charging 
port and universal power outlet.  The headset connector is also here 
under the cocktail mini table.  This is the headset provided 
in premium economy class.  Its noise cancelling effect is okay.
However, if you have big ears like me,   you may also find it is not quite 
comfortable to wear after a while.  It will be better if you bring your 
Bluetooth headset as it can now be   paired to the entertainment system.
The stunning 15.6-inch 4K screen   is fixed on the bulkhead.
As it is a bit far from   the seat for touch control, you can use 
the remote control to navigate the menu. Unlike the traditional remote control,   this one works like a trackpad, 
but it is quite intuitive to use.  The award-winning inflight entertainment 
system with new movies, TV series, podcasts,   and music added every month.
You will definitely find   something you're interested to watch.
Complimentary Wi-Fi is now offered to   cafe members in premium economy class.
However, if you entered other frequent   flyer membership at check-in, you 
cannot enjoy this offer like myself. Although you can find a cocktail 
mini table here, no welcome drink   was offered on this short haul flight.
There was also no hot towel service either.  Not a big deal. However, if Cathay wants 
to attract more revenue customers booking   premium economy class on short haul flights
These are actually some premium features   that customers would expect and 
it is not too costly to offer.  Here you can find your 
foldable table in the armrest.  As this flight departs before 
10:00 a.m., breakfast is served.  If it departs after 10:00 a.m. local time, 
nuts and drinks will be served before lunch.  There was no printed or onscreen menu, and the 
two breakfast choices are always dim sum set,   and egg and sausage.
As I had egg and   sausage on my flight from Manchester, 
I chose the dim sum set on this flight.  To be honest, breakfast in economy class 
and premium economy class are quite similar.  The only differences are croissant 
is served instead of white row   and food is served in stonewares.
Note that Prosecco is only   served in long haul flights.
Although the breakfast served on   this flight was nothing special, the late lunch or 
dinner served on my return flight was much better.  I had steak and mashed potato on 
the flight CX549 to Hong Kong.  If you have not tried dim sum before, these 
were actually quite tasty and worth a try.  The main dishes in premium economy 
class on Japan routes are similar   to that offered in business class.
Whereas on shorter routes like flights to   Shanghai, the same economy class menu was served.
On this route, try to pick a seat on   the left hand side.
If you're lucky that   the weather is fine, you will be able to see 
Mount Fuji when the flight approaches Tokyo.  This time I can barely spot 
it for a few seconds only.  Let me wrap up this short haul premium economy 
class experience with Cathay Pacific here.  First of all, the hardware, i.e. the seat 
is a big improvement. The big 4K TV and   the privacy wing are remarkably good.
I also love having the TV fixed on the   bulkhead instead of stowing under the armrest as 
I can still watch it during takeoff and landing.  This also makes it easier for passengers 
in the window seat to leave the seat.  About the service, to be honest, there was 
no notable difference from economy class   except the food was served in stonewares.
I was on this short haul premium economy class   only because I booked premium economy class 
return tickets from Manchester to Tokyo.  My honest opinion is that if I booked the short 
haul flight separately, I would definitely not   be paying the premium price for this slightly 
better seat for a duration of only 3.5 hours.  Last but not least, thank you very 
much for your time watching this video.  If you find it useful, please 
like and share this video.  Your subscription to my channel 
is also much appreciated.  Please enjoy the rest of the video for the 
approach to the Tokyo International Airport.

I'm not even kidding when I say that this thing was ancient, and I won't even edit this clip because I want to show you how slow this thing actually was so you can understand my complaints after spending thousands of dollars for this. And, another thing I want to mention is that I got super lucky not having a neighbor because when you're sleeping, you're basically touching feet with each other. But, now that we're moving up in levels and have Lufthansa as the baseline, from here on out, ratings will be broken down into four different categories: the seat, the food, the amenities, and the overall value to see just how much better things can get. reviews.transcript_full: Many passengers in this travel tips community are worried about their medication being flagged in airport security. The Transportation Security Administration is on high alert for anything that can pose a safety risk to crew or passengers. I made the other parts of this video in the airport, ready for a drastic lighting change, but the sound is going to be good and the travel tips and travel hacks are going to be excellent for your trip. I forgot to tell y'all that my selfie stick broke in the airport, so I'm waiting on it to get here and you should just see the whole contraption that I have lifted up my camera with. We're going to make it work. Every medication has to be screened, including the equipment that we travel with. On the TSA website as of 2026, they say to inform the officers if you're carrying medication and to facilitate this process, which really means make it smoother, faster, easier for you and less stressful, clearly label your medication. That is a huge sigh of relief and update for 2026. And I'm going to go through tips later. Here's a quick fire round of the rules in airport security of things that I get asked most often about from passengers bringing medication. One rule is that you must inform the officers before screening begins that you have liquid medications or IVs, pumps, or syringes. Does informing them add more stress to you? No, that is not hard. You're just telling them that you have this stuff. Another rule is that you then are supposed to put the medication and the equipment in the bin for screening. But, an update in 2026 is they most of the time do not want you to take them out if you have informed them you're carrying them. The next rule says that liquid medication does not have to follow the 3.4 oz rule. Those liquid medicines are exempt from the rule. Even over-the-counter medication, like contact solution, eye drops, my shampoo prescription that I fly with a lot, none of those have to fit into 3.4 oz containers or less. I'll go into this later, but if it is a prescription liquid, have that liquid prescription with you. So, here are some easy travel tips to save you stress before you even leave your house for a trip. Number one, have your liquids ready to be pulled out, either all of them in a gallon bag, or at the top of your personal item bag for easy access, because you're going to facilitate the process. We're making everything smoother. Number two, do not put liquid medication in your TSA compliant quart-size bag. Here's one travel tip, when you want to know what medicine is allowed in the TSA line, like insulin, for example, that's one of the most frequently asked questions that I see, you go to the tsa.gov website. In the top right corner, tap on what can I bring, and then you're going to just type insulin, for example, and it will search, and it will tell you that yes, you're supposed to, number one, inform the officers that that you have diabetes and you're carrying insulin equipment or wearing it. 90% of the time they'll say just keep everything in your bag, because that machine knows what insulin looks like when it's screened. Just so you know, when I say the alarm goes off, it's not this loud flashing sound or light. By the way, I'm going to talk about powder and supplements later on in the video cuz that's another frequently asked question. They are medical items. Number one, inform the officers that you cannot stand without this item. reviews.transcript_full: Welcome aboard Business Class in Cathay Pacific's A330 The video includes a tour of Cathay Pacific's The Pier Lounge  This video shows the full Cathay Pacific Business Class flight This includes Business Class menus, meals, and amenities The flight takes us from Hong Kong to Phnom Penh The video ends at Asia's newest, empty mega-airport Welcome to Hong Kong International Airport The airport sits on Chek Lap Kok island in the South China Sea The airport opened in 1998 and was built on reclaimed land Hong Kong airport handles 70 million passengers each year  The airport operates 24 hours a day without closing The Pier Lounge is located near Gate 65 in Hong Kong Airport This is the largest lounge in Cathay Pacific's network The lounge design focuses on comfort and a calm atmosphere Each solo chair includes a reading lamp and side table The lounge was created by the London studio Studioilse Cherry wood and limestone are used throughout the lounge Natural materials create a warm and understated interior Local artwork adds a subtle connection to Hong Kong The lounge concept is inspired by the streets of Hong Kong The 'Food Hall' offers an excellent buffet spread Fresh coffee is prepared by professional baristas daily At the heart of the Pier Lounge is a bar area The bar's large windows provide views over the airport tarmac A noodle bar serves Cathay Pacific’s signature dishes Dan dan noodles are prepared fresh throughout the day Guests can also enjoy dim sum and steamed buns here The Tea House offers a calm space away from the crowd A tea specialist serves a selection of premium teas This is the Airbus A330-300 that will fly us to Phnom Phen Aircraft registration number: B-HLN (built in 2001) I am the first passenger to board today's flight This Airbus A330 features 24 Business Class seats The Business Class cabin is arranged across four rows in total Seats are configured in a traditional 2-2-2 layout Cathay Pacific operates several A330 Business Class layouts Some aircraft feature modern 1-2-1 Business Class cabins The seat offers a generous 45 inches of pitch A hot towel is offered upon boarding A welcome drink is served as well The Cathay Pacific captain welcomes passengers onboard Have you ever flown with Cathay Pacific? Leave a comment Cathay's safety video celebrates its home city Hong Kong Safety instructions are woven into city life scenes Cabin crew guide viewers through iconic locations We're leaving the gate at 8:40 am (on time departure) We pass several Cathay Pacific Airbus A330s while taxiing Cathay Pacific operates 43 Airbus A330 aircraft. Cathay Pacific is one of the largest A330 operators in the world Cathay's A330 fleet has an average age of around 17 years The A330 mainly serves Cathay Pacific destinations across Asia  New cabins are being introduced on selected A330 aircraft. Cathay Pacific has ordered 30 Airbus A330neo aircraft The new A330neo fleet will arrive from 2028 onwards Cathay's A330s are powered with Rolls-Royce Trent 700 engines  Cathay Pacific is one of Asia’s most respected airlines Cathay Pacific was founded in Hong Kong in 1946 The airline was started by an American and an Australian pilot Cathay’s name refers to an ancient term for China Hong Kong has always been the airline’s home base Cathay helped shape Hong Kong as a global aviation hub We get a nice view of Hong Kong Airport after takeoff Hong Kong Airport replaced the city's famous Kai Tak Airport Let's have a look at the Cathay Pacific A330 Business Class seat  The entertainment controller is stored under the armrest Seat controls are located on the center armrest Personal entertainment screens are installed at every seat. The screens are small by modern standards The tray table folds out from the seat in front The seat uses a shell-style reclining design. Reclining does not affect the passenger behind you Amenities are limited since this is a short, regional flight A pillow and duvet are provided Let's have a look at the menu of today's flight Dim sum selection: chicken beancurd roll, shrimp fun gor, pork siu mai, seafood dumpling with spinach skin, sticky rice roll Breakfast is served with yoghurt and seasonal fruit Cathay's A330 has 2 lavatories for Business Class passengers The entertainment library offers a decent movie selection TV series and music span multiple genres and regions The entertainment system also includes flight maps Flight time from Hong Kong to Phnom Penh is two hours The captain announces that we’ve started our descent We will land at Phnom Penh's new Techo International Airport The new airport is nearly four times larger than the old one The airport is designed to handle 50 million travelers per year Techo International Airport is designed by Foster + Partners Phnom Penh’s new mega-airport is sparking debate  The new airport looks massive… but it’s empty Techo Airport is bigger than Cambodia’s current travel demand The airport is designed to support Cambodia’s projected growth  Cambodia invested more than $2 billion into this mega-airport Techo Airport is designed to become a Southeast Asian hub The airport’s runway can handle giant Airbus A380 aircraft The airport aims to become one of the greenest in Asia Solar energy powers much of the new terminal complex Techo Airport mixes Khmer culture with futuristic architecture  Thank you for watching my Cathay Pacific Business Class video

reviews.transcript_full: This week's flight was an absolute disaster. >> This has gone terribly. >> But it wasn't just the flight that went wrong. In a flight formula first, I also managed to mess up the microphones. Now, I would generally be inclined to just throw this all in the bin and move on to the next video. Except in this case, I'm basically just using this flight as a as an excuse as a Trojan horse to talk about the illustrious aviation career of F1 legend Nikki Lauder. Yes, this short hop across the English Channel on an airline called German Airways has a link to Nikki louder. I admit it's an incredibly weak link, but it does exist and we'll get into it later in the video. So, I guess let's get into it. This is a bit different, isn't it? Yeah, we're trying something new. I guess >> I CAN I'LL WRITE IT AND WE'LL DO IT LIVE. >> ANYWAY, Nikki Louder. For those of us who aren't necessarily hardcore Formula 1 fans, Nikki was one of the most legendary drivers the sport has probably ever had. He won three world championships. There was, of course, the 1976 Nurburg Ring crash, the famous comeback 6 weeks later, and decades after that, he played a major role in the modern Mercedes AMG team. But this is Flight Formula, not Flight Formula 1. So, what are we doing here? Well, the racing part was only half of Nikki's story. The other half was that he was completely almost comically obsessed with flying. The story goes that in 1974 while he was still racing for Ferrari, he took a ride in a small Cessna and from that point on it was game over. He got his pilot's license. He bought a Cessna Golden Eagle. He kept adding type ratings and by 1979 he had his own Leah Jet 36 that he used to fly himself to races in. Now to be fair, plenty of racing drivers have their pilots licenses. Jim Clark, Jackie Stewart, even Michael Schumacker. That's not the weird bit. The weird bit is that where most of them treated aviation as an expensive hobby, Nikki went and started an airline. Actually, he ended up starting three of them. And these weren't vanity projects. Nikki was building real international airlines. He fought Austria's national carrier. He partnered with Luansa. And he would get into a public fight with Boeing after a fatal crash. Which raises the obvious question, how did a Formula 1 driver do this? The answer, I think, is that Nikki was never just a racing driver. He was a businessman, an entrepreneur who just happened to be extremely good at driving cars. And you can see this right at the beginning of his Formula 1 career. Formula 1 is and probably always will be a rich kid sport. And Nikki was no different here. He came from serious money. His family had paper factories in Austria, but crucially, they hated the idea of him racing. And so they cut him off financially. He had no backing. His grandfather reportedly said a louder should appear on the front pages of the Austrian newspapers, not in the sports section. So from the very start, Nikki's career was not just about being fast. It was about almost turning his Formula into a business. He had to get people to back him. He was taking massive personal risk. And he was basically betting it all on the fact that he was good enough to make it. And look, starting an airline is rarely a good idea, but really this was just Nikki taking the next step in his career, finding the next thing to throw all his energy into. So, it's 1979. Nikki was 30 years old at this point. He had two world championships under his belt. He had, of course, survived the Nurburgring crash, and he was driving for Brabbom, the Formula 1 team owned by Bernie Eccleston. Eckleston would of course later go on to be the all powerful commercial boss of Formula 1, but in 1979 he was merely just a team owner. Well, sort of. It's complicated. Again, this is not flight Formula 1. Anyway, in September of 1979, halfway through the Canadian Grand Prix weekend, Nikki decided he was done. He cut short a practice session and told Bernie he wanted to retire immediately because he had no more desire to continue the silliness of driving around in circles. >> So, you know, it's all it's all not funny anymore. So, get get really does get boring. >> He was not mincing his words there. And then on the same afternoon, he flew from Montreal to Long Beach, California. Not to decompress, not to sit on a beach, he went to visit McDonald Douglas and put down a $300,000 deposit on a DC tent. This was not some ridiculous private jet retirement present. This plane was for the airline he had started 5 months earlier. This was, of course, the very aptly named Louder Air, but the Louder Air that existed when Nikki landed in Long Beach looked nothing like a DCT10 operator. It was a tiny airline stuck between, I guess, a rock and a hard place. What am I talking about here? Well, in 1979, Austrian Aviation was locked down. The government-owned Austrian Airlines had the scheduled routes. It had the political connections and it had the official place in Austria's international air agreement. So if Nikki wanted to fly a normal scheduled service from say Vienna to Frankfurt, Vienna to Munich, or quite frankly Vienna to anywhere useful in the world, he couldn't. The bilateral system stopped him before he even started. On paper, that probably should have been the end of this whole story. But this was Nikki, so he found a side entrance. Charter flights. Charter was the one part of Austrian commercial aviation that wasn't completely locked down. But I guess it still was a little bit locked down. The system didn't just issue fresh permits to new airlines. So Nikki had to find a small Austrian company called Alpair. And then he had to buy their Bed Bas concession. Yeah. Their charter permit. It would let him carry paying passengers on demand. But he wasn't allowed to do regular routes. There was no proper scheduled services. Just one-off charter flying. But this permit also had a ceiling. In Nikki's own telling in his book, the practical limit on aircraft size was 44 seats. So, Louder Air started with two used 44 seat Fauler F27 turborops. These were the planes Louder was flying in that September of 1979 when Nikki was in California putting money down on a widebody. Now, the original plan for the airline was to be polite, stay small, stay charter, and stay out of Austrian's way. In Nikki's own words, I'd have a much easier life just flying tiny turborops in a corner of the Austrian market that Austrian Airlines didn't really care about. Except Austrian Airlines did care. Every expansion attempt hit resistance. Every aircraft application stalled. Every route request hit a wall. Otmar Lens, Louder's CEO at the time, watched it happen up close. By his account, Austrian wasn't just defending its monopoly. It was actively using its political network to obstruct louder air everywhere it could. So Lens told Nikki the obvious thing. If Austrian was going to treat him like a threat anyway, he might as well become one. Stop trying to politely avoid them. Go get a widebody. Go after the longhaul markets they couldn't easily serve. That finally was what this trip to Long Beach was all about. The DC10 gave him a path to something bigger. If Ladder Air was able to grow and get funding, it had a wide body on order. And if it didn't, the DC10 had a three-year long waiting list. so he could just sell the delivery slot, maybe even for a small profit, and walk away. Except within weeks of his deposit, two DCT10 crashes destroy the aircraft's reputation. Suddenly, nobody wants one. Nikki's slot is worthless, and the growth side of the airline is failing, too. Austrian Airlines doesn't let up. The scheduled rights still don't come. So, when the next interim payment comes due a year later, Nikki doesn't have the cash to pay for it, and there's nobody to sell it to either. So, Nikki goes to his old friend Bernie Eckleston looking for advice. Bernie basically just reminds Nikki that he is the Nikki Lauder. McDonald Douglas won't want the public scandal of a famous F1 world champion walking away from an order at the exact moment the DC10 is already getting battered by the press. Nikki of course follows this advice. Macdonald Douglas lets him walk away from the deal penalty-free. But this means that Louder Air is now really stuck. By 1981, with no widebody coming and just a small charter operation that Austrian Airlines still won't let him grow, Nikki effectively retreats. He leases out the [ __ ] to Egypt Air and Louder Air shrinks down to running just a few executive jets out of Vienna. Just enough to keep the company technically alive. For Nikki, that might have been the worst possible version of failure. This is a man who turns problems into motion. But Louder Air is not being beaten by one simple problem he can engineer his way around. It's being squeezed by a whole country. And then almost annoyingly, Formula 1 starts looking interesting again. In August of 1981, Nikki turns up at the Austrian Grand Prix as a television commentator. He's barely cared about Formula 1 since walking away in Canada. But now the cars are different. Turbos are arriving. Ground effect is changing everything. And then Ron Dennis at McLaren comes calling about the 1982 season. And yes, the joke version is that Nikki comes back to Formula 1 to fund his failing airline. And like a lot of good jokes, there is probably a bit of truth to it. But it's not just the airline that gets him into the car. It is this new era of cars. reviews.transcript_full: British Airways completed the overhaul of their Dash 8 Dreamliner fleet in early 2026, replacing the old Yin Yang Club World product with Collins Aerospace's Super Diamond Club World Suite. One-way business class seats on this route normally cost over $3,000, but the frequent sales often brings the one-way cost to under $2,000. We managed to book four round-trip award flights during peak season using BA's Avios. Here's how we did it. Check-in in Cincinnati was quick with little to no wait time due to this being the only British Airways flight of the day. The dedicated Club World check-in desk only had one person ahead of us in line for document verification and bag drop. It took about 15 minutes, including the time spent waiting in line, to complete the check-in process. Contrast this with Heathrow, where even with multiple Club World check-in desks, it took over 30 minutes to complete the check-in process. Security was one area where Heathrow and Cincinnati were pretty similar. The short time to clear security was due to fast-track security at Heathrow provided to Club World passengers in TSA pre-check in the States. Lounges, however, are where Heathrow takes the lead. Once a hub for Delta, CVG had European service to Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Rome, Manchester, and Zurich in addition to the current flights to Paris and London. That history left CVG with one large Sky Club and two common access lounges, The Club and The Escape Lounge. Since none of those lounges are One World member lounges, Club World passengers at CVG are given access to the Escape Lounge. The current Escape Lounge at CVG is small and lacks a bathroom, but it does offer decent enough hot food, cereals, and snacks. The lounge also has a full bar, though without any self-serve options, and generally has great staff. However, a few of the staff on this visit were far less than helpful. Overall, this is not a lounge I would go out of my way to visit. However, that is about to change. In part due to the demand of this British Airways flight, the new Escape Lounge is set to open in April 2026. The new lounge will be in a space once occupied by a Delta international lounge and be about four times the size of the current Escape Lounge at 6,700 square feet. Club World passengers will retain access to the newer larger lounge, which should help ease overcrowding when British Airways changes the Cincinnati route from a 787-8 with 31 Club World Suites to a 777-200ER with 48 Club World Suites. At Heathrow, overcrowding remains an issue despite Terminal 5 offering Club Lounges at Galleries North, South, and the B Gates. On this visit, the Galleries South Lounge had the lowest occupancy and open seating was plentiful. The lounge offered clean, family-friendly restrooms, a well-stocked buffet, and self-serve wine. If British Airways had announced our gate more than 30 minutes prior to boarding, we would have gone to the lounge in the B Gates as our departure was at a gate B36. Boarding was straightforward for both Cincinnati and Heathrow, and with priority boarding, we had plenty of time to get acquainted with the suite. The first difference I noticed between this Club World Suite design and the old Club World product, other than the door and direct aisle access, was the storage. The Club World Suite has storage near your shoulder where you'll find the amenity kit and water, a storage bin near your foot, storage under the footwell, and two side storage compartments, one of which houses the IFE remote. On either side of the remote, you'll find an electrical outlet and the headphone jack for the BA branded headphones. And for larger items, there is ample overhead storage. And the most obvious difference will be the privacy door. At this height, the door won't make the suite feel totally or partially enclosed, but when seated, the suite feels private without feeling cramped and feels on par with most other business class products. After takeoff, the FAs should enable the door to be closed, but if they forget, you can find the door release mechanisms on the wall just behind the door. One other notable difference is the IFE screen. Club World Suites comes equipped with an 18-in screen up from the 12-in screen of the old Club World product. The IFE provides a helpful seat guide and presents BA's High Life entertainment options. High Life has every major new release movie as well as some from popular British franchises. There's a fairly wide breadth of TV options as well, meaning almost anyone can find something to watch, even kids. One cool feature for kids was the dinosaur-themed flight map. And if you're unable to reach the touchscreen, the IFE can be controlled through the remote. Lastly, controls for the seat layout and the lighting can be found near the armrest. As we completed boarding, the FAs brought out menus and pre-departure beverages and started the safety video after pushback from the gate. >> Welcome, everyone. We will now demonstrate the safety features of this aircraft, and your attention is essential as this may be >> On both flights, after having reached cruising altitude, the crew came around to take meal service orders. On the flight out of Cincinnati, I started with the grilled citrus prawns and had the ribeye steak for my main. For dessert, I chose the festive options mousse cake. For drinks, I chose the Johnny Ginger to go with my starter and the Sura pair with the steak. However, the Sura was not loaded this evening, so I settled for the Pinot Noir. The prawns were served with warm bread and an artichoke and sun-dried tomato salad. The prawns served cold were great and the spice on the prawns was well balanced by the mango salad. After the strong start, I had high hopes for the steak. The steak, however, was disappointing. While well seasoned, the steak was overcooked, but I did get to see how well built the tray table was as I struggled to cut through the meat. My dinner service on this outbound route ended with the well-executed mousse cake. The breakfast service commenced roughly 2 hours outside of London. I opted for the chia pudding with seasonal fruit and muffin. The chia pudding, while listed as a strawberry pudding, was topped with coconut flakes and was much better than expected. However, British Airways could have saved money by not offering the muffin. And the best part of the breakfast was the fresh fruit. On the outbound dinner service from London, I started with the burrata and had the traditional Christmas dinner for my main course. And for dessert, I had the brioche bread and butter pudding. On this return flight, I only had cocktails, opting against the wines they had on offer. I paired the winter warmer with my starter and main course and at the behest of the FA, I had the Singleton Scotch with dessert. The winter warmer and the burrata with the tomato and basil pesto set this meal service off with a great start. The great service continued with the Christmas dinner. The FA tasked with preparing the meals managed to heat the turkey without drying out the meat and the cabbage was near perfect for a reheated airplane meal. Rounding out the meal service was the bread pudding. For the pre-landing service, I had the niçoise salad and a roasted ham sandwich. Catering on British Airways usually makes the headlines for the wrong reasons, but the catering and the flight crew on this return leg outperformed BA's usual reviews. The FAs were even great with the kids meals, helping us make modifications to best fit my children's preferences. Between the dinner and the breakfast service on the outbound flight, I tried out the bed in Club Suite. The bedding from The White Company comes with a small seat cover, duvet, and pillow. When converted into a bed, the seat is long enough to fit most heights and the footwell wide enough to be comfortable for most back sleepers. However, the lack of mattress topper places BA's business class behind some others like United and Qatar. Overall, Club Suite is a huge upgrade over the old Club World product. The main downside for both, however, is the lack of onboard Wi-Fi, though BA has begun to add Starlink to the 787 Dreamliners. While not the best value for a points redemption and the high taxes when traveling through Heathrow, if you have the points to burn and need to fly to London, BA still offers a better value over some other airlines like Delta. Booking 355 days out, we booked the four award seats that BA released for each leg of the trip. In total, we used 720,000 points and paid 3,000 in taxes and fees for a roughly $19,000 round trip ticket for four passengers. We didn't utilize any sign-up bonuses to earn the points for this trip. Rather, the points were earned using our normal spending that was driven primarily by our American Express trifecta and also our Capital One Venture X card. Both American Express and Capital One transfer to British Airways at a one-to-one conversion and the process to transfer the points is simple and fairly quick. Some other airlines may have better beds and higher cent per point redemptions, but the wide availability of British Airways' transfer partners and the upgraded Club World Suite make British Airways a worthwhile use of points. And most importantly, the FAs on both of the flights were great and made the trip feel special for my children. Until next time, thanks for watching.

The window seats that are closer to the window provide a good amount of privacy. You're not in a closed suite, but unless you lean forward, you can't really see your neighbors. And I appreciated the adjustable armrest, which adds a bit of shoulder space when you're lying flat. That said, this seat does feel a bit tight, and the footwell is extremely narrow, which makes moving around, especially when sleeping, pretty tricky. I also noticed some visible wear and tear on the surfaces. Still, it's functional and comfortable enough for a mid to long-haul flight like this. Soon after reaching cruising altitudes, service started with a warm towel, followed by a welcome drink and some nuts. The menu offered a great variety, plenty of drinks, multiple main courses, and options for various dietary preferences. >> I chose the ravioli, which was nicely presented and tasted good, though it wasn't particularly memorable. The main downside was that all the courses were served at once, which takes away from that refined multi-course dining feel. Also, the drink glasses were a bit dirty, which is a real letdown, especially in business class. Unfortunately, the restroom was easily the weakest part of this flight. It was incredibly cramped and the sink didn't drain properly. Furthermore, there were no special amenities, just soap. Definitely below what you'd expect in business class. Each passenger received an amenity kit designed by one of various South American artists that collaborate with LATAM. On this flight, I got one by Judy Kaufman. These amenity kits are reusable and collectible, which adds a fun touch to it. Inside, you'll find earplugs, an eye mask, lip balm, hand cream, socks, a bamboo toothbrush, and toothpaste. Most of them from Feito Brasil, a luxury Brazilian brand that specializes in artisanal, vegan, and sustainable cosmetic products. It's great to see that LATAM puts real thought into the design and eco-friendliness of these kits. Also, them coming in multiple designs is somewhat unique and makes you want to collect them all. The in-flight entertainment setup was actually quite nice. The screen was perfectly sized for the distance from the seat. It was responsive and had a solid mix of movies and TV shows, both new and classic titles. The noise-canceling headphones worked very well, and so did the remote control, although getting it out of its holder was a bit awkward. Unfortunately, there was no Wi-Fi on this flight, not even for purchase, which is a big miss in 2025. And the moving map wasn't available, either. Still, the system performed well overall and kept me entertained throughout the flight. When it came time to rest, I put the seat into bed mode. The pillow and duvet were super plush and comfortable, and the cabin was kept at a pleasant temperature throughout the flight. Unfortunately, the sleeping experience itself wasn't great. The seat felt narrow, and the foot well made it almost impossible to turn your body. The lowering right armrest does give you a bit more space, but overall, I wouldn't say this bed setup is very comfortable. About an hour and a half before landing, the pre-landing meal was served. There was a choice between a roast beef sandwich or a falafel burger, with dessert options of chocolate ganache or seasonal fruit. I chose the roast beef sandwich, which came with chips and the chocolate ganache. It was okay, edible but far from impressive, and presentation was pretty basic. The cash price for this business class flight with LATAM Airlines I took in late May of 2025 was around $2,000, but instead of paying cash, I redeemed 50,000 Virgin Atlantic points and paid $55.80 in taxes and fees. But thanks to a 30% transfer bonus from American Express, I only had to transfer around 39,000 MR points. With that bonus, my redemption value came out to be about 5 cents per point. A fantastic deal, especially for an 8-hour international business class flight that includes Delta One Lounge access. But now, let's see how I'd rate this business class experience with LATAM Airlines. The ground experience. The ground experience gets an 8 out of 10. The standout elements here were definitely the priority security line and access to the Delta One Lounge, both of which made the pre-flight experience feel truly premium and stress-free. However, aside from those highlights, the rest of the ground experience, including check-in, boarding, and arrival, felt pretty standard and didn't really offer anything above what you'd normally expect. The seat and cabin. The seat and cabin gets a 6 out of 10. The seat itself is decent and visually appealing, with a good level of privacy and a comfortable cabin environment overall, but in bed mode, the space feels tight and the narrow footwell makes it difficult to get comfortable. On top of that, the onboard restroom was a major weak point, cramped and lacking in amenities, definitely below business class expectations. The onboard dining. The onboard dining gets a 6 out of 10. There's a solid foundation here with a good variety of options and meals that are decent in both taste and presentation. However, a few execution issues really hold this back, things like the dining service style and the poor cleanliness of the glassware. The IFE and amenities. The IFE and amenities get a 7 out of 10. There are definitely some strong points here, especially with the amenity kit, which is both stylish and thoughtfully designed, and the overall entertainment system, which offers a good selection of content. But the biggest drawback is the lack of Wi-Fi, which is a major miss for a long-haul business class flight today. Limited storage space at the seat is another small downside. The onboard service. The onboard service gets a seven out of 10. The crew was friendly, professional, and did their job well throughout the flight. That said, the service felt more reactive than proactive, and there weren't many personalized touches that made the experience feel truly special or memorable. Averaging everything out gives this business class experience with LATAM Airlines an overall score of 6.8 out of 10. It isn't among the elite products, but it's a solid and mostly comfortable way to travel, especially when you factor in the amazing Delta One Lounge access and the great redemption value using points. The seat could use an update, and the food and restrooms definitely have room for improvement, but for an overnight 8-hour flight to South America, I'd say it's absolutely worth it and would fly in this business class product again, especially if booked with points. But ladies and gentlemen, that is just my opinion. What do you think of LATAM's business class product? Would you fly it, or would you fly to South America with another airline? Let me know in the comments section below. But for now, I just want to say thank you so much for watching, and I will see you in the next one. Take care.

reviews.transcript_full: Good morning from Singapore. After a fun few days of taking my mom around Singapore, we're headed to Japan flying by a Taiwan. There's a lot of great choices between the two countries, most notably China Airlines, EVA, Starlux, and Singapore. >> [music] >> Today we'll be flying both Singapore and EVA back-to-back. Longtime viewers of this channel will remember I did nearly an identical routing my on my last around the world, but flying EVA and Starlux. How does Singapore's regional business class stack up against the other great airlines in the region? Let's find out. We paid 45,000 Air Canada miles to fly from Singapore to Taipei to Tokyo, which is a great price for more than 6 hours of business class flying. Singapore's Changi Airport is incredible. I've covered the Jewel with its giant waterfall, movie theater, and shopping arcade before. Today I got to explore some of the other features, like this koi pond, and this two-story butterfly garden. Seriously, where else can you have an experience like this in an airport? We next headed to the Singapore Airlines lounge. It was the same as last year and is supposed to be renovated over the next few years. I really like it. The main room has a large buffet and made-to-order stations. But like before, we sat in the quieter area off to the right. There's a smaller buffet here and the dual bar barista station. Except it was actually open this time. I had a hearty breakfast that was quite tasty and overlooked the koi pond. We headed to the gate and went through security, which is done at each gate in Singapore. We boarded and turned down the jet bridge for business class. I was warmly greeted and walked to my seat. The 787-10 has Singapore's regional business class seats. The same we saw on the regional A350 and on Turkish Airlines. While I do like them, as we'll see, they are a bit tight when trying to sleep. The seats alternate between those closest to the aisle and the window. There's the annoying little wing thing on the side with some lights and a nice size storage cubby. I've covered the seats in detail as many times before, but I think they're quite functional on a daytime flight such as this. The crew confirmed my meal pre-order, offered apple, orange, tomato juice, or water, offered to hang my coat, and gave us hot towels. Our pushback was delayed due to congestion, then it took quite a while to taxi to the runway at Changi. Flying time to Taipei was 4 hours and 15 minutes at 35,000 ft. The thing I was most excited for about this flight was the food. This is now my fourth Singapore Airlines business class flight, but the very first where I was actually departing from Singapore. That means I had access to the full Book the Cook menu, rather than more limited options such as in New York, Seattle, or no option in Ho Chi Minh. Even though it was breakfast, I went for the lobster thermidor, one of Singapore Airlines' signature dishes. Without Book the Cook, you had the option of scrambled eggs, rendang, and dim sum. First was a course of fruit, bread, butter, and jam. Next came yogurt and muesli, which I skipped to save my appetite. The lobster thermidor was good, really good. They've changed the recipe since COVID to make it a tad lighter, but it was still rich and unctuous. It was served with asparagus, potatoes, and pumpkin, and I polished off the whole thing. I think it's clear that Singapore's home catering really lives up to the hype. Even though it was a daytime flight, Singapore dimmed the windows and cabin lights as if it were night. EVA had done the exact same thing on this route a year ago. So, let's check the bed. I found it comfortable enough, but it still is tight around the shoulders, even if you move the armrest. There's just so much wasted space between the seat and the window. And the footwell, as on Turkish, is really too tight. Singapore's in-flight entertainment is the same excellent offering as on their long-haul fleet. Wi-Fi is also still free for business class passengers. We began our descent into Taipei Taoyuan and flew over the island, but approached from the northeast. So, we had a great view of Taipei and even Taiwan Songshan Airport in the distance as we came in to land. So, Singapore's regional business class on the 787-10 out of Singapore. Honestly, it was as good as could be. Fantastic service, excellent food, and a lie-flat seat. Passengers taking this configuration on longer flights, say to Australia, may have some legitimate complaints about the narrowness of the seat and the footwell. But on a regional flight like this, it's a wonderful treat. Like my last Singapore business class flight, I actually wish the flight were longer, and I don't know of any higher endorsement >> [music] >> than that. But enough of what I think, what did my mom traveling with me think? She gave it a nine out of 10. >> [music] >> In her eyes, the crew were so polite and gracious, the food good, and she found the seat mostly comfortable, but found it a tad stiff, and it hurt her back in a way that the long-haul A350 seats did not. And notably, she wasn't bothered by the narrowness of the seat and footwell like I was. That's the thing with reviewing airlines, though. At the end of the day, so much of it is indeed subjective. But next time, we'll have perhaps one of the best direct comparisons, as we fly next on EVA's own 787-10 out of their hub of Taipei. Thanks for watching, and I'll see you on the next one.

reviews.transcript_full: Good afternoon, everybody, from Taipei, Taiwan, Taoyuan International Airport, Terminal 1. My name is Hugo, and I'm very excited cuz today I'm going to be flying on probably the most hyped airline in the world, Starlux. It's a pretty new airline, quite a unique one, which is often called one of the world's best, and I'm going to be flying on one of their A350-900s in economy class from here in Taipei to Hong Kong. But without further ado, let's go and see if Starlux is really that good. I just arrived in from Hong Kong, by the way, so that's why I didn't have to go landside. Okay, so I've made it airside. I already had a mobile boarding pass, so I was able to skip the counters and just head straight through security. So that was pretty easy, and now I'm airside. This is quite an interesting, very long terminal. Like it doesn't end. Online check-in worked well, by the way. Taipei, Taiwan, Taoyuan Airport has sort of three terminals. Well, there's Terminal 1 and 2, and then the new Terminal 3, which is only partially opened. I'm not too sure about Terminal 3, but airside, the Terminal 1 and 2 are connected into four concourses. So Starlux operates from both Terminal 1 and 2, depending on where you're flying to. Hong Kong seems to be Terminal 1. I think there's a shuttle train between the two terminals. Terminal 1 was built in 1979. It's the original terminal. There's lots of luxury shopping that can be done here, but at least in Terminal 1, there's surprisingly limited food and beverage outlets. It's also very closed in. There's not much natural light. I'm finding it a bit confusing to navigate, and there's long walking distances. This is my first time here, by the way. I went to see if I could walk in and buy lounge access to Starlux Galactic Lounge here, cuz I was able to pre-book it, but you can't walk in. There doesn't seem to be heaps of great places to blind spot here. I just happened to be in a cafe with a good view at the time when my ride to Hong Kong was arriving. Bravo 58508 is a 2024 built Airbus A350-941, which was delivered new to Starlux in December of 2024. Starlux was founded by K.W., former chairman of EVA Air, a subsidiary of the Evergreen Group, founded by K.W.'s father. It's an interesting story as to how he ended up founding a competitor airline to EVA Air, One that was covered by a great and fairly light-hearted video by Flight Forum Yard. The vision for Starlux is to offer a curated world-class experience. The design and experience is very space-themed, which we'll see later. It appears as though every aspect of its design has been well thought out. They even partnered with BMW Designworks to design their cabins. Starlux launched in early [music] 2020, bad timing as they had to suspend passenger operations shortly after due to the [music] pandemic. Especially impressive considering there are two other premium carriers, EVA and China Airlines, in Taiwan, Starlux had already posted an operating profit in 2023. Its fleet consists of A321neo's, A330-900neo's, A350-900's, and more recently the dash 1000. All factory fresh aircraft with an average age of just over 3 years. The gate area is downstairs from the main terminal, but you can just go back up. I got my boarding pass printed at the gate desk, which is a very cool boarding pass by the way. And I also asked how much an upgrade was. It was 1000 USD to premium economy. I think it was 4000 to business. That is mind-blowing. It's nowhere near that to just book it outright. Apparently the flight's not very full. I currently have a spare middle seat. Weather seems to be getting worse. I was just wondering where a plane I was wanting to spot was, but it had to go around. Makes sense cuz there's windshear. Boarding looks like it'll be done by zones and starts only 30 minutes before departure. Never mind, boarding started slightly early. >> Hello. Versailles. >> Thank you. >> Welcome on board of one of Starlux's A350-900's. Very cool to be able to say that. Which are at the front feature four first class suites in a 1-2-1 configuration, which though it's not full first class as such, it's still a very rare thing to see a startup airline have and reflects how luxury Starlux is. Then behind that there's 26 business class seats with modified Collins Aerospace Element seats in a 1-2-1 configuration, followed by 36 premium economy seats with the Recaro PL3530 in a 2-4-2 configuration, followed by 240 economy seats with the Recaro CL3710 in a 3-3-3 configuration. First impressions, there's a nice scent coming from business class. The cabin feels cozy but fancy and I think that's how it's meant to feel. The cabin is stunning. Since this is such a new plane, this Airbus A350 is one of Airbus' new production standard, which has wider cabins, which actually enables a 3-4-3 configuration, like what you'll find on Philippine Airlines' new A350-1000s. [music] So, it's nice that Starlux went 3-3-3. Not entirely surprising though. My seat for this flight will be 64K. Each economy seat features a nice headrest adjustable both vertically and on the sides and you might be able to adjust neck support as well. Waiting for me at my seat was a pillow with a nice fabric cover, which is great though a little unnecessary for such a short flight. Here's the recline, which seems excellent. Oh wow, the window has a dimmer. I wasn't even thinking about that but that's also an option of the new production standard. I think Starlux is the launch customer. The cabin also feels huge. By the way, the crew are very friendly during boarding. Each seat features a huge 13.3 inch entertainment screen, which is adjustable and on the bottom of it you'll find a USB port and an audio port. On behalf of captain and the entire crew, we wish you a pleasant flight with us. >> Welcome aboard Starlux Airlines. Also, the screen appears super high resolution. Now, while we're waiting, let's take a quick look at the in-flight entertainment screen. It's super responsive, pretty much like an iPad. The selection of movies and TV shows including in English is, to me at least, shockingly good. There's Bluetooth connectivity, which is fantastic. There's a menu feature, which on this route you can see they rotate the addition to the beef, which I gather they get from a special partner, so that's cool. Looking forward to seeing what it's like. If you're enjoying this video so far, and you found it interesting, I'd really appreciate it if you consider liking and subscribing. For whatever you do, thanks in advance, even if it's just watching this video. >> Takeoff, please make sure your seat belt is firmly fastened. Thank you. >> [music] >> Hello everyone, during today's flight we will provide you with a beverage and meal service. Wi-Fi and duty free sales are also available. Now meanwhile, we will provide you with an in-flight duty free sales service shortly. Please contact our cabin crew if you wish to make a purchase. >> For the meal service, there's just one option of course as expected. It's a 1 and 1/2 hour flight. It's beef noodles. Not only was there a hot meal, but a couple sides too. There was some fresh fruit, a cutlery packet including metal cutlery, some rice crackers, and a mixed juice box. With the noodles there was also a meatball of some description. The beef noodles were delicious and very hot. The beef in particular was amazing. I wish there was more. The noodles also seemed great quality. The fresh fruit was nice and so were the rice crackers. The mixed juice box was very tasty and I think it was pretty healthy, too. The metal cutlery tell that a nice premium touches. The window dimmers do work better than on the 787. What's your opinion on window dimmers? I'd be interested to hear in the comments below. The meal service was completed about only 40 minutes after takeoff. Rubbish was collected a few times. Now, let's take a quick look at one of the lavatories. This lavatory is insanely good. It's big, especially for economy. It's got some additional amenities. There was spray of some sort and something else. There's succulents for decoration and even spa music and water sounds in economy? Wow. It was also super clean. Online check-in works well, [music] and it was good I was able to get my boarding pass printed at the gate. Crazy upgrade prices though. It's very comfortable, spacious, and super modern. I think the best economy seat I've ever experienced overall. These new A350s are very nice, too. Having all factory fresh aircraft [music] is a unique opportunity for a startup airline to make the experience truly theirs and design it from scratch, and StarLux nailed it. reviews.transcript_full:
Today I am adding a new airline to my 
list. My flight on All Nippon Airways   takes me from Sydney to Tokyo Haneda on 
their Boeing 787 Dreamliner. But with   JAL and Qantas also offering this exact 
route, where does ANA fit in? Stay till   the end because I'll show you how to fly this 
airline’s business class for less than 1000   AUD.
 
 
The check in line was completely empty   as I arrived just 90 minutes before my flight.
The baggage allowance in Economy is 2 checked   bags, each up to 23 kilograms — which is 
actually quite generous compared to most   carriers. Thanks to their partnership 
with VA, if you happen to have Velocity   Gold status or above, you get an 
extra 23kg of baggage allowance. After check in, it was through 
immigration and security,   and then a seriously long walk to Gate 53.
Unfortunately, the Velocity partnership with ANA,   doesn’t extend to lounge access - another 
casualty of the mis-mash of Velocity partnerships.  But by the time I got to the gate, 
it was already time to board anyway. The boarding process was impressively organised. 
In what I think is a first for Economy class,   ANA boards its window seat passengers 
board first. If you think about it,   this makes sense and should at least in theory 
reduce that awkward shuffle in the aisle.   ANA was the launch customer for the Boeing 
787. It has a fleet of 86 of these types   with many more on order. Today we are on 
the 787-9 specifically the international   configuration with 192 economy class seats. The 
seat configuration is the standard 3-3-3 layout. The disappointing part of this seat layout   is that they used to run a wider 2 4 2 
configuration, but this didn’t survive.   That leaves Japan Airlines the only one that 
has stuck with 8 across layout on the 787. At around 17 inches wide, today's 
seat is on the narrower side.  On the seat pitch front, at 33 to 34 
inches, it is among the best you'll   find in economy. The seat itself covers the 
basics well with a coat hook, USB C charging,   split seat pockets and AC power under the seat.   The footrest is a genuinely nice touch that 
you don't see on many economy products anymore. Amenities wise, you get a pillow and blanket 
— simple but appreciated on a 9 hour flight.  And after all those comments about seat width,   I lucked out today with two empty seats next to 
me, which made a very comfortable difference. We pushed back right on time as ANA treated 
us to their Pokémon themed safety video. One   of the most charming safety videos I've 
ever seen and very on brand for Japan. Shortly after takeoff, the crew came 
through with the pre meal service.  Wet wipes, a packet of rice crackers — which were 
actually really tasty — and some orange juice. The tissues on board are made 
from recycled green tea leaves.   It's a very Japanese touch and 
I thought that was really cool. Since this was my first flight with them,   I played it safe and went with a special 
option specifically the Hindu meal.  And right away, one thing 
stood out, the metal cutlery.  I don’t know about you, but for me, that's 
a mark of a premium airline even in economy. The tray itself was pretty substantial. 
Alongside the main there was a salad,   cheese and crackers, fruit and dessert. The 
main was a chicken curry with rice — fragrant,   well seasoned, decent portion. It actually 
reminded me of the meal I had on Malaysia   Airlines. Although thankfully I didn't spill 
this one. Overall, a solid meal service for   economy and better than I expected. Maybe I 
don’t need to order a special meal next time. After the meal service, the cabin windows were 
dimmed even though this was a daytime flight.  I took the cue and managed 
to get a few hours of sleep. Before that though I spent some time with 
the entertainment system. And this seems to   be a bit of a theme with Japanese airlines 
— the content library is well stocked, but   titles are displayed as lists rather than grids, 
which makes finding anything a bit of a chore.  On the plus side there was WiFi on board, and 
the messaging version was completely free.  On a day flight that was pretty valuable and 
it made the whole experience far more passable. In between the meal services, the galley was 
stocked with snacks and drinks that you could   help yourself to — water, juice, light snacks.
Here is a look at one of five lavatories in   Economy class. It was pretty clean 
as you would expect from a Japanese   airline. This one was fitted with a change 
table and of course, it came with a bidet. With around two hours to go, as we flew 
past Guam, the second meal service came   around — a snack box. Inside was a bread 
roll, some fresh fruit and dried fruit.   It was decent but honestly a bit light for 
a 9 hour flight. The second service could   have been more substantial — but this has become 
pretty standard across the industry these days. The rest of the flight was uneventful and we 
eventually began our descent into Tokyo-Haneda.  So where does ANA sit among the 
three airlines on this route?  Against Qantas, I think ANA wins pretty easily 
with a newer aircraft type offering a better   hard product and features like WIFI on board. 
Against JAL, it's a closer call. JAL still has   the edge in terms of seat comfort with their 
2 4 2 layout. The food and onboard services   were similarly good to each other while 
the IFE was equally bad in both cases.  Overall, ANA economy is a solid product 
and is a comfortable way to get to Japan.   But I probably won’t rate is as high as JAL. 
Let me know what you think in the comments. So, to that business class upgrade tip. ANA is 
a Star Alliance member and their flights can be   redeemed using other Star Alliance program 
including Avianca's LifeMiles program. I   paid 25,000 LifeMiles for this economy 
ticket flying out of Sydney. But here's   an interesting quirk — if you book from the 
Tokyo end, economy drops to just 20,000 miles   and business class exactly double that at 
40,000 miles. Buy those 40,000 miles during   a LifeMiles sale and you could be sitting in ANA 
business class for less than 1000 AUD. That is   the real sweet spot on this route. Just keep 
in mind that award availability is limited,   so always check this on the Aviance website before 
you buy — and never purchase miles speculatively.

Aer Lingus kept producing extraordinary things and every single one of them ended up bigger than the place it came [music] from. reviews.transcript_full: First class, business class, premium economy, and economy. What's the difference in all four cabins on British Airways? And is it worth paying for those more premium cabins? I've personally flown all four multiple times, and today I'm breaking down what to expect in each class from the ground experience to the seats, to the onboard dining, drinks, and overall experience. So, let's start with the experience on the ground at check-in. In economy, or World Traveller as BA calls it, you'll use the standard check-in desks, and checked luggage allowance varies based on the exact fare type. Basic fares come with no checked luggage, where a standard fares get one 23 kilo bag. In premium economy, or World Traveller Plus, you'll get a dedicated check-in area at Heathrow, and at out-stations you'll be able to use priority check-in lines. Each passenger can check in two 23 kilo bags. Once checked in, both economy and premium economy will then head through the standard security lines. In business class, or Club World, you'll get dedicated check-in area, two 32 kilo check bags, and you can head through fast track security. This fast track security doesn't often make a huge difference at Heathrow, but at some airports and at some times a day, it can be a big time saver. First class passengers will get access to the first class wing, a closed-off check-in area that's recently been refurbished with a new burgundy design that feels very Qatar Airways. There's an area to sit and get refreshments, but generally check-in here will be very quick and much more friendly than I found at the other desks. Once checked in, you can then make your way through a separate security area and a very fast security channel that then deposits you directly into the first class lounge. It is worth noting, too, that status with BA and its Oneworld partners can allow you to access some of these perks regardless of travel class. For example, silver status will also get you business class check-in and fast track. Gold will allow you to use the first class wing, and both grant extra luggage. Once through security, economy and premium economy passengers who don't have status will be killing time in the terminal before boarding. Business class passengers, or those with silver status, will have access to BA's network of business class lounges. At Heathrow Terminal 5, which is BA's main hub, there are three business class lounges: the Galleries North Lounge, Galleries South, and the B Gates Lounge. The North Lounge is the most conveniently located near security, but as such it tends to be the most full. The South Lounge has the biggest capacity, but can also get very busy. The B Gates Lounge tends to be the least busy and a little more relaxing, but it has the inconvenience of being located over the B Gates, which can be a bit of a walk if you're departing from the A Gates. All of these business class lounges will feature a variety of seating options, a buffet of food with quite a bit of variety both in terms of choice and quality. I've had some pretty terrible and some very good food from here, but for the most part it's decent, nothing special. You'll also find bar areas with self-service beer, wine, sparkling wine, spirits, and some pre-mixed cocktails. If you're traveling outside of Heathrow or from Heathrow Terminal 3, then you may access some nicer versions of BA's own lounges, as well as access to lounges of their One World partners, such as Cathay Pacific, Qatar Airways, or Qantas. First class passengers, meanwhile, will arrive in the first class lounge straight after security. However, although this lounge is called the first class lounge, you'll find very few first class passengers in here. The lounge is mostly used by those with gold status and offers a slightly elevated offering compared to the business lounge, including some improved food options, free pour champagne, and a manned bar for cocktails. But for those actually traveling in first class, who want to exit the first class lounge and move over to the Concorde Room. This is exclusively for those who have first class ticket or the very difficult to acquire Gold Guest List status. In here you'll find a quieter space with Concorde memorabilia, including a Concorde nose cone out on the terrace, an elevated drinks offering including high-end spirits and champagne, plus the a la carte Concorde dining room. Plus, if you're here for a longer connection or just want a bit of privacy, you can book some time in one of the private cabanas. These are already set up for rest, work, and showers. And after a bite to eat and maybe a few cocktails, it's time to head over to your gate to board the flight. BA board their flights in boarding groups, and your group will be determined by the higher of your status level or ticket class. Gold guest list go first, then it'll be first class or gold status passengers, followed by business class or silver, then premium economy and front status, and then finally economy. And once on board, this is where we start to see the biggest difference in the experience. So, let's start with the seats. In economy, as you'd expect, the seat is pretty basic, but I've got to be honest, I do always pay for the extra legroom ones. Even though I'm only just turning 36 at the time this video comes out, my legs and knees can't really handle not being able to stretch out on a long flight. But in terms of the seat itself, it is pretty narrow and firm, but it does at least have an adjustable headrest. You get a small in-flight entertainment monitor, which on these exit row seats is stowed in between the seats, and you also have a small tray table stowed in here, too. In premium economy, you get a bigger, wider, and overall much more comfortable seat. Plus, even the standard seats here have plenty of legroom. reviews.transcript_full: Marrakech, a city full of color, chaos, and energy. And just a few hours away from London. But the real story starts before we even get there. This is British Airways business class, or at least that's what they call it. Same seats as economy, no screens, and a 3 and 1/2 hours flight. So, what are you actually paying for? Let's find out. BA Euro Flyer is a wholly owned subsidiary of British Airways. They are based here in London Gatwick and started operations in 2022. With a fleet of 25 A320s and A321s, they serve mainly short-haul, low-cost leisure flights to European and North African destinations. I've always traveled out of London Gatwick through the North Terminal. This is my first trip to the South Terminal as far as I can remember. It does look smaller and busier. Luckily, BA has its own check-in area and a separate area for first and Club Europe or business class travelers. The check-in counters appear quite busy, yet the process took less than 10 minutes to complete. Speaking of check-in, you might have used an official airline's app or two to handle your pre-flight check-in. The official BA app received an astonishingly low score from users. I don't normally talk down on any company or product, but I have to agree with everyone else's opinions as soon as I sign up. The app could still provide basic flight information before you register. Strangely enough, it simply could not connect to or display anything useful after you register. My advice is just to use their website and save yourself all the trouble and frustrations. With that out of the way, so why not check out the South Terminal a bit and then kick back in the lounge before the flight. I wouldn't exactly call the airside area huge, but there are indeed more shops and restaurant than I expected. Getting to the lounge is easy. Just follow the signs and then go up one level. Welcome to the BA Club Lounge. My first impression is this lounge is bigger and has more surfaces than I expected. Like bar tending surfaces and full service shower rooms near the entrance. Continental breakfast is served here. Nothing too fancy, but you won't go away disappointed either. Otherwise, coffee, tea, pastry are available here. Interestingly, for a lounge this size, they offer a large selection of alcohol. The lounge got quite busy the morning I was there. If you want somewhere quieter, consider going up to the loft through these stairs. Hardly anyone got up here the morning I was in. I bet you can chill or get some work done here. Not only that, you can treat yourself to a craft beer or two. For those traveling with kids, there is even a playroom with toys and a PS5. This is the place to be if you're an aviation geek. Not only is the apron in full view, you are also facing runway 26 left. As you know, Gateway is a single runway airport. You can just sit back, relax, and see all the takeoffs and landings here. I guess it is also my boarding time. Oh, I didn't know you could actually see the cargo area in action near gate one. As I mentioned earlier, their fleet consists of all Airbus A320s and A321s. They are between 18 and 21 years in service. Once again, I didn't know what to expect before I got on board. Let's just say the seating configuration is quite creative. The supposedly 2-2 configuration is actually a 3-3 arrangement in reality with a tray set up between two seats on each side. There is also no in-flight entertainment system for this regional flight. Otherwise, you can find the standard reading lights and air vents. Need to charge your phone? The socket is under the seat. Be sure to have a UK three-pin plug or USB cable. Pushback commences slightly ahead of schedule despite a full flight. That allows the crew plenty of time to do a safety demo. Remember I said Gatwick is a single runway airport? In fact, serving over 40 million passenger, it is one of the busiest, if not the busiest. So, even though we left the gate early, we still had to wait in the queue for takeoff. At least you get to enjoy plenty of planes making their final approaches up close. Takeoff was pretty standard and uneventful. And we had to stop almost immediately after we gained altitude. There was no meal service in the economy class. Passenger can purchase food and drinks from the menu. Thankfully, food and beverages are included in business class. I ordered a Bloody Mary for myself about 25 minutes after we took off and enjoyed the view outside. Lunch service began an hour after we took off. The menu wasn't fancy, but it was good enough. I got myself this chicken dish. The white wine went very well with the chicken. It was satisfying. There wasn't much to choose from for dessert, so I got myself a cookie instead. The business class toilet is in the front. It is very small, but it was kept relatively clean and tidy. I think it passed the mid-flight cleanliness test. We finally reached the North African coastline about 3 hours later. Over the Moroccan airspace, cities, villages, and desert all came into view. And then we were making our final approach into Marrakech. Overall, it was a smooth and uneventful flight. Flight time was just over 3 and 1/2 hours. But let's be honest, this is business class in name more than in seat. You are essentially paying for the space next to you, lounge access, and a meal, not a different on-board experience. If you go in with the right expectations, it works. Just don't anything premium. Have you flown this route before? Let me know in the comments. I will see you in the next video.

Is Emirates' Business Class on the A380 still one of the best? Many travelers rank Emirates as the best airline in the world Let’s judge the seat, food, service & comfort on a real flight The 9 hour flight takes us from Bali to Dubai Enjoy the full Emirates Business Class experience & hospitality Welcome to Bali, the Island of Gods (and traffic!) Denpasar International Airport is the main airport of Bali The airport is also known as Ngurah Rai International Airport The airport is named after the Balinese hero I Gusti Ngurah Rai Over 20 million passengers pass through the airport annually Emirates offers dedicated check-in for premium passengers The International terminal has a Balinese architectural theme  It features statues inspired by Hindu mythology Emirates doesn't have its own lounge at Bali Airport Instead, Business Class passengers use the Tujuwan Lounge  The lounge welcomes passengers from different airlines The lounge is small and feels crowded during rush hours The food and drink choices are nice but limited
  It's a short stroll from the lounge to the fgates This is the Airbus A380 that will fly us to Dubai
  Aircraft registration number: A6-EUX (built in 2017) This Emirates A380 has a two-class layout with 615 seats The Business Class cabin is located on the upper deck There are 56 Business Class seats, spread over two cabins The seats are laid out in a staggered 1-2-1 configuration The cabin design is bold, ornate, and unmistakably Emirates 10A is my seat for the 9 hour flight to Dubai Each Business Class seat is 18.5 inches (47 cm) wide  Seat pitch varies from 48 inches (122 cm) to 39 inches (99 cm) Next to the window seats are storage compartments In front of the Business Class seat is a 17-inch TV An ottoman under the TV adds legroom and storage space A side console holds the power outlets and the IFE handset Each Business Class seat comes with a personal minibar A tablet controls the suite's lighting and inflight entertainment A panel for the seat controls is located in the side table  The tray table is released at the push of a button A welcome drink is served prior to takeoff The captain welcomes the passengers We're leaving the gate at 7 pm local time Emirates uses a no-frills safety video Bali International Airport also only has one runway  The A380 is powered by four Rolls-Royce Trent 900 engines One of Emirates A380's great features is the tail camera The tail camera offers a unique forward-facing view Have you ever flown in an Emirates A380? Leave a comment Emirates has currently 110 Airbus A380 in its fleet The carrier's A380 aircraft have an average age of 10 years The smaller Business Class cabin features 18 seats  The larger Business Class cabin features 44 seats  Business Class passengers receive a luxurious amenity kit Men receive Bvlgari toiletries, deodorant, and shaving items Loungewear is provided on flights over nine hours The loungewear is made from super-soft premium modal Slippers and an eye-mask are offered as well Bedding includes a blanket, plush pillow and mattress topper Noise-cancelling headphones are provided Let's have a look at today's menu A hot towel is provided prior to the dinner service Aperitif, served with mixed nuts Starter: salmon tataki with red radish, furikake and soy dressing Main course: vegetable pappardelle with parmesan Dessert: salted caramel cheesecake Post-dessert treat: chocolates Emirates' A380 features a bar at the rear of the upper deck The onboard bar is open to Business Class passengers It's time for some rest ... Window and center seats reach 79 in (200 cm) when fully flat Aisle seats extend to about 70 in (178 cm) when flat Emirates A380’s mood lighting creates a relaxing ambiance Emirates offers one of the best inflight entertainment system Emirates calls its inflight entertainment system ICE ICE stands for Information, Communication, Entertainment The ICE system features movies, TV shows, and live TV Entertainment is available gate to gate on many flights Emirates offers complimentary Wi-Fi in Business Class Passengers can track the flight with live camera views ICE also features a live moving flight map A breakfast is served 90 minutes prior to landing Main course: French toast with spiced apple date compote The pilot announces our descent toward Bali Emirates was founded in 1985 with just 2 aircraft (A300 & B737)  Both aircraft were leased from Pakistan International Airlines Today, Emirates operates a fleet of over 250 widebody aircraft Emirates employs more than 100,000 staff worldwide The airline carries over 50 million passengers per year Did the aircraft land outside the designated touchdown zone? Any expert aviation opinion is welcome :-) Emirates is the biggest operator of the Airbus A380 Emirates has currently 110 Airbus A380 in its fleet The carrier's A380 aircraft have an average age of 10 years Emirates A380 is an icon of modern commercial aviation The airline also runs the world's largest Boeing 777 fleet My heart goes out to everyone in the Middle East right now May peace and hope conquer darkness and war Thx for watching my Emirates A380 Business Class video
