reviews.transcript_full: Tonight I'm flying China Airlines A350 business class between Sydney and Taipei, a quick overnight run, and honestly one of the most comfortable ways to cross this route. My flight was scheduled for 10:10 p.m. Sydney time, and it pushed back right on time. Before boarding, I stopped by the SkyTeam Lounge at Sydney Airport, but for some reason it was absolutely packed that night. [music] So, I didn't stay long, and I basically skipped food and drinks there. On board, China Airlines A350 business cabin is a 1-2-1 layout, so everyone gets direct aisle access. The cabin feels spacious, and even with the middle overhead bins removed, there was still plenty of overhead luggage space, >> [music] >> which is always a nice surprise on a full flight. Service from the cabin crew was top-tier throughout, >> [music] >> and I really appreciated the cabin temperature, comfortable, not too warm, and not freezing, [music] which makes sleeping so much easier on an overnight flight. The travel kits were excellent, >> [music] >> a pair of slippers and a Moschino vanity kit with genuinely good quality skin care items, plus a really cute Moschino luggage [music] tag, which I actually want to keep. I also loved the little table lamp. It's a small detail, but it makes the whole space feel more premium and cozy. Because it's an overnight flight, >> [music] >> I mainly slept. I didn't spend much time with the entertainment system, but I did notice one thing missing. There are no external cameras, so you can't watch the outside view from different angles like on some other airlines. That said, they do offer free Wi-Fi, and the speed [music] was good enough for messaging, including photos and using most of my usual iPhone apps without issues. After departure, dinner was served with an entrée, soup, and main course. I chose the seafood, and it was honestly delicious, especially since I hadn't eaten much before boarding. The drinks list was impressive, too, and I had a glass of Laurent Perrier Brut Millésime 2015, a vintage champagne you don't see every day. It was absolutely divine. I got about nearly 6 hours of sleep, then woke up for a Chinese-style breakfast, which I really enjoyed. We arrived in Taipei at around 3:45 a.m., about half an hour early, great for punctuality, but not ideal if you're actually going into the city. At that hour, hotels aren't ready for check-in, and public transport is limited, so it can be inconvenient unless you're transferring to an early morning flight. On the way back, departure was 10 to 12 at midnight, [music] and I used the China Airlines Lounge at Taoyuan Airport T2. Compared to the SkyTeam Lounge [music] in Sydney, the food and drink here were much better. It felt like a proper preflight meal. Because it's such a late departure, I prefer to eat before boarding and go straight to sleep. I asked the crew to move my main meal to the morning and cancel the original breakfast, and that plan worked perfectly. After takeoff, I slept really well, nearly 7 hours, which is exactly what I want on a flight like this. Finally, I need to talk about the seat. The seat itself is very comfortable for sitting, and the overall personal space is great. My only real critique shows up in bed mode. When you go fully flat, the seat base stays firm and flat, but then your body can feel the inward curve on the backrest section, which creates a small gap behind your lower back. It's uncomfortable to lie on an uneven bed, but not a deal-breaker. I believe a thin mattress pad would probably fix it completely. Overall, China Airlines A350 business class between Sydney and Taipei is a really solid product. Great service, a comfortable cabin, strong food and drinks, and reliable Wi-Fi, just with that one small bed mode gap that I hope they'll address with a mattress pad in the future. Thanks for watching.

reviews.transcript_full: Hello everyone. Welcome back to our channel. Today, we're taking you along on our journey flying ANA Premium Economy departing from Vancouver International Airport to Tokyo Haneda. We'll also share our experience at the Plaza Premium Lounge. Our trip actually started in Seattle. We drove about 2 hours to Vancouver. This is one of our favorite travel hacks. Flying from Vancouver to Japan is usually 20-30% cheaper than flying from Seattle. We parked our car at Vancouver Airport's long-term valet parking, which cost us about $200 for 4 weeks, significantly cheaper than parking at SeaTac. For this flight, we paid $826 USD per person one way from Vancouver compared to about $1,182 USD from Seattle. Quite a big difference. With Premium Economy, you were allowed two 23 kg checked bags each. Since we had five bags, we paid an additional $150 baggage fee. After check-in, security was quick and smooth. We made our way into the international terminal, explored some duty-free shops, and then headed to the Plaza Premium Lounge near gate D67. The lounge was clean and not too busy when we arrived, but it's definitely on the smaller side. I can imagine it getting quite crowded during peak hours. >> Soup options included tomato soup and chicken soup. Pork ribs and maple chicken. Grilled vegetables and fried potatoes. Salads and desserts. There are not a lot of options for food selections. For drink, there is a coffee machines for lattes and cappuccinos. Canadian wines from Okanagan Valley and Niagara Peninsula. A few basic spirits like Bacardi rum and Canadian whiskey. And of course local lager and pale ale beers. We grabbed a glass of wine and some snacks and just sat back for a bit. Overall, the lounge is functional, but not memorable. It's a decent place to relax, but don't expect a luxury experience. After 30 minutes, we headed to our gate, which was just a few minutes walk from the lounge. Hi, hi. So, we are flying from Vancouver to Tokyo. We stay in Tokyo for 4 days. We will enjoy it. Shop to lot of shopping in Tokyo. Then, we will fly to stop by Korea for 10 hours. And then, Mongolia. Soon, it was time to board our flight, a Boeing 787. Walking into the premium economy cabin, the layout is a 2-3-2 configuration, creating a more spacious feel compared to standard economy. However, our first impression of the seats was slightly mixed. While the space itself is generous, the seats did feel a bit worn and dated, especially compared to JAL's newer cabins. One thing we noticed, compared to JAL, ANA's premium economy seats do not include a privacy divider between seats. On JAL, that divider gives you a bit of personal space helpful when you're sitting next to someone you don't know. The amenity kit is simple and functional. You get slippers, eye mask, toothbrush, basic headphones, but to be honest, compared to JAL, the amenities feel a step below. JAL offers more thoughtful touches like their heated eye mask, which really enhances comfort on long flights. And also, it comes with a bag. With ANA, everything is there, but it feels more basic and minimal rather than premium. You get a 38-in seat pitch, giving you significantly more legroom, a recline function with leg rest, which really helps on long-haul flights, a wide seat design, making it easier to relax without feeling cramped. The 15-in touchscreen is bright and responsive, and there's also a universal power outlet, USB charging port, personal reading light. Overall, while the seat design isn't the most modern, it still delivers a comfortable and practical premium economy experience. ANA provides noise-canceling Panasonic-branded headphones, which is a nice touch in terms of branding, but in terms of comfort, we found them just okay. After wearing them for a longer period, they started to feel a bit uncomfortable around the ears. Shortly after takeoff, we were served a welcome drink including champagne along with a small snack of rice crackers. For the main meal, we had several options. Minced pork sauce over steamed rice, seafood turmeric rice, ANA's original chicken cutlet curry. We chose the minced pork dish. The meal was arranged with smoked salmon macaroni salad, fried potatoes with shiso, cheese crackers, and a small dessert gelato. The flavors were balanced, not fancy, but satisfying. After the meal, we enjoyed some matcha tea with a milk biscuit. Japanese snacks and baked goods just hit differently. Simple, but incredibly well done. Throughout the flight, there were also light snack options available including instant noodles. On long-haul flights like this, one of the biggest challenges is staying comfortable and avoiding inflammation. We always fly with the Hyperice Normatec Legs Compression System and Firefly devices. It's a portable leg compression device designed to improve circulation and reduce swelling, which is helpful when you're sitting for more than 4 hours flight. About midway through the flight, she put it on and it helped increase blood flow circulation and reduce inflammation. The device gently inflates and deflates in cycles, applying pressure from the feet upward, almost like a massage for your legs. We already have reviews for these devices and feel welcome to watch it in our channel. Now, let's check out the lavatories. As expected from a Japanese airline, the bathrooms were consistently clean throughout the flight, something ANA does very well. A standout feature is the bidet function, which adds an extra level of comfort and hygiene. However, one limitation, premium economy passengers cannot access business class lavatories, so you'll be using the shared economy section. That said, they were well maintained and never felt overly crowded during our flight. In between meals, ANA also offers light snack options, which is always a nice touch on a long-haul flight. One of the highlights was their instant noodles, and they actually offered two options, a vegetarian version and a regular version. We tried both and they were delicious. About an hour before landing, we were served a light meal box with a small sandwich, yogurt, apple slices. It was fresh and clean, but compared to JAL, it felt slightly less premium and less memorable. Overall, ANA premium economy feels like a more simplified version of JAL's premium economy experience, especially when it comes to service details, food, and overall comfort. That doesn't mean it's bad. In fact, it still offers a comfortable seat, solid in-flight service, and a reliable long-haul experience. But when you compare it side by side with JAL, you start to notice the differences in the finer details, things like seat privacy, amenities, and dining quality. Those small touches are where JAL really stands out. So, I'd say ANA delivers a good and dependable premium economy product, but there is definitely room for improvement to reach that next level. After landing, we made our way through immigration, which was smooth, by the way, and then headed to baggage claim. And this is where something really stood out. Watching how luggage is handled in Japan is impressive. Now that we're starting our descent into Frankfurt, I have to reiterate that ANA is a fantastic airline to travel with. reviews.transcript_full: Isn't this just the most fascinating airport on Earth? I'm actually not being ironic here. This is Shannon Airport. It started its life as one of the most important refueling stops for early transatlantic flights, but today it's a pretty quiet regional airport on the west coast of Ireland. Except for some reason, some of China's most powerful leaders have a habit of visiting [music] this place. This is of course Xi Jinping at Bunratty Castle, 15 minutes down the road from Shannon, enjoying a banquet in 2012. Why is he here? Well, they describe these visits as pilgrimages. [music] Pilgrimages to the place that changed their country's economy forever. So, what happened at Shannon? >> [music] >> Shannon's story actually starts well before the airport ever existed. All the way back in the mid-1930s, planes couldn't yet cross the Atlantic non-stop. They had to stop and refuel, and Ireland's west coast was [music] the natural place to do it on the European side. It started with flying boats operating out of a base on the Shannon Estuary, a place called [music] Foynes. The Estuary is a wide, deep, naturally sheltered stretch of water, essentially a perfect runway, waterway for these flying boats. Then, during World War II, a purpose-built airport was constructed just across the water. This was Shannon Airport, and after the war it became one of the most important aviation hubs on Earth. Pan Am, TWA, BOAC, KLM all were flying through here. But, as aircraft improved throughout the '50s, the reason to stop started to fade. It didn't vanish overnight, and we'll get to why in a second, but while it lasted, Shannon was an incredibly busy stopping point. And back then, flying was expensive. The people passing through here were some of the wealthiest people on Earth, and they're all stuck in this terminal with money in their pockets and nothing to spend it on. Nothing until one man looked at the situation and came up with an idea that would, through a few twists and turns, eventually change the world. So, I just arrived. There's no duty-free shops, though. That was a big part of this. Duty-free shops are pretty important for Shannon in the history and how it changed the world, so let's get into that now. The duty-free shop, the one you walk through at basically every airport, was invented right here at Shannon all the way back in 1947. Unfortunately, we were landing into Shannon and not flying out of here, so I couldn't actually see it with my own eyes. But, anyway, the person behind it all was a guy called Brendan O'Regan. O'Regan was born in 1917 into a family that owned hotels in County Clare. That's the county Shannon sits in. In his early 20s, he trained in hotel management across Europe, and by his mid-20s, he'd built up enough of a reputation that the Irish government gave him a franchise to run all of the catering at Foynes flying boat base. When the operation moved across the Estuary to Shannon, he moved with it. Now, this franchise bit is important. The government didn't just hire O'Regan, they made him a private contractor with the right to 1/4 of the profits. They essentially outsourced the entire catering operation and let him run it like his own business. The reason they did it this way is pretty straightforward. They needed a talented operator with real skin in the game, not a civil servant on a flat salary, and that's exactly what they got. O'Regan is looking at this airport, and he's seeing something no one else is seeing. Hundreds of the wealthiest travelers in the world stuck in the terminal for hours with foreign currency in their pockets and nothing to spend it on. Now, coincidentally, the Irish government had just done something that was going to turn out to be pretty important. In 1947, they passed the Customs Free Airport Act. The idea behind it wasn't about shopping, it was about making Shannon work better as a transit hub. Most of Shannon's traffic was just passing through on the way to somewhere else. So, the government figured why make them deal with customs at all? Just declare the airport outside Irish customs territory, strip out the formalities, and make it as frictionless as possible for passengers, cargo, and airlines. This was the first legislation of its kind anywhere in the world. But, O'Regan looks at this legal framework and sees something the government probably didn't intend. If Shannon is technically outside Irish customs territory, that means goods sold inside the airport are exempt from Irish taxes. So, [music] he can sell things to passengers at massively reduced prices. He opens a small duty-free kiosk with Irish goods, linen, souvenirs, [music] and it does all right, but it's not setting the world on fire. And it probably would have stayed that way if O'Regan hadn't been sent on a trip to the United States. After World War II, America had launched the Marshall Plan. This was a massive aid program designed to rebuild and modernize European economies. Part of it wasn't just money, they were also bringing people over, government officials and business leaders to study how the Americans did things. Things like productivity, efficiency, modern business practices. The idea being that they would bring all this knowledge back home and improve Europe. O'Regan gets picked for one of these delegations in 1950. And the funny thing is, all of this American business knowledge he's supposed to be absorbing, that's not what changes everything. It's the ship ride home. On board the SS America, somewhere over the Atlantic in international waters, he notices that they're selling duty-free alcohol and [music] tobacco, and people can't get enough of it. That's when it all clicks. He's got the legal framework, he's got the captive audience, he's already got a duty-free kiosk. [music] He's just not selling the right thing. He comes back to Shannon and sets up a little timber hut selling bottles of whiskey for $1.50, a third of what it costs outside of the airport. It was an instant hit. Then came the cigarettes, the perfume, the Leica cameras, and the Omega watches. Within months, international manufacturers are fighting for employed around 1,000 people and accounted for roughly 20% of Ireland's total dollar exports. Shannon was the only airport on Earth with a duty-free shop for several years before Amsterdam Schiphol adopted the model in 1957. So, duty-free was big, but it led to something even bigger, something that changed the world. The free zone. Let's get into it. >> [laughter] >> So, here's the thing. Right around the time duty-free is proving itself as this massive success, a new generation of jet aircraft is arriving that can fly non-stop across the Atlantic. The very reason all of these wealthy passengers were stuck at [music] Shannon in the first place, appears, at least on the surface, to be under threat. Now, it didn't actually collapse overnight, and there was a couple of reasons for that. First, Ireland had signed a bilateral agreement with the United States back in 1945 that tied all US transatlantic services to Shannon. If you wanted to fly the Atlantic to Ireland, you had to land here. And then there was Ireland's neutrality. It never joined NATO, which made Shannon one of the few places in Western Europe where the Soviet Union could comfortably land. By the late 1970s, Aeroflot was running around 2,000 flights a year through Shannon on the way to places like New York, Washington, and even Cuba. [music] So, for a while there, you had this extraordinary thing. American carriers on one side, legally required to be there, and Aeroflot on the other, [music] choosing to be there. All at this one airport in rural Western Ireland. Shannon was still busy, but the threat was real, and O'Regan could see exactly where this was heading. He wasn't going to assume the Americans would stick around forever. [music] He wanted to build something that didn't depend on airlines being forced to be there. He'd heard about something called a free port, places like the Colón free port in Panama, where companies could import goods, store them, repackage them, and re-export them again without paying any duties. But, these were really just trading hubs. The idea of actually setting up factories inside one of these zones and producing things on an industrial scale, nobody had really done that before. And that's where O'Regan's final idea was different. What if you took that customs-free concept, and instead of just warehousing and shipping, you used it to attract actual factories? Now, keep in mind, Ireland at this point was still a pretty protectionist economy. Foreign companies couldn't easily set up shop there. So, the idea of opening up a zone where foreign manufacturers could come in and operate freely, that was a big ask. But, the Irish government actually liked it. In 1958, they amended the exact same Customs Free Airport Act that made the duty-free shops possible in the first place, and turned it into something much more ambitious. They designated a zone next to the airport where companies could set up, import raw materials, manufacture products, and then export them, all completely tariff-free. And on top of that, companies operating in that zone paid zero tax on their export profits for 25 years. What followed was the Shannon Free Airport Development Company, or SFADCo, established in 1959 with O'Regan as chairman. This was not a normal government department. It operated more like a startup that just happened to be backed by the state. It could build factories, offer grants, handle customs paperwork, train workers, market internationally, everything under one roof. Now, O'Regan's nickname was Bash on Regardless, a play on his initials B.O.R., and that's exactly what he did. His first move was to start building factories before they even had any tenants. Advanced factories is what they called them. They were pre-built, ready to go, just plug in your machinery and start producing. The early tenants were not exactly world-beaters. There was a Dutch piano manufacturer, a plastic button factory, but O'Regan's bet was that any signs of life would attract bigger fish, and he was right. Standard Press Steel moved in from America, and then Sony, the first postwar direct manufacturing investment in Europe by a major Japanese corporation. De Beers, the diamond company, GE, they all followed, and by the mid-1960s, the zone employed around 4,000 people. O'Regan also does something pretty wild here, too. There was no town. There was an airport, and there was a bog. That was it. So, O'Regan just built one, Shannon Town, the first new town built in Ireland in almost 300 years. >> [music] >> In 1976, a Shannon economist called Tom Callaher wrote a handbook for the United Nations on how to build a free zone from scratch. It had organizational templates, customs frameworks, even a blueprint act [music] that governments could copy into their own legislation. It was basically an instruction manual for how to replicate what Shannon had done. Throughout the '70s, delegations from places like Malaysia, South Korea, and Thailand were arriving at Shannon to see it for themselves. But then, in 1980, the big thing happened, the thing that would change the world. But first, guys, I'm heading to Korea in just under 2 days, and it's that awful time again. It's time to pack. But thanks to today's video sponsor, Extra, it's a little bit easier this time. It's currently pretty chilly in Seoul, so I'm going to need some warm clothes. Thanks to Extra's travel pack vacuum kit, I can make it all fit. All we do is simply unzip the travel pack, put in all of our bulky clothes, zip it up, and then, simply using Extra's handy-dandy rechargeable vacuum pump, this thing gets about 15 uses per charge, and it's rechargeable using a USB-C cable, I simply hook it up, and then hit the magic button. And just like that, we've reduced the size of my warm clothes by about 60%, meaning they'll easily fit in my bag for my trip to Korea. And you know what else I'm taking to Korea? My new Extra Card Holder Pro for MagSafe. This is the MagSafe version of their very famous Card Holder Pro. It holds up to seven cards, it's RFID blocking, and quite obviously, it magnetically attaches to the back of my phone. Now, if you're watching this on or before April 13th, Extra's currently running their spring sale where you can get up to 45% off your order. If you use the discount code Flight Formula at checkout, you can get an additional 20% off your order. I'll leave a link to Extra down below in the description, or you can scan the QR code here. Big thanks to Extra for sponsoring this week's video. Now, let's get back to our regularly scheduled programming. It's castle. It's castle. This is Bunratty Castle. It was built in about the 15th century, and it's a magnificent thing to come and see. It's located about 15 minutes away from Shannon Airport. But more importantly, over the past three decades, six of China's most powerful leaders have all come here to enjoy banquets. So, why have they all made the trip to Western Ireland to this random country castle? Well, it was the duty-free, it was the free zone that led to an idea that changed China's economy, and well, arguably, the world's economy forever. So, how does an idea travel from rural Western Ireland to the other side of the world? Well, it starts with a problem. By the late 1970s, China was in ruins. Mao's Great Leap Forward in the late 1950s had killed tens of millions of people. The government had ordered farmers to abandon their fields and smelt metal in their front yards. Yes, this actually happened. The country starved. Then the Cultural Revolution tore the place apart for another decade. Schools were shut down, factories were closed, intellectuals were sent to labor camps. And on top of all of that, there was the century of humiliation, decades of exploitation by Western and Japanese imperial powers. China's economy was devastated. Its institutions were broken, and its people were leaving. Hundreds of thousands of mainland Chinese had been risking their lives to cross the border into places like Hong Kong, swimming rivers, hiding in the hills, many of them dying in the attempt. And then, in 1978, [music] Deng Xiaoping takes charge. Now, his actual title is a whole other thing. China had abolished the position of president during the Cultural Revolution, so technically there was no president. Deng's official title was vice chairman of the Communist Party. There was this other guy who was the actual technical leader, but he consolidated power, and historians call him the paramount leader. But the point is, Deng, by 1978, was the guy that was running the show. >> [laughter] >> And Deng was a pragmatist. He famously said, "It doesn't matter if a cat is black or white as long as it catches mice." One of the first things he does is he sends delegations out into the capitalist world to study how other countries had modernized. China had been almost completely closed off for decades. They knew things were bad, but they hadn't really faced just how far behind they'd fallen. And what they found shocked them. One delegation goes to Western Europe and comes back genuinely stunned. The head of the delegation reportedly described what he saw as a galloping economy, [music] nothing like the collapsing capitalism they'd been told about. Then Deng goes himself. In October of 1978, he visits Japan. He tours the factories of Nissan and Panasonic, rides the bullet train, and reportedly said, "This type of train would be perfect for us." He then comes back to China and announces the reform and opening-up policy. China is going to open up parts of its economy to foreign investment. But he can't just throw the doors wide open. In a communist country, that's ideological suicide. He needs a contained experiment, a zone where capitalism can be tested without contaminating the rest of the system. And this is where it gets really interesting. The man who proposes exactly where to put these zones is, and I'm going to butcher this, Xi Zhongxun, the top Communist Party leader in Guangdong province. Rather incredibly, really, that guy was Xi Jinping's father. He goes to Deng and says Guangdong should be allowed to create special zones to attract foreign investment. Deng's response was, "Right, we'll set up these special zones. The central government has no money. You have to do it yourself and break through." The government would go on to approve four special economic zones. Three of them you may or may not have heard of, Zhuhai, Shantou, and Xiamen. But the fourth is set up just across the border from Hong Kong at a small fishing village that you've almost definitely heard of, Shenzhen. The legislation passes in August of 1980, and one of the men who personally presents it to Chinese Parliament is a senior official named Jiang Zemin. But there's a problem. They don't have a playbook for how to actually run one of these zones. So, they go looking for someone who does, and this is where the story comes back to Ireland. In October of 1980, eight senior Chinese officials are sent on a 6-week trip to examine free zones around the world. And out of those 6 weeks, three of them, half of the entire trip, was spent in one place, Shannon. They have classroom sessions, they do site visits, they have detailed briefings on the nuts and bolts of actually running a free zone. Now, on paper, Ireland and China could not be more different. But Brian Callanan, a SFADCo planning officer who helped host the delegation, said something happened during those 3 weeks that nobody quite expected. The Irish hosts started to share their own history, and not the charming bits, centuries of British colonial rule, the Great Famine, then decades of grinding poverty even after independence. And the rural west, County Clare, the place where Shannon sits, was one of the most economically depressed regions in all of Western Europe. [music] Before 1980, Shenzhen's economy was less than 1/5 of a percent of Hong Kong's. By 2018, it had overtaken it entirely. [music] And China didn't stop at four zones. The idea kept mutating, development zones, high-tech zones, free trade zones. Each generation a little different, but the principle always stayed the same. By the late 2000s, China's various economic zones accounted for roughly 22% of the country's GDP and 60% of its exports. But if we zoom out even further, this was the real turning point. Before 1980, China was one of the poorest countries on Earth with virtually no foreign investment and decades of self-imposed isolation. Average growth of around 10% a year for three decades straight. 800 million people were lifted out of poverty. He famously stood on top of Tulla Glass Hill overlooking the industrial zone for a quiet moment of reflection. One of China's top leaders standing in silence above a small industrial estate in Western [music] Ireland. Then we have Xi Jinping in 2012. reviews.transcript_full: Crossing the equator is more than just a flight. It's a commitment. 15 hours, two countries, and the slow shedding of a Canadian winter for the warmth of the south. This time, the journey to Santiago started with a question. Is a business class seat on a shorter widebody plane worth the premium? I'm taking you through the full experience, the lounges, the food, and the honest reality of the longest flight I have taken to South America. Our morning began at the Maple Leaf Lounge in Toronto. It's spacious, dependable, and exactly the kind of stillness you need before a 6:00 a.m. departure. A quick bite of omelette and fresh fruits and we were off. Looking forward to what lay ahead. Stepping onto the first leg. The configuration is a classic 2x two. It feels more like an upgraded lounge chair than a futuristic pod, though. At 5 hours and 42 minutes, it's a bit of a light version of business class. No pillows or amenity kits here. The seats were comfortable, though. I did spot a speck or two of dirt that felt a bit out of place for a premium cabin, but overall it was a fairly clean cabin. The layout is older, so the buttons are manual and need a bit of a wiggle, but they offer great ergonomic control, including a leg rest and footrest that keeps you nicely elevated. I did find one quirk though. The TV pulls out from the armrest, which is a bit nostalgic to the economy exit rows, but at least there's a dedicated plug for charging. Then came the service. We started with orange juice served interestingly in a paper cup. But when it came time for breakfast, we hit a snack. By the time the flight attendant reached us in row 9, they had already run out of the savory egg options. You know what the funny part is? The attendant still asked me what I wanted. I mean, you only have two options, French toast and an egg. If one of them is not available, why even ask the question? It wasn't much of a choice, and unfortunately, the taste didn't make up for the lack of options. The presentation was lovely, though. The soul was missing. It was a quiet disappointment, saved only by a croissant, a posh pear, and a glass of champagne to toast to better things ahead. The crew must have seen it in my eyes because they brought out extra nuts, sensing I was still a little hungry. It was an okay start. But wait, don't make up your mind just yet. As we started our descent into Panama, I realized that travel is rarely a straight line. It's a series of reset. If you're enjoying this honest look at the journey, I'd love for you to join the community here. Hit subscribe because next we are heading deep dive into Chile and Peru and I don't want you to miss a single moment. Touching down in Panama City felt like a reset. We headed straight to the Copa Club. It's a massive bustling space. The food here was a highlight. Tasty hot options like chicken, rice, and potatoes. Big massive machines for coffee and different kinds of sodas. They even have a full stacked bar for you to enjoy. We only had a short stay this time, but I knew I'd be seeing a lot more of this lounge on the way back. If leg one felt like a light experience, leg 2 to Santiago was the full story. As soon as we boarded the 6 and 1/2our flight, the difference was clear. plush pillows, warm blankets, and a proper amenity kit was waiting for us. We were in the first two rows this time, so no running out of menu items here. We got water bottles and a golden frog, dark chocolate, a 60% cacao treat that tells a Panama story. It was the sweetest addition. Even the champagne served in mini flutes this time felt like a step up. Heat. Heat. Heat. Heat. The meal service was a complete 180. We started with a fresh tomato soup and salad that actually had soul. For the mains, I went with the salmon in a rich cream sauce while my partner had the chicken and rice. Both were flavorful, well paced, and followed by a chocolate drizzled ice cream that made the 30,000 ft view even sweeter. This was the business class I was expecting. On the way home, the experience stayed consistent. I finally got my breakfast eggs. But the real highlight was our long layover. On the return trip, we used our layover to actually breathe in Panama City. Thanks to the breezy immigration process for Canadian passports, we stepped out into the heat, found a local cafe, and wash the city pulse before heading back to the Copa Club. The lounge is beautiful. This time we took a hot shower and enjoyed a mimosa by the window while watching the airport bustle. A perfect end cap. After some research, I found the secret to Copa. Under 6 hours, it's a streamline service. Over 6 hours, they pull out all the stops. It's an interesting rule and I'm curious, have you noticed this on other airlines? At just under $3,000 per person, this wasn't just a flight for me. It was the ability to arrive in South America feeling present and rested rather than depleted. If you are looking for luxury that feels accessible and a way to make the long haul to the south feel like part of the vacation, this is a strong contender. 15 hours later, we were finally crossing the southern hemisphere and Chile was waiting for us. Next up, I'll show you what that journey led to from Atakama desert to Patagonia. See you in Chile. Ciao. Hey, hey, hey.

reviews.transcript_full: It's Air China today and I'm giving it a 4-minus for long-haul business on Airbus 850.  When talking about newcomers who made it into the premium aviation league, most think of  Emirates or Qatar.  Yet Air China with almost 500 aircraft is only few years younger.  It all started in 1988 when China decided to break up at Stadeau Naviation Company.  Out of it emerged Air China in Beijing, China is turning Shanghai and China's southern  in Guangzhou.  Air China inherited the long-haul fleet and the intercontinental routes, arguably the most  prestigious part as well as flag carrier status.  It clearly had the strongest foundation to become China's premium global carrier.  Today the numbers look impressive, but scale does not always automatically translate into  elite status.  So the real question is, where does Air China actually stand today?  Let's explore together the cabin, food, service and the whole experience on board of these  850-900 on an 11 hour flight from Beijing to Milan.  I'm flying from Beijing capital, one of the two Air China main hubs in Beijing.  I'm connecting from a domestic flight and need to change to international terminal.  Navigating through Chinese airports is never straight forward task.  It's a midnight with few people around, making the task even more challenging.  It's interesting to see that Hong Kong and Macau are still serviced from international  terminal, even if being part of China for almost 30 years by now.  Beijing capital used to be main city airport, but you can see that glory days are over.  It's still the largest of Beijing two airports, but it doesn't look like investments are coming  here anymore.  In contrast to night buzz of Dubai or Qatar, it feels half deserted.  So without a doubt I had to air China lounge.  Beijing capital is their main hub.  It should be a flagship lounge here, so I'm anticipating being impressed and pampered.  But the lounge is closed due to plumbing issues.  And I'm redirected to first class lounge.  A bit strange reason, but I get a chance to experience first class, so no complaints.  I'm greeted by a cute giant panda and he becomes pretty much the best thing I can tell  about this lounge.  Well, not true.  It was also clean.  But honestly, if this is the luxury of first class, then I'm even afraid to think what  you can expect in its poor cousin, business lounge.  First impression, very simplistic and functional.  Old furniture, simple food stations, basic bar.  Food and drinks seem to be very much focused on Chinese passengers and might look a bit  strange for foreigners.  The lounge looks like it came all the way from the 90s.  And this starts telling a story what air China could be about.  Fortunately, I don't have too much time till the flight, which means I don't have to  force myself to enjoy the questionable luxury of the first class lounge.  I'm heading straight to the gate and managed to get a good look at my today's ride.  It's a brand new 850 with only two years of age.  Air China has a very distinctive livery which makes it easy to spot.  It's a clean and a little retro look.  Those blu-chit lines come all the way from the design book of 70s.  Making a bold statement that stability and consistency is more important to our China  than being cool or modern.  Our 850 comes with 32 business seats in one to one reverse heading bow on staggered  configuration, which on paper is already a good sign for comfort and privacy.  Now let's see what that means in reality.  Well, it's definitely a modern cabin with a sweet style seats which offer a very good  level of privacy.  Air China uses recarulated 6720 seat design.  Besides Air China, it's only a Beary that used it so far.  The Abeary's version however has a sliding door, while Air China stayed short of it.  They claim it's for better service.  But I wonder if the main reason was that the door comes with extra 50 kg of weight.  And Air China didn't want to add an extra 1.5 ton of weight for the sake of being what.  More cool?  That doesn't sound there China at all.  Besides that, it's still a very solid product.  Even without the door, the high shell of the seat gives you a good cacoon-like feeling.  Unlike a Beary which has a bare-bone model with cheapest finishes, Air China's seat was  customized with better materials, built-in storage drawers and a Chinese style lamp.  However the quality of materials and finishes is good but not great.  And it doesn't give you the luxury look and feel that you can get in a catei area or  catearchus with.  The seat is long, confiant functional.  Maybe not the absolute top tier in space, but pretty good for a long haul snooze.  7 to 8 inches long and 21 inches wide, it's not beating any records but seats right after  bestened class.  It's a bit firm and Air China doesn't provide any minimatrices, so you better like firm  bedding.  There is a fully adjustable headrest but it's too small to be fully comfortable.  The narrow foot well is the standard issue of those seats.  There is nothing that Air China could reinvent about that.  The seat comes with 18 inch HD screen, respectable but on the low end of what you expect  today actually.  20 inches of becoming standard and catei areas with comes with whopping 24 inch 4K display.  Still it's perfectly fine for watching one to our movie on a night flight.  But given that this is a new business cabin for a China which will likely last for another  10 years, not sure why they didn't go for a larger screen and 4K.  It's clear that current Air China tech will start looking more and more outdated already  in few years.  All additional seat equipment is clustered around mini table on your side.  Controls are simple and I appreciate the modern remote with built-in screen.  Power outlets are easy to reach but surprisingly for a brand new plane, no USB type C.  Besides standard reading light we also have a mini lamp in a Chinese style.  It's definitely custom made feature requested by Air China and I love it.  This is how airline can show its character.  Also an interesting small vanity mirror, a simple thing but quite handy.  You do get bored on those 10 plus hour flights so it gives you one more thing to entertain  yourself.  One thing that strikes me is that so many amenities are packed in plastic bags.  This is both unfortunate and very typical for China but somehow you would expect better  from flag carrier.  I'm going to look further into those amenities few moments later.  It's late night and there are only 3 main things on my agenda.  Take off, dinner and sleep.  So far this is a very solid modern business seat.  Not the most luxurious but definitely competitive.  The hardware here goes ahead of soft elements which I start to suspect is the style of Air  China.  I'm putting on a very decent pair of slippers which is definitely a Chinese thing and  all ready for the flight.  The pre-flight service brings again few surprises.  I'm offered the choice of champagne or Air China's signature red lantern drink.  I go for the later which proves to be an interesting but kind of polarizing choice.  It's a sort of savoury sparkling tomato juice which sounds intriguing but tastes rather  weird to European tastes.  Well curiosity killed the cat but for sure it's an experience.  Another surprise is that there are no menus.  A flight attendant is just asking if you prefer western or Chinese and let you wonder what  kind of mystery meal you will get.  Reminds a small family restaurant where a grandma tells you a menu of the day.  Kind of both cute and frustrating at the same time.  While crew is serving those drinks I'm enlisting Air China in my safety video competition.  I like comparing how airlines use this otherwise boring thing to tell something about who  they are or not.  Air China video might not be very creative but it's clearly authentic and has a lot of  Chinese flavor.  I'm meeting again my friend Panda from the lounge.  Hopefully this time he's not going to be the only highlight of my experience.  Fast forward few moments and here comes the dinner service which perfectly continues the  service standard set by the lounge.  It's a mix of something which is a little average and a little different.  There is no multi-course gourmet dinner with restaurant quality as in Turkish or Cathay.  Everything comes at once.  It doesn't look very sophisticated and somehow it feels like it was sitting in the fridge  for some time.  It's the culinary equivalent of a highway motel.  Functional does the job but leaves you wondering what happened to ambitions of the owner who  wants dreamed to open a witz Carlton.  The main course is something which is a mix between a burger and a pizza with some roasted  pork inside.  Comes with fried rice and broccoli on the side.  Somehow it reminds me of Gansa food.  The purpose is not to impress but to feed.  There is no starter but to desserts.  A fruit platter and some strange tasting cheesecake which most likely is not a cheesecake  at all so comparing it doesn't help.  I also got a glass of wine.  It wasn't bad but I still don't know what it was.  The flight attendant neither seemed to know the wine list.  No was very fluent in English.  At the end we stopped our discussion at a smile and a white wine.  I didn't risk to go for a coffee and washed my meal with a cup of tea.  This worked perfectly well.  Still a tea bag rather than a pot but rich and good and with a nice porcelain cup.  I start to realize another thing about air china.  It just doesn't try to be multicultural if it's some standards like Emirates, Cathay or  Singapore Airlines.  And many things that look strange for me are not about good or bad but rather this is  how it works in China and it's okay.  Done with the dinner so let's finish now exploring the amenities.  Air China doesn't have any official partnerships like Etihad has with Armani or Air France with  Cloron.  The amenity pouches brand it looks it on which is respectable.  But once you take it it feels a bit plastic if not outright cheap.  Makes you wonder if this is really endorsed by the brand.  Once I open I can't hold a smile.  It looks more like a lunch box or a first aid kit than something that should give you  a premium wipe.  There is a lot inside but all that gives a feeling of pick and mix rather than something  designed to purpose.  This set there is Loxytone, body lotion and lip balm and then a full line that would  make proud anything for 10 cents store.  Toothbrush, hairbrush, hair plugs, eye mask, all with over engineered packaging.  Very much Chinese and very much excessive, unplastic, not unluxury.  But maybe this is how it works.  Let's move on, headphones, my soft spot for long flights.  Comes in a dedicated case which often signals a branded pair.  I flew with a smaller competitor of Air China, high nine airlines and they had an excellent  set of power and welkins.  But here I get a typical generic set.  It got noise cancellation and it's generally passable but nothing outstanding.  After 30 minutes you start feeling a bit uncomfortable wearing those headphones.  A pass but not a score.  And finally bedding set.  I mentioned that we don't get mini mattress which is clearly a miss, only pillow and blanket.  Both are generally okay but there is no mistake that this is not Armani Casa like on Etihad.  Rather something which was optimized for cost and durability.  But while missing on aesthetics they do the job as good as any other.  It's just a soft reminder that Air China is not there to be cool.  And all those plastic bags somehow bring more of a spirit of student dorm rather than a  business class on a major airline.  Once you finish unpacking you are left with a pile of plastic bags which makes you feel  like you just came back from a supermarket.  Before going to bed I still check the in flight entertainment.  After all the content choice is very big but it's clearly optimized for Chinese passengers.  International content is surprisingly new and decent but quite limited compared to choice  of local movies and series.  This could be fair if Air China would only target domestic audience but might be questionable  choice if it aims to bring international travelers and transit traffic.  Still it's much better than what I had on China Eastern and China's Haozorn.  The other two main legacy Chinese airlines.  Now it's finally time to sleep.  I put the bed into life-flat position, it does feel a bit stiff but I'm tired so I'm sure  this is not going to be any obstacle.  I learned to think about Air China by now.  Hard product over soft and definitely prioritizing domestic tastes and practices.  It's there for China not to please foreign tastes.  Everything comes with breakfast my final important task on this flight.  If you don't count the landing which I have to say is quite important too.  After a short exchange with flight attendant I failed to advance my understanding of breakfast  options beyond Western and Chinese.  And while still remembering the fate of the curious cat I again decide to go for Chinese.  The breakfast comes with a set of dim sums, marinated cucumbers and mushrooms and something  which looks like porridge but it's actually a sweet rice dessert.  Same fruit as for dinner too.  And as a cherry on top this boiled egg with a plastic leaf as decoration.  It's not the most conventional breakfast by European standards but it was for sure interesting  and actually not bad.  But that egg with plastic leaf somehow became for me a symbol of Air China service.  It's now very locally focused and with very little attention to details and style.  It's the end of the 11 hours flight and I do have one final torture test for Air China,  Lava Turis.  And they pass, it's clean and well maintained.  It's a standard 850 Lava Turi but it would not be a Chinese airline if there would not  be a small gadget.  This automatic flap for trash can really makes me smile.  And actually they got some interesting toiletries here from Herberist, a premium Chinese brand  with East meets West aesthetics.  Wonder why they would not build the whole amenity kit around them, would make much more sense  and send a different vibe.  I won't patent this bright idea, it's all for Air China.  Now it's all for this flight and a time to conclude.  I'm giving Air China for minus for this flight today.  My first impulse was 3.  But then I have to admit that their hard product is actually quite good.  It's the service where they suffer.  And to a large extent this could also be about famous cultural differences.  Air China is making efforts, new fleet and growing international network on top of its  domestic backbone.  Their new cabins are not best in class but definitely very competitive modern business  product.  I know it's below Qatar and Qatay but generally in line with KLM, Air France and Turkish.  And way better than Lufcanza.  But they still struggle to understand or care much what premium experience means.  From the lounge to onboard service, crew training and food and drinks, it's all just  average if not mediocre for modern long haul business flight.  These days just having a seat and a meal doesn't cut it anymore.  Air China's functional approach may still work for their domestic market but it will  not help them with international expansion.  Something that they're trying hard these days.  Interesting experience, no regrets but still falls short of something that you would like  to repeat.

reviews.transcript_full: Hi and welcome to Amsterdam's Gibral Airport.  Today's review is all about Catholic Pacific Long Hall Business Class and I'm super excited  because we get to fly all the way from Amsterdam to Hong Kong on a Catholic Pacific Airbus 351,000  so let's see what it's all about.  Apparently according to some, Catholic Pacific suffered more than most in the pandemic  and some say they haven't bounced back yet, so let's find out if that's true or not.  Now our trip actually started in Helsinki where it was freezing cold and loads of snow,  so we haven't actually used the check-in facilities here at Amsterdam's Gibral,  and we're travelling handbagged only, so we haven't used our check-in bag allowance either.  Now, whatever the inflight service is like, one area where cafe definitely excels  is in its own and operated business and first-class lounges.  Now unfortunately in Europe there is only one lounge and that is at Heathrow Airport,  so here at Amsterdam we've used the one-world lounge which is operated by a spire.  All I want to say about the lounge is that it is situated a long way away from our gate.  I don't know if they always go from G6, but if they do, then the lounge is at least a 15-minute walk away.  It's okay, it's nothing to write home about, but if you want a glass of champagne and some popcorn, go there.  So, yeah, enough of all that, let's go and get on the plane.  Boarding was quick, orderly and efficient.  We have no one-world status on this flight,  so we are in the process of switching our allegiance from British Airways to Alaska,  so we were in group two.  We boarded at the front of the two doors and was greeted by the cabin manager  who was very friendly and visible throughout the whole flight.  Immediately on boarding we were offered a welcome drink of water, juice or champagne,  and shortly after we were given a hot towel.  The cabin is light and airy, and first impressions of the seat is that it is roomy, but don't worry.  After we talk about food and service, we cover the seat in lots of detail.  We should also say at this point that these are not Cathay's most modern cabins.  They're more modern cabins feature the area suite,  however this review will be relevant for years to come.  Since of Cathay's fleet of roughly 140 wide-body aircraft,  only around a dozen currently have the new suite.  As soon as all the passengers had boarded, the crew started taking drinks and meal requests.  Quite rightly they appeared to start with passengers who presumably have Cathay or one-world status.  I'd requested the beef online a few days before the flight,  and clearly it worked because they said they had my order  when all I needed was to select my starter and drinks.  We noticed that the cabin manager was welcoming all passengers, including us by name,  starting with one-world status members first.  The drinks were delivered about 30 minutes after takeoff, accompanied by this amuse-bush.  Whilst waiting for the drinks and meal, I explored the Wi-Fi.  I'd already planned by the Wi-Fi package as the flight was over 11 hours,  but to my pleasant surprise it was free to business class passengers,  and this covered web surfing as well as messaging,  and included the ability to switch between devices as well.  Internet coverage was a bit patchy, especially over Western China,  and if I'd paid for it I might have been a bit grumpy,  but for a free service it was more than adequate.  Next came the immunity kit.  At first we thought that the different coloured kits were tailored specifically for him and her,  but it transpires that they all have the same contents.  Nothing stood out from the immunity kit crowd,  except perhaps that the eye mask looks particularly robust,  and should stand the test of time.  One small criticism is that on one hand this pre-ordering of breakfast seems to be a great idea,  but maybe they could have included a pen to allow you to make your choice  without scrabbling round for a writing instrument in your hand baggage.  Our tables were covered with a cloth and the starter arrived via a trolley and this tray,  along with warm bread and balsamic dressing.  We both ordered the soup which was really delicious,  and it was served along with our correct choice of wine,  retailing at $60 per bottle, both our wines proved to be top choices.  Within 15 minutes the mains arrived.  Whilst both were tasty, they were perhaps not memorable.  Additional drinks were not offered,  but when we asked for another glass of wine they were served within a couple of minutes.  Then came the cheese and more drinks and lots of desserts were served from a trolley,  and then we were offered tea or coffee and offered chocolates, what a nice touch.  Overall, the meal service for this daytime flight felt very efficient, yet nicely relaxed,  and at this point we should say just how hard the crew worked,  from the moment we boarded until the end of the meal service four hours later.  Let's talk about the seat.  The design is a few years old now and we were concerned that it might feel dated  or lack privacy compared to the latest creations from British Airways and Qatar,  which typically include a door that allows them to be bagged as a suite,  rather than just lifelad.  In reality, our seat proved to be a great space in which to spend 11 hours.  The one two one Herringbone layout means that all seats have aisle access,  are forward-facing, and they have been designed so you can't actually see your neighbour,  even if sitting in the middle two seats.  There's no divider between these two seats,  but if you're not travelling with a person next door, it doesn't feel obtrusive.  The controls here are simple and effective,  and this cupboard stores your headphones, a bottle of water, and the amenity kit.  Tucked away behind are your in-seat power and USB points.  There's a great little storage space here, which is perfect for stuff like your own headphone case,  chargers, and so on.  The seat feels spacious, partly because of the addition of this padded area here,  and also this small section here, which can be raised after takeoff to widen the seat area even more.  This armrest is movable and acts as a storage for your water.  In all important bed mode, the seat easily accommodated my 6-foot 2-inch frame,  and the ability to stow away your TV monitor and tray to either side  means that you're not at all limited when lying down or turning over,  and the foot area does not taper significantly,  so all in all, it was very comfortable.  The linen is supplied in this smart bag, and the duvet is the nicest we've experienced on an aircraft,  when added to the full-length mattress topper, and the lovely pillow,  we were pleasantly surprised by how much we loved this seat.  Cathay has paid for external cameras on its A350,  and this greatly enhances the entertainment value during approach and landing,  especially if you don't have a window seat.  The now essential toilet tour reveals this novel feature, a Lou with a view.  Yep, there's a window.  Service in-flight continue to be quick and efficient,  with crew answering the call button almost instantly.  We had to sample the famous Cathay snack burger,  which is available at any time, apparently, during the flight.  And as I demonstrate here, you can see why it's so well regarded.  It was absolutely delicious.  There is also a tray of snacks for you to help yourself to during the flight,  so we did.  The cabin lights were turned on gradually from two hours before landing,  and breakfast service began about 30 minutes later.  We'd been encouraged to pre-order our selections,  so the service was particularly quick and unobtrusive,  which allowed those who still wanted to continue to sleep to do so.  We were offered top-ups of hot drinks,  and the cabin secured a good 20 minutes before landing.  This embarkation at Hong Kong was quick.  We were connecting onto an Airbus 330 flight to Sabu,  which we planned to review in due course.  So we had to pass through transit security.  Whilst beyond Cathay's control, this was not the easiest of processes,  and we were glad that due to an earlier arrival,  our planned 60-minute connection time turned into nearly two hours.  There is no fast track for business class passengers.  We didn't film here,  but the whole area feels like an afterthought,  compared to the rest of Hong Kong airport,  which after all is only 25 years old.  So one of the acid tests of an airline is whether you look forward to flying with them again.  And whilst we are having a fantastic time in the Philippines for once,  I am actually looking forward to the 14-hour flight back home with Cathay Pacific.  So as far as we're concerned,  any rumours about Cathay's performance dropping since COVID are very wide of the mark.  Even despite the older seat design,  we still found it incredibly roomy and very comfortable,  and the service was absolutely top-notch.  So whilst the food is probably not memorable and perhaps not quite up to the standards of Eti Had and Cathay,  it certainly stood up to the likes of British Airways.  So I hope very much that you've enjoyed this.  Thanks very much for watching,  and look out for the other airline reviews on our channel,  and we'll see you again soon.

reviews.transcript_full: Have you ever heard of a first class service where a Porsche takes you right to the aircraft and you can even enjoy a bath before your flight? Today you're coming along for a ride in the fantastic Lufansza first class from Frankfurt in Germany to Tokyo Haneda in Japan. What's up guys? This is DDN. First class passengers can use the dedicated check-in counter at Frankfurt airport terminal 1. You can check in here but should use the separate first class terminal for the full service. I walked about 5 minutes outside the terminal to reach [music] the first class terminal. The first class check-in lounge is located on the second floor. There was no separate drink service as it connects directly to the lounge, but there were spacious sofas and Bang and Olivesson speakers. I had little time to sit because staff quickly handled everything from printing tickets to checking bags. I entered the lounge fast thanks to them. Security screening takes place at the lounge entrance. It is unique that staff take your passport and return it right before boarding. The lounge inside is modestly sized. At first glance, it feels like a welldecorated business lounge. However, the Lufansza firstass lounge has three unique advantages. First, dining service starts before boarding. You might think first class dining is common, but this is special. While waiting for food, you receive the unique Lufansza first class ticket and rubber duck. The ticket comes in a paper case. It is very practical with a hole cut out for the barcode. They also give you a cute rubber duck. The design and color change periodically, [music] and I received a unique one with a white body and blue beak. The [music] lounge dining menu ranges from simple egg dishes to steaks. I ordered tuna tatakei salad and Australian Wagyu. The food was better than expected despite low expectations for German cuisine. I enjoyed it with a glass of lauron perier champagne. Besides the single menu, the buffet offers various cheeses, desserts, hams, and salads. I give the lounge dining service a very high rating. Second, private rooms and bathrooms are available to all lounge guests. The two private rooms operate on a first come, first served basis, so use them when empty. The space is cozy like a hotel room. From [music] the provided water to the German Verther's original caramels, the details are impressive. Private rooms alone are common in other first class lounges, so they might not have a huge impact. At the very back of the Lufansza first class lounge, there is a bathroom with a separate bathtub in addition to the standard shower rooms. Since there are surprisingly many guests in the lounge, you should book quickly if you plan to use the bathtub. Like a hotel bathroom, it provides robes, bath salts, various toiletries, and balain amenities. I wondered if bathing before a flight was necessary, but it felt great. I felt relaxed enough to fall asleep immediately upon boarding. I think the duck souvenir was meant for playing in this bathtub. It was a special service unique to the Lufanza first class lounge. Finally, the strongest point, the Porsche chauffeur service seen in the thumbnail. Each first class passenger has a dedicated staff member who finds you when it is time to board. Following their guidance down the elevator, you receive the Porsche service from the lounge to your plane. I realized I hadn't gone through immigration yet. A separate immigration process for first class passengers takes place here. I also received my passport back, [music] which they had kept earlier when I did check-in. You must wait inside and cannot go out until your vehicle arrives. This area has casual tables and chairs with nice touches like popcorn and ice cream. Finally, my Porsche has arrived. Unbelievable. Riding a Porsche to the plane is such a special experience. Not all chauffeur services use Porsches. [music] Sometimes Mercedes vans are provided. I was lucky to ride a Porsche Cayenne to the aircraft. I thought I would ride alone, but I shared it with another passenger. From then on, it was a sequence of thrilling scenes for any aviation geek. It was an honor to see various Lufansza aircraft parked at the airport up close. I wondered when else in my life I would ever travel to an aircraft in a private vehicle. The B747-8 I am boarding today, registration D- A B YQ has appeared. While other passengers were waiting in line, the Porsche drove up and stopped right next to the aircraft. Uniquely, Lufansza aircraft are nicknamed after German regions or cities. The aircraft I am boarding today is nicknamed after Germany's northernmost state, Schlesvig Holstein. I took a commemorative photo before boarding and headed up the stairs into the plane. The B747-8 I am boarding today is the only double- deck commercial aircraft along with the well-known A380. Unlike the A380, it is not a full double-decker. Only the front half has two levels. It is nicknamed the queen of the skies due to its distinct humped nose shape. Lufanza's B7478 has a total of 364 seats across. [music] First, business, premium, economy, and economy. Like Korean Airs B747-8i, Lufansza's first class is located at the very front of the first floor. The seats are uniquely positioned even further forward than the cockpit. Unlike Korean Air which has six first class seats with three on each side, Lufansza has eight seats by adding two in the back. There is a communal table in front of the center seats. Sometimes newspapers, snacks or chocolates are placed here. The seats are over 2 m long, perhaps designed for tall Germans. Sitting down, it is nearly impossible for your feet to reach the ottoman. With four windows assigned per seat, the space is very generous. The first class seat design fits [music] Germany well. Areas passengers touch like the seat and ottoman are gray while the rest is a yellowish beige. It looks like a gray seat nestled within beige walls. [music] The fabric seats are massive, nearly 80 cm wide. There are antenna-like reading lights at the headrest. Leather is used for the armrests which hide the entertainment and seat controls. The opposite side of the seat uses completely different colors. Beyond the colors, the single red rose by the window stands out. This rose is a symbol of Lufansa first class. KLM also uses fresh flowers in the cabin. [music] The front of the seat has a unique design with a monitor mounted in the middle of a narrow glossy white partition. While most first class seats are very enclosed with high walls, Lufansza's first class feels open at both the sides and the front. This is an unusual design compared to the current trend of adding high walls and doors to business class for privacy. You can raise the sidewall using the controller in the armrest, but most of the seat remains open. Because the seats are densely arranged and the structure is open, the lack of privacy feels like a significant drawback. Below the monitor, the ottoman is layered with different tones of dark gray and beige. It serves as a spacious drawer, [music] perfect for storing shoes during the flight. The window side is decorated with light [music] beige leather. Since the seat is nearly 10 years old, the age is somewhat noticeable, but it feels surprisingly well-maintained and clean. Practical storage spaces are placed throughout, and the windows are covered with soundproofing panels, making it the quietest [music] space in the cabin. The table is incredibly large and sturdy, and it was very convenient that it could move all the way from one end of the seat to the other. The floor uses different materials and colors from the aisle to clearly distinguish between private [music] and public space. While I was looking around the seat, the flight attendant brought a welcome drink along with macadamia. I was also given a voucher containing a code for in-flight Wi-Fi. Around the time I finished checking the aircraft type, [music] the plane began push back and prepared for takeoff. While modern aircraft like the A350 or B787 are the current industry trend, there is a heavy charm unique to superlarge aircraft like the B747 or A380. In fact, many B747-8i models are used as private jets for heads of state or royalty, including in Korea and the US. However, since 4ine aircraft like the B747 and A380 [music] are practically discontinued, they will likely be hard to find in about 10 years. The in-flight meal service began as the aircraft passed over Hungary. [music] An amuse bouch of sea bass topped with carrots was served with an apparatif. Two types of champagne were offered. And since I am not a strong drinker, I ordered the Lauron Perier Alexandra Rosé 2007 vintage because it looked nice. Uniquely, unlike most airlines that take orders early in the flight, Lufansa took meal orders only after serving the amuse bouch. Since it was a flight to Tokyo, I had a choice between Japanese and Western menus. I was craving Japanese food, but I ordered Western since this is a German airline. Both the western and Japanese courses begin with caviar service. I like the detail of serving the lime wrapped in a small cloth to catch the seeds and neutralize any fishy scent. But several elements considered basic to caviar service were missing. To preserve its flavor, caviar, which absorbs metallic smells, is typically served with a mother of pearl spoon. Lufansza is the first airline I've encountered that serves caviar without one. Furthermore, the absence of blinies, Russian pancakes, or biscuits to serve the caviar on left me feeling that the composition was somewhat lacking. On the other hand, I liked how the meals were brought out on a two-tier cart. They paid great attention to the visual details of the cart itself, even including a three tier tray. For appetizers, you can choose from three options served on small plates. Although I usually eat light, I turn into a big eater on planes. So I tried all three. There was venison served with yuzu mayonnaise and asparagus mousse, lobster kung fit with king crab and Italian barata cheese. A salad with Dijon mustard dressing was also served. I didn't have much expectation for the in-flight meals, but everything was surprisingly decent. [music] The Australian Wagyu steak served with bo sauce was tender, juicy, and delicious. They didn't ask for a specific dness when taking the order, but it seemed to be served medium. For dessert, I had cheese. Coffee was served with Belgian noy house chocolates. In fact, there is a separate chocolate menu, and a selection of chocolates is set up on the center table. I was full, of course, but the service felt like the fastest and simplest firstass dining experience I've had. I suppose you could call it a practical Germanstyle meal service. After finishing my meal, I tried to catch up on some work, but I felt cold and requested a blanket. Interestingly, my laptop wouldn't charge because the aircraft voltage was too weak. So, I gave up on editing and decided to sleep. I went to the lavatory to brush my teeth and change into pajamas. Being a firstass lavatory, the toilet lid was covered in leather like a seat, and there was even a window. While not huge, it was stocked with various toiletries, including razors, shaving cream, and facial mist. Most of all, the single red rose in the lavatory was quite romantic. The pajamas were placed on the ottoman when I first boarded, along with slippers and the amenity kit. The dark navy pajamas with a mandarin collar were very soft and comfortable. When I returned after changing, the turndown service was complete. On top of the 180° flat seat, a mattress pad and a thick hotel style duvet were prepared. I used the pillow I received at boarding and got ready to sleep. Breakfast is served as the aircraft enters South Korean airspace. Thinking about the 12-hour layover in Tokyo before catching my flight to Gimpo made me want to grab a parachute and jump out. I woke myself up with some [music] refreshing orange juice. Once again, the food was brought out beautifully on a cart. Bread, cheese, various berries to mix into yogurt and coffee were served. At the time, the Korean Peninsula was experiencing heavy monsoon rains, so the aircraft shook quite a bit, and I failed to get a nice shot of the table setting. The strawberries looked beautiful, but tasted sour. Eggs and bacon were also provided, and the Lufanza specific condiment set was quite pretty as well. While the second meal is usually simple on most airlines, this one felt particularly modest for a first class meal. Let's take a quick look at the in-flight amenities before landing. The first class amenity pouch contains a toothbrush, toothpaste, and skin care products from Augustina Bowder. It also includes socks, an eye mask, a shoe horn, earplugs, a comb, and mints. I wondered what was inside the thin metal tin, and it turned out to be a clever foldable shopping bag. Since there's a lot to carry when disembarking first class, [music] it's great for packing everything up. True to Lufansa's generous reputation with chocolate, each passenger is also given a separate box of chocolates as a gift. As for the headsets, they used to provide bows, [music] but recently they've switched to the AKGN700, the same model used by Korean Air. After looking through the amenities, the final service of hot towels and juice was provided and the 12-hour flight came to an end. When we talk about glamorous first class, we usually think of Middle Eastern, Singaporean, or East Asian airlines. It is true that there are generally fewer expectations for service from Western airlines. However, having actually flown Lufansza first class, the service was excellent and comparable to Middle Eastern carriers. In particular, the ground services provided at the airport, such as check-in, chauffeur service, and lounge service, seem to be top tier compared to any airline in the world. The quality and attention to detail of the cruise service and the provided amenities were also excellent. However, the most crucial elements, the seats and the in-flight meals were quite disappointing. While the seats themselves were spacious and nice, it was very regrettable that they were an open type design with no privacy protection. The dining service, which should be the highlight of the flight, was also lacking compared to first class on other airlines. Fortunately, these drawbacks seem to be well addressed in Allegris. The new first class being installed on Lufansa's A350. The meals were certainly a bit underwhelming, but they weren't entirely bad as there were several nice details throughout the service. Lufansza First Class may not be the best in the world by my standards. However, the premium service, which is rare for a Western airline, and the unique experience of being driven to the aircraft in a Porsche, are truly unrivaled. This was DDN. Thank you.
