reviews.transcript_full: Hey everyone and welcome back to my channel! Today, I'm flying Starlux Airlines business class from Taipei to Los Angeles I've flown Starlux in economy a few times before and I thought their economy experience was incredible, so I'm really excited  to try their business class product today The business class experience started with a great first impression at check-in A dedicated staff member on the floor proactively grabbed my luggage to place it on the conveyor belt for me This was a premium touch I've never experienced when checking in for business class before After a smooth check-in, I headed to Starlux's GALACTIC lounge in terminal 2 The welcome was incredible Upon handing my lounge pass to the agent, he personally walked me into the lounge, helped me with my carry-on at the lockers, and gave me a thorough introduction to the layout of the space The lounge is spread across two floors with seating areas and bathrooms on both levels The two shower suites are located downstairs, while the luggage lockers are exclusively upstairs Both floors feature the same buffet spread, but you'll find certain items like some desserts and the hot dogs, only on the upper level If you're looking for a dessert recommendation, there was a pudding from LOOL that was a total standout I'm not usually a pudding fan, but the combination of its incredibly soft texture and rich, deep flavor made it probably the best I've ever had As for the hot dogs, the flavor was actually great, but interestingly there were no buns to eat them with In addition to the buffet, you can access a full made-to-order menu via a QR code at every table I highly recommend the items under the "Star Rated Cuisine" section of the made-to-order menu One thing I really appreciated was the portion sizes They were small enough to give you a full sense of the flavors without being so large that they felt overwhelming to finish  It allowed me to try several different dishes, which is exactly how I like to eat in a lounge I particularly love the Biang Biang Noodles They were wide and chewy with a nice kick of spice that wasn't overwhelming I actually ordered them twice since they were so good The futuristic aesthetic of the lounge continues into the shower suites, which feature the same gray metals and bright yellow accents The setup here is consistent with what you'd expect from a premium lounge The showers are stocked with THANN Eden Breeze shampoo, conditioner, and body wash However, I did notice slippers aren't provided and the towels aren't wrapped in plastic, but these are minor details in an otherwise well-designed space The shower queuing process is quite manual You have to hand your boarding pass to the front desk And they'll ask you where you'll be sitting and tell you they'll come find you when it's your turn Because there are only two shower suites, I'd recommend putting your name in as soon as you arrive In my experience, you may need to be a bit proactive I think a staff shift change happened while I was waiting for the showers and my request seemingly got lost in the shuffle, so I had to follow up myself to get access It's a great space to freshen up, just be sure to check back in with the desk if you've been waiting for a while Soon it was time to head to the gate Since the lounge is located near the D gates and my flight was departing from the B gates, it was a solid 20-minute trek I'm a fast walker, and even I found it to be a pretty long walk, so definitely budget enough time to get there Business class passengers are in Zone 1, so you're among the first to board Today's aircraft is an A350-900 The cabin features 26 business class seats in a 1-2-1 configuration When I was booking my flight, the Starlux website actually flagged that rows 3 and 7 have partially obstructed window views I really appreciated that transparency, and since the other window seats in rows 2 through 5 were already taken, I opted for seat 6K Waiting at my seat was a plush pillow and blanket, along with a pair of slippers and the Starlux amenity kit Once I was settled in, a flight attendant gave me an incredibly detailed seat tour The entertainment screen is impressive I measured it at about three-and-a-half iPhones wide by two-and-a-quarter iPhones tall There is a digital panel for seat and lighting adjustments, as well as physical "quick buttons" for immediate shortcuts into takeoff or sleep positions For storage, there's a deep side cabinet that houses the handheld remote and universal outlets It also features a wireless charging pad, though I couldn't get it to work despite trying several different placements The cabinet comes stocked with a bottle of Acqua Panna, noise-canceling headphones, and a Onelux facial mask Rounding out the space, there's a lamp at the seat， an additional side compartment for smaller items, as well as a coat hanger by the seat entrance The seat also has a sliding door that was easy to operate and made the space feel private Before takeoff, the crew came by to offer pajamas and asked which size I wanted These pajamas are the new 2026 pajamas that are a part of a collaboration with Paul Smith and replace the old version As we begin to prepare for takeoff, I buckled the over-the-shoulder belt that is required for takeoff and landing Dinner service started soon after we were in the air I'll flip through the menu and wine list quickly here, but feel free to pause if you want to see the full selection I pre-ordered my meals online, which is a service available when managing your trip on the Starlux website from 21 days up to 24 hours before departure It's definitely worth checking out the site because they often have online exclusive dishes that aren't on the regular in-flight menu I chose the Taiwanese menu by YuenJi, a Michelin one star restaurant in Taichung, Taiwan The tea smoked pork and the pumpkin flavored stir fried rice noodles were delicious It was a sophisticatedly and balanced, light meal However, the service tempo felt rushed My main course arrived while I was still working on my starters Having both courses on the table at once created this awkward pressure to choose between finishing my starter or eating the main while it was still hot, which took away from the relaxed, paced dining experience you'd expect During the dinner service, I also tried the boba latte While it wasn't the best boba I've had, it was my first time having it on a plane, and I thought it was a fun, unique offering from Starlux After dinner, the crew came by to ask if I wanted the mattress pad put on my seat I checked out the amenity kit It included a small pouch with products by THREE, including a balancing stem moisturizer, a balancing overnight oil serum sq, and a balancing protective lip bar There was also a dental kit, a comb, earplugs, an eye mask, and socks The lavatory is well-designed, featuring a main mirror with a magnifying section and a waist-down side mirror I also like that they automated the experience: the toilet button is sensor-activated, so you never actually have to touch it They also provide toothpicks, mouthwash, and fabric hand towels Even though they were wrapped in plastic, having actual towels in the restroom is a nice premium touch that I just don't see in other business class cabins It's something I've only ever seen before in ANA first class I changed into the new 2026 Starlux pajamas, which are a collaboration with Paul Smith They were comfortable I actually found them to be a bit more comfortable than the pajamas I had in ANA first class I've heard a lot about the legendary reputation of the previous version of Starlux pajamas, so I'm curious if this new version lives up to that standard For those of you who have tried both the old and new sets, which one do you like better? Let me know in the comments what your experience was Returning to my seat, I prepared for bed I'm 183 centimeters, or six feet tall, and in the full lie-flat position, the legroom was ample The armrest is also adjustable with three different settings: the standard position, a higher position for lounging, and a lower setting that levels with the lie-flat seat Putting it in that lowest position gives you a bit of extra width for sleeping I also tried the seat's Zero-G function, which shifts the chair into a dentist-chair like position and is supposed to trigger a relaxing pulsation on your back However, when I first set it to Zero-G mode, I couldn't feel the sensation at all I even set the pulsation intensity to the highest level using the digital control panel, but even then, the movement was barely noticeable so definitely don't expect a full massage feature here I'll be honest, I didn't sleep well on this flight The cabin air was a bit warm, which made my throat feel dry and the blanket, while comfortable, was a bit too warm for the environment Also, if you're a light sleeper, I'd definitely recommend using the earplugs from the amenity kit or the noise-canceling headphones From row 6, the operational noise and talking from the galley between business class and premium economy were quite noticeable Since I couldn't sleep, I spent some time exploring the in-flight entertainment The library is massive, with a wide range of English-language films, TV shows, and music alongside plenty of Mandarin, Korean, and Japanese content They even had Angry Birds in the game section It's been a long time since I've played that so it was a fun throwback A feature I really like is the heart icon, which lets you favorite movies, TV shows, and music and quickly access them from the menu bar The flight map is also fantastic If you zoom into a city, it displays points of interest complete with pictures They also have a new "live discovery" feed at the  bottom-left hand side of the screen that suggest landmarks and locations related to your destination, which is a great way to get excited about the journey The remote is actually quite unique It has a clean design without too many buttons and features a trackpad area to control a cursor on the screen I love that the remote displays the remaining flight time and has dedicated buttons for quick volume adjustments However, while the trackpad is an interesting innovation, it felt less efficient for navigating the interface than traditional directional left, right, up, down buttons would have been Since the screen was easily within arm's reach and very responsive, I found it much faster to just touch the screen directly I also tested the free business class WiFi To get connected, you just enter your email, last name, and birthday Unlike economy, which is usually limited to texting, the Starlux business class experience included full web browsing While it was a nice option to have, the speeds were very slow If you get hungry in the middle of the night, the crew comes around with snack baskets filled with items like cereal sticks, dried mangoes, chocolate, and rice crackers There is also a snacks menu you can order from I decided to try the Lion's Mane Filet Burger One thing to keep in mind is that even though this is on the "snacks" menu, the burger is actually quite large, so plan your appetite accordingly I feel like there was just too much bun for the size of the patty, but the plant-based patty itself was actually quite interesting I also ordered the peach sparkling drink which was a refreshing and great non-alcoholic option About 90 minutes before landing, the breakfast service began Being a big fan of wagyu, I had pre ordered the wagyu burger for breakfast While the flavors were great, it was a heavy choice for a morning meal In the future I'd likely opt for the lighter congee set that was offered for breakfast from the Asian menu The real highlight, however, was the bread basket which featured a fresh croissant, almond oatmeal honey bread, and a yogurt banana scone They felt like they came straight out of the oven and had this soft, almost cloud-like texture Even the scone, which I thought would be hard, was surprisingly soft and light We finished the service with fresh fruit, and I also ordered the hojicha latte Since I already had the boba latte earlier, I was glad I got to try the other signature drink now I really appreciated the nutty aroma of the hojicha latte, though both the boba and the hojicha lattes were a bit watery Soon, we were preparing for descent and the cabin crew came by with a tray of various candies I appreciated this thoughtful touch and grabbed one of each flavor So, what's the final verdict on Starlux's business class First, in terms of the hard product, there is no denying that this business class cabin can easily compete with some of the best in the industry Everything feels brand new and sleek, and you can tell that they put a lot of thought into the aesthetic However, I did find some of the tech choices to be a bit superfluous For example, the seat's Zero-G has a pulsation function that was barely noticeable even at its strongest setting It didn't really contribute to or detract from my comfort Similarly, the trackpad remote was less functional than traditional directional left, right, up, down buttons would have been, especially since it was often easier to just use the responsive screen within reach While these features were certainly novel, they felt more like bells and whistles As for the soft product, my first impressions were incredible From the seamless check-in to the lounge experience and the initial welcome on board,  the level of proactive, attentive service made this feel like a first class experience on a business class ticket However, during the flight I noticed a consistency gap I interacted with 6 or 7 different crew members, which felt high for a cabin that wasn't even half full I wonder if they were using this mid-week flight for crew training With so many hands involved, this service lost a sense of consistency Onboard, the flight attendants I interacted with most were truly exceptional: attentive and personable in a way that felt very premium But when you receive  such a world-class level of warmth from one person, the transition to a colleague following a more standard, functional service flow becomes very apparent It wasn't that the other staff were lacking, but rather that the  elevated standard wasn't a consistent thread across the entire team Starlux already has a world-class hard product, but I think they're still polishing the gold to reach that final layer of seamless, end-to-end consistency found on legends like ANA or Cathay Pacific Once they do, Starlux clearly has the ceiling to be the best in the sky For those interested, this flight cost 75,000 Alaska Airlines points and $46.63 USD in taxes and fees If you enjoyed the video today, please hit the like button and the subscribe button I really appreciate your support as it really helps the channel and I'll see you in the next video

reviews.transcript_full: American Airlines screwed itself over big time. This isn't exactly rare in the aviation industry, Allegress. [clears throat] But in the world's most profitable and busy airline market, the US, that is especially painful. You see, 10 years ago, the US airline industry looked vastly different to what it does today. Back then, American Airlines had just gulped up US Airways, creating the largest airline in the world. They were profitable, and most importantly, not noticeably lower quality than their competitors. By contrast, United in the process of merging with Continental, was in a rather weak position. In 2017, former CEO Doug Parker famously declared that American Airlines would quote, "Never lose money again." As he said that, the industry had started to diverge. Two separate strategies were taking hold. On the one hand, Delta had decided to invest in its passenger experience. That entailed two major investments that American was not willing to make. investing in their on-time performance and providing modern interiors with seatback TVs for all passengers. American, on the other hand, decided that their network was their USB. They'd be the airline that could get you anywhere in the US with one stop. Unlike Delta, they actively decided to remove seatback TVs, believing that the future would be BYOD, allowing them to cut costs and optimize efficiency. Fast forward to 2020. The world shuts down and the US airlines face their biggest crisis since 9/11. So what does each airline decide to do? American, focused on domestic flying, retires all their 757s, 767s, and A330s. Delta, focused on premium brand perception, is also not entirely focused on long haul and retires their newly reconfigured trip 7s. A move that also seems like a mistake in hindsight. United however looking at Delta is set on becoming premium and realizes unlike Delta and American that longhaul is the key to appealing to premium travelers flying to Polarmo is more appealing from a marketing perspective than flying to say garden city Kansas so they do not retire a single longhaul aircraft as we all know post pandemic international travel has been all the rage and the trend has not slowed down despite economic and social instability which airline made all the wrong strategic moves by not only cutting longhaul flying but also going less premium. American Airlines and unfortunately undoing mistakes takes a long time in this industry. That brings us to the Airbus A321 XLR, the longest range, most capable single aisle aircraft in the world. I cannot think of another airline for which this aircraft is more important than American Airlines. American Airlines now has a shot at redemption. In the next 2 years, American will take delivery of 50 A321 XLRs, enabling flights between most of Europe and the US Northeast and from Miami to deep in South America. Given that they have hubs in New York, Philadelphia, and Charlotte for European flights, and Miami for South America, these aircraft will finally allow American to expand its reach globally in a way they haven't been able to since their pandemic retirement. Keep in mind that so far Delta has not even ordered the A321 XLR. So, could this aircraft allow American to out compete Delta in terms of network? Not only that, but the aircraft seems to offer a pretty impressive passenger experience. Something that until recently hasn't been a concept I'd associate with American Airlines. I'm Dan, a professional airline critic who has flown over 200 different premium products in the close to 12 years that I've been reviewing airlines. Come along today as we fly American's brand new A321 XLR, only the second one in their fleet from New York to Los Angeles to experience American Airlines game changer firsthand. As fun as it is to have some snow, it's going to be nice to get some heat as we fly down to LA. We're traveling carry-on only today as part of a round the world trip. So, we pass checkin and head straight for the premium security line, which is much appreciated. Once through, we head to the Greenwich Lounge, which is one [music] of three premium lounges co-operated by American and BA at JFK's [music] Terminal 8. I've praised this lounge before and I'll say it again. This is a really nice space. And I surprise and hear is that the lounge manager came up to me and said, "Sir, I see you're filming." I love the seat finishes. This is a very similar seat to JetBlue Mint. In fact, it's basically the same. But if I'm not mistaken, given that it was about 15 months since I flew JetBlue last, this is just way more private. This is frankly one of the most private business class seats I have ever flown. You cannot see anyone else. I can see the feet of the person across from me, but that's it. There might as well not be anyone else on this aircraft, especially here in the last row. It just feels so nice. So, with that, let's go back to before takeoff when we had much better lighting so I can show you around. Looking straight ahead, obviously, we have our entertainment screen which comes out and can be angled down or up to suit your position. A rare feature in business class actually. Below that is our footrest, which will mainly be of use in bed mode, and to the side of that, our exit. To the right, our storage area houses a headphone hook, a moody light/drink tray. Our charging, which includes a 60W USBC port, a remote, and a pop out mirror. Below that, our seat controls that are beautifully placed with no risk of accidentally being hit. On my left, I've got my tray table latched onto the wall, and I love the fake marble finish. Then, finally, I've [music] got my soft, comfy seat. There are movable armrests on both sides of it. And on the left, I've also got a wireless phone charging surface, which works unusually well. Also, a water bottle and a handy closable storage bin. This seat really maximizes space, but manages to still feel roomy. We also have a door, which would honestly make this one of the most private business class seats in the sky. [music] But unfortunately, it hasn't been cleared by the FAA, so for now it's unusable, a problem that's becoming increasingly common in the industry. Overall, I wouldn't say we need it in this seat. reviews.transcript_full: As of early February 2026, Bombardier, sorry Airbus, has delivered just over 480 A220s,  out of close to 1000 currently ordered. Now, it's hard to find exact figures for any given date,  but it's currently estimated that between 80-90 of these are grounded. That's just under 20%  of the global fleet. Why? Well, it's not because the plane itself is particularly faulty, no.  It all has to do with the engines. This week, we're going to dive deep into the story of the  Pratt and Whitney Gear Turbofan engine. A brilliant piece of engineering, decades in the making,  that has also become the catalyst for one of the worst engine crises in modern aviation.  The airline we're flying here from Paris to Zurich is air-boltec. Well, it's complicated,  but we'll get to that in a minute. Now, apart from this flight being massively delayed,  we've got a change of pace. And me generally being confused by Charles de Gaulle's Terminal 1,  this escalator goes over a hump. Air-boltec is a particularly interesting airline because they went  all in on the A220. They've built their entire fleet around this one plane, and are now living  with the consequences of that bet. We'll get back to Air-boltec later in the video, but first,  let's understand what's going on here with these engines.  Let's start with being precise about what we mean by grounded here. I don't mean temporarily  out of service for a scheduled check. I mean perfectly good aircraft sitting in long-term storage,  four months, or even a year waiting for one thing, an engine, or at least engine parts from Pratt  and Whitney. So what is going wrong here and why does it hit the A220 especially hard?  The A220 only has one engine option, the PW 1500G. Part of the Pratt and Whitney  geared turbofan family of engines that also powers a big chunk of the A320 Neo-fleet. But the  crucial difference here is that the A320 Neo has two engine choices, and only around 43% of them  are fitted with that Pratt and Whitney option. So when these engine problems ground aircraft,  the overall impact on the global A320 Neo-fleet stays manageable. Air lines with that other option,  the CFM leap engines carry on unaffected. But the A220 doesn't get that luxury. If your PW 1500G  is down, the aircraft is down with it. It's worth mentioning Embraer's EJET E2 here. They also  exclusively use Pratt and Whitney geared turbofans and have faced similar, if not quite as extreme  groundings. But I'm flying on an A220 here, so let's focus on that. Before we dive directly into  the problems, it's worth touching on what Pratt and Whitney has actually achieved here, because the  geared turbofan isn't just an incremental improvement. It's a bit of a step change in JET engine  technology. Let's start with a super quick, overly simplified JET engine explainer here.  Turbofan JET engines have two main sections. There's a big fan at the front that shoves a ton of  cool air backwards at reasonable speeds. And then there's the engine's core, the turbine.  This is the bit that burns the fuel and makes everything spin. It does also shove air backwards,  but it's doing it a lot quicker and with a lot more heat. Now this is where we get to bypass ratios.  This is the split of how much air flows around that core turbine versus how much goes through it.  A bypass ratio of 10 to 1 means that for every one part of air that goes through the core,  10 parts get pushed around the outside by the fan. If we go back to the 60s, this concept  barely existed. Early JET engines were turbo Jets, not turbo fans. They had a bypass ratio of zero,  but modern engines chase higher and higher bypass ratios. Because in subsonic flight,  this is the most efficient way to generate thrust. You don't want a JET that throws a small  amount of air backwards at a ridiculous speed. You want a JET that pushes a huge amount of air  backwards a little quicker. This gives you the same amount of thrust for less energy,  less noise, and overall better fuel economy. So on a modern airliner, the fan is the thing that  generates the majority of the thrust. And that core turbine is the engine that powers the fan.  Mostly, this is overly simplistic. The problem with classic turbo fan engine design is that the  fan at the front is directly coupled to that center turbine. But the fan and the turbine want to  operate at completely different speeds. The fan wants to spin relatively slowly, whilst the  turbine wants to spin fast. So for decades, engine designers just split the difference.  The big fan at the front spins faster than it wants to, and the turbine that drives everything  spins slower than it wants to. And they just accepted that they were leaving performance on the  table. Now, the obvious solution here is to put a gearbox between the two sections. Let them spin  at different speeds. Problem solved. Engineers obviously knew this decades ago.  The first gear turbo fan to actually fly was the turbo maker Aspen, way back in 1952.  It powered a French test aircraft called the Fouga Gemot. The concept worked. Through the 60s  and the 70s gear turbo fans appeared in smaller applications. The Garrett TFE 731 became one of the  most successful business jet engines ever built. Over 11,000 were produced. They've been flying  for over 100 million flight hours. And we also have the likeoming ALF 502. Another gear turbo fan  that's been powering the BAE 146 since the 80s. This one was particularly famous for being whisper  quiet. But these were smaller engines. Around the 7,000 pounds of thrust mark. The A220 needs around 24,000  pounds of thrust. And the A321 Neo needs upwards of 33,000 pounds. Scaling up a gearbox to handle  that kind of power was the problem. In the mid 1980s, Pratt and Whitney and Rolls Royce actually  tried. They worked together in a consortium called IAE. They attempted to build a large  geared turbo fan for the Airbus A340. It was called the Superfan. This Superfan promised bypass  ratios of 18 to 1 or even 21. And a 15 to 20% reduction in fuel consumption. Airbus made it  the launch engine option. The dancer in North West signed up. But then the program collapsed.  In large part due to the gearbox simply not being able to handle the power. The whole thing was  cancelled in April of 1987. Airbus had to redesign the A340 and switched to more conventional engines.  This was probably the thing that doomed the whole A340 program. But I covered that more in my A340  video. I'll link that up above or down below. The lesson the wider industry learnt here was the  geared turbo fans at airliner scale just didn't work. They were too complex and too risky.  But Pratt and Whitney didn't give up. After the Superfan died, a small team quietly kept working  on the gearbox technology. Over roughly three decades, they invested somewhere north of $10  billion in geared turbo fan development. And the result was this geared turbo fan family of engines  we see causing problems today. The big engineering challenge here is creating a gearbox that can  continuously transmit around 30,000 horsepower for tens of thousands of hours in an environment  with extreme temperatures, vibrations and G forces. And it has to be light enough that the weight  penalty doesn't eat away at the efficiency gains. Their solution here was a planetary reduction  gearbox. What they call the fan drive gear system. I won't bore you with the details, but the  result is a 3-to-1 speed reduction. The turbine spins at around 9,000 RPM while the fan spins  at around 3,000 RPM. Each component near its optimum speed. The performance gains here were  significant. The bypass ratio jumped to 12-1, doubled the previous generation and it achieves  in the region of a 16% reduction in fuel burn. It is truly an engineering marvel. Well, kind of.  Other modern turbo fans like the CFM Leap, the other option on the A320 Neo and the only option  on the 737 MAX also achieves similar performance gains without a gearbox. They instead mostly focused  on the turbine design side of things to increase efficiency. But either way, if we put all of that to  the side, what is the problem Pratt and Whitney are having today? Surely it has to be this gearbox,  right? This was the impossible part. No. Across millions of flight hours, the gearbox has been  essentially flawless. The revolutionary part of the engine works pretty much perfectly. The  problems came from somewhere else entirely. When the Pratt and Whitney gear turbofan first ended  service in 2016, it had multiple durability and reliability issues. By July of 2017, 46% of  gear turbofan powered A320 Neo's had been out of service for at least one week. For comparison,  the other engine option, the Leap was at just 9%. But these were solvable problems that just  required new seals, revised liners and software updates. By 2020, Dispatch reliability had climbed  up to 99.98%. The teething phase seemed over. But then came the real crisis. In March of 2020,  a Vietnam Airlines A321 CEO suffered an uncontained turbine disc failure during takeoff in Ho Chi Minh City.  A chunk of the high pressure turbine disc flew out of the engine. Luckily, it missed the fuselage.  That aircraft was powered by a V-2500. An older conventional engine, not a gear turbofan.  But the investigation into that failure would eventually expose a problem that affected both  engine families. Because while the V-2500 and the gear turbofan are very different engines,  some of their most critical components come from the same manufacturing process,  occurring at the same pattern Whitney-owned plant. And that plant had a problem. To understand  what went wrong, we need to touch on how you actually make these parts.  Let's just imagine that you need to manufacture a turbine disc. A critical rotating component  that's going to spin at 9000 RPM in 1000 degree heat for tens of thousands of hours. Normal  metals can't survive that. So these components are made from nickel-based super-alloys.  Metals specifically engineer to maintain their strength at extreme temperatures where steel  or aluminium would soften and fail. But having the right alloy is only half the battle.  How you form that metal into a disc matters just as much. I guess to be clear here,  whatever method you use, the part will eventually be precision machined into its final shape.  But it's the way you create the raw material that makes all the difference.  The classic method is forging. You start with a solid block of the super alloy,  you heat it up, and you smash it into shape under enormous pressure. Think of it like shaping hot  clay. This is good because it makes the metal's internal grain structure line up in a strong way.  Similar to how wood grain makes timber stronger in one direction. But it also means the metal isn't  perfectly uniform throughout. Maybe one spot has a tiny floor or one area is slightly different  from another because of how that original block was made. Those tiny inconsistencies can become  weak points later on. But then we've got powder metallurgy, the more sophisticated approach.  Instead of starting with one big block, you atomize the super alloy into a fine powder,  like super fine sand. Then you put that powder in a mold, press it into shape,  and then subject it to extreme heat until it fuses into a single solid piece. When done properly,  the advantage is remarkable. The finished piece has uniform properties throughout,  and every part has identical material properties. So you've got no weak spots or variations.  At least that's the theory. At a Pratt and Whitney facility in Clayville, New York,  microscopic particles had contaminated the powdered metal between late 2015 and mid-2021.  Nearly six years of production. These particles became stress concentrators. Tiny floors buried  inside the metal that act as crack initiation sites. And this is where powder metallurgy's  greatest strength becomes its greatest weakness. With traditional forging, floors tend to work  their way to the surface, where they can be spotted during inspection. But because powdered  metallurgy fuses all of these tiny particles together, contaminants get locked deep inside  the finished part. And conventional inspection techniques, like ultrasonic inspection,  are only really effective at catching surface and near surface defects. Not microscopic floors  buried deep in the interior. So we've got contaminated parts,  entering service with defects that nobody can see. And these are slowly growing under the stress  of every flight cycle. Now Pratt and Whitney had become aware of this after the investigation  into that Vietnam Airlines incident in 2020. This clearly took some time because the contamination  only stopped in mid-2021. But by mid-2022, the FAA had issued an airworthiness directive that  essentially said, for engines manufactured in this period, there's a risk of high pressure  turbine failure. And this risk was considered at this point manageable. The affected parts needed  to be inspected, but those inspections could happen at the next routine shop visit. But on  Christmas Eve, the 24th of December 2022, a Viva Airbus A320 Neo in Guadalajara suffered a  rotor separation during takeoff. This time, it was a geared turbofan engine. And that's when  Pratt and Whitney realized the scope of the problem. Roughly 3000 engines, 93% of the operational  fleet at the time, contained components from the contamination window. The regulatory response  flipped from the maintenance approach of inspect at the next scheduled visit to control the risk  right now. The most affected parts had to come off within 100 flight cycles, typically under a  month of flying. These were parts that were meant to run for years and all of a sudden had hard  deadlines. And this is how this whole engine problem becomes a grounded aircraft problem.  Accelerated removals and replacements drain the spare engine pool. Maintenance slots end up  overwhelmed. Turn around times that used to be 60 to 90 days stretch past 250. These planes  need inspections in new parts, but they simply can't get them in any reasonable amount of time,  so they end up in storage. Now, to be clear here, Pratt and Whitney has fully acknowledged the  problem and is working on fixes. There's new inspection protocols, they've expanded the maintenance  capacity and they've worked on durability upgrades. RTX, their parent company, expects total costs  of around 6 to 7 billion dollars from this crisis. Much of it is going directly to affected  airlines as compensation, but money doesn't fix everything. Pratt and Whitney has said that they  expect this all to be fully resolved by the end of the decade. The desperation around all of this has pushed airlines to extreme measures. There's a long and complicated history of the A220 that I won't cover here.  In short, it used to be a bombardier jet and then Airbus bought the program. I covered it all in  this video. They currently operate 52 of them.  And that's it. Nothing else. On paper, this makes a lot of sense. Single type fleets simplify  everything. Training, maintenance, spare parts, cruise scheduling. And the A220's economics were  perfect for their network. Connecting the Baltic capitals with thin, medium-distance routes that  can't fill say a 737. They even found a way to squeeze more value out of their fleet. Starting in 2019,  Air Boltzik began wet leasing spare capacity to the left-hands of group. Lapvia, Estonia, Lithuania,  as seasonal markets. When demand dips in winter, why not lease your planes and crew to someone who  needs them? The idea started small, but got addictive, especially after COVID. Airlines needed  capacity fast and Air Boltzik filled a lot of that gap. Air Boltzik operated 30,000 wet leased flights that year, roughly 39% of their total flights,  and this generated about 20% of their revenue. A single-type fleet perfectly matched  the network with a side business that kept utilization high year-round. Two customers,  passengers buying tickets, and airlines buying capacity. It was a great strategy,  until these engine problems. When the crisis hit, Air Boltzik faced an impossible choice.  They were contractually obliged to operate flights for the left-hands of group. reviews.transcript_full: Today we're up in the north of Scotland to take one of the UK's longest into city trains,  the LNR Highland Cheafedon Service down to London Kings Cross.  So come along with me and let's experience this near 600 mile trip in first class with  complimentary meals, snacks and drinks throughout along with some of the very best train window  views the country has to offer.  The journey starts in Inverness, the most northerly city in the UK and capital of the Scottish  Highlands.  The German settlement here dates back to at least 5,800 BC and nowadays it's home to  around 48,000 people.  The edge of the famous Loch Ness is located just 6 miles to the south west of Inverness  City Centre, making it where most people start their journey to try and find Nessie.  Anyway let's fast forward to the next morning and head to the station to get this epic  trip started.  It's about a 10 minute walk from my hotel and the harsh winters in the far north of Scotland  mean it's around minus 8 degrees here this morning.  Inverness Station has seven platforms and opened way back in 1855 and is the terminus  of the far north line, the Kylavlokhoush line, the Inverness to Aberdeen line and the Highland  main line the latter of which we'll be taking today.  Inside there is a staff ticket office and travel centre along with some automatic ticket  machines and a few shops.  There is also a heated waiting room, free to use toilets and paid luggage lockers.  Our train this morning is the LNER Highland Sheet and Service to London Kings Cross, departing  at 7.55 am.  Let's check out the route.  We head southbound from Inverness making seven stops in the Highlands and Central Scotland  before calling a dead imbra and then crossing into England for seven further stops and  then arriving in London around 4 o'clock this afternoon.  Our train is ready and waiting on platform 1 so let's head over there now.  It is formed of this 9 car LNER Class 800 Azuma by mode train.  These have a top speed of 125 mph on both diesel and electric power.  They have a capacity for 611 passengers across two classes of travel, 510 in standard class  and 101 in first class where we'll be sitting today.  These trains have had a pretty mixed reception since their introduction back in 2019 and  we'll go through the main issues once we get going.  Wheelchair users will need to request the use of a mobile ramp from station or train staff.  Otherwise there is a small step up from platform to train.  Coach M at the front of the train on southbound trips is where you'll find the two first class  wheelchair spaces along with companion seats.  The accessible toilet is in the adjacent vestibule.  Luggage can be stored on the large stacks at the ends of the coaches or on the overhead  racks which run above all seats.  First class is in a 2 plus 1 configuration with a mix of airline style, bay and solo seats  which are particularly good for business travellers.  Wow the lights sure are unnecessarily bright in here.  With Valentine's Day approaching let me tell you a little love story.  It's not about a person but the love I have for travelling by train.  There has always been something so special to me about relaxing into my seat and looking  out the window at the scenery passing by and listening to the sounds of the rails beneath.  Whether it be a snowy trip through the Scottish Highlands like today which evokes memories  of family childhood holidays at Christmas time, we'll m used to have a large gathering  to celebrate the new year with aunts, uncles and cousins from all over the country coming  together.  We would always travel by train and I still remember watching the magical scenery slide  by outside as I wrote Happy New Year on the fogged up window.  Likewise today there's nothing I enjoy more than sipping champagne on a high speed  euro star service on route to Paris to start another one of my epic euro trips.  Nothing beats the romance of a train journey for me.  From planning my destination to good value fair finding to the purchase and delivery of  the e-tickets, train pall has been supporting me every step of my journey and by my side  throughout every trip with an absolutely seamless experience using the train pall app  Zero Hassel.  Click the link in the description below to download the train pall app today.  Start planning your next rail adventure and fall in love with train travel just that little  bit deeper, just like me.  We depart on time at 7.55am.  The route from Invaness to London Kings Cross is scheduled to take us 8,7 minutes of travel  time, covering a distance of 581 miles.  Prices for advance non-flexible tickets start from 120 pounds in first class and from 54  pounds in standard class.  They are all dynamically priced and can be quite a lot more expensive closer to travel  at peak times or on holidays so book as early as you can.  Right after departure the complimentary service begins with orange or apple juice and water.  Orders are then taken for breakfast as we wind our way through the very snowy and even  more barren landscapes as the sun begins to rise.  I went for the full vegetarian which consisted of meat free sausages, a fried egg, spinach,  mushrooms and beans.  It was ok but certainly nothing to write home about.  The Highland mainline connects Invaness and Perth covering 118 miles and broadly following  the route of the A9 trunk road.  There are 8 intermediate stations but we will call it just 3 of them today, Avymor, King  Rossi and Pidlockery.  Ok, time to check out the seats here in first class.  Reservations are displayed on the digital panel above the window.  The seats themselves have an ok shape but they are just very hard with little padding  on the base or back.  There is a slightly winged headrest, a missing head cushion and adjustable armrests.  There is a small recline using this button but only the base slides forward.  The tables are large and sturdy and will easily fit any laptops.  Each passenger has access to 1 UK 3 pin power socket and 1 USB-A port.  The laptops can be found on the back of the seat in front or on the wall next to you.  Lastly, windows are equipped with very good sunblines.  Overall it is not a terrible first class product but it really could be better, especially  the seats.  It is such a beautiful and peaceful morning, even the notoriously bad ride quality on  these trains isn't causing a problem right now due to the maximum speed on the line  being 80 miles per hour until we are south of Perth.  I recently tried out the latest version of the Class 800 series, the East Midlands Railway  Class 810 Aurora, to see if any improvements have been made. The city is home to around 47,000 people and is capital of the county of Perth and Kim  Ross.  The beautiful station building is arguably one of the most ornate in Scotland and dates  back to 1848. We have now been on the go for two hours and are running a few minutes early so I can  hop out to stretch my legs for a moment, but not for long as it is still below freezing  outside. We will soon be coming into the Scottish Capital suburbs and we will be passing by the airport. This Interurban tram system has just a single line and runs for a total of 11.5 miles.  On the way into the city, we pass by Murrayfield, home to the Scottish National Rugby Union  team.  This seats 67,144 people, making it Scotland's largest stadium and the 5th largest in the  UK.  Then on the left is the Haymarket Depot, the main Scotwell Maintenance Facility in the area.  We then call at Haymarket Station where the crew drops a bombshell.  Our train will be terminating at Edinburgh Waverly the next station.  Hopefully we will be coming into one more 18 and this train you will be gearing to  be a one more two.  The plane is here so you will be one of the instant you will be passing.  And in fairness to LNER, that is exactly what happened.  Some rare quick and joined up thinking on UK railways.  And with absolutely no delay at all, we depart Edinburgh Waverly and pass some of the  impressive Scottish Government buildings on the left hand side.  One thing that ultimately did change with our train swap was the onboard catering offerings.  The onboard buffet and at sea ordering service is now open.  Also, LNER have three different menus within their first class service, Delhi, Dish and  Dine, with each train designated with one of these service levels.  Basically, it's just a slightly different menu.  Delhi is the most basic one.  Dine is the best which we had earlier, but now we are on a Dish train.  Around 20 minutes after departure from Edinburgh, the crew swung into action with the lunchtime  meal service as it is now approaching midday.  This time I went for one of the LNER signature hop on board golden ails, a pack of crisps  and a salted caramel dessert pot.  I also ordered the vegetarian risotto which will follow soon.  Before long, we are steaming from the borders region in Scotland into Northumberland in England,  as we parallel the rugged North Sea coast.  Next stop, 400 miles away in that direction, Denmark.  Three miles further south, we crossed the Royal Border Bridge, a grade one listed brick-wireduct  spanning the river tweed below, giving some impressive train window views.  It is 659 metres in length and has 28 arches in total.  Just after barrack upon tweed, my lunch is served.  It is quite a delicious risotto with pearl barley, mushrooms and a roasted shallot on top.  Free Wi-Fi is available for all passengers on board.  This wasn't particularly fast and the signal was weak in rural areas.  However, it was fairly strong throughout most of the journey south of Edinburgh.  The next major calling point for us today is in Newcastle upon Tyne, England's most northernmost city  and home to 320,000 people.  The line converging from the left here forms part of the loop around the city centre  with the other local lines heading off east to Sunderland and west to Cumbria.  You can also change here for Transpenin Express services to Leeds, Manchester and Liverpool,  as well as the Tyne and Weir Metro system for the local area.  Newcastle is situated on the river Tyne, which we cross on departure from the station.  If you look down to the left, you can see five further bridge crossing spanning the river off in the distance.  Here we are passing non-stop through Durham.  Again, off to the left, after the station, you will see the stunning 11th century Durham Cathedral,  a UNESCO World Heritage Site.  On the approach to York, right next to the station is the National Railway Museum.  It's a great place to visit for three or four hours with large static displays of trains  from the UK and around the world, and it's completely free.  York Station is, without doubt, one of my favourites in the country  with its large metal and glass train shed spanning the Sutherland platforms.  I'm not sure I was due a third meal service, but one was offered after Donkaster anyway,  so I grabbed the Coronation Chick-P-Wap, which was also pretty decent.  There were some serious flooding on the river Trent as we're coming up to Newark.  This is one of the main reasons the last remaining flat crossing on the UK Mainline network,  seen here, hasn't been able to have been replaced yet.  We zoom through Newark Northgate Station non-stop and continue south.  I have covered this section of the line in much more detail in my LNER Intercity 225 review  from York to King's Cross, so you can check that out if you want to know more.  Our final intermediate stop today is in Peterborough, the largest city in Cambridge,  with a population of 192,000.  This is the northern terminus of the Temslink London commuter trains,  and most of the lines south of here are quad-tracked to cope with a much increased capacity demands.  When travelling at or close to the maximum line speed of 125 mph,  you can certainly notice the ride quality deteriorate.  There are frequent rattles and bumps which are quite uncomfortable at times.  As we are now fast approaching the end of today's journey,  let me summarise my experience onboard this LNER Highland Cheafed in service from Inverness to London King's Cross.  Overall, I had an enjoyable trip, but there are definitely improvements that could be made.  Eight hours on a train in any situation is a long time,  so I really think they need to address the seat comfort situation in both classes urgently,  and turn the light brightness down,  likewise with the bad ride quality at speed,  although this is an inherent problem with the whole Class 800 series,  not just LNERs, so I don't know what could be done to address this.  It's also very poor that there was no food service available at all for standard class passengers  for the first half of the journey.  However, the other amenities are good, with well-sized tables, power sockets,  and all the accessible facilities you'd expect on a modern train,  well, except-level boarding.  The staff were friendly enough, and the first class service was good.  There was plenty of choice and quantity of food and drinks available.  I also think that the cost is very reasonable if you get an advanced ticket,  although be aware of the very expensive last minute and on the day prices.  Lastly, good job with our train swap in Edinburgh,  being clearly explained on board and not losing us any time.  We actually arrive at London King's Cross a whole 10 minutes early,  at 3.52pm, making the total journey time today, 7 hours and 57 minutes.  Have you been on any long distance UK intercity trains before?  If so, which ones? How did you find them? Let me know in the comments below.  I'm always open to new video ideas,  so if you have something you'd like to see on the channel,  then drop me a DM on Instagram, Blue Sky or Twitter.  Don't forget to subscribe, thanks for watching to the end,  and I'll see you in the next video.  Bye.

Today we're flying on one of the most anticipated 
new cabins, the Aria business class suites from   what many would consider to be one of the most 
highly regarded airlines, Cathay Pacific. Over the   past few years, Cathay has definitely had a bit of a 
rough go of it amongst political tensions in Hong   Kong, being shut down for an extended period of 
time due to 2020, and the struggles with employee   morale. Not to mention that competition with other 
airlines has only grown fiercer over the years.   But with the release of their brand 
new Aria business class suites,   is this Cathy's signal that they are back to take 
their place as the crown jewel of the skies? Let's   find out on today's 11 hour and 35 minute 
flight from Hong Kong to Vancouver, Canada. But first, our trip starts off here at the Hong 
Kong airport terminal 1 at the Cathay Pacific   the Pier Business Class Lounge. Hi. So, let's 
talk about Cathay's lounges a little bit. So,   as a business class customer, you 
do have access to three of Cathay's   lounges here in Hong Kong airport. There is 
The Wing Business, The Bridge, and The Pier   Business where I am right now. For those of 
you who are looking for shower facilities,   keep in mind that only the Pier Business and the 
Bridge have shower facilities. The Wing does not,   and the Wing is also the smallest 
out of the three. So, like I said,   you can access all three if you want. If you 
have the time and you want to lounge hop,   you can definitely do that. Or you could just 
go to the one that's closest to your gate. For   those of you who are interested in seeing 
what the Bridge and the Wing look like, I   did cover them as part of my other video on Cathay 
Pacific when I covered their older business class,   which I will link in the description box below 
for those of you that want to see that. But in   the meantime, let's check out the Pier Business. 
Cathay Pacific's The Pier Business Class Lounge is   located in Terminal 1 by gate 65. It's the 
largest of Cathy's business class lounges   and spans over 3,300 square meters or 35,500 ft. There is a 
buffet with both Western and Asian food options,   a full service bar, and of course, their famous 
noodle bar, which serves an assortment of dim   sum and multiple noodle options. I of course had 
to get a bowl of my favorite, the dan dan noodles. In the meantime, let's check out the shower 
rooms. The shower rooms are stocked with Bamford   soaps and lotions, as well as other amenities 
like dental kits and cotton pads. Although,   you can request additional amenities like 
deodorant and slippers at the front desk as well. And even though the shower rooms are quite small,   I always find them to be clean and 
well-maintained. So, no complaints here. All right, that's it for the lounge. Now,   let's get going to the gate so 
that we can board our flight. Today, we'll be boarding out of gate 23. And 
since our aircraft today doesn't have first class,   we'll get to board in group one as business class 
passengers. Our flight does depart slightly late   today, but eventually we get boarding. I'm just 
thankful that the flight wasn't cancelled. And as   I make my way towards the seat, I didn't notice it 
at the time, but looking back at this footage now,   you'll notice that the guy in front 
of me is stealing random pillows.   Here he is taking one pillow. And then here 
he is taking a second pillow. Not sure what   he plans on doing with these, but I feel bad 
for whoever seats those are. All right, that's   enough about the pillow thief. Our 777-300er 
today has a 1-2-1 configuration in business class.   And we will be seated in seat 16K today. And here 
they finally are, the long awaited Aria suites.   These new seats have a 21 inch or 53 cm width in 
between armrests, although the width does extend   to 25 inches or 63.5 cm at the shoulder area. As 
for row pitch, you'll get 43 inches or 109 cm. Hidden   inside the side table, there's a small storage 
compartment where you can store some small items.   There's also a storage locker where you'll find 
the headphones, a bottle of water, and a mirror   that flips out. And just down below, you'll also 
find another small storage compartment. In terms of   charging outlets, you'll get a USB A port, 
two USB C ports, and a universal power port.   Side table also has wireless charging, although 
it is hard to miss if you don't look closely.   And finally, we have every introvert's favorite 
part, which is the privacy door, making this a   fully enclosed suite. Before takeoff, the crew 
stops by and gives us hot towels for our hands. They also come by with some welcome 
drinks. There was a choice between   orange juice, champagne, and Cathay's 
signature drink, the Cathay Delight,   which is a mint kiwi drink. It's very 
refreshing, and I highly recommend it. Now that we're in the air, let's check out the 
food and beverage menus. We'll start with the   beverage menus first. This was the wine and 
champagne list. And then here's the beer,   spirits, cocktails, and non-alcoholic beverages. 
For food, we have the main menu as well as the   all day menu. And then, of course, the pre-arrival 
meal menu, which is breakfast. There was also an   online exclusive menu which had eight additional 
options for the main meal if you pre-order online   beforehand. The crew then stopped by and dressed my 
table with the tablecloth. I did pre-order one of   the online exclusives. I ordered the steamed 
halibet which was done in collaboration with   Louise, a one-star Michelin restaurant in 
Hong Kong. The halibut arrives and it's served   with chorizo sauce, basque piperade, which is a stewed 
vegetable dish made from tomatoes, onions, garlic,   and esplette peppers. This was so good. You can see 
how easily the fish flakes here. It was cooked   perfectly and it was very flavorful, especially 
with the chorizo sauce and the basque piperade. There's also a slice of bread with butter. 
And I did order a glass of champagne and a   cup of Hong Kong milk tea as well. And 
to end the meal, I did order dessert,   which was also done in collaboration with 
Louise Restaurant. I got the vanilla panna cotta,   which was served with green apple 
compote and shortbread crumbles.   This was creamy and delicious and 
most importantly, not too sweet. After dinner, the crew also stopped 
by and offered some chocolates.   I chose the sesame one, which is 
my favorite. Highly recommend it. All right, now that dinner is done, let's check 
out the amenities and the IFE. Here's what the   amenity kit looks like. It's a leather bag by 
British brand Bamford. Inside the amenity kit,   you'll find an eye mask, lotions, and lip balms, 
and pillow mist from Bamford, a dental kit,   mouthwash, and a pair of earplugs. Oh, and you 
also get a pair of slippers. And this is what   they look like. Now, let's take a look at the 
headphones. They are noise cancelling and I   found them to be pretty good. The IFE does 
have Bluetooth capability as well if you   prefer to use your own though. Now, as for 
the IFE it's a 24 inch 4K touchscreen display,   and there is a remote available if you prefer 
to use that as well. In terms of entertainment,   there are over 4,500 hours of movies, TV shows, 
music, podcast, and games available. They even had   Disney Plus, HBO Max, and Paramount, so there's 
no shortage of entertainment to keep you occupied.   They also have the watch together feature so 
that you can coordinate and watch a movie with   someone else on the flight as well if you want. 
But if you'd rather be a keener and do some   work to make the rest of us look bad, there is 
complimentary Wi-Fi for business class passengers.   For me personally though, the stand out of 
the IFE was of course being able to see the   availability of the lavatories. Green means 
the lavatory is available whereas red means   it's occupied. Brilliant. And speaking of the 
lavatories, let's take a look at them now. There   are three dedicated lavatories for 45 business 
class passengers available, making it a 15 to1   passenger to toilet ratio. In terms of amenities, 
there were Bamford soaps and lotions. And tucked   away in the drawers, there were some antiseptic 
hand gel and antiseptic hand wipes, and there's   also a foot pedal to open the garbage bin lid, 
which we always love to see, of course. Lastly,   there's also a full-length mirror along 
the back wall. Now, before we head out,   let's take a moment of appreciation for these 
custom door locks on the lavatory doors. This   is my first time seeing custom locks like this in 
a lavatory door on an airplane, and they really   give it a premium feel. And just one more thing, 
on your way back from the lavatory, make sure you   check out the small art gallery that they have 
on board, which features art from local artists. All right, now let's finally head back to our 
seats so that we can get it into full liat mode.   Back at our seats, let's get everything set up. 
I slip on the mattress cover and there are seat   controls at the edge of the side table to get 
it into lie flat mode. In fully lie flat mode,   the bed is 79 inches or approximately 200 cm. The bed 
sheets are also by Bamford and they're quite nice.   I did find them to be thick enough to keep me warm 
throughout the flight. Most importantly though,   this is what the footwell space looks like in lie 
flat mode. I do think it's more narrow compared   to their older cabins, but I personally didn't 
have any issues with foot space. I am quite short   though at 5"3' or 160 cm, so taller people, you 
might have more difficulties. Overall, I found the   bed to be very comfortable. And once you get the 
door closed, it felt very private as well. I even   managed to get a couple hours of sleep. And after 
a nice little nap, let's check out the all day   menu. I decided to order two classics. The first 
was the shrimp and pork dumpling noodle soup.   The noodle soup was warm and delicious, and the 
pork and shrimp dumplings were thick and juicy.   You can never go wrong with this one. Second 
thing that I ordered was an egg tart or a dan tat   in Cantonese. This is always a must order for me 
whenever I fly with Cathay. All right, now before we   get to the pre-arrival meal, let's talk about how 
much all this cost. So, let's talk about how much   all this cost. So, I did use points for this and 
I used British Airways Avios. And one way between   Hong Kong and Vancouver was 92,750 British Airways 
Avios plus $181.90 Canadian in taxes and fees. But   at the time when I booked this, there was a 30% 
transfer bonus between Amex and British Airways   Avios. So, I got 30% of those points back. So, 
it was basically like I paid just under 65,000   British Airways Avios. I also had the option of 
using Asia Miles. I could have booked this using   88,000 Asia Miles, but since British Airways 
Avios and AMex had the transfer bonus, I decided   to go with British Airways Avios instead. Before 
the pre-arrival meal, we're given a hot towel   for our hands and the trade table gets dressed 
with a tablecloth. I went for the Chinese   breakfast, which was congee with chicken and oats 
and stir-fried rice vermicelli with vegetables and   soy sauce. The congee was great, but the vermicelli 
noodles were kind of boring and flavorless. And as we start to make our descent into 
Vancouver, let's talk about Cathay Pacific   for a little bit. Overall, I think Cathay 
has done a great job with these new cabins.   My one small criticism is that the footwell 
space is smaller compared to the older cabin.   But otherwise, these new seats are much more 
modern looking, comfortable in bed mode,   and the IFE is fantastic. But let me know 
what you think about Cathay Pacific's new   Aria business class suites. Are they enough 
to put them ahead of the competition, or would   you rather still fly on other Asian carriers like 
Singapore Airlines, EVA, ANA, and Japan Airlines?   As always though, thank you for joining me on 
board today. And if you've enjoyed the video,   please do like and subscribe so 
that we can fly together again soon.

yt_comments.author: @markjones2781
yt_comments.text: Hmm, The showers at the CX Pier Lounge are dark and tiny (I'm 190cm tall and fairly lean at 90kg). Moving about or even taking off your shoes is a challenge. The clammy humid air is suffocating. The showers at Changi are much better! As for the Aria Suite itself, despite its Instagram wow factor, it has many down sides. The IFE screen is just too damn big. It's like sitting in the front row of a cinema. The leg space/cubby hole is cramped and you can't swing the IFE screen out of the way like in the old cabin. Just what is the point of storages spaces so small you can't drop a handbag or whatever into? The wireless charging spot doesn't work in the real world of a moving/vibrating plane. There is no reading light! For those of us who still read books this is a tragedy. Finally, the door offers little privacy from people or crew walking up and down the isle and yet takes the claustrophobia level to an extreme. In summary, the Aria suite is a step backwards not forwards. Thankfully, the CX crews are simply fantastic and go some way to making up for the deficiencies of the new hard product.

I had way worse on a plane. But, for an airline like Qatar on a flight of this length, I honestly would have expected a hot meal service. Afterwards, little bottles of water were handed out, too. As we're cozying up for the night, let's have a look at what the in-flight entertainment system has to offer. The interface looks the same compared to the one we encountered aboard the Airbus A350-1000 just now. You can tell the touchscreen isn't the newest anymore. Content-wise, the selection is all right for the length of flights this aircraft operates. Obviously, it's a notably slimmer variety compared to the one aboard the A350. Speaking of releasing dangerous gases, the lavatories of this plane are small, but have got everything you need, including a changing table, some paper cups for when you brush your teeth, face and hand towels, hand soap, and eau de toilette. Around halfway into the flight over northern Turkey, the cabin lights came on and the crew started another round of service. This time, a hot breakfast. A snack service and a full meal service on a 5 and 1/2 hour flight that departs in the middle of the night is incredibly impressive. But, I can't help myself but be annoyed by the timing. Qatar Airways once again offers three options, either a frittata with chicken sausage, which is what we've got, an omelet with sweet potato, or some sweetish I didn't really understand. But, I prefer savory breakfast anyway, so here we are with our frittata, served with creamy spinach, a rösti, and a chicken sausage. Alongside our breakfast dish, we received a warm croissant and some strawberry jam, as well as a bottle of water, a cup of raspberry yogurt, and some fresh fruit. And come on, these are the same plastic cups we saw in the lounge, aren't they? To drink, my morning combo of coffee and orange juice, and once again, some metal cutlery. The beverage selection is extensive and includes complimentary alcoholic drinks, too. They even offer real French sparkling wine in economy class, with their brand of choice currently seeming to be Veuve Clicquot. It's basically champagne, but just from a different region of France. Quality-wise, this is a 10 out of 10, an all-around phenomenal breakfast service with a diverse and tasty main course, sensible additions like a warm croissant, yogurt, and fruit, and presented nicely alongside bottled water, beverages of choice, and metal cutlery. So, now lights are off again, and we go back to sleep? What the intention here is continues to elude me. I think even the world's best is allowed to not be perfect, but this level of imperfection just makes their marketing seem disingenuous. Should you choose Qatar Airways when you come across a good deal? Absolutely. They're not a bad airline by any means. But, are they better than every other airline on the planet? Of course not. reviews.transcript_full: Today we're back in Pakistan to fly from what is said to be the world's second most dangerous airport.  We'll travel with Pakistan International Airlines down to Islamabad and we'll see some  of the most stunning scenery I've ever seen from a plane window.  So come along with me and let's experience this together.  I have just done a week long guided tour of these northern regions and honestly it was  the most interesting trip I've done in this part of the world.  Seeing the unspoilt natural beauty of the Karakura mountain and its surrounding valleys  was truly breathtaking.  The fun started when we were heading back to the airport on the penultimate day of the tour.  There was some huge protests against the government for cutting some regional subsidies  to the people of the northern regions of Pakistan.  So they took to the streets in the towns and even fully blocked the main road from Islamabad  to the Chinese border.  This delayed us by about six hours in total.  Anyway I spent the night in Gilgit and the next morning headed to the small airport in the town  for my flight back to the capital Islamabad.  This opened back in 1949 but was upgraded with this new terminal in 2014.  This is well known for being a treacherous airport to fly to or from due to the high mountains  surrounding it on all sides and the runway not being well aligned with the narrow valley in or out.  Security is super strict here too with this being the first of five checkpoints I will pass  before getting on the plane.  Nothing like an AK-47 in your face is a welcome greeting.  After I received a pat down and my bag received an X-ray,  it is then searched with the guard being particularly interested in my padlock and a pack of coffee for some reason.  I'm then allowed to proceed to the check-in desks.  There's no such thing as online check-in here.  Hello.  The staff were friendly and helpful and I was soon presented with a boarding pass for flight PK604.  So let's check out the route.  We depart Gilgit on runway 07 to the northeast and immediately make a sharp 180 degree turn and a steep climb.  The 8000m plus Karakaru mountain range is to our left and the 7000m plus Hindu Kush range to our right.  We then head down to the Lowlands and make an easely approach and landing in Islamabad.  I must now check out of this region with a security officer.  They like to keep track of where all foreigners are before heading through another X-ray and metal detector security checkpoint.  Now finally through to the departure lounge where there is a small food and drink stand and a large waiting area.  At least it's air conditioned.  There is also a prayer room, toilets and a free water dispenser located here.  I was just catching up on some emails when a guy bought me some biscuits and a cup of tea, free of charge.  No idea.  Happy 2026 from nonstop Euro trip and my partnership with Level 8 Luggage which is now in its third year.  I've had a good chance to check out most of their fantastic range and Level 8 is the only luggage I will use now.  They are durable external shells where the lightweight polycarbonate or elegant aluminium are as functional as they are stylish.  And internally there are many pockets, dividers and straps to help compartmentalize your packing.  Every case where the carry on or check in also comes with tier-sare approved latches or locks and go anywhere 360 degrees spin or wheels.  And finally for your peace of mind a limited lifetime warranty is included on all luggage.  As a new year's gift you can grab anything from the Level 8 website and get 10% off at all by using code nonstop10.  Just click the link above now, in the description below.  Anyway around 15 minutes after I've scheduled departure time, our plane arrives on its inbound service from Islamabad.  I was very glad to actually see it in person as this was the first day in the past 5 that it had actually run and it wasn't tracking on the flight radar 24 app.  It's a Pakistan International Airlines 80R 42-500 twin turbo prop regional plane. This was 17 years old at the time of filming.  Just a couple of minutes after the last of the inbound passengers have elated, boarding commences and we walk the short distance from the terminal to the waiting aircraft.  And what a beautiful background for this experience and it seems like a perfect day for flying. The Alpine view should be great.  I'm welcome by the flight attendant and pointed towards my seat, a last row window seat on the left side of the plane.  The seats are pretty standard but they are well padded and do recline.  The leg room is quite tight but I'm sure it'll be fine for this short flight.  Boarding is complete in a little over 10 minutes and once the bags have been fully loaded, the doors are closed and the cones removed from outside.  We then start our short taxi to the single runway here at Gilgit nearly 1 hour late at 2.10pm.  We line up on runway 07 pointing straight towards a mountain which is a bit concerning.  But we then accelerate hard, take off and immediately bank right and start the full turn south towards Islamabad.  Today's route is 274 km in distance and is scheduled to take 1 hour and 15 minutes of travel time from gate to gate with a flying time of approximately 55 minutes.  My tour agency booked my tickets but they cost around 14,000 Pakistani rupees if you buy direct with the Alpine.  It's not long before we start to get the first of today's spectacular plane window views out towards the Caracara mountains off to the left hand side.  Shortly after, the complimentary food and drink service begins with the flight attendant serving himself first.  I receive a small snack box with a sandwich and cake along with the choice of a hot or cold drink.  Most people are now glued to the windows.  I'm not 100% sure which mountain this is but K2, the second highest peak in the world at 8,611m is off to this direction somewhere.  If you want to watch my Mount Everest sightseeing flight review in Nepal next then click the link in the description at the end of this video.  Nice to see that PIA have a monkey box kit loaded in an air-Austral storage box.  This flight is scheduled to run twice daily but it's frequently cancelled due to bad weather up here or dust storms in Islamabad of the 14 planned weekly flights.  It sometimes only runs 2 or 3 times.  Before long we have left the mountains and are starting our descent through the haze down to the Pakistani capital's large international airport.  We land on runway 28 left after 55 minutes in the air.  In the end it was a pretty uneventful flight but endlessly scenic.  I had the option to return to Islamabad with the guides by car at no extra cost but that would have taken around 10 hours and I was keen to experience this flight.  So for the $50 cost I think I made the right choice.  I'll leave a link to the full guided tour I did around the north of Pakistan in the description but it cost $980 for a 7 day all inclusive trip for 2 people and I would highly recommend it.  It's a fascinating and beautiful place.  We are light the plane and board a bus for the 5 minute drive to the terminal.  Have you been on any scenic flights before? If so which ones and on which routes? How did you find them? Let me know in the comments below.  Our bags are already arriving on the carousel as we arrive in the beautifully decorated baggage claim area.  I'm always open to new video ideas so if you have something you'd like to see on the channel then drop me a DM on Instagram, Blue Sky or Twitter.  Don't forget to subscribe thanks for watching to the end and I'll see you in the next video.  Bye bye.

reviews.title: Airlines are banning power banks (but it kinda makes sense)
reviews.transcript_excerpt: It must be kept in a protective pouch or transparent plastic bag and within arms reach under the seat or in a seatback pocket…

captions.text: It must be kept in a protective pouch or transparent plastic bag and within arms reach under the seat or in a seatback pocket
They want them kept accessible under the seat or in a seat back pocket, where they can be monitored by passengers and crew.

yt_comments.author: @Kai_meL30n
yt_comments.text: Even at airports recently I found that finding an available wall outlet to charge my stuff was a challenge! Sure there were charging 'stations' but those are in high demand and good luck getting one. So what's the alternative? Power banks. But alas, you also need to charge those, lol! I also found the usb outlets on board the planes to be mostly a non-option. Either they are too low powered, or the port itself is damaged and your cable cannot maintain a proper connection. So it's rather messy this whole power bank situation. Great video btw!!

yt_comments.author: @rgseidl67
yt_comments.text: Qi2 in the seat in front of you to the rescue. USB power outlets are mechanically fragile and airlines typically don’t want to give passengers a full mains socket (globally inconsistent plugs, voltages, high aggregate electrical power, fuses etc.)
