article_text: Entertainment & Connectivity , Thought Leadership & Brand

As travelers grow to expect the same digital experience in the sky as they do on the ground, inflight entertainment screens are now at the center of the cabin experience. These systems have evolved from basic seatback screens to intelligent, connected platforms that blend entertainment, personalization, and connectivity. This shift has transformed how passengers experience content and how airlines express their brand. For the Airline Passenger Experience Association (APEX), that evolution marks a key moment in how the industry represents innovation and collaboration.

The proposed addition of an APEX Board seat dedicated to major inflight entertainment screen manufacturers highlights how essential display technology has become to the overall passenger journey. As airlines integrate entertainment, personalization, and connectivity into one seamless experience, APEX members will decide which of these candidates will help guide that next phase of progress. This story profiles the three nominees: Ben Asmar of Safran, Andy Masson of Panasonic Avionics Corporation, and Kurt Weidemeyer of Thales. Each brings a unique perspective shaped by years of leadership, creativity, and innovation that continue to define the future of inflight entertainment.
Andy Masson, Panasonic Avionics Corporation

Panasonic Avionics Corporation has become a driving force in the evolution of inflight entertainment, combining decades of aerospace expertise with deep roots in audio and visual technology. Since joining the company in 2021, Andy Masson, Vice President of Product Management and Portfolio Strategy, has helped transform the seatback screen from a passive display into a connected, interactive, and sustainable experience.

“Panasonic Avionics has always believed that the passenger experience sits at the center of aviation innovation,” Masson said. “Our mission is to deliver technology that feels human, responsive, and intuitive, designed around how people actually travel.”

At Panasonic, Masson led the development of Astrova, the company’s most successful inflight entertainment system to date. The platform features advanced OLED displays, Bluetooth audio, and high-power USB-C, complemented by a modern industrial design. More importantly, it was built for the future: lightweight, energy-efficient, and modular, allowing airlines to upgrade components without replacing entire systems. “The industry must innovate responsibly,” Masson explained. “With Astrova, we designed a system that performs at the highest level while reducing waste and long-term costs.”

For Masson, joining the APEX Board represents an opportunity to connect technical innovation with the broader passenger experience community. “We are entering a new world of on-demand and streamed media powered by ultra-fast satellite networks,” he said. “Through APEX, we can align the interests of airlines, technology providers, and content creators so that everyone, from passengers to studios, benefits.”

Before joining Panasonic, Masson built a career that connected entertainment and aerospace. He began as a live sound engineer and later founded Audiosys, a professional audio-visual company serving large-scale events and recording artists. He then moved into aerospace, leading cabin engineering and modification programs at Boeing’s Continental Data Graphics, before becoming CEO of Adient Aerospace, Boeing’s joint venture focused on aircraft seating. Each position reinforced his belief that technology and comfort work hand in hand to define the passenger experience.

Looking ahead, Masson hopes to utilize his APEX role to help the industry continue to lead in entertainment and connectivity. “Aerospace has always set the standard, from pioneering on-demand video to bringing satellite connectivity to passengers,” he said. “Now, as we move into the next era of inflight media, our challenge is to deliver smarter, more flexible systems that make every journey personal, sustainable, and inspiring.”
Ben Asmar, Safran

Safran has become a leading voice in redefining how passengers experience inflight entertainment, combining creative design with advanced engineering to make air travel more immersive and personal. At the center of that effort is Ben Asmar, Vice President of Product and Innovation, whose 17-year career in aviation has been devoted to blending technology, empathy, and design to elevate the passenger journey.

“As connectivity becomes faster, more accessible, and in many cases free to passengers, it opens new opportunities for suppliers like Safran,” Asmar said. “It allows us to make IFE systems more engaging and connected, enabling real-time personalization and linking inflight entertainment with ground-based content. Instead of being limited to monthly updates, airlines can now refresh shows, push news, or stream live sports every day.”

Asmar has overseen major advances in seatback display technology, enabling Safran to deliver systems that provide passengers with a more cinematic experience. “Seatback screens have come a long way,” he explained. “Today, we’re offering 4K displays, even in economy. When you’re sitting close to a 13-inch screen with Bluetooth audio and noise cancellation, you see and hear content the way the director intended. It’s like having a movie theater in the sky.”

To Asmar, serving on the APEX Board offers an opportunity to guide the industry through rapid technological change. “Technology moves faster than ever, and aviation needs to keep up,” he said. “If APEX can help remove barriers that slow innovation, we can bring new systems to passengers much sooner. Safety always comes first, but progress shouldn’t take ten years.”

Personalization remains a core focus for Asmar and his team. “We’re working with airlines to create experiences that continue across journeys,” he said. “A passenger might start a movie on one flight and pick it up on the next. The next step is ensuring that personalized experience can follow travelers across partner airlines so their preferences move with them.”

Asmar believes APEX is key to uniting airlines, suppliers, and partners around shared standards that enable scalable innovation. “Airlines and suppliers can’t do this alone,” he said. “Progress happens when both sides collaborate to make technology feel human and meaningful. Through APEX, we can move faster, stay connected, and keep the passenger experience at the heart of aviation’s next chapter.”
Kurt Weidemeyer, Thales

Thales has emerged as one of the driving forces shaping the digital future of inflight entertainment, combining decades of aerospace expertise with a forward-looking approach to connected travel. Leading that effort is Kurt Weidemeyer, Vice President of Product Management, who oversees Thales’ global strategy for inflight entertainment, connectivity, and digital solutions. With more than 20 years of experience at Honeywell, Inmarsat, and now Thales, Weidemeyer has focused his career on merging technology, creativity, and reliability to create seamless passenger experiences.

“For years, inflight screens were simply a place to watch a movie,” Weidemeyer said. “Now, with advances in software, hardware, and connectivity, we can help airlines deliver a fully curated experience. Passengers can log in, pick up a film they started on a previous flight, or access recommendations tailored just for them. Anything you can do on the ground, you should now be able to do in the air.”

Under his leadership, Thales introduced FlytEDGE, the industry’s first fully cloud-native inflight entertainment system. “FlytEDGE is a platform in the sky,” Weidemeyer explained. “It gives airlines full control over their digital environment. They can update content, refresh the user interface, and make changes instantly, even while the aircraft is in flight. We built it so our customers can move faster and operate with full autonomy.”

Weidemeyer’s candidacy for the APEX Board of Directors reflects his goal of strengthening collaboration across the passenger experience community. “I’ve been involved with APEX for more than ten years, both as a member and a panelist,” he said. “What makes APEX powerful is how it brings everyone together, from airlines and suppliers to content partners, to make meaningful progress. It is the only forum where the entire industry can work collectively to advance technology and improve the passenger experience.”

One initiative especially important to Weidemeyer is APEX STREAM, which aims to standardize digital rights management for airline media. “We recently launched edge caching for streaming services like Netflix, Prime Video, and Disney+, the first in the industry,” he said. “That technology is exciting, but the next challenge is the legal side. Through APEX, we can bring airlines, content owners, and technology providers together to define how rights are managed so passengers can access the content they love safely and seamlessly.”

Weidemeyer believes that APEX is essential to helping aviation keep pace with rapid technological change. “The fastest progress happens when we move forward as a community,” he said. “Every airline is different, but we share common goals like improving satisfaction, driving efficiency, and creating new value. Through APEX, we can set the right framework, bring innovation to passengers faster, and deliver lasting benefits for airlines and travelers.”
Elevating Entertainment into Experience

While the three nominees represent different companies and perspectives, Kurt Weidemeyer of Thales, Andy Masson of Panasonic Avionics, and Ben Asmar of Safran share a common goal of redefining inflight entertainment as a complete passenger experience rather than just a platform for content.

For each candidate, innovation means more than sharper displays or faster systems. It is about turning the screen into a central part of the journey, one that connects travelers to the airline’s story, adapts to personal preferences, and blends design, technology, and connectivity into a seamless experience.

Their shared commitment to collaboration, standardization, and creativity reflects APEX’s mission to keep raising the bar for the passenger experience through real, measurable innovation. The addition of a dedicated inflight entertainment seat on the 2025–2026 APEX Board highlights the industry’s recognition that screens are now vital to both passenger engagement and airline identity.

Together, Weidemeyer, Masson, and Asmar represent the growing influence of the inflight entertainment community within APEX and across aviation. Each brings a distinct viewpoint shaped by experience and expertise, yet all share the same vision: to make every journey more connected, intuitive, and memorable.
A Vision for the Future
As APEX members prepare to vote, the new inflight entertainment screen manufacturer seat stands as a marker of the industry’s progress and its potential.

“The inflight screen connects every part of the passenger journey, from entertainment and comfort to discovery and engagement,” said APEX/IFSA CEO Dr. Joe Leader. “The leaders from Thales, Panasonic Avionics, and Safran demonstrate how creativity and innovation continue to shape our industry. Their vision reflects the spirit of APEX, bringing technology and people together to make every flight more personal, inspiring, and connected.”

article_text: The latest Inflight Entertainment (IFE) trends reveal a significant shift from traditional content delivery to sophisticated, psychology-driven passenger experiences.

This was the outcome of a panel discussion at APEX Global EXPO , moderated by Maryann Simpson , Director at Jetway Communications, which featured insights from three airline IFE leaders: Dominic Green, Director of In-Flight Entertainment at United Airlines; Miguel Ferreira, Digital Onboard Experience Manager for TAP Air Portugal; and Blake Rittenberg , Manager of In-Flight Entertainment, Tech and Partnerships at JetBlue. Each brought unique perspectives from their respective carriers’ approaches to passenger engagement and entertainment strategies.

According to the panel, airlines increasingly view their IFE platforms as integral parts of their digital ecosystem rather than standalone entertainment systems. “We’re really trying to evolve our IFE away from being purely a media player,” explained Dominic Green, Director of In-Flight Entertainment at United Airlines, who noted that United is deploying its newest platform across more than 30 aircraft in their mainline fleet.
Passenger psychology plays a crucial role in modern IFE strategy. Rittenberg pointed out that when in aircraft, passengers are “hurling through the air at 35,000 feet at 500 miles an hour.”

This understanding drives airlines to create experiences that help passengers feel more comfortable. Interestingly, flight map features have emerged as crucial comfort tools, with airlines reporting that an overwhelming majority of passengers engage with mapping products during flights. As Rittenberg explained, “It’s almost like an illusion of control. Being able to see how high you are, how fast you’re going, and how long until you arrive at your destination gives you this false sense of control.”

The streaming revolution has strengthened, rather than weakened IFE’s position. “IFE is actually like the last place on earth where you have all of this content from all of these streaming services living side by side,” Rittenberg pointed out, highlighting how fragmented streaming services have made IFE more valuable as a comprehensive entertainment hub.

Cultural identity and personalisation are becoming key differentiators. TAP Air Portugal has leveraged its platform to showcase Portuguese culture, launching initiatives like an exclusive onboard film festival and interactive wine tourism content. “With IFE, if you have the right redesign and the right functionalities, you can liberate the experience of content discovery,” noted Ferreira, adding that “passengers are not commenting on the mainstream; they are commenting on this niche content that makes a difference.”

Data analytics is revolutionising content curation and advertising strategies. Airlines are moving beyond traditional demographic targeting to create more nuanced, journey-specific experiences. United Airlines has implemented sophisticated data collection from its new platform. However, Green noted that understanding how passenger behaviour changes onboard still requires “a bit of an art and science to it.”

The challenge of creating interfaces that work for all generations has emerged as a critical focus area. JetBlue emphasises designing systems that accommodate digital and non-digital natives, ensuring all passengers can easily access features from basic entertainment to Wi-Fi connectivity.

Advertising within IFE systems is evolving toward more sophisticated, less intrusive models. Airlines are implementing targeting capabilities based on route, nationality, and passenger preferences while working to standardise advertising systems across the industry. “As an industry, we should standardise this… and make them (advertisers) feel it is easy to buy ads inside of our product,” Ferreira suggested.

Looking ahead, airlines are focused on creating more connected, personalised experiences throughout the entire journey. This includes pre-flight content previews, seamless continuation of viewing experiences, and better integration with airline apps and services. The emphasis shifts from pure entertainment to creating a comprehensive digital experience that enhances the travel journey.

The evolution of IFE systems reflects the industry’s broader move toward more personalised, data-driven passenger experiences. As airlines continue to invest in new technologies and partnerships, the traditional IFE system is transforming into a sophisticated platform that serves as a crucial touchpoint in the airline’s digital ecosystem.

article_quotes.text: Air France partners with Apple TV for IFE content - Aircraft Interiors International News Aircraft Safety Aircraft Seating Airline News Airframer News Cabin Design Catering & Onboard Retail Galleys & Monuments Industry News Inflight Amenities Inflight Connectivity In-flight Entertainment Materials.

In the newest cabins, the anti-glare screen is equipped with a Bluetooth connection for connecting personal headphones or earphones Air France has expanded its lineup of inflight entertainment (IFE) through a partnership with the Apple TV streaming service.
Customers can also enjoy free access to Apple TV content directly via Air France’s new high-speed wi-fi portal, which is being progressively rolled out across the airline’s entire fleet.
Apple TV on long-haul flights On all long-haul Air France flights, customers can access original Apple TV series, such as Ted Lasso, The Morning Show , and Severance .
Series promoting French lifestyle, like Carême , are also available.
Customers will not be able to watch entire series on the IFE system though: only the first three episodes of each series are featured in a dedicated channel.

Air France also offers one week of free access to Apple TV content on personal devices via its new high-speed wi-fi portal Coming soon: Apple TV via cabin wi-fi Air France also offers one week of free access to Apple TV content via its new high-speed wi-fi portal.
Air France is gradually rolling out its new high-speed wi-fi service across its fleet, including regional aircraft.

reviews.title: Singapore Airlines Business Class — Is It Still the Best in the World?

captions.text: Many travelers rank Singapore Airlines above Qatar or Emirates
Lounge amenities include showers, meeting rooms, and Wi-Fi
In front of the seat is a large 18-inch HD screen
KrisWorld includes hundreds of movies, TV shows, and playlists

reviews.transcript_full: Is Singapore Airlines the world’s best Business Class airline?  Many travelers rank Singapore Airlines above Qatar or Emirates Let’s judge the seat, food, service & comfort on a real flight The 13 hour flight takes us from Singapore to Brussels Enjoy the full Singapore Airlines Business Class experience! We're arriving at Singapore Changi Airport Changi consistently ranks among the world’s best airports The airport is home to the world’s tallest indoor waterfall The Rain Vortex is 40 meters (131 feet) tall At night, the Rain Vortex glows with shifting colors and music The airport spans 4 terminals arranged in an inverted U-shape The airport connects to 400+ cities across the globe Singapore Airlines offers a dedicated Business Class check-in Changi Airport serves 70 million passengers annually Let's visit Singapore Airlines' SilverKris Business Class Lounge Located at T3, this is Singapore Airlines' flagship lounge The lounge is split into a left and right section upon entry Both lounge sections feature their own buffet & drinks stations Seating ranges from sofas and armchairs to dining tables Food quality exceeds that of most Business Class lounges The lounge's other section feels more intimate This part of the lounge has a buffet station with open kitchen The spirits selection includes several premium brands Live cooking stations serve noodles and pastas The buffet includes a mix of Asian and Western dishes Lounge amenities include showers, meeting rooms, and Wi-Fi The lounge is open 24/7 for eligible passengers Let’s head to the gate for our flight to Brussels A Singapore Airlines A380 is parked right next to our gate This is the Airbus A350 that will fly us to Brussels Singapore Airlines is the world’s largest A350 operator Singapore Airlines' crew arrives at the gate (please count them) I count 6 pilots and 26 crew members (!!!)  Is this the most staffed flight ever? :-) Usually, there are 13 cabin crew & 3 pilots on a long-haul flight It's time to board the aircraft Singapore Airlines’ A350 features 42 Business Class seats Spread over two cabins, the seats are arranged in a 1-2-1 layout 20A is my window seat for the 13 hour flight to Brussels The seat is one of the widest in the airline industry Seat pitch is 153 cm (60 inch) and width is 71 cm (28 inch) Center seats include a partition screen for privacy Let’s take a detailed tour of the seat prior to takeoff The seat controls are located in a panel in the armrest In front of the seat is a large 18-inch HD screen A small compartment with vanity mirror sits beside the screen The seat features an ottoman (foot rest) to the side A side console offers storage, power outlets, and a reading light Next to the console is the IFE remote and a small storage box The tray table is stored in the armrest The crew welcomes passengers with a drink and hot towel We have a full Business Class cabin on tonight's flight The pilot welcomes the passengers Have you ever flown with Singapore Airlines? Leave a comment We're leaving the gate at midnight (on time departure) The safety video is a beautifully produced film  The iconic Singapore Girl delivers the safety instructions Safety instructions are paired with Singapore’s landmarks The cabin lights are dimmed for takeoff The A350 is powered by Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines We get a nice view of Singapore Changi Airport after takeoff Business Class amenity kits are available upon request The kit includes skincare items from Le Labo Slippers and socks are offered A large pillow and a soft duvet are provided as well Noise-cancelling headphones enhance the inflight experience Let’s take a look at the inflight menu World-class chefs design Singapore Airlines' menus Aperitif: a choice of drinks, served with mixed nuts Starter: marinated smoked salmon with capers Main course: herb-crusted roast lamb chops, garlic confit mash Dessert: Milo dinosaur cake We encounter moderate turbulence above the Straits of Malacca  The region around Malaysia and Sumatra is prone to turbulence Converging trade winds create big thunderstorms The A350 has three lavatories for Business Class passengers The lavatories are stocked with Payot toiletries Singapore Airlines' cabin crew assists in setting up the bed When fully flat, the bed measures 198 cm or 78 inches in length Legs are positioned at a slight angle in bed mode The IFE system is controlled using a handheld remote Singapore Airlines calls its IFE system KrisWorld KrisWorld includes hundreds of movies, TV shows, and playlists Singapore Airlines also offers free Wi-Fi in Business Class The flight can be tracked in real-time with an interactive 3D map Light bites are served upon request throughout the flight Mid-flight snack: Singapore carrot cake with prawns Breakfast is served 90 minutes prior to landing Breakfast service starts with a hot towel to refresh a little Breakfast includes sliced fresh fruits and flavored yoghurt Lobster Thermidor is served as a main course The captain announces the start of our descent into Brussels Singapore Airlines is one of the world’s most awarded airlines The airline’s story began in 1947 as Malayan Airways Its first aircraft was the twin-engined Airspeed Consul In 1966, it became Malaysia-Singapore Airlines, or MSA MSA split in 1972, creating two national airlines Singapore Airlines quickly emerged as a global carrier Singapore Airlines has often led aviation innovation It pioneered free meals, drinks, and headsets in Economy In 2007, it also launched the Airbus A380 into service Thx for watching my Singapore Airlines Business Class video

reviews.title: Why this Aviation YouTuber Is Surprisingly Controversial
reviews.transcript_excerpt: Over the past few…
reviews.transcript_full: Over the past few years, aviation YouTuber Sam Chui has slowly earned a reputation that many find increasingly questionable. The groundwork for this downfall was laid the moment people began to wonder whether the personality shown on camera truly matched reality. In his highly polished videos, Sam Chui comes across as friendly, passionate, and deeply invested in aviation. Everything appears carefully crafted to make him likable. Yet an increasing number of signs suggest a very different picture behind the scenes. And those warning signs did not appear recently. They began showing up years ago. You see, Sam Chui began making videos at the very dawn of YouTube, uploading his first content as far back as 2007. As the platform grew, he grew with it. Over time, he became widely viewed as one of the OG’s in aviation YouTube. But according to some, as his audience expanded and his influence turned him into one of the biggest names in the niche, his ego grew alongside it. Or as this reddit post states “Sam Chui’s ego is massive now and he’s at the point where he thinks he’s untouchable.” With other viewers noticing the same shift in his content. “Used to love his videos… “, “Stopped watching and unsubscribed almost two years ago” Meanwhile Traveler MSY says that “He started as a hobbyist because he liked aviation, but now he’s a publisher/presenter.” Things however took an even darker turn after a flight on Kazahkstans national airline, Air Astana, with his then-friend Josh Cahill. In a video released later, Josh alleged that during this flight, Sam Chui assaultetd members of the cabin crew. In his podcast with Aviation Youtuber Swiss he stated that this is a recurring theme. To be fair, Sam Chui was not always the primary cause of controversy. The 2022 incident involving Nepal Airlines is a good example of that. In a video filmed on a Nepal Airlines flight, Chui appeared in the cockpit together with the airline’s chief pilot, Vijaya Lama. Several media outlets described this as a violation of aviation safety regulations. Later, on a Nepalese podcast, Lama himself referred to the incident as one of the biggest mistakes of his career and claimed that Sam Chui had been paid by airlines in general. In situations like this however, responsibility lies primarily with the flight crew. Access to the cockpit is strictly controlled, and only the pilot in command has the authority to grant or deny entry. Chui did not enter the cockpit on his own initiative; he was invited in by the chief pilot. For that reason, placing the main blame on Chui feels misplaced. The regulatory and safety responsibility rests with the pilot, not with a guest who was allowed into the cockpit by someone in a position of authority. But this is not the only time when chief pilots got in trouble for Chui entering the cockpit. In May 2023 for example, Chui was suspected of violating Taiwan’s Aircraft Flight Operation Regulations after entering the cockpit without the required authorization. As a result Taiwan’s civil aviation authority opened its investigation against Chang Kuo-wei, who was flying the aircraft at the time and is also the founder of STARLUX Airlines. Chang was summoned for questioning, and authorities concluded that this incident constituted a regulatory breach. With the relevant regulation stating that: “No person may be admitted into the flight crew compartment of an aircraft except for the authorized personnel and Flight Dispatchers of the operator.” However it is undeniable that there is a broader pattern of Sam Chui frequently appearing on camera chatting with pilots or filming inside cockpits during active flights. These moments give viewers access that most other aviation YouTubers simply never get. However this level of exclusivity not only fuels curiosity, but also skepticism by his viewers. Many viewers ask how this level of access is even possible. Others openly question whether Chui cooperates with airlines behind the scenes, or whether his videos function as promotion rather than independent documentation. Chui himself repeatedly insists that his content is authentic and not sponsored. According to him, airlines do not pay for coverage and he retains editorial control. Yet a quick look at comment sections tells a different story. A large share of viewers clearly doubts this narrative. According to some viewers, the lack of authenticity in his videos is obvious, with one critic even calling him a paid cheerleader without integrity. The combination of privileged access, unusually friendly cockpit interactions, and consistently positive portrayals makes many people unconvinced that these videos exist without some form of financial support by the airlines. That gap between Chui’s claims and audience perception therefore remains one of the most persistent points of tension surrounding his work. In general, Sam Chui’s videos are highly polished and rarely focus on negatives. That alone is not a flaw. This style clearly resonates with a large audience and has helped make his content some of the most popular in the aviation space. Chui himself repeatedly emphasizes that he is not a reviewer. His work reflects that position. There is also clear demand for this approach. Many viewers prefer watching unique and impressive insights into aviation rather than constant conflict or outrage. For them, Chui’s videos offer escapism, access, and spectacle. And that appeal explains his sustained success. At the same time, it is difficult for many to ignore that his videos often carry a promotional tone. Even without explicit advertising, the consistent positivity, exceptional access, and cinematic presentation create the impression of marketing. This does not automatically mean the content is sponsored, but it does blur the line between documentation and promotion. That ambiguity sits at the core of the debate around Chui. His content satisfies a real audience need, yet for a significant portion of viewers, it still feels closer to brand-friendly storytelling than to neutral aviation coverage. When you look at Chui’s videos, they are usually not labeled as sponsored. On the surface, they appear independent. However, occasionally the content contains hints that suggest otherwise. For example, some videos include links in the description pointing directly to the airline or organization featured. A clear case comes from his coverage of the EBACE Airshow. At first glance, it seems like regular reporting, but a closer look reveals a connection: the video description contains links to EBACE itself. A little research confirms this was indeed a cooperation, as the organizers explicitly state in a press release. Now don’t get me wrong here: promotion in itself is not inherently problematic. Sponsored content provides creators with additional revenue streams, reducing reliance on YouTube ad revenue and giving them more financial freedom to produce high-quality content. The issue arises when sponsorships are not clearly disclosed. Failing to label paid content can be seen as disrespectful to viewers, as it misleads them about the independence of the content. But non-disclosure may also violate YouTube guidelines, which explicitly require creators to label sponsored content. Beyond platform rules, undisclosed sponsorships can also conflict with media and trade laws in many countries. In the United States, where Chui’s channel is based, the Federal Trade Commission Act requires that any material connection between an endorser and marketer must be clearly and conspicuously disclosed. This is meant to guarantee transparency so viewers understand when content carries a promotional element. In Chui’s videos, you usually won’t find any explicit sponsorship labels. I’m not a lawyer, but it’s easy to see why people make these allegations. In Chui’s early days, to many his content felt more authentic. His passion seemed genuinely focused on aviation, and that authenticity attracted a loyal audience. Over time, however, perceptions shifted. Many now view the channel as primarily a money-making machine. Despite Chui’s claims that his content is unsponsored, he maintains a dedicated page on his website for sponsorships, highlighting how attractive his channel is for potential partners. This contradiction between public statements and the promotion of sponsorship opportunities fuels skepticism and raises questions about transparency. Cases like these certainly eroded trust among his audience and explain why some viewers gradually turned away. Claims that he was paid by the subjects of his videos certainly contributed, but there’s more to the story. Because another notable incident started to take shape in 2023, involving a dispute with fellow YouTuber Josh Cahill. I’ve made a dedicated video covering that case, so I won’t go into full detail here, but you’re welcome to watch it after this one. To be honest, I was a bit biased in that video and, in retrospect, I’m not particularly proud of it. But anyway here’s a quick summary of why the conflict erupted between the two: Now, there had already been minor disputes between the two, including a Twitter argument where they exchanged jabs. After that, they seemed to get along and even met in person. But the feud escalated when Josh Cahill claimed that Sam Chui had been paid by the Indian airline Vistara. Chui viewed this as defamation and, in a now-deleted YouTube comment, accused Cahill of blackmailing the airline. In response, Cahill released a video detailing the whole situation. This triggered a huge backlash against Chui, forcing him to apparently temporarily block comments on Instagram. The incident clearly damaged his public image, splitting the community, with those critical of Chui forming the seemingly larger group. After some time, Chui posted a statement video, apologizing to Cahill while also defending his own positions. However, as of December 2025, that video appears to have been removed from his channel. but in December 2025, Josh Cahill posted a video titled: “Still BANNED by QATAR AIRWAYS? Let’s fly them and see what HAPPENS!” In that video, Cahill explained why he had been banned from Qatar Airways and alleged that the airline had engaged in bribery to secure sponsored content. He further claimed that Qatar Airways later collaborated with Chui, suggesting that these efforts aimed to improve the airline’s public image. The video reinforced the perception among some viewers that Chui’s access and coverage could involve covert partnerships with airlines, fueling skepticism about the independence of his content. Now, you can think whatever you want about Josh —he has his own reputation for drama—but it’s clear he is not the only one raising concerns about Chui. Well, the aim of this video is not to gossip or to defame anyone. Disagreement in my comments is not only allowed but welcome, as long as it remains civil and respectful. But all in all being fair to viewers matters. When someone buys a product, books a flight, or engages with content, they expect unbiased information. Transparency and honesty are the key, and that’s what this video aims to highlight. Shortly after Cahill’s December 2025 Qatar Airways video went live, he discussed the situation on his Josh Cahill & Swiss Show. In their latest episode, Chaill claimed that Sam Chui’s damage-control videos were not a single incident but a pattern: every time he posted a negative video about an airline, it was soon followed by a positive one from Sam Chui. He further alleged that people from Qatar Airways told him that the airline provides Chui with unique access, accommodates his requests, and essentially lets him operate freely. He also claimed to have emails and screenshots supporting that Sam Chui had been asked to “fix the mess” created by prior coverage. Clearly we’re dealing with two major creators accusing each other, so where the truth actually lies isn’t for me to decide. That said, it is true that Chui sometimes portrays airlines with a negative reputation in a positive light. There is, however, one airline with a particularly bad reputation that he can’t cover anymore because its license has just been revoked. How this “corrupt mafia airline” fell—you’ll see in this video. Thanks for watching, and see you soon.

and weight. Soft, but structured and long   enough for some head to toe coverage.
Last up the mattress pad which was folded   into itself serving as a second support pillow 
if you wished. The pad itself was one of the   best I’ve seen in Business- maybe the best. It was 
actually squishy foam and made a true difference   in the comfort of the seat and bed.
The meal service began a little   under an hour after take off.
Here’s the menu for the flight- you’ll   notice it’s missing a bit of info. The menu card 
is only for the main dish of the first meal- which   can also be chosen online prior to the flight. 
Note that choosing online will give you at least   one additional choice than just the on board menu.
Service on the flight was efficient and friendly-   in that order. The crew were warm at 
attentive but there wasn’t much time   for chit chat or explanation of the dishes- for 
the wine, it was simply, Spanish or French Red.  The appetizer was some sort of seasoned shrimp 
with a really fresh salsa verde. The shrimp were   a bit like rubber bullets, but the flavor 
was very good. The cheese course was also   served- an odd thing since they don’t expect 
you to keep this plate through the service.  The main meal followed and I chose the online only 
option which was jumbo shrimp with seasoned rice,   fried plantains and tequila sauce. 
Flavors here packed a punch and if it   wasn’t for the shrimp again being very 
firm, I’d definitely order it again.  This was served alongside a side 
salad and a section of breads.  Last up for dessert we had a small 
tres leches cake and vanilla ice cream.  In total, the meal lasted around 45 
minutes and wasn’t rushed for me,   but I can see how it may have been 
for some. I just wish there was a full   menu. Overall I’ll give the meal a 7.7/10.
Wifi vouchers were passed out for Business   class though the pricing was also very 
fair. $22 for the full flight and free   messaging was available for everyone.
In flight entertainment was available   on the large bright screen and had a 
great selection along with a couple   live tv channels and a beautiful moving map.
Headphones on this flight- different from the   previous one were surprisingly comfortable 
with the suede like ear cups- though I   suppose this might give my identity 
away, but my ears aren’t rectangular.  Here’s the bed in full flat mode with that 
fantastic bedding. I slept like I was at home for   a solid five hours. That is a massive win for me.
When I woke up, I noticed they had a full bar and   snack bar setup. Besides the Virgins and Emirates 
of the world- this was one of the largest spreads   I’ve seen before. It was so well laid out and 
there was even a Nespresso machine- a self   service Nespresso Machine. You know that alone 
earned them an extra point in the total score.  They gradually started to wake the cabin up around 
80 minutes before landing for the second meal   service. Before that, let’s take a look at the 
very stylish amenity kit and get freshened up.  The kit is from Etro and makes for quite 
the statement pieces as far as eye masks go.  Restrooms were stocked with the same Etro 
products and were kept clean throughout.  I’d love to know if this was the 
intended flower. It’s a bold choice.  Choices for breakfast were eggs or waffles. I 
went with the eggs and these were actually really   delicious. Every airline should serve their eggs 
with some sort of salsa. Along with that was a   fruit cup and a pot of yogurt. Overall a nice- 
not too big- tasty breakfast service. 8.2/10.  As we were approaching Sao Paulo from 
the northwest, the sun began to rise.  Note that for the entirety of 
the “dark” part of the flight,   the windows were locked at a ⅗ dimmer 
setting, which I think is fair.  Super efficient crew, fantastic sleeping 
experience, decent food, self service Nespresso   and a nonexistent lounge sums up this flight. 
For the sake of the rankings- not the score-   I’m going to disregard the lounge access since 
those should be open soon after this comes out.   So again, I think I’m going to bump them up to a 
6.5 which will round to a 7. Give me full menus,   a lounge, next time I won’t order the shrimp 
and maybe, they could get a full 7 or 8.   That bedding though had a lot to do with 
this ranking because it simply shows me   what direction they’re trying to go in.
So I really hope you enjoyed this trip   report today, if you did please be sure to 
click the like button and subscribe with   notifications on so you don’t miss my my twice 
weekly videos. I’ll see you next time for a   special one from the Park Hyatt Kuala Lumpur. 
As always, thanks for watching until the end.

Being business class, we were also entitled to use the fast track. As one of the check-in staff had to head to the lounge anyway, they decided to escort us there, which was lovely. It's important to state China Airlines has its own lounge in Bangkok, but because it closes earlier in the evening, that meant this Redeye flight uses a third party lounge. There is a big emphasis on food with a live food station at one end and plenty of seating. It's fairly stylish, but there's [music] really only a few relaxed seats towards the back of the lounge. The rest of them seem to be designed for those wanting to eat. [music] After relaxing for a little bit, we headed to the gate. I've always found Bangkok's [music] airport somewhat confusing to navigate as everything always looks the same. But at least the signposting is easy to follow. And before we knew it, we were at the gate ready to board. As soon as we arrived, boarding had just [music] started and we were boarded first. And I have to admit, I was pretty surprised by this interior. Unlike China Airlines other aircraft, there's a fresh, light air aesthetic with warm lighting and brighter, more youthful colors at play with sky blues, sunset colors of peach and blue. It's really a pleasant boarding lighting scene. The economy seats are well padded and every seat has a large if screen. In business class, there are just 12 seats arranged in a 2x two configuration across three rows. >> [music] >> The cabin is a sea of design details with beautiful oceanlike carpet designs and dappled lighting. The seat fully recines into a fully flatbed. And it's a nice touch to see those Pokémon pillows, which perhaps added to the more playful interior aesthetic. There's a big leather adjustable headrest which helps add a bit of height to the pillow when sleeping. In between the seats is a personal storage unit in blue which includes this stylish illuminated seat control and a privacy divider which again is lined in blue. An auspicious color in Taiwan. And check out this little mirror. There was also a small cocktail table which housed the noiseancelling headphones and even slippers were offered on this 3-hour flight. [music] Another nice touch was the incredible bedding, perhaps the best I've had on a short hall flight like this. The surprises kept on coming as we were handed a full wine list and a food menu and we were served China Airlines signature mocktail. Now let's take a look at the extensive menus for this flight. I mean, this is kind of obscene really, but what's even better is the fact that you can actually also pre-order meals even on shorter hops like this. Hot towel in hand, we push back on time at 2:30 in the morning. After takeoff, the cabin crew prepped the cabin to try and minimize any disruption for those wanting to sleep. While I charged my phone using the wireless charging, which actually worked, the cabin crew set up my seat for dinner. What was even more incredible was the fact that the dinner was preceded by a drink and nut mix served on this gorgeous plum blossom plate. The meal was served shortly afterwards. And look at this feast. European carriers take note. This was a wanton noodle soup with a side salad and some [music] fried fish balls. It was delicious and made even better by dessert, which was a hazelnut and caramel tart. [music] After heading to the well pretty standard toilet stocked with Moroccan oil amenities, I set up the bed to try and get some sleep. [music] Now, I have to say the seat by far isn't long enough and the footwell is very restrictive. That said, I was so tired I basically went straight to sleep for approximately an hour before the cabin was being prepared for landing. And we were offered some water as soon as we woke up. Before landing in Taipei, we were offered hot towels. Now, considering this is just a 3-hour flight, this first sector blew us away. And with just a one-hour connection, we headed straight to our next flight. Sadly, no time to visit any of China Airlines lounges. If you wanted to see what the lounges look like, feel free to check out our other China Airlines videos on the channel. If there's one frustration with Taipe's main international airport, it's that the terminal is very long. And while it's easy to connect, be prepared for some walking. Arriving at the next flight's gate, the boarding was just about to start, and we were greeted by a view of the gorgeous A350 waiting to whisk us across to London. After a few minutes, we were invited to board, and China Airlines uses separate [music] jet bridges for business class, which is always a nice touch. The A350 cabin in comparison is a lot more muted than the A321 and there's a warm natural glow which helps lift the muted metallic and wooden finishes that create a bit of a design drama in the cabin. The seats in the cabin are arranged in 1x 2x1 configuration [music] and the center pairs are perfect for those traveling together. While these seats don't offer doors, they are incredibly private. There are nice design touches such [music] as the blue storage pocket, the dragonclaw lamp, and there's plenty of storage, including a shallow pocket, a deeper one with a mirror, and a large biffold [music] tray table. The seat features lovely textures and details, and the linen available on this flight is substantial. The team also set up the seat as soon as you arrive. Although the mattress topper is more of a protector than offering any real padding, but it is lovely that they set up the bed even before you take a seat. It is one of my favorite seats in the [music] skies for sleep. I always find it spacious. As soon as I sat down, I was offered a welcome mocktail again. Now, sadly, there's no champagne. That's now only offered after takeoff. A nice upgrade to the experience, taking over from Northace, is the new Moschino immunity kits, which are a lot more luxurious and are stacked with products, including a luggage tag. Now, that's a nice touch. In the razable armrest, the noise cancelling headphones [music] are stored and they aren't terrible. The if is still the same with lots of options of movies, TV shows, and a great [music] moving map. Hot towels were offered before we pushed back and headed to the runway, [music] as well as the menus, which are pretty impressive, featuring three Michelin star [music] chefs. China Airlines always splits their menus into [music] Western and Asian cuisines. And now they also have some pretty interesting partnerships with bubble tea brands, for example. The wine [music] list is also incredible. After takeoff, the crew hurried into action, handing out fasttrack cards [music] for London, followed by an amuse bouch and after takeoff drink. Although I had entered into a new stage of delirium, this selection of snacks were delicious and paired perfectly with the champagne on offer. But nothing could prepare me for this Michelin starred meal ahead of me. It looked delicious and was partnered with a range of beautiful accompaniment. While it looked great, the food was okay, it's not as good as previous dishes I've had with a carrier. But one thing hasn't changed. The food always [music] looks great. Just look at these desserts. And the bowl is stunning, too. After dessert, I was basically forced the cheese plate, which I paired with a New Zealand Sven Blanc. Feast complete and still 11 hours ahead of us, I headed back to the Sky Bar, which is a smaller version of the Trip 7 product they have. is a lovely social space with a range of Taiwanese snacks, teas, coffees, and spirits. The crew are always so proud showing it off. Snacks safely stashed away at the seat. I headed to the toilet, which is stylish. It features abstract Taiwanese art, and it's even got its own soundtrack that plays throughout the flight. [music] Heading back to my seat, I set it up for sleep as I was pretty exhausted from the previous flight. Waking up about 6 hours later, I opted to dive into a mid-flight feast, which started with a cheeseburger, which was actually delicious. But for the sake of the review, I also opted for a cold noodle bowl, which was a little less tasty, but I guess it felt fresh. I was also encouraged to try a bubble tea as it's new to the airline and an exclusive partnership apparently, but the taste wasn't really for me. I watched a few movies afterwards, had another glass of champagne, and before we knew it, the cabin was coming to life for the second meal. Just before landing, I felt like the cabin crew went fullon lighting scene mode as we cycled through some really gorgeous lighting as the crew handed out hot towels. Our [music] tables were laid, and this time I had pre-ordered a maple bacon and pancake breakfast, which was delicious, even though I actually had no idea what meal I was meant to be eating at this [music] point. As this lengthy flight came to a close, I am left reflecting on one of my favorite airlines. China Airlines is a myriad of design details. Whether it's on the new A321 with its stunning interiors featuring butterflies, dappled lights, and textures, or the A350, which is the flagship of the airlines fleet, there are no shortage of elements that create a really comprehensive passenger experience. Sure, there are elements that would elevate the experience further, such as pajamas, the return of other Michelin star chefs, and in the case of the A321, slightly longer beds. But overall, these can be forgiven when the airline seems to be doing so much right. I love the fabrics, the textures used, the small design details like the beautiful platear, the coasters, the new menu design, and even the addition of the amenity kits feels more in tune with the rest of the passenger experience on the A350. I still love the bar area. is a lovely space to interact with the crew and having experienced the A321. I really love the time spent on creating a really special entryway. As I touch down in Heathrow, I can't help but think that the carrier is headed in the right direction. China Airlines continues to make small tweaks, modernizing the design pallet and appealing to a more international consumer. With news of the airline not resting on its laurels and updating its widebody interiors already, I hope this is yet another step forward. Thank you so much for watching once again. Please like, comment, subscribe and do get involved. And until next time, safe fly.

Today, I'm flying up to Heathrow from Switzerland to  avoid taxes. No, not those types of taxes. I'm talking departure taxes which are astronomical  if flying out of the UK but much lower if flying out of other points in Europe. After a gorgeous  morning hop up to London, we pull into Terminal 5. reviews.transcript_full: Today I'm flying from Bangkok to Hong Kong on a Cathay Pacific Airbus A330 This plane is definitely on the more dated side and features the oldest cabin in Cathay's fleet but hopefully in this video you'll see why even when you're not in their most modern cabin Cathay Pacific still offer a very solid experience... I started off my journey by taking the airport train from the centre of Bangkok to Suvarnabhumi Airport which is quick and only cost me 15 Thai Baht, or about 35 British Pence In the airport itself it's huge and somewhat overcrowded, and this is actually my first time flying out of this airport so I can't say I'm that familiar with it but my overall review of it is that it's just fine The Cathay Check-in area is in the S Zone and 2 hours before departure there was barely any queue and check-in was very quick Impressive as Cathay operate about 7 flights a day from here, mostly on massive aircraft like the Boeing 777  or Airbus A330 I was on today Airport security was pretty slow as they seemed to be doing a secondary inspection on almost everyone me included, but I'm pretty sure that was because I had a big cake and some fruit in my bag so it was probably my own fault once through to the departure zone there are loads of shops and restaurants and these cute little cleaning robots but the whole place is laid out in a few long thin corridors absolutely crammed with people and it's a big building so walking anywhere takes a while  One cool thing I noticed though which I haven't seen at other airports is the departure board which says how long it takes to reach each gate, and the direction you need to go to get there anyway, I made it to our gate and whilst watching this Myanmar Airways plane our plane for today just happened to appear out of nowhere, what are the chances hey? and some more perfect timing, that's another Cathay Pacific plane taking off in the background as ours parks at the gate Today we're flying on an 18 year old Airbus A330-300 with 262 seats in total 223 of which are in Economy class, and the Airbus A330 is really the workhorse of Cathay's short haul fleet, with them operating 43 in total making them the largest operator of he type in the world and as these old planes age out, they'll eventually be replaced with the much newer Airbus A330neo It was soon my turn to board, and whilst walking down the jetbridge another Cathay A330 was pulling up alongside showing just how many flights they do to bangkok Now, before we step on board, here are the stats and route map for today's flight, where a 40 minute late departure would see us land 20 minutes late in Hong Kong and all the pilots said about the delay is it was due to Chinese airspace restrictions which I'm slightly dubious of as I feel every flight I've ever taken in or around China has said the same thing but in anycase, here is the plane's cabin, and as someone who always sits by the window the A330 is probably my favourite plane to fly thanks to its 2-4-2 layout I chose seat 61A here which was free to select and the thing I like about this plane is I only have to climb over one person to reach the aisle so it feels much less claustrophobic if you're in one of the window aisles like I was today Now looking at the seat itself, legroom is good with 32" of seat pitch, much better than the 29 or 30" you'll see on most narrowbody aircraft It has a nifty folding tray table which folds out like this Then a small storage shelf just above that... and a little drink holder so you can have a drink without needing the table down The screen is pretty small at 9", maybe one of the most noticeable flaw of this slightly dated cabin and as you'll see shortly, the touchscreen is pretty laggy, but it's still perfectly usable another noticeable thing is the seatback is actually quite short I'm only 5'6" and you can see my head pokes above the headrest, so taller people might need to crank the headrest all he way up to be comfortable The headphones meanwhile are some of the best I've used in Economy, also, the crew went through the cabin offering blankets, I didn't bother get one though and the seat back pocket has plenty of little storage pouches so very convenient Now for the TV, it has Cathay Pacific's award-winning IFE system with a really good selection of movies, tv and games in fact, it was rated the best entertainment system in the world by Skytrax in 2025 However, on the A330 the tv is a bit too old to run it properly, so you can see here it's just a bit slow and laggy not an issue on their newer planes but it is noticeable here, especially coupled with the small-ish screen we started pushing back about 30 minutes behind schedule and the safety video started playing so here's that... one of the better safety videos I've seen actually and shows a nice bit of Hong Kong culture Now getting ready for takeoff the sun was just about to set which made for some very scenic views,  so stay tuned for that coming up in a second... Despite being a short 2.5 hour flight, this is Asia we're flying in so of course we had a full meal service I can't remember exactly but I'm pretty sure this was pork noodles with warm bread,  a fruit bowl and their signature Haagen Dazs ice cream on the side Everything was good and it's just a solid service for a short haul flight plus you get actual metal cutlery and Haagen Dazs is a premium touch There's also an inflight magazine with some interesting articles in both Chinese and English, especially this one about the cats of Hong Kong and speaking of cats, here's mine, he wants you to like and subscribe to support the channel and help fund his ice cream addiction back to the magazine though, it has a cool route map which I always love to see and they have a bit about their fleet, which I amusingly noticed already includes the 777X even though it's been delayed for years with no end in sight last of all as we approach Hong Kong for landing, they do have inflight WiFi but you have to pay for it so I didn't bother Worth noting that Business, First and Diamond status passengers get it for free though anyway, here's the landing in a dark but somewhat light-polluted Hong Kong also I noticed as we were landing a big gap in the fencing and lighting around the runway and that was actually due the the Air ACT Boeing 747 which had crashed into the sea 2 weeks before this flight and I guess they hadn't rebuilt the fence at that point so you could still see the big gap So as we disembark the plane it's time for my final thoughts... Cathay Pacific just offer a very solid shorthaul experience on their Airbus A330 It might not be as snazzy and modern as their A321neo or A350  but it's comfortable and the inflight service is top notch the price was very competitive too, being about 20% cheaper than a similar time with Thai Airways and similar to budget airlines like Hong Kong Express when you factor in things like food, seat selection and baggage costs... So I'll just give them a solid 80% score accross the board and on my airline tier list they keep their spot as a 10/10 airline in my opinion,  mainly because in the past I've had some really good experiences with them and even though this flight wasn't perfect, it was still very solid for a short haul trip now if you want to see something that was a 10/10 experience then check out the flight I took after this one a 14 hour flight from Hong Kong to London in their Airbus A350-1000 Economy Class which was just an exceptional flight in every way I'll also have reviews of Oman Air, Jet2, Air Europa and Air France to name a few coming in the next few weeks so subscribe to keep up to date with that like and leave a comment if you enjoyed this video thanks a lot for watching and good bye

reviews.transcript_full: Greetings everyone from Taipei Taoyuan Airport T1. Thank you for joinning us!  Today, we'll be flying to Fukuoka with Starlux Airlines, which has been honored with the Global Excellence Progress Award. Despite only being in operation for five years since its inaugural flight. Starlux Airlines has already achieved a 5-star airline rating and is highly regarded by industry experts. Let's experience it and see for ourselves the premium service Starlux Airlines offers. The check-in process was quick and efficient, with every detail clearly explained to passengers. Now at the security check area. There's quite a crowd here! Past security check, let's head to the Starlux Airlines lounge! This lounge is located in Terminal 1, near the A-side gates. Although the lounge is not large in area, cleverly utilizes the space to set up a resting area, a dining area, and a working area. Hot meals and snacks are still offered during non-meal times, along with a menu for ordering. Steamed brown sugar buns Stir-fried vegetables and mushroom rice Sweet and Sour Meat and Stir-Fried Chicken This bowl of Japanese ramen makes me feel like I am in Japan—delicious! The walkway to the boarding gate is so beautiful! The business class seats are arranged in a 1-2-1 staggered layout. The economy class features a 2-4-2 configuration. The cabin's color scheme feels very soothing while also exuding a sense of premium quality. The Snoopy-themed screen interface is a real eye-catcher. Time to check out my nest for the next two hours in the air! The legroom is a bit tight, but it's perfectly adequate for a quick nap during the two-hour flight. The flight attendant greeted us warmly and offered a hot towel and welcome drink. The safety video is quite entertaining! All set, and the plane is starting its pushback! Next, let's experience the complete journey of the Airbus A330-900 as it accelerates and takes off. I can really feel the powerful acceleration during takeoff, and the noise levels are remarkably well controlled! Taipei to Fukuoka covers a distance of 1,291 km, with an actual flight time of 1 h 50 min. The sky feast beginning! Japanese set meal. Cheers! The entertainment system offers an extensive content library, and the touchscreen is highly responsive. The lavatory maintains the same color scheme. Honestly, there's nothing particularly special about it. With a simple touch of the control panel, the seating position transitions into a bed. Night has fallen, and we'll soon be descending into Fukuoka. Let's enjoy Fukuoka's beautiful nightscape together!

reviews.transcript_full: In today's video, I take a gruelling 14 hour flight from Hong Kong to London in Cathay Pacific's brilliant Airbus A350-1000 Economy on what would actually end up being one of the best flights of my life so you'll find out why after flying over 60 airlines Cathay Pacific are one of my favourites and also I'll show you a useful trick which helped me get one of the best seats on the plane completely for free so buckle up and enjoy this Cathay Pacific Trip Report! and we start at an eye-wateringly early 5am in the morning in the impressive departure hall of Hong Kong Airport This is actually my first time flying Cathay Pacific Economy long haul, though back in 2018  I actually flew their Business Class from London to Tokyo via Hong Kong and remember those being some of the best flights of my life Just things like the cabin crew greeting me by name as I boarded and being able to order burgers in the middle of the flight not to mention that was my first time on an Airbus A350 too and the seat is really good plus their Business Class lounges in Hong Kong are probably the best in the world and up until that point in my life I'd only ever flown Business with British Airways and Virgin Atlantic which I don't think are bad airlines per se, but flying Cathay was just such an eye opener to what  a real world-class airline is like anyway, all that to say, I was exciting to be flying Cathay Pacific today, even if just in Economy... Hong Kong Airport is pretty good too, and I think is best summed up with the word efficiency though I feel like for an airport of this size there's actually not many shops or food and worryingly, the shopping area was filled with Labubu statues here I was thinking that trend had died down by now but clearly not in Hong Kong as you can see here, the airport is also pretty big, my gate happened to be all the way over here, literally the furthest you can get from the entrance so there was a lot of walking involved and I was lugging about fifteen kilograms of luggage so reaching the gate took a while and yes, that much carryon is vastly over their seven kilogram allowance... but they don't weigh bags at the gate, and I wanted to bring home a lot of souvenirs and snacks... anyway, now that the sun has started rising I have to say Hong Kong Airport is amazing for planespotting there are so many widebody aircraft here including a whole fleet of 747 cargo planes making it a feast for the eyes and the backdrop of skyscrapers and mountains makes for a lovely view in terms of seating though,  there isn't that much by each gate actually and I think if our plane was full then there wouldn't have been nearly enough seats for everyone Now here's our plane for today, a 7 year old Airbus A350-1000 registered B-LXI which had just arrived a few hours earlier from Boston it has 334 seats in total, 256 of which are Economy Class also this was the only one I caught on film but I got a great view of many cool takeoffs whilst I waited around for boarding to start and start it did, about 45 minutes before scheduled departure One way that Hong Kong Airport is living in the future is that they have these cool biometric gates so you don't even need to show your passport and boarding pass it just scans your face and lets you through after a few seconds hugely efficient and really speeds up boarding, not that that was necessary today as the flight probably wasn't even half full Now before we step on board here are the stats and route map for today's flight where we would actually take a pretty indirect route over North China around the Himalayas whilst avoiding Russia to land slightly early with a flight time of 13.5 hours, but about 15 hours actually sat on the plane due to a slightly delayed departure and as I alluded to in the intro, there's a good trick you can do with many airlines to find the best seat for free Cathay Pacific let you view the seat map online right up until departure I saw the best exit row seat 60K was actually still available, but cost £156 extra so I ignored it and thought I would be happy with the seat I'd been allocated 46K, this locked-in window seat but then the thought of spending 15 hours trapped by the window reminded me of this scene from White Lotus... So I went up to the gate agent, showed them the seat map and asked if I could have that exit row seat and to my surprise they did it for free very quickly so that was great you'll see how good this new seat was in a moment, but moral of the story is, just keep an eye on the online seat map and even if it's not an exit row you should be able to ask them to change you to the best seat available and even better, the two seats next to me ended up being empty too making this literally the best seating setup you can ask for in Economy Class obviously all this was largely due to the luck of having an empty flight,  but hey, I'm just reviewing my experience and this is just how it turned out now obviously legroom is fantastic and in this seat you get direct aisle access too and actually, the non-exit seats are also pretty good with 32" of seat pitch and 6" of recline the tv is a decent sized 11.1" too so overall it's a very competitive seat You get quite a nice soft pillow, no scratchy disposable cover here... and what is probably one of the better Economy Class blankets out there, soft and very large, plus I had 3 of them since my row was empty... a well padded adjustable headrest and a very nice wing view also something pretty rare to see in Economy Class these days, they actually give you a printed menu which first of all, just feels a bit more premium, but it's also nice being able to read it and decide what you want well ahead of time, rather than making an on the spot decision when the food cart comes round also the entire drinks menu is here, so you don't have to guess at what they have or don't have also they give everyone a water bottle after boarding, vital on a long flight like this and the headphones are actually pretty decent for Economy Class... though I've recently started using this Bluetooth transmitter instead which lets me connect my wireless headphones instead and makes for an infinitely better audio experience Amazon affiliate link in the description if you want one for yourself This is the new Naked Gun movie by the way, extremely stupid but I enjoyed it a lot and that brings me to the IFE System, which is actually really good so good in fact that Skytrax ranked them as having the best inflight entertainment of any airline in the world this year and they basically have everything you could want, loads of movies in many different languages a nice slick interface, tv shows, music, games quality of life things like airport guides and connecting gate info two external cameras in very high definition which I always enjoy watching... plus the inflight map is pretty good too they also have the full inflight menu here in addition to the paper menu handed out during boarding and the full Cathay Pacific Shop, which has a satisfying range of quality-looking branded merch Boarding finished very quickly due to how empty the flight was but of course, the pilot announced a 40 minute delay due to of course, air traffic restrictions over China which seems incredibly common due to how restricted China's airspace is and was mildly annoying, but we still ended up arriving 20 minutes early in London so it wasn't the end of the world and now here's the safety video, which I liked a lot,  makes me want to visit Hong Kong again and eat some claypot rice with a side of egg tart and milk tea After a bit of taxiing and some more waiting we were finally ready for takeoff and I definitely made the right seat choice as the view of Hong Kong on takeoff was jaw-dropping so get ready for that, coming up now... and here's something weird you can see here so genuinely curious if any pilots watching could explain... after fully raising the flaps the pilots lowered them again, only to raise them a few seconds later here they are going down after being fully raised... and here they are going up again... please leave a comment if you have any idea why? anyway, apart from that the views of Hong Kong taking off were incredible The contrast of the skyscrapers and mountains with the bay make for one of the coolest takeoff views in the world and hear you can see Guanzhou, which is just an absurdly big city and it has one of the busiest airports in the world which you can see here Pretty soon after takeoff breakfast was served, and the service was rapid due to how empty the plane was and I can report that this was easily the best airplane breakfast I've ever had mainly because they had proper dim sum and it was actually pretty good, which I've never seen on a plane before also metal cutlery make it feel fancy There was a prawn dumpling, a meatball thing and this yellow dumpling, all very tasty Then a well-seasoned congee which I mixed the meatball into They also give you a towelette, butter, jam and a bread roll which was actually warmed up then lastly a strawberry yoghurt, fresh fruit and orange juice to drink Then on top of all that I got a Hong Kong milk tea to drink which is pretty big in Hong Kong and also a unique thing offered by Cathay Pacific Another cool feature of the seat is they have a device holder built in not so useful on the exit row seat, but it's well placed here on the regular seats I got up to stretch my legs, and you can see here just how empty the plane was, back here I would say it was maybe only 20% full, with a lot of people just laying down on a full row and I'm aware Cathay took a very big hit after Covid, but I'm surprised they still seem to be struggling to fill planes Now for a loo review, toothbrush kits are available but I had to ask the crew for one and the toilets were kept clean throughout, with crew constantly going in to clean them Also, this is by far the biggest sink I can remember seeing in a plane toilet even when compared to most Business Class loos Another nice quality of life feature is they show you the flight timeline letting you know when to expect food and drinks services throughout the flight Halfway through the flight it was time for meal number two, and I got  sweet and sour pork with pineapple, rice and vegetables then for the starter a chicken and jicama salad, which I had to look up, apparently a jicama is a vegetable from Mexico then fruit, Haagen Dazs ice cream, and warm bread and butter to round things off and ginger ale to drink The cabin then stayed dark for the rest of the flight prety much, and I ended up watching Mulan If you get hungry or thirsty there's a drink and snack stand in the galley, plus you can just ask the crew to get you either cup noodles or a Hong Kong egg tart and I got an egg tart which was a nice mid-flight snack and all I needed as the two main meals were tasty and filling enough then right before landing the crew came round and handed out these Palmier biscuits which were also very nice so overall a fantastic flight when it came to food and Cathay Pacific clearly know how to  keep you well fed throughout a super long flight We then began our descent into a very overcast London which brings me to the very last feature of this review, the WiFi all I can really say is that it exists, and it was too expensive for me to bother trying it would be nice to see them catch up to many competitors who offer free WiFi Like Qatar Airways or British Airways but that's pretty much the only criticism I have for Cathay today... and now the landing... it was raining when we landed so the window instantly fogged up but to summarise, if you couldn't tell already, I just really like Cathay Pacific and they're probably my favourite airline and this super long haul flight confirmed that for me and as someone who mainly flies Oneworld Airlines, Cathay are my airline of choice when flying to Asia if the price is right also this was a personal record for me, it took maybe 4 minutes from stepping off the plane to passing through customs and there was no queue at all for immigration so that was very satisfying, and I just made a quick stop at M&S to buy these cookies,  which are the best in the world by the way, before heading home I used miles to pay for this flight and it cost a very reasonable 31,000 Avios plus £81 and sure, not everyone will be as lucky as me and get an almost empty flight to relax on but I'm just judging based on my experience on this flight so I'm giving Cathay an 82.5% and putting them up to a 10/10 on my airline tier list, the same rank as Singapore Airlines, who are maybe a bit better if I'm being completely objective but either way, I think Cathay have earned their place at the top of my list Now if you're looking for something else to watch then check out my recent review of Oman Air's Business Class a super underrated airline with one of the best Business seats out there and some fantastic food as well as part of this trip I also flew Oman Air's 787 Economy, and Cathay Pacific's short haul A330 and I have many more videos in the pipeline so don't forget to like and subscribe to stay up to date with all that! thanks a lot for watching and good bye!
