reviews.transcript_full: This week we're heading to Philadelphia on American Airlines, but we'll hardly touch on that.  Instead, I want to focus on money.  More specifically, Delta Airlines and two interesting aspects of their business.  First, we'll look at an interesting way that they make money,  and then we'll examine, investigate, get eyes on one strange way that they save money.  Oh, and we'll also touch on the history of airport lounges.  Why in the world are there these semi-exclusive buffets in almost every airport?  We're starting this one in Boston at an airport lounge.  Unfortunately, it's the American Airlines lounge.  We're not flying Delta here, but I do want to focus on them.  And let's start with a simple question.  Are they a profitable airline?  This may sound a bit silly, they're the world's largest airline by revenue,  and the most profitable if we don't include the privately held Emirates.  But are they actually making money flying people around?  Well, rather interestingly, the answer is no, not really.  Delta does a pretty good job at breaking out all of their revenue sources  in their financial statements, and from all of that, we can figure out that the core airline  part of the business, you know, flying people around, runs at roughly a 2.5% loss.  But once we add in their loyalty program, and a few other, miscellaneous revenue sources,  but mostly the loyalty program, the overall company runs at a 10.5% profit margin.  Delta is not alone here.  In fact, we can see, from some great analysis by visual approach analytics,  that the five biggest US airlines all have similar, if not more dramatic economics.  Now, I think we all know that loyalty programs for airlines are massive money spinners.  One of those classic old sayings is that airlines are credit card companies that fly planes as a side hustle.  But the scale and profitability of these programs and the way in which Delta,  specifically, has transformed their business over the past decade to really revolve around their  loyalty program is truly remarkable, or ridiculous. I'll let you be the judge of that.  I want to focus on Delta's shift towards premium travel and loyalty revenue,  and how these have gone hand in hand to make them one of the most resilient airlines in the world.  At least, resilient in terms of airlines. This is not an easy business to be in.  So let's start with the premium travel part of this picture.  Over the last decade, Delta has successfully pivoted towards the premium market.  If we look at some numbers, back in 2011-2012, before this pivot, roughly 20% of the seats on their  planes were premium, think business or domestic first class. But of these seats, only 14% of them  were generating any revenue. They just weren't able to sell them. Now look, they weren't empty,  they were being given away as upgrades to high status loyalty members. But today, this is flipped.  Roughly 30% of the seats on their planes are now premium, and they're selling 88% of them,  for cash, real money. So how have they done this? Well, there's a few factors with the first  big one being they simply dropped the price, at least on short hold domestic flights.  Back in 2010, a first class seat was roughly 13 times the price of an economy seat.  Today, it's more like three to five times the price. But they've also better segmented their  cabins. There's now first class premium economy, comfort plus standard economy,  basic economy. Instead of having this huge jump up to first or business class,  they now have a bunch of more affordable little hops that entice passengers to buy a more premium  option. Of course, we can't forget the actual experience. They have put a lot of money into  upgrading their premium offerings, both in the sky, with the seats, and on the ground in the  lounges. This has not only helped them generate more high margin revenue. It's also helped them to  become the world's most valuable airline brand for the last seven years running, at least according  to brand finance, a business valuation and strategy consulting firm based in the UK. But at the same  time as this premium push was occurring, they've also turned their loyalty programs, Sky Miles,  into a cash machine. Sky Miles has been around since 1981, but it really started to print money  when Delta launched their first Sky Miles credit card, with American Express back in 1996.  It was one of the earliest airline credit card programs, and it initially started as a nice  little partnership that led to some side income. But it slowly over the last three decades become a  major driving force behind Delta's profitability. The amount to MX is paying out to Delta over the years  has grown from under $2 billion in 2010 to over $7 billion in 2024. And they have a long term  target of growing this to over $10 billion in the near future. This is seen as highly profitable  and durable revenue that now generates a disproportionate share of Delta's profits relative to their  airline business. I mean, they're an airline, it's a bit crazy. But how does this all work in practice?  Let's quickly run through it, and I was a bit surprised with one specific element of all of this.  Let's say you sign up for a Delta Sky Miles gold American Express credit card. Congratulations.  And then you spend, let's say, $60 on an annual wine tracker plus subscription. Not only do you now  get alerts on great wine deals, you also receive 60 Delta Sky Miles for that purchase. Those  miles aren't just appearing out of nowhere. MX is purchasing them from Delta, but how? Well, the  merchant, me, in this case, receives something like $58.50 after the interchange fees. Basically,  MX takes a cut of $1.50 from that sale. Out of that $1.50, MX has to spend, and these are not  public figures, but it's roughly estimated, around two cents per mile. So out of this transaction,  Delta is getting a dollar 20, and MX is getting 30 cents. This seems heavily skewed towards Delta,  doesn't it? And it is, to some degree. But we'll get back to MX in a second. Without getting too  deep into the balance sheet and accounting here, I was always under the impression that airlines  basically take the money for the miles and book it as an IOU. They have to keep it as a liability  towards future travel. They're not booking the money made from selling miles as revenue straight  away. Those miles will be used for seats on planes at some future date, and when that date comes,  they then get to recognize that money as revenue. I was always under the impression that they were  essentially arbitraging the value that they sell them out versus the value at which they get  redeemed. For instance, if they're selling miles to MX for two cents, they want you to redeem  them at a value of less than two cents, and this is almost always the case. They control which seats  get released when and how much they charge for them, so they'll always make a decent cut. It's  basically a casino and they're the house. But of course, it isn't quite that simple, and this  is the bit that really surprised me. They're actually able to instantly recognize a large chunk  of the sales of miles as marketing revenue. This is truly a beautiful business. This means that  from the roughly $6.9 billion in cash that Delta received from MX in 2023, they were able to  instantly book just under three billion of it as their marketing cut. MX is using their branding  on the cards, so Delta gets paid. This percentage seems insanely high to me, but it seems to be  roughly the industry standard, and it's almost entirely profit. Now let's get back to MX. They're  handing over most of the money they make on the interchange fees, so why are they doing this deal?  Well firstly, they don't mind because they're able to make a healthy profit off the annual card fees  and off the interest payments from revolving credit card debts. Delta cards represent 21%  of MX's worldwide card member loans. They generate around $15.5 billion a year in net interest income,  so once you take into account credit losses, they're likely generating around $2.5 to $3 billion  a year in interest income from Delta card holders. MX also doesn't mind giving Delta such a big cut  because it helps them win new affluent customers. And this is why I emphasized earlier that the  premium market push goes hand in hand with the increased loyalty revenues. If we zoom out here,  the cycle is fairly simple. Delta goes more premium and they improve their overall brand. This leads  to them competing less on price and having a wealthier customer base. The perfect fit for the  already premium MX. Co-branded credit cards are perfect here. Affluent people want all of the  perks on their premium travel with Delta. And so they get and spend with these credit cards.  This makes Delta more highly profitable revenue that isn't tied to flying, which in turn allows  them to spend more to maintain and improve their further premium position in the market and the  cycle goes on and on until Delta is the only airline left and the sun has engulfed the entire  solar system. No, not quite. They're of course competitors, but Delta is seemingly leading the  packier in terms of how much money they're able to squeeze out of the credit card market.  So that's one way that they make a lot of money, but let's now head to Philly where we'll  discover a unique way that they save a lot of money.  New York is out there somewhere. We're making a quick pit stop in New York here at LaGuardia Airport.  I've stopped in at the American Airlines Admiral's Club. Now, this lounge, well not this specific one  because they recently rebuilt LaGuardia, but the original LaGuardia Admiral's Club was the first  ever lounge built in the world, all the way back in 1939. Why here? Well it comes down to the airport  and the man it's named after. Mayor Fierrello LaGuardia. Back in the early 30s, New York's main airport  was Floyd Bennett Fields in Brooklyn. It was located a long way from Manhattan, so airlines shifted  their New York services to New York in New Jersey. Fierrello did not like this at all. In 1934 when  he was flying home from Chicago on TWA, his plane landed at New York, like almost every other New York  flight back then, but he refused to get off. His ticket said New York so he demanded to be flown  to New York. After some back and forth, the crew obliged to flying just him to Bennett Fields.  It was a pierced hunt, but it lit the fuse for a new airport closer to the city. By 1939,  that new airport opened in Queens. It was modern, glamorous, and the mayor loved it. Now, there's  often repeated story out there that LaGuardia himself had a large office at this new airport,  and that this caused a lot of criticism from the press. This criticism,  eventuated with him abandoning the office and American Airlines taking it over,  building the first airport lounge. This is not quite true. He did have an office at the airport,  he loved greeting visiting dignitaries, and yes, the press criticized it. But the lounge space  that American Airlines leased was planned from the start. American Airlines were major supporters of  this new airport, and this allowed them to lease a space and open an invitation only members club  for VIPs, celebrities, and politicians. reviews.transcript_full: Today we're talking about what it's like to fly business class on Copa Airlines. I took not one but two flights recently from Panama City, Panama to Jamaica for the first time as a Jamaican citizen. And while both were in business class, they were not quite created equal. Oh, and I'm also giving you a tour inside the Copa Lounge in Terminal 2 at Tokaman International Airport in Panama City. So, if you're wondering whether flying business class on Copa is worth it, stick around and make your own decision. Let's start with the flight experience for both flights. Copa Airlines is Panama's national carrier and is part of the Star Alliance. On my first leg of my Jamaica trip, I had a more traditional seat layout, the kind you're probably used to. There was a built-in screen in the back of the seat in front of me with the controls and tray table in the armrest. Behind the seat, they had a light and associated controls and a little nook that had a cup holder and ports. There was plenty of leg room with a little space for your feet. They have one button for your legs and another one for the seat to recline. The seats recline a decent amount for you to get really comfortable for a quick nap, but I couldn't sleep cuz I was too excited for this trip. Now, this is where it gets interesting. My second business class flight back home to Panama from Jamaica had a completely different setup. No TV screen inside at first because the screen actually popped out of the armrest and was adjustable. You just push the button to release it and then pull it up and rotate it to your liking. It could be controlled by the buttons on the TV and also on the screen. Controls for your seat are located on the center console and there was decent leg room. The tray table was in the armrest to my left. On both flights, we were offered water or orange juice while people were boarding. Before the flight took off, flight attendants came around and took your lunch orders. The two options were a quesadilla with turkey and cheese, and the other was a ham and cheese sandwich. Oh, and it comes with real silverware. I actually enjoyed the lunch on both flights. I will say I missed having the snacks you usually would get in economy, so I asked for some. They always have great snacks that I end up becoming addicted to living in Panama. The team members on both flights were very pleasant, kind, and helpful. The Copa Lounge in the Tokman Airport in Panama City, Panama can be found on the second floor if you take an immediate left after security in terminal 2. yt_comments.text: some more facts about pegasus for those who wonder: - planes are named after daughters of the employees. - most of 321neos are based in Istanbul SAW, 320neos and 737 are based in secondary cities (Antalya, Izmir, Ankara and others.) - PGSUS is the code for its stock in Istanbul Stock Exchange. a couple of years ago, it joined to BIST30 index (top 30 stock in istanbul exchange). never pays dividends. - seats don't recline. - there is no screen in seats but in many planes there is in flight entertainment used via wifi. no internet, tv shows and movies etc. (paid or premium packages) but you can check your location in map, and other flight info in real time (this is free) - bolbol points are useful especially to buy upgrades. one return flight would give enough points for your next flights meal or seat selection.

reviews.transcript_full: This is an ultra low cost carrier, and I am as shooketh as you are.  The airline Pegasus, the flight Frankfurt to Antalya, the video a deep dive into one  of the best run low cost carriers out there.  Because today I will take you along a journey on Istanbul based Pegasus, where we will explore  what they do differently, look at how they doubled in size over the past decade while still  remaining one of the most profitable airlines on the planet and find out if they offer  a good value after all.  I am glad you have decided to join me on this trip, so let's get going.  Aviation geeks and frequent flyers welcome to this new episode of our flight review series  Brutally Honest.  I am at Frankfurt Airport this 3rd morning about to fly down to Sania Antalya, the heart  of Turkey's Mediterranean coast.  And for the majority of travelers, a trip to Antalya begins on one of two airlines.  Sun Express, which is a joint venture between Turkish Airlines and Loftansa, or Turkey's  second largest airline, Pegasus.  The airline is headquartered at Istanbul's second airport, Sabihagguktsin, where it operates  a massive hub, offering countless connecting attenuaries between almost 150 destinations  in 50 different countries.  This already differentiates the carrier from most of its ultra-low-cost peers, where  connections are despised.  Even on my flight from Frankfurt to Antalya, they were connecting passengers.  Checking in in front of me was a couple travelling via Antalya to Kirgistan's capital Bishkek.  This makes the carrier an attractive choice for price-conscious travelers on plenty of  thinner routes.  We actually flew with them back in 2018 from Vienna to Kuwait before non-stop flights  between the two cities existed.  We're heading to Terminal 2 here at Frankfurt Airport right now, where Pegasus operates  out of.  As I was amongst the first passengers there, check in was a breeze, and we can already  make our way to the gate.  The fare I booked includes a checked bag.  Pegasus offers bundles ranging from basic, all the way to Comfort Flex, at pretty fair prices  if you ask me.  With the most premium package being just 40% more expensive than the cheapest, the airline  naturally guides you to pick the more premium bundles.  Getting you to pay up is something the airline is really good at.  As of the first quarter of 2025, Pegasus makes around 29 euros per passengers in so-called  and silery revenue, meaning things that go beyond the package that you booked.  That's even more than textbook low cost carrier Ryanair, which reported around 2350 in  an silery revenue per passenger in the last fiscal year.  Among these ancillaries are an option to make your ticket flexible for 13 euros, selecting  seats which costs at least 12 euros to, making the advantage bundle more attractive for  me, so I switched to that which included most seats for free to see how they make you  pick the more expensive bundle.  A popular example of how companies structure prices to make you pick more expensive options  is Apple.  You'll see the cheapest iPhone and might think you'll get that, but then a bit more  storage isn't that much more expensive.  But then you might want to go for the pro phone after all, and then get extra storage  for the pro too.  Pegasus employs the exact same strategy very well.  By pricing their different bundles so close together, the barrier to spend more money  is low enough for people to pay up, and I am a prime example for how well that works.  Other charges you might want to know about are their additional baggage fees which are  insane, 100 euros for an additional 20 kg, that is egregious even Ryanair only won 60  bucks for that.  Compared to that the fees for transporting various types of sporting equipment seem fine,  but the one thing you'll want to splurge on is their pre-order hot meals, but more on  those later.  Pegasus also offers a reward program, I'm specifically not calling it a frequent flyer  program because it does not offer any perks for frequent flyers, but with each flight  you earn ballboard points that you can use towards future purchases with the airline.  Ballboard is Turkish and means abundant.  During a low cost airline their flights use remote stands here in Frankfurt, with their  flights to Ankara, Istanbul and Antalya boarding next to each other.  When I booked this trip I had to choose between Pegasus and this fairly new Turkish charter  airline called Mavigook Airlines, and back then their flight was scheduled to be operated  by a 737.  But had I known they'd send their flagship triple 7 today.  Something as down to Antalya today is Tango Charlie, November Charlie Kilo, a 2020 build  Airbus A320 Neo.  Pegasus used to be a big 737 operator, but in recent years they have switched almost completely  to A320 Neo family aircraft, having 46 A320 Neo's and 61 A321 Neo's in their fleet  as of July 2025.  They're also supposed to get another A321 Neo basically every month for the rest of  the decade.  Currently they're left with just 977, but late last year have placed an order for 1077  Max10s with another 100 options, so the airline is certainly not done growing.  One thing that has amused me for years is how Pegasus underlines on every single one of  their planes that they are an Iata member.  They're so proud of that, even though well almost every airline is an Iata member.  North Korea's Air Corio is an Iata member.  Anyway entering the plane through door 1 we are greeted by a typical low-cost cabin.  Arranged in the A320's usual 333 configuration this A320 Neo holds 186 passengers, just  shy of its rated maximum, but in line with what you will find on most other low-cost carriers  including the A320 Neo's of Air Asia and Wizair.  The seats do not come with adjustable headrests or headrest covers.  For my height of 180cm the legroom could be worse.  I can manage these 3 hours to Antalya.  There's also a standard tray table as well as a high literature compartment.  All air vents and personal reading lights can be found in the ceiling above.  I picked seat 4A for the engine view of course.  Now let's sit back relax and get ready for departure.  Shortly after climbing out of Frankfurt the  pre-ordered meals were handed out.  This is where Pegasus shines.  A good hot meal is something I am always willing to pay up for.  There is just something about having a good meal on a mode of transit, be it on a plane  or on a train that I just find deeply relaxing.  Looking out the window moving across the globe and having something delicious to enjoy  that with, I love that.  And Pegasus offers an unbelievable variety of hot meals to pre-order on virtually all  of their flights.  There are breakfasts, sandwiches, wraps, schnitzel, pasta, steak, chicken, gifte, fish,  kits meals, salad, fruit, a hard-shaped cake, vegetarian kosher infant gluten-free, low-fat  low-sodium, low-calorie meals if you don't find a meal you like to pre-order here, something's  wrong with you.  Ranging from 5 to 8 euros for the sandwiches and 11 to 20 euros for the meals, I also find  the prices totally fine.  And quality wise, you're unlikely to complain either as Pegasus uses Do and Co as their caterer.  Do and Co is a high-end catering company that does upscale in-flight catering for airlines  such as Qatar Airways, Turkish Airlines and Austrian Airlines as well, headquartered in  my hometown of Vienna and founded by Mr Do-Dun, an Istanbul-born businessman of  Turkish and Austrian ancestry.  This is also why Do and Co does both fantastic Turkish and Austrian dishes, which is why I  had to see what their schnitzel is like.  We've got chicken schnitzel, which is a bit atypical, but Veel gets very tough when  heated up on airplanes and a turkey-based airline won't serve pork for obvious reasons, so  chicken it is.  It was served alongside classic Austrian parsley potatoes and a lemon wedge, wrapped to keep  the seeds from falling onto the dish like it would be in a fine Viennese eatery.  We've also got a cold bread roll and butter, a little side salad with a bell-sameg vinaigrette  and some chocolate mousse for dessert.  And then, and I completely forgot about that, the advantage bundle that I booked also includes  a sandwich.  All in all, for 11 euros, that is an amazing meal and absolutely worth its price.  Just listen to this, that's actually reasonably crispy for something heated up on a plane.  Not included in the meal was a beverage, and everything, including water, needs to be paid  extra for on Pegasus.  Our low-cost carrier water price comparison shows that Pegasus is in line with what most  other European low-cost carriers charge, which is a bit more than you'll have to in other  parts of the world.  Other beverages, hot or cold, non-alcoholic and alcoholic, as well as snacks and a limited  number of hot meals can also be purchased on board.  Pegasus equip their planes with Inflex Equilux, Arrow, Lux1, Wireless Digital Services platform.  A variety of movies and TV shows are available to stream to your device, those are included  with the more expensive bundles or can be purchased on board for an extra 4 euros.  Some games and an Inflite-Mapping application is offered too.  Since the plane is not equipped with power ports though, you should charge your device  before the flight or bring a power bank.  The crew did two rounds of service on this flight, or you could say two attempts at selling  you snacks and beverages, one ride after takeoff, and one around an hour before landing.  And as we're beginning our descendant to Andalia, I have to underline my admiration for  how well run this airline is.  Obviously it's a low-cost carrier, therefore I won't complain about the limited legroom  missing power ports or somewhat stiff seats.  Also, most of the luxuries displayed in this video were paid extra 4.  The windows seat reservation, the sandwich, checked bag and Inflite and attainment combined  came as a bundle that cost 30 euros more than the cheapest one would have, and the pre-ordered  hot meal was another 11 euros.  However, in total I paid just 130 euros for this one-way ticket, and 130 euros for a  three hour flight, including a checked bag, seat reservation, streamed to my device entertainment,  and a good hot meal is more than alright if you'd ask me.  And I believe it is the value that health pecs has grown so rapidly over the previous few  years.  Obviously the cost-based for running an airline is way lower in Turkey compared to other  European countries, but they don't shy away from making good strategic decisions as well.  For example, over the past few years, as they have gradually switched from 737-800s to  primarily Airbus A321-Nios, their average number of passengers per flight has also increased  from 149 A-Decadego to 182 last year.  This improves the economics of each soul seat even further, and combined with their young  fleet, the great value offered by their Enceleries, and the low cost-based that a country  like Turkey offers, while having access to many high-income markets in the region, and  its efficient route network planning, enabling fairly high aircraft utilization, and play  of good connections, it is no wonder that the airline is amongst the most profitable  in the world, regularly achieving double-digit operating margins.  That might not sound like much, but airlines are notoriously thin margin businesses, where  most struggle to even get close to 10%, let alone surpass that consistently.  So if you come across a good fare on Pegasus, and you're willing to sacrifice a bit of  seat comfort, I think you'll have a splendid time with them.  And with that, welcome to Package Holiday Hell.  Welcome to Antalya.  I hope you have enjoyed this video and will join me again on another trip soon, special  thanks to all those of you who support our work with a paid sponsorship.  Thanks to you, we can take our time to do deep dives into airlines such as this one,  and spend more time on videos that might not be that interesting, but are still useful  if you consider flying with set airline.  If you want to support our mission to create the most detailed no-nonsense flight reviews  possible, click on the join button beneath this video to learn more, where the lowest  support tier starts at just 2 euros per month, which is just 24 euros per year.  Even that amount helps us pay for some extra services like the meal on this flight, who  showcase as much of an airline's product as possible.  But whether you are a sponsor, a subscriber, or simply stopping by for this one video,  thank you very much for watching and coming along.  If you're down for another video, why not check out this episode about Pegasus main competitor,  Sonic Express, a holiday carrier that's a joint venture between Loftunza and Turkish  airlines and somehow ended up with neither of their characters leaving very little impression.

reviews.transcript_full: Good day and welcome back to the Flying Doctor channel.  On today's one minute flight review, we'll go from Belan, Brazil to São Paulo on a Latam A320 in  premium economy. I use the self-service kiosk to check in and print my boarding pass before  heading airside to catch a few special livery's.  Premium economy with Latam is similar to your business where all seats are economy but the  middle seat is blocked. The FA created each passenger by name and handed them a bottle of water  before we were pushed back and sky-borne. About 45 minutes after takeoff, I was offered the choice  of a frittata or sandwich. I opted for the beef and cheese sandwich which came with a bag of chips  and granola bar. Lager room was comfortable and power options were available if I needed.  No IFE on the seatback but a catalog of movies and TV shows are available after connecting to  the inflate Wi-Fi. The ability to message and serve the web costs a few extra bucks.  I paid $154 for the premium economy seat which was only about $30 on top of basic economy.  Considering you get a light meal, early boarding and additional baggage allowance,  I think it's definitely worth the extra money.  If you want more information on this particular flight, check out the following  through review in the description. As always, thanks for watching. See ya!

reviews.transcript_full:
Today, we're flying ITA Airways Business Class aboard a 
brand-new Airbus A330neo from the Maldives to Rome The video features the full Business Class experience on
ITA Airways (seat, meals, service, entertainment, amenities) Welcome to the International Airport of the Maldives We're taken to the main terminal by a Four Seasons luxury car Check-in is smooth, with dedicated Business Class counters We’re taken by bus to the remote aircraft stand The new international terminal at Velana International Airport 
in the Maldives is officially set to open this summer The Maldives’ old terminal was built for 1.5 million passengers
but now serves over 2 million, causing major congestion The new Maldives airport expansion will ease congestion 
and handle the growing number of travelers This is the Airbus A330neo that will fly us to the Maldives
(aircraft registration: EI-TYC; named Stefano Baldini)  ITA Airways operates a total of 23 long-haul aircraft in its fleet:
11 Airbus A330-900neo, 6 Airbus A350, and 6 Airbus A330-200 ITA Airways' fleet has an average age of 5.7 years Have you ever flown with ITA Airways?
If so, what was your experience? Leave a comment ITA Airways' A330neo Business Class cabin is arranged in a 
1-2-1 configuration, giving each passenger direct aisle access 6L is my Business Class seat for the flight to the Rome The seat model is the Thompson Vantage XL,  
an excellent seat type used by several leading airlines What makes ITA’s version unique is the bespoke Italian styling Window seats alternate between true window seats (set closer
to the fuselage) and aisle-adjacent seats (set closer to the aisle) In the center section, seats are arranged in a paired layout, 
designed with couples or traveling companions in mind ITA Airways' A330neo Business Class cabin features a
stylish decor, reflecting Italy’s legendary design sensibility A hot towel and welcome drink are offered upon boarding Nineteen athletes, including Olympic and Paralympic
medalists, demonstrate the procedures in the safety video We're leaving the gate at 1 pm local time (on-time departure) We pass a Dreamliner of Neos, an Italian airline specializing 
in leisure travel and a competitor of ITA Airways Male Airport has 2 runways measuring 45 × 3,200 m
(148 × 10,499 ft) and 60 × 3,400 m (200 × 11,150 ft) ITA Airways' Airbus A330neo aircraft
are powered by Rolls-Royce Trent 7000 engines The Trent 7000 engine delivers a thrust of 72,000 pounds
(one engine has the push of 100 Ferraris racing flat out) This enables the A330neo to achieve a non-stop range
of up to 7,200 nautical miles (approximately 13,334 kilometers) We get some terrific views of the Maldives after takeoff The Maldives' islands and atolls
are the visible tips of an oceanic volcanic mountain range The Maldives has 1192 coral islands & sandbanks: 200
islands are inhabited & 140 islands are home to resorts Let's have a closer look at the
ITA Airways Airbus A330neo Business Class seat The seat features a 17-inch high-definition TV screen A spacious footwell is located under the TV Passengers can hang their jackets with a built-in hanger The seat's side cabinet keeps belongings handy
and also holds a modern, elegant light and the power ports The side table under the cabinet holds the entertainment 
handset and seat controls for easy comfort adjustments The seat's tray table is smoothly released via a simple latch Let's explore ITA Airways' Business Class amenities The kit is an elegant clutch in sustainable and reusable canvas,
and contains a dental kit, eye mask, socks, and earplugs Business Class passengers also receive a second kit: a soft 
cosmetics bag by international wellness company QC Terme The kit includes shower gel, shampoo, 
sanitizer, face cream, body cream, and hand butter Bedding includes a pillow, duvet and slippers Noise-cancelling headphones are also provided Let’s explore today's inflight dinner menu ITA Airways’ Business Class wine list features 
a curated selection of fine Italian and international wines Aperitif, served with mixed nuts Starter: pumpkin and parmesan cheese flan
with mushrooms and toasted pumpkin seeds Turnip greens Orecchiette pasta: Italian pasta dressed
with anchovies of Cetara, tomatoes and bread crumble Main course: braised beef cheek, 
accompanied by roasted cubed pumpkin and sautéed chard Fresh sliced seasonal fruit plate Dessert: tiramisu with coffee glaze and dark cocoa crumble ITA Airways' A330neo Business Class has 3 lavatories: one 
at the front, and two shared with Premium Economy at the rear With the push of a button, the Business Class 
seat reclines into a fully flat bed The bed measures 80 inches (203 centimeters) in length Let's explore ITA Airways' inflight entertainment The program offers the latest Italian movies, Hollywood 
blockbusters, TV shows and immersive music playlists ITA Airways offers Wi-Fi on its Airbus A330neo fleet The flight path takes us over Abu Dhabi We encounter some turbulence in the Iraqi airspace It's time for a midflight snack: assorted Italian cheese board
served with pear mustard, dried apricot and pistachios A light dinner is served 90 minutes prior to arrival: 
a slice of gourmet Napolitan stone baked pizza The pizza is served with a walnut brownie as dessert We're approaching the Italian airspace ITA Airways is Italy’s national airline,
founded in 2020 as the successor to Alitalia With its striking blue livery and Italian flair,  ITA Airways 
represents a new chapter in Italy’s aviation story ITA’s fleet features modern Airbus aircraft, including the A220, 
A320neo, and the sleek A330neo & A350 for long-haul routes Despite a challenging start in a competitive market, ITA
is expanding its network across Europe, the U.S., and beyond Thank you for watching my video about 
ITA Airways' Airbus A330neo Business Class

As soon as I sat down in my very nicely 
equipped all aisle access flat bed business   class seat- like when I really sat down to 
settle in, the first question that came to   mind was: Wait a minute, is this seat 
actually better than their old 2-2-2?  Everyone always wants a modern all aisle access 
flatbed, for the record, myself included. But,   this was the first time that I’ve ever sat 
in those traditional lie flat seats followed   by a tight squeeze of a staggered seat just 2 
hours later and well, I have opinions to share.  By the way, the price that I paid for this and 
every flight I take is always in the description.  Let me welcome any of you who may be new to the 
channel, my name is Kevin. I’m here to give you   a self-funded and honest look at some of the 
best- and some of the not so best- airlines and   hotels in the world, which I’ve been bringing 
to you full time for the past four years.   Check out my hundreds of videos, scan 
the QR code or click the link in the   description to learn more about how I do 
things. Let’s get into the trip report.  I just arrived here in Santiago from Sao Paulo 
and when I say “just” I mean seconds ago and now   I need to high tail it through what honestly felt 
like a never ending maze from the new additions   here at Santiago’s international airport. 
Editions that Google Earth hasn’t even added yet.  I was meant to have around a 2 hour layover. 
Short, but relaxed and was really looking   forward to visiting the LATAM lounge since I 
love their lounge in Sao Paulo and this one   is meant to be even better. But, the winds 
over the Andes today were extreme and so   we had to take a very out of the way route to 
get here, adding an hour to that first flight   and meaning that I needed to walk directly to 
my next gate after passing through security.  As I arrived they were already pre-boarding 
so I was glad I decided to come straight here.  Tonight we’d be hitching a ride on a 7 
year old 787-9 of which Latam group has   27 of with 19 more on the way- along with 
10 787-8s. This flight was originally sold   showing the older configuration 2-2-2 
seating as you saw in my last video,   but around a week prior to the flight, the 
seating was updated to the newer layout.  I should mention though, while today’s layout is a 
very modern seat, LATAM has also revealed a third   layout featuring seats with doors which they 
begun installing, I believe to eventually   replace both of these existing layouts.
Like I said, multi national airlines with   fleets spread out over five countries 
can get a bit complicated at times.  Stepping on board I was warmly greeted and 
quickly found one of my favorite cabin designs   flying these days. I had previously reviewed 
this product- and I use air quotes around this   product because on the 777s, especially in the 
bulkheads, the layout is wildly more spacious.  On board our 787 tonight, all of the finishes 
that I loved from that 777 are the same here,   from the really satisfying squishy interior of 
the shell, to the red leather accents and even   what I swear is real stone on the side tables. 
It’s one of the classiest cabins you can find.  If you’re enjoying the video and would like to 
support the channel there are many ways you can   do so. A quick like on the video and subscribe 
helps videos with the algorithm. You could join   my Youtube Memberships to get early access to some 
videos and access to all of my Community Posts or   you could check out my Patreon where I post the 
most and can help out if you have travel related   questions. Whatever you do, thanks for doing it.
Next to you you have an open storage area with a   small integrated closed area what is built 
like a tank and really satisfying to click   close. The build quality of it makes me wonder 
if it was originally meant to have a lock,   which would have been pretty cool.
Controls, remotes and outlets are   thoughtfully laid out and easy to use and access.
The seat itself though is quite narrow, as is the   aisle to access the window side seats. Generally- 
tight as it may be- I can fit my size 12 foot in   this space, but that wasn’t happening today.
Same as my previous flight, no pre departure   drinks were served but there were 
bottles of water at each seat.  The foot cubby is quite shallow but tall and 
doesn’t have space under it to stow anything.  To get fully situated you’re going 
to need to macgyver it in this seat.  So about what I was saying. Of course, it 
is wonderful to have your own private space   and I have sat in these staggered lie 
flat seats more times than I can count,   some of those times on other airlines on 787s but 
here they were clearly trying to pack these seats   in as tightly as possible. I’m 6’ tall or 181cm 
and while I was seated it was one of those cases   where both of my knees were touching parts of the 
seat and the monitor just felt needlessly close.  I checked the seatmaps of ANA and EVA air who both 
use similar seats on their 787s- both of which,   especially EVA felt extremely roomy 
and they all look to be fitting the   same amount of seats in the same space- 
so, I’m not sure what was going on here.  Anyway, it’s less a complaint and more just 
an open question about the pros and cons of   certain 2-2-2 seats vs certain all aisle access 
seats. The safety video began and we pushed back.  The first drink service started 
promptly after take off, but first   let’s take a look at the comfort items on board.
First up, love a really good quality and cushy   pair of slippers- that along with a great pillow 
are investments I wish more airlines would make,   they can really make a good flight great.
Luckily, LATAM got the message and the pillow   was fantastic in size and fluff- nearly 
as good as Iberia’s but not quite there.  There’s a duvet style blanket in 
the bag as well, one that is soft   and cozy and a good weight as well.
Finally there’s also a mattress pad   which I’ll show you in action in a bit, but 
for now, another creative storage solution.  The drink cart came down the aisle and 
I had a glass of Sauvignon Blanc along   with a sad bowl of cold and somewhat stale nuts.
Here’s a look at the full menu. Prior to take off   orders were taken and I went for the special dish 
of the day, part of their Sabores que Transportan   or flavors that transport a series of local 
inspired dishes created by locally renowned   chefs- a type of program I love to see on board 
any airline, I’ll blindly order whatever they   recommend. Unfortunately when I did order it, it 
had already sold out, so I went with the beef.  Luckily, shortly after take off my 
very friendly member of crew came   by and let me know she found one for me and 
it turned into the highlight of the flight.  The full meal is served all at once which 
is standard for Latam. For the starter   there was thinly sliced Chilean Abalone with 
lemon and potato salad and a green salad.  The main dish, which to their credit looked 
incredibly similar to the photo in the menu   was Smoked pork tenderloin with smashed Chancado 
potatoes with paprika oil, caramelized apples and   plums. Give me pork and apples together and I’m 
there for it all day and this was no exception.   Overall I’d say the dish was lighter in flavor 
than I was expecting but was still a delight to   eat. I can’t tell you how refreshing it is to try 
something truly new on an airplane of all places.  That was finished off with a Dulce de Lech Mousse 
with Chocolate Ganache and brownie chunks which   was perfectly indulgent and a great finish to 
the meal. Overall, the full meal gets a 9/10.  I know some don’t like full tray services 
but for a late departure like this,   I thought it was a good way to go. My tray 
in the last row was cleared just an hour and   25 minutes after take off, leaving plenty 
of time for sleep on this 10 hour flight.  The entertainment on board was decent with 
over 200 movies on offer from all types   of genres as well as a great newest 
generation moving map. Quality noise   canceling headphone were available as well.
Here’s the bed in full flat mode. It is a bit   of a tight squeeze around the knees 
but it gets the job done. At least   that food cubby is tall enough to not also 
restrict you in that direction. That said,   this is not a seat I can comfortably 
sleep in as a flat bed as I’m not   part of the mummy sleeping crowd.
The sleeping pad was thin but very   nice and squishy foam which even while sitting 
up made for a much more comfortable surface.  I enjoyed a few hours of wine assisted half 
reclined sleep and came to as we were approaching   Florida, just before the sun began to come up.
Let’s take a look at the amenity kit and   get ready for the breakfast service.
I loved the kit. These and the smaller   kits offered on my previous flight are both from 
the same artist collection of kits that they   had rotating through different designs. While I 
don’t need socks or ear plugs or stuff like that,   the number one thing I look for in a good 
kit is whether it’s practical to use again   and this surely, for something, is.
Bathrooms on board were sparse but   kept mostly clean throughout the flight.  The cabin was woken up around 80 minutes prior 
to landing and I was served around 15 minutes   later. A much appreciated efficient service again. 
LATAM really understands what important on these   overnight flights that often stay in the same time 
zone. There’s no need for jetlag if you can get a   decent sleep and LATAM’s service allows for that.
For breakfast there was a choice of scrambled   eggs, a ham and cheese selection or crepes with 
dulce de leche and strawberries. Now, crepes   or pancakes are something I never order unless 
necessary for breakfast on a flight- but also,   I have a rule which requires me to order anything 
that ever has dulce de leche- a rule I adopted   many years ago during my time in Argentina.
Well, today it was a mistake. The dulce de leche,   it can do no harm, was good, even the 
overheated nearly burnt part. But,   the crepes turned into a globbual of sticky hot 
dough as the individual layers fused together.  I also had some yogurt, a small fruit plate 
and… ⅓ of a muffin? Are we rationing muffins   now? Overall, the breakfast gets a 6/10.
Service on board was exactly what I want on   an overnight flight. Friendly and efficient 
during meal services and hiding in between   them for all I care. I also appreciate that 
they never locked the dimmers on the windows.  This flight on it’s own I’d say is 
a 7, but averaged out with my other   LATAM flights I think keeping them at a 6 is fair.  A gorgeous morning approach over 
Sandy Hook and into JFK is coming up.  So, LATAM is a solid airline and I wouldn’t 
hesitate for a moment on flying them again-   though I would be on the lookout 
for their new seats or at least   their 777s which was vastly more comfortable.  So I really do hope you enjoyed this wonderful 
flight with me today. If you did, please be sure   to click that like button and subscribe with 
notifications on so you don’t miss my weekly   flight and resort reviews. I’ll see you next time 
for my final installment from Punta Cana for a   video that I honestly didn’t want to 
make which sounded really tempting to   watch. You’ll understand when you see. As 
always, thanks for watching until the end.

reviews.transcript_full: This video is sponsored by AeroLow.  British Airways Longest Route connects London and Sydney in a flight time of 21 hours. Flight BA-16 has a roughly 1.5 hour layover in Singapore to refuel, recader and to switch  crews.  In today's episode of our Flight Review series, Brutally Honest, I will take you along  the longest nonstop flight British Airways currently offers, clocking in at a whopping  15 hours and 30 minutes with no break in between.  And since here at Simply Aviation we put a focus on economy class products, we'll do  that flight in coach.  15.5 hours, the rough equivalent of flying from London to Chicago or Delhi, turning around  and flying all the way back to London.  I'm excited to bring you along, so let's get going.  Aviation Geeks and Freak & Flyers, welcome to this new episode of our Flight Review  series, Brutally Honest.  My name is David and we're in Tokyo this morning heading over to Hannida Airport to catch  our flight back home to Europe. Additionally, the wind is a bit unfavorable today, meaning our flight will be exceptionally  long, even beating the longest British Airways nonstop route by great circle distance,  which is London to Santiago de Chile.  I'm honestly quite surprised I even got a ticket for this flight.  This route hasn't reached me for a while, but a one way from Tokyo to my hometown of  Vienna is consistently priced at at least 1,360 euros on British Airways. Boarding for premium cabins is zone one and includes both business and premium economy passengers. There are only three zones in total. Everyone had to have their carry-on items searched prior to boarding, and they held us on the jet bridge for another 5 minutes before we were allowed to board. Boarding for all passengers was at the front of the plane, leading to a lot of foot traffic and liloos in the business class cabin. We saw several economy passengers stowing their bags in the business class overhead bins, and the flight attendants didn't seem to care. This is a Boeing 767300 ER with 20 business class seats and 213 economy seats. This aircraft also features 39 LATAM plus seats which feature additional legroom. The business class seats are arranged in a 1 121 staggered layout and all seats have direct aisle access. We are in seats 3A and 5A today which are the window seats closest to the windows. Even rows are closer to the aisle. Each seat has a 16-in touchscreen, USBA, and universal power plugs. The universal power plugs didn't get turned on on our flight, or they weren't working, unfortunately. The seat has a decent amount of storage space. There's a small closing compartment below an open area to the side of the seat. A goodiz counter with a real stone surface. [Music] The seat surface uses three-dimensional textiles to help improve air flow and temperature. The seat was a bit narrow, and I found that I often hit the seat controls with my elbow, causing my seat to move unintentionally. The seat has a pitch of 45 in and a width of 19 1/2 in and recines to a fully lay flat. As a bed, the seat was comfortable. I think more comfortable than as a seat where it was a little too flat and didn't have much lumbar support. The footwell was a bit tight, but as long as you lay on your back, Trevor found it comfortable, and it was long enough for him to lay completely down, even at 6'4 in. When in bed mode, it is a little difficult getting in and out of the seat. That's one of the problems with the 767. The cabin is narrower than newer aircraft models, so the seats tend to be a little tighter. There were accent lights above the literature holder and storage area and you can control their light level. There's also a reading light which you can adjust the brightness on. Waiting at our seats was a mattress topper, duvet and pillow. The linens were good quality, the pillow a decent size and the duvet was quite large also welcome. The amenity kits are eco-friendly and focus on sustainable materials throughout. The bags feature designs from South American artists. Inside the kit features a bamboo toothbrush, eye mask, socks, earplugs, a refreshening towel, lip balm, and hand cream. Push back was prompt, but the taxi and wait to depart took about 20 minutes. We took off to the south and quickly escaped the cloud cover. [Music] On board, the in-flight entertainment system is called LATAM Play. With over 300 movies and a thousand TV episodes, there's a decent selection available, and the system was responsive. There were also music and games available and a flight tracker. This aircraft did not have Wi-Fi. Some LATAM 767s have it installed and they're working to install Wi-Fi across the fleet. No pre-eparture drinks were offered, but they did take our meal orders on the ground. On this flight, there was a lunch service and a hot snack service just before landing. Just after takeoff, mixed nuts and sparkling wine were served. LATM has refocused their onboard dining experience recently and now provides Latin American focused meals with a focus on the local flavors of the departure point. For lunch, we both ordered the Amazonian shufa, which is a fried rice dish, and Luca mimoose for dessert. The starter was a take on a kowsa, a traditional Peruvian potato dish, although a bit deconstructed. The shrimp were fine, a little tough, but fine. Overall, this dish lacked flavor. The salad was literally three leaves of lettuce and a basic vinegarette. I guess it counts as a salad, but it could have just been a garnish at that point. The starter was fine, not great, not bad. The main dish was their signature dish from a local chef, Ilia Garcia, and it was great. It was flavorful, and anything with plantains is always a plus to us. The Luca Mimoose was light with some tart mango fruit bits on top and then cookie crumbles on the bottom. It was good, but the mango on top was what made this. Overall, the lunch was good. We're glad to see local flavors on board. And while the starter wasn't anything special, we did enjoy the rice dish. About 70 minutes before arrival, a snack service was served. It was a sandwich and a dessert. Trevor ordered the lentil burger and dol de leche pudding and a Coke Zero. I skipped the snack. Trevor said the sandwich was pretty good and had mozzarella, lettuce, and tomato on top of a lentil patty. It was served with potato chips and an ioli. The pudding was very light with a few cookie bits on top and fresh blueberries. Overall, the dish was decent and more than some carriers will offer on a flight of this length. For comparison, we flew Delta down to Peru and there was no second meal or snack service offered in business class. We arrived into Atlanta around 8:00 p.m. This was a completely daytime flight. [Music] Evenings are a bit busy at ATL, but we got a good sunset view as we taxi to our gate in the F concourse. [Music] We found this flight to be comfortable. I slept a good chunk of this flight since I wasn't feeling great. I found the bed to be long enough and the footwell decent, although I found it more comfortable to sleep on my side than my back due to the contours of the seat. Trevor felt like he could have slept, but it wouldn't have been the best sleep due to the space restrictions around his shoulders and legs. The service was good, the food was enjoyable, and had a unique flare to it. The flight attendants were present throughout the flight and were personable and friendly during service. I think this product is fine for a mediumh hall flight. We got a great fair for our trip and had a good experience. Would we fly LAM again? I'd say absolutely for a mediumh hall flight like this one. Our biggest complaint about service was the fairly indifferent LATAM ground staff in Lima. Once on board, the flight attendants were friendly. One important thing to note is that we booked this trip through Delta. Latam has a joint venture with Delta. And while LATAM is not part of the Sky Team Alliance, Delta medallions get many perks and benefits with LATAM. This includes priority boarding, check-in, etc. We also earn Delta miles and elite MQDs on this flight. Have you flown Latam? Let us know in the comments what you think of this airline. And don't forget to hit that like button and subscribe to keep up with our latest travels. Thank you for watching. We'll see you on the next adventure. [Music]

reviews.transcript_full:
Welcome on this Air France Business Class
flight in an Airbus A330 from Paris to St Martin (Caribbean) The video features the full Air France Business Class
experience, from seating & meals to amenities & bedding This Air France Business Class video also includes
the A330’s landing at St Martin’s iconic Princess Juliana Airport Our journey starts at Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris,
Europe's third busiest airport (after Istanbul and Heathrow)  Unfortunately, my Air France Business Class 'light' ticket does
not include access to the lounge for some pre-flight relaxation We’re taken by bus to the remote aircraft stand This is the Air France Airbus A330-200 that will
fly us to St Martin (aircraft registration number F-GZCN) Air France has 11 Airbus A330s in its
long-haul fleet with an average age of 22 years The Air France Business Class on the Airbus A330
features 36 seats spread over six rows in a 2-2-2 layout There are two Business Class cabins: a front cabin
with 24 seats (4 rows) and a rear cabin with 12 seats (2 rows) The Air France A330 Business Class cabin has a sleek look 4A is my seat for the 9 hour flight to St Martin Air France installed Equinox 2D Business Class
seats by Stelia Aerospace on its Airbus A330 fleet The Air France Business Class seat on the A330
has a pitch of 78 inch (198 cm) and a width of 22 inch (56 cm) A retractable screen provides privacy between seats I’ll take a detailed tour of the 
Air France Business Class seat after takeoff A hot towel is provided to refresh a little Air France’s safety video is an elegant and stylish movie We’re leaving the aircraft stand at 10 am (on-time departure) Air France’s A330s are powered by General Electric engines  Air France’s A330-200s are being replaced
by the next-generation and larger Airbus A350-900s Let’s have a look at the Air France A330 Business Class seat Each Business Class seat features a large TV screen,
with a storage cabinet and footrest underneath  Directly next to to the seat’s head rest is a small
cubby for storing headphones, water and small items The power plug and passenger service unit
(remote control for IFE) are within easy reach The arm rest houses a large tray table Let's have a look at the Air France Business Class amenities The Air France Business Class kit contains the following items:
a dental kit, earplugs, eye mask, socks, and Clarins cosmetics A soft microfiber pillow and a warm blanket
are offered to all Business Class passengers All Air France's Business Class passengers get slippers Air France branded noise-cancelling headphones are provided  One hour into the flight, we're leaving Europe behind us
and will now fly over the Atlantic Ocean for the next 8 hours  I am a very nervous flyer, especially over the ocean Are you also scared of flying over the ocean? Leave a comment As we start the Atlantic crossing, the Air France crew
hands out the Business Class menus for the inflight meals Appetizer: cream of smoked sweetcorn soup,
girolle mushrooms and toasted buckwheat Air France also serves its Business Class passengers
crepes fourrées (stuffed pancakes) during the aperitif Starter: Camargue red rice, sweet potato,
and rainbow trout salad with raspberry vinaigrette Main course: beef chuck, peanut sauce, celery, Taggiasca olives Mustard in grains from the prestigious moutardier 
Edmond Fallot in Dijon is served with the beef  Cantal, Fourme d’Ambert, & Chabichou du Poitou cheeses Dessert: crispy hazelnut and caramel cake Air France's Airbus A330 is equipped with
two lavatories for the 36 Business Class passengers The Air France Business Class seat on the A330 can be
reclined into a fully flat bed with a lenght of 197 cm (77 inches)   Have you ever flown in Air France Business Class?
If so, what was your experience? Leave a comment Air France’s inflight entertainment system
offers a wide variety of movies, shows, music and games Snacks & drinks are available in the galley during the flight A light meal is served 90 minutes prior to landing Smoked salmon, tangy creamy sauce, 
pearl pasta with vegetables, and orange & pink grapefruit The Air France A330 pilot addresses
the passengers as we are approaching St Martin’s airspace There's a lot of traffic at St Martin airport, and we
have to circle for 30 minutes before starting our descend  We get some great views of the Caribbean during the descent St Martin has one of the world’s most scenic airport landings Maho Beach on St Martin is famous for being
next to the international airport, right at the end of the runway Thanks for flying with me in Air France Business Class Don't forget to like, comment,
and subscribe for more flight reviews!

reviews.transcript_full:
This video features a spectacular seaplane flight in the Maldives Enjoy the Maldives seaplane flight and the magnificent views! The destination of the flight is Soneva Secret,
the Maldives' newest ultra-luxury resort Welcome to Male International Airport in the Maldives, where
Soneva hosts meet guests who arrive by international flight The Soneva hosts also assist guests with the check-in
at the airport counters to secure seaplane boarding passes The Maldives has two seaplane operators: 
Manta Air and TMA (Trans Maldivian AIrways) Next, guest are transferred to the seaplane terminal by a Tesla The drive to the seaplane terminal takes only 5 minutes The new seaplane terminal was inaugurated in October 2022 At the seaplane terminal, Soneva operates its own
lounge, where guests can wait for their flight to the resort The lounge’s interior reflects Soneva's signature eco-design Snacks (cheese, chocolates & ice-cream) and beverages
are served, and complimentary WiFi is provided The lounge also features a play room for children The lounge features a large outdoor terrace, with views of the
seaplane docks, which is the world's largest seaplane terminal Prior to boarding, passengers are escorted 
to a small room, where a safety video is played Soneva has its own fleet of luxurious seaplanes Maintained and operated by Manta Air,
the Soneva seaplanes offer a superior travel experience The Soneva seaplanes have only has 8 seats
(for comparison, a regular seaplane features 16 seats) Aboard the plane, leather interiors welcome passengers Twin Otter seaplanes have short take-off and landing abilities They have a range of 886 mi (1425 km)
and a cruise speed of 173 mi (270 km) per hour Have you ever flown onboard a seaplane in the Maldives?
If so, what was your experience? Leave a comment Flight time from Male to Soneva Secret is 75 minutes
(a stop-over is made at Soneva Fushi along the way) All pilots in the Maldives are commercially trained and
they fly the plane with bare feet or flipflops (so cool!) A seaplane flight in the Maldives is a breathtaking journey
as it offers some of the most incredible views in the world The first part of the flight crosses the North Male Atoll - home to
the airport and capital city Male - which consists of 50 islands The first hotel in the Maldives opened
in the North Male Atoll in 1972 and had only 30 rooms The seaplane is flying over the famous One&Only Reethi Rah
Resort, located on the outer edge of the North Male Atoll We're making a stop-over at Soneva Fushi to drop some guests Soneva Fushi is regarded as the first luxury hotel in the
Maldives, setting of the trend of luxury holidays in the nation Opened in 1995, Soneva Fushi is still one of the Maldives' best 
resorts, blending ultra-luxury with environmental responsibility Welcome to Soneva Fushi International Airport,
probably the tiniest airport in the world The stop-over at Soneva Fushi takes only 5 minutes The plane takes off at short distance from the resort
as not to disturb the guests on the island Here we go again ... We get a spectacular view of Soneva Fushi after takeoff Soneva Fushi is located in the Baa Atoll,
a designated UNESCO World Biosphere Reserve The Baa Atoll is home to 1200 fish species, including manta
rays, sharks, and an abundance of sea turtles and dolphins The Baa Atoll consists of 75 islands of which
13 are inhabited with a population of over 11,000 people Two luxury resorts can be seen in the distance:
Anantara Kihavah Villas and Four Seasons Landaa Giraavaru As the seaplane leaves the Baa Atoll, the Maldives' 
next atoll - the Raa Atoll - comes into view Surfers and sailors flock to Raa Atoll
for its excellent surf spots and idyllic sailing routes We get a nice view of Joali Being Resort from the air This is Joali Maldives, the sister resort of Joali Being We're leaving the Raa Atoll and now head towards the
Haa Dhaalu Atoll, the most remote atoll in the Maldives We get our first glimpse of Soneva Secret,
the Maldives' most exclusive resort Soneva Secret is located in the bluest lagoon I've ever seen The only resort in the Haa Dhaalu Atoll, Soneva Secret is set on
Dhipparufushi Island at the westernmost tip of the Maldives Soneva Secret features only 14 water & island villas; each villa
comes with a dedicated team of three (including a butler & chef) This is how the landing looks like from the cockpit ... From the landing site, it's 5 min by speedboat to the resort The resort staff is waiting for us on the beach 
(it feels like a scene from the White Lotus, only the real version)

reviews.transcript_full: Over the years, few airlines have fascinated me as much as China's Junyao Air.  It's not a widely known airline, but I think it should be, especially when you're  into aviation because there are so many interesting things about them.  For example, they are currently the only so-called Star Alliance connecting partner, meaning  they are not a full member of the alliance but work closely with them by offering connecting  at Tineraries and let Star Alliance frequent flyer status holders enjoy their benefits on  Junyao Air flights as well.  And the airline isn't even that small.  Despite only commencing operation in 2006, the airline has already grown to more than 100  planes, including a fleet of 9 Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners sporting one of five unique colorful  liverys.  These are some of the most stunning paint jobs you'll find on any Dreamliner if you  ask me.  And with their three digit number of aircraft, Junyao is amongst the largest airlines in the  world to have started operation in this century.  They mostly focus on domestic routes, primarily from airports in the Yangtze Delta region,  from which they also operate a small number of long-haul routes.  As of March 2025, they connect Shanghai Pudong with Helsinki, Manchester, Brussels, Athens,  Melbourne and Sydney, as well as fly from Henan Province's capital Changzhou to Helsinki  and Milan, Malpenser.  Today I'm very excited to bring you along a flight aboard Junyao Air and share more  of the airline's unique intricacies as well as dive into the intriguing contrasts of  domestic air travel within China on our journey from Shanghai Hong Xiaotang to Shenzhen.  I'm glad you're joining me on this trip, so without further ado, let's get going.  Ibeation geeks and frequent flyers welcome to this new episode of our Flight Review series  Brutally Honest.  I'm just about to leave my hotel here in Shanghai and make my way over to Hong Xiaotang  International Airport.  The city of Shanghai is served by two airports, the older original one being Hong Xiaotang  in the city's west, and right before the turn of the millennium, Pudong International Airport  was inaugurated, which now serves as the main international gateway to the region and has  surpassed Hong Xiaotang's size.  Due to its proximity to the city center, Hong Xiaotang Airport mainly caters to domestic  flights these days, as well as a handful of cross-border short-haul flights to other inner  city airports like Taipei Songshan, Seoul Gimpo, and Tokyo Haneda.  This early in the morning, taking a cab from the Bund takes only half an hour and costs  around 80 yuan or roughly 10 euros.  Usually, I would take the subway, which also wouldn't be an issue for a 730AM domestic  departure, but when booking this flight, there was no way to reserve a seat.  I appreciate my 150 USD ticket, including a 20kg checked bag, but I would have also been  willing to pay a few bucks to ensure I would be getting a window seat.  Even emailing their customer service to no avail as their inbox was full.  So my last resort is going to the airport as early as possible in the hope I'm able  to snag one of the remaining window seats at check-in.  There might be a possibility to do it online and Mandarin, but even with translation apps,  I wasn't able to figure it out, and neither in their own app nor on platforms like WeChat,  which sometimes are the key to getting what you want in journeys in China.  First, we're passing a brief security check followed by us being allowed into the check-in  area.  Junyao staff gave all of us waiting in line already about and then opened the check-in  desks perfectly on time.  And we got our window seat.  Personally, there are many things I love about Chinese airports.  They are usually pretty efficient and reliable, despite the masses of people.  I also appreciate how well connected to public transit they are.  Junyao is a particularly great example as it is not only connected to three different  metro lines, which also connect to Pudong Airport directly, but also one of the main high-speed  railway stations of Shanghai.  Although saying it's connected is somewhat incorrect, as the train station and terminal  two were built as one super-sized intermodal transportation hub which opened in 2010.  Naturally being a nerd for air travel and transportation in general also means I take  a deep interest in urban planning, and this is a text book implementation of intermodality.  And the Chinese are, rightfully so, proud of that, displaying this super-fascinating 3D  model of the terminal complex at the Shanghai Urban Planning Exhibition Center, an interesting  museum about how Shanghai is designed and works.  Connecting high-speed intercity rail lines with major airports is something that needs  a bigger focus in the future.  There are many examples of where this makes travel easier already, such as in Amsterdam  and Frankfurt.  Both airports that arguably wouldn't have gotten as big as they are had they not been that  well connected within their respective countries.  Another aspect that Chinese airports generally do well in is the plentiful availability of  lounges, which are often accessible with lounge access programs such as priority pass or  with premium credit cards.  Just look at how many different ones there are.  Thanks to my credit card I was allowed into the Juniao Air Lounge, despite traveling in  an economy class.  It's a chic space with elegant, French-inspired interior in the airlines' distinct color scheme.  The lounge offers a self-service buffet with a variety of hot and cold beverages and a scrumptious  food selection with local staples like T-eggs, Malai Gal, Golden Fried Rice and Yo-Tiao.  Let's inhale this gorgeous breakfast and then make our way to the gate.  Cross Hong-Tiao Airport you'll find a large variety of western brands, which I didn't  expect as it mainly serves domestic routes.  There's a Starbucks now, which is a local iteration of Starbucks exclusively offering  products to go mainly through mobile ordering so the brand can compete more effectively against  local rivals such as Lucan Coffee.  There's also a Shake Shack, a Hardies and a Lulu Lemon, as well as a Japanese Ramen  chain, and a relay, a type of convenience store you really only see across European train  stations, which for me as a European seems amusingly out of place at a Chinese airport.  The Dreamliner down there will take us to Shenzhen today.  Registered Bravo 20 Delta Tango, this Boeing 787-9 is the 100th Boeing 787 to operate in China,  which is commemorated by a decal at the front of the aircraft.  It was delivered to Jun-Yao Air in 2019 and wears a delivering featuring Chinese Pienese,  which is known as the King of Flowers in China.  What's unique about the boarding passes on some Chinese airlines is that they tear on  both sides.  That's so the staff can confirm your presence at the check-in counter and again at the  plane which is usually only done when buses and remote stands are involved.  You can see my ticket having been torn on this side, but I still have another terrible  slip on the other side remaining.  Entering the plane through door 2, the business class cabin is to our left, which consists  of 29 121 configured Thompson Vantage XL seats.  We're back here in Economy Class though, where 295 Recaro CL3710 seats are fitted in  the Dreamliner's Classic 3333 configuration.  Waiting for us on the seat already is a pillow with a soft reusable cover.  The headrests of each seat are adjustable in three ways on the sides, vertically, as  well as down here for some extra next one.  With my height of 180 cm, the legroom is phenomenal, also for a long-haul flight, but  especially so for a 2 hour domestic flight like this one.  Above a standard seat back pocket is a bifold tray table and a high literature pocket  a signature element of many Recaro seats.  Universal power ports are not installed, but you will find a USB-A port at the bottom  of the entertainment screen.  The port hooks are offered too.  There is a notable amount of advertising around the cabin, including the C-through stickers  at the bottom of the windows promoting their new road from Chunchaw to Milan, as well as  large stickers on the over-at-binds.  In the ceiling there are adjustable reading lights but no personal air vents.  Like all Dreamliners, this one too has dimmable windows.  The triple-7300E are parked next to us as about to depart to Beijing.  If you are curious about what China Easton's triple-7s are like on long-haul routes, we  have an in-depth video covering a flight from Frankfurt to Shanghai and Economy class  available on our channel as well.  If you enjoy detailed flight reviews like these ones, please consider subscribing to our  channel and ensure you won't miss our many upcoming reviews.  As we are texting for departure, let's use the time to have a brief look at the  plans in flight entertainment system.  Junyao's Dreamliners employ the popular Panasonic X3 Entertainment System with adjustable touch  screens installed at every seat.  There is a comparably small number of movies and TV shows available to watch on demand,  including a handful of international options.  I love how the TV show section has its own category just for Genshin Impact.  The subsequent games are offered too, as is a state of the art in-flight map.  I don't know if these are apartments or offices, but either way I dig the view from there.  Now we are finally ready for departure.  Junyao Air's logo is prominently featured on their engines, the aircraft's tail, the  headrest covers and so on.  It depicts a stylized version of a Rue E-sector.  A Rue E-sector is a type of talisman symbolizing power, good fortune and prosperity and is deeply  rooted in Chinese culture.  The name Junyao by the way is not technically the name of the airline.  Well, yeah, technically it is.  After all that's what it says everywhere, but it's not the airline's Mandarin name.  In Mandarin, Junyao Air is called Tsisyang Hong Kong, Hong Kong simply meaning airline,  but the term Tsisyang means auspicious, full of promise.  So naturally I wondered, then what does Junyao mean?  Junyao is actually the name of the parent company of Tsisyang Hong Kong.  And the Junyao group does all sorts of things, including trying to build cars, kinda looks  like a pre-is knockoff to be honest.  Anyway, the Jun in Junyao stems from one of the characters in the name of their founders,  and Yao Kunwe's high quality and excellence.  Right for takeoff, the crew handed out breakfast boxes, alongside a hot main dish.  This was the only option available, which was ham and eggs and some steamed vegetables,  including potatoes, broccoli, a cherry tomato and corn.  It's at the box, there is a cold bread roll, some nuts, a pack of ketchup, and a cart  of a probiotic yogurt drink.  As for beverages, I asked for a cup of water and some coffee, which automatically came with  milk and sugar already in it.  No black coffee on this flight.  The meal was totally fine, it wasn't spectacular in terms of overall airplane food quality,  but it's miles better than the hot breakfast dish's air China serves.  The aside though, getting a complimentary hot meal on a domestic flight at all is remarkable.  The lavatories of the plain are pleasant too.  I like the faux wood pattern on the wall and appreciate the sentiment of the plastic flower.  The cabin of the plain is plastered with advertising, in this case for the China merchant's bank,  which isn't all that uncommon for the country as you are bombarded with ads from the moment  you enter China.  Duneo Air also sells airplane models of their Dreamliner Sunboard, which is super cool,  and 10 bucks for a 1-500 model doesn't seem bad, but I wouldn't know what the quality  of the model is like.  As we're cruising over Chao Chou, just north of Shanhou, it's time for a quick conclusion  about this journey, but it's important to know that this is not the end of the video  because our arrival airport, Shanjian Bao An, is one of the most architecturally stunning  I have ever been at, and there are some interesting things I want to show you about the baggage  claim area.  As for Duneo Air and today's flight, one word, marvelous.  There was nothing I can fault the airline for.  A $150 US dollar one-way economy class domestic flight, and we get a check back for free,  got the seat we wanted for free at the check-in counter, a lovely little lounge, a modern  comfortable aircraft, a state of the art and a team and system, a comfy pillow, impressive  legroom, and a complimentary hot meal.  What more could I even ask for?  Only two things left me a bit puzzled, both because I'm a foreigner and not Chinese.  With the former being that I wasn't able to select a seat online and wasn't able to  get in touch with anyone at the airline, that sucked, but wasn't that surprising.  The second was that sweet milky coffee, which simply isn't my taste, but that's what  you get in China, it's a tea country, not a coffee country after all.  Apart from those two pedantic little complaints, this was an S tier domestic flight.  And even after having been to China a couple of times, there are things I simply won't  understand.  Like the fact that fake Prague down there, for some reason, is a Huawei Research and  Development Center.  I'm not even joking, that's a Huawei office campus.  Like, what?  Well, what better way to welcome you to China Silicon Valley.  Welcome to Ginger.  Up in wanting to see the airport stunning Terminal 3 in person for years and I'm so  excited to finally be here.  The Terminal was opened in 2013 and features a unique roof design that looks as stunning  from the inside as it does from the outside.  And baggage claim is quite different from what I'm used to as well.  Staff already positioned carts everywhere so you don't have to get your own.  There is staff making sure your belongings don't come out damaged and there is a life  feat of the containers being unloaded downstairs so you can see your suitcase before it comes  up.  Airport staff also scans your baggage slip and the tag to make sure you got the right  bag and are not walking out with somebody else's.  What a journey and what a video this has turned into.  How many things there are to show on a 2 hour flight?  It's incredible.  If you enjoy deep dives into air travel around the world, you are at the right place.  Here at SimpliViation we've made it our mission to take you along the journey of as many  different airlines as possible and with this video we have ticked another 1 hour list,  our 250th or something.  What we're not even close to being done, many more videos will come out soon so subscribing  to our channel is certainly worth it.  And if you share our passion and want us to be able to dedicate more time and resources  to this channel, please consider becoming a paid channel sponsor. All of these amazing people have chosen to help us out with their own hard earned money  already and we are immensely grateful for their contribution to this channel.  As we said, many more videos are coming soon, including the next flight of this journey  where we will show you what Cathay Pacific's new Airbus A321 Nios are like in economy  class.  As always, thank you very much for watching and coming along, I will see you guys for  a new video next week and until then, safe travels.
