Your author recently experienced his first actual, real-world 4K video on board a Cathay Pacific A321neo this month, in conjunction with Cathay’s launch of 4K HDR content last month (for which, full disclosure, he was a guest of the airline), and the experience was an absolute joy. Content service provider, Anuvu, started providing 4K content to Cathay’s A321neo aircraft in 2021 .
Cathay is also rolling out its newest graphic user interface (GUI), and the system is very similar to the one on board Cathay’s latest Aria business suite product .

On sitting down in the excellent Collins Air Rest seats , Panasonic’s 15.6” 4K HDR screen, from its NEXT generation of systems, is expansive and beautiful, with a lovely Hong Kong screen saver on boarding, offering buttons providing easy access to both the excellent flight map and delightful inflight cameras.
Modern cabin design has to take into account the amount of space, light and attention from the enormous modern screens. Image: John Walton

At the top right of the main screen there is a small line of useful information and control buttons, although these are mixed together rather than being separated into categories: wifi availability, a sleep icon, the overhead light, the crew bell, and a combined double-button for the settings and Bluetooth connectivity for headphones.

It feels like this could use a card sort exercise or some other categorisation work, perhaps separating the lighting and crew call buttons from the IFEC control and status buttons, with consistent button size. Thinking of my enthusiastically travelling 83-year-old mother and other travellers who might be less familiar with the iconography (what does “crescent moon” mean: sleep? do-not-disturb? qiblah?), perhaps the button sizing might also be increased, and some guidance text included.

New to the latest GUI is a Watch Together function, a welcome delight to this frequent flyer, well used to having to set up a movie side-by-side with his partner and then having to do a 3-2-1 countdown, with the inevitable need for a resynchronisation effort at some point during the film.
With an empty seat next to me, I was able to try out the Watch Together function. Image: John Walton

Cathay has intelligently balanced ease of use with the potential for abuse here, with a mention in the Watch Together notification that this feature can be turned off in the settings menu, and given that the sending seat is identified it should be relatively simple to identify anyone abusing the system.
I liked how Cathay had clearly considered the possibilities for abuse of the Watch Together system. Image: John Walton

The content library was overall wide-ranging, with 4K HDR content limited to a fairly small selection of films, most of which are classics like The Godfather , Shawshank Redemption , and The Lord of the Rings , with some praiseworthy Hong Kong classics included as well. Other content remained at standard definition, shown only too plainly on the 15.6” Panasonic NEXT screens.
The Hong Kong classics’ run-time made them a good choice for the route. Image: John Walton

Cathay executives told RGN during a follow-up interview that the blocker to more 4K content is upstream of the airline, with the content owner, content service provider and IFE system provider not yet working well enough together for a wider library of 4K content.

And that’s the rub: on this short flight of under 3h30, sitting down for a full viewing of any of The Lord of the Rings movies is playing flight time chicken with the end of the movie, especially given that there were regular screen-stopping announcements in no fewer than four languages (Cantonese, English, Japanese and Mandarin) before takeoff, after takeoff, during the several periods of turbulence, and before landing.
One of the Lord of the Rings movies is longer than the flight in total runtime. Image: John Walton
On which note: the entire screen freezes to an audio-representation announcement page during every single announcement, which was frankly a poor user experience during a short flight like this.

Cathay executives are in agreement on that, and tell us they are working with regulators to see what might be possible, perhaps including restricting screen-freeze to during only one language’s worth of announcements, guided by the IFE language the user selected.

Overall, though, the new GUI worked excellently and the 4K visuals are beautiful. But expanding this to more content, including shorter options like documentaries and episodic television will be crucial.

Your author selected the one single episode on board of the cinematographically superlative Deadliest Catch — winner of more than a dozen Emmys and many other awards for its visuals, and available at home in 4K — and the experience was worse than watching the show on an iPhone, because the big beautiful 15.6” 4K panel makes every compression artifact and other visible visual loss all the more painful.
Why can’t the content pipeline get the one episode of Deadliest Catch on this system in 4K? What’s the risk? Image: John Walton
Cathay Pacific provided flights to enable this article, but all opinions are unfettered and the author’s own.

article_text: Safran Passenger Innovations (SPI) has enjoyed an impressive trajectory in embedded inflight entertainment and today is seen as delivering proverbial ‘Cadillac’ IFE systems to airlines around the globe.

In the less than 15 years since its RAVE-branded IFE debuted with all-new innovations — first via predecessors IMS and later Zodiac Inflight Innovations which was acquired by Safran — SPI has seen its system installed on thousands of aircraft, with many airline contracts seemingly never even publicly announced, such as the IFE hardware aboard Starlux’s A350-900s or Icelandair’s Boeing 737 MAX twinjets.

Also of note, SPI is a key partner to Lufthansa as the airline rolls out its Allegris nextgen long-haul product. And a joint ideation project between SPI and Lufthansa led to the launch of new docked companion tablets that enable Allegris business class passengers to control their IFE, seat functionality, lighting and thermal environment with the device. SPI confirms it is not bound by exclusivity and can supply similar products to other airlines.

But SPI is also focused on what it says is a more sustainable approach to embedded IFE. And so, when it set about to design its next-generation system, it didn’t just adopt new display and processor technology — 4K miniLED HDR 10+ Liquid Crystal Displays for the former and Snapdragon for the latter — it also worked to slash weight to reduce CO2 emissions.

The result, RAVE Ultra plus, was first announced in 2023 with a promise that it will achieve, depending on aircraft type, up to 23% in weight savings over its immediate predecessor, RAVE Ultra, by using smaller and lighter line replaceable units and optimizing cable weights.

Some of the hardware was later showcased by SPI at the 2024 Aircraft Interiors Expo (AIX) in Hamburg. At that time, the manufacturer also committed to offering the new miniLED LCD displays beyond just premium classes but rather across all travel classes and screen sizes: 13.3″, 15.6”, 17.3” and 32”.

RAVE Ultra plus builds on the foundation of SPI’s award-winning RAVE Seat-Centric IFE, which broke the mold in aviation with local storage and docked screens that can be easily replaced or upgraded, and RAVE Ultra, which served as SPI’s foray into a new kind of architecture whereby each screen system contains local content but also works as part of a cloud of drives to open up terabytes of storage for thousands of hours of content. The RAVE Ultra displays are also backward compatible with SPI’s legacy RAVE meaning airlines can mix and match displays on the common backbone.

Impressively, however, the “plus” part of the new nextgen RAVE Ultra plus system takes this cloud-based architecture to another level, and represents a variety of new technologies, company vice president of products and strategy Ben Asmar explained to RGN at AIX 2024.

For one, the move to bring much more powerful Snapdragon processors on board allows SPI to “take all of the displays we have on the aircraft and put them together into a cloud networked storage and processing solution. So, we’re taking the same concept that, say, an Amazon does on the ground, where they have a ton of servers all communicating together with virtualized environments to serve applications and we’re replicating that on the plane by knitting all these screens together to make a virtualized server infrastructure and storage infrastructure,” Asmar said.
“So we’ll have the power of 300 Snapdragon processors [on a widebody] that can do distributed processing for anything you can imagine on board.”
This in turn eradicates the need for a heavy head-end box, saving crucial weight. “The only thing we need the head-end for is aircraft interfaces,” he noted.

“There is going to be a terabyte (TB) in each of these displays which means I can provide 300 terabytes of storage space which allows us to do really interesting things in the future” including facilitating edge caching (storing streaming video locally after it has been accessed online by a passenger) as part of SPI’s new RAVE Cloud Services portfolio.

SPI showcased its new miniLED LCD displays at AIX 2024. It is also offering the option of a new tethered second screen device which can be used as a remote control (the passenger’s own device can also be paired with the IFE system).

Also driving weight savings is a decision by SPI to tuck a lightweight DC power system into the seat leg to power its RAVE Ultra plus 13.3″ displays in economy class and provide up to 60W of USB charging per passenger. “It doesn’t take any room from the passenger,” Asmar noted.
The DC power system/seat leg integration is discreet.

SPI also developed a product that allows AC power in economy to be selected as an option, explaining thusly: “The solution is deployed by distributing AC power directly to AC outlets located in every seat from a small number of power distribution points located throughout the cabin. This means AC power can be offered in every seat without the need for an AC seat power box in every seat group – an industry first.”

As ever with the RAVE product line, the RAVE Ultra plus system features inherent modularity. For example, below each 13.3″ display sits what Asmar calls “the little pill at the front” which features the USB ports and the audio socket, presently available in four combos (including USB-A and/or USB-C).

So if a passenger manages to jam something into one of the ports and breaks it, no worries. “Rather than replacing the whole display, all I’m doing is replacing this small pill, which means I’m serviceable,” said the SPI executive.
The same holds true for when it’s time to phase out USB-A; the peripherals can be easily swapped out and upgraded.
For RAVE Ultra plus, SPI has also adopted what’s called ‘reduced paired Ethernet’ — technology it borrowed from the automotive industry.

Describing the solution to RGN, Asmar said: “An Ethernet cable is eight wires. Reduced paired means there’s only two to still deliver 1000BASE-T Ethernet. There’s roundabout a kilometer-and-a-half of IFE cabling on an aircraft. So, if I can reduce its weight by over half, then I’m saving an enormous amount of weight that’s actually not seen by anyone.
“I’m not reducing any passenger services, but I’m saving an incredible amount of weight and sustainability is one of the key elements of what RAVE Ultra plus is about.”

All in, the choices made by SPI for RAVE Ultra plus bring the Brea, California-headquartered firm much closer to reaching the Holy Grail vision described by IMS to your author nearly 15 years ago, wherein the head-end box is removed, and rapid content delivery is supported but cable weight is reduced.
The new screens are expected to debut in premium cabins in the near future, and the broader RAVE Ultra plus ecosystem should be flying in a couple of years.
SPI vice president of products and strategy Ben Asmar demonstrated the products to RGN at AIX 2024.
It seems Safran Passenger Innovations is seeking to leave no weight-reduction or sustainability stone unturned in its pursuit of a more environmentally-conscious embedded IFE system.

article_text: As part of Icelandair’s recent Airbus A321LR delivery , there was a major uplift in the passenger experience, with seating provided by Geven Seating and the debut of Panasonics Astrova IFE system.
Geven Comoda-Materia seats with Panasonic 16″ Astrova Screens installed – Imge, Geven

This delivery introduces Icelandair as the first customer to feature Geven’s New Comoda-Materia Pack for Business Class and Elemento for Economy Class, both of which are integrated with the Panasonic Astrova IFE solution for the first time.
Comoda-Materia Pack for Icelandair – Image, Geven
Elemento on Icelandair’s A321LR – Image, Geven.

This program is particularly notable as it represents Geven’s first implementation on a narrow-body aircraft. While debuting on the A321LR (A320 family), both seating solutions have been designed for long-haul operations. They are also slated for delivery on the A330 and A350 fleets, allowing for versatile deployments across different aircraft types.

In Business Class, Icelandair passengers will experience the latest evolution of the New Comoda-MateriaPack, which has undergone a custom redesign to reflect the airline’s brand identity. This bespoke version includes enhanced features such as cradle functionality, a spacious central console offering storage, and design elements that provide increased luxury and privacy.
In the back of the aircraft, the Elemento seat makes an appearance, which is designed for comfort – but also for weight.

However, if you’ve kept up with this blog, you would know that the other big launch on the route was Panasonic’s Astrova platform . This deployment marks the First-ever integration into a seating product.

The Comoda-Materia Pack seat is equipped with 16-inch Astrova monitors, while Elemento features 13.3-inch Astrova monitor s. This demonstrates the effective use of lightweight, flexible Astrova OLED screens to improve the passenger experience while meeting challenging design and certification requirements.
In addition, the upgradeable peripheral bar on the Astrova screens should reduce servicing and replacement times whilst in the field.
The cooperation with Panasonic began in July 2023, and within 12 months, the seats with integrated IFE were successfully certified in a short lead time for both Comoda – Materia Pack and Elemento.
In Quotes
Alberto Veneruso, Geven Managing Director, said:

“We are incredibly proud to have accomplished these results with Icelandair and Panasonic Avionics. This partnership marks a significant achievement for Geven, showcasing our commitment to innovation and passenger comfort. As the New Comoda – Materia Pack and Elemento are also set to debut on the A330 and A350 fleets, we are excited to see these solutions shaping the future of long-haul travel. We look forward to supporting Icelandair in offering their passengers an exceptional flying experience .”
Helga Huld Bjarnadóttir, Director of Customer Experience & Loyalty at Icelandair said:

“Designing a new cabin is a complex and collaborative process that starts with designing an exceptional customer experience. This process relies on the expertise of multiple partners and great collaboration. For the whole seating and In-Flight Entertainment design, it was a pleasure to witness the innovative solutions and dedicated efforts from Geven and our shared focus on delivering an outstanding experience for our passengers.”
A First Deployment

With every brand-new deployment, there are lessons to learn as partners work together on the finished product and how to integrate it. From the look of things, the partnerships between Geven and Panasonic Avionics have come out well, giving both companies lessons learnt, as well as an advantage for Geven if they wish to deploy the screens to other airlines.

Similarly, Panasonic Avionics will be looking carefully at the deployments, this being the first time Astrova (as well as some of the additional features that Icelandair have signed up for) and seeing the impact of the product in the real world.
But the result for the flying passenger should be a comfortable experience, along with some of the best screens in the sky.

reviews.title: 17 HOURS ON THE QANTAS A380 Business Class Review from Dallas to Sydney

yt_comments.author: @high-reshallucinations
yt_comments.text: Pretty good overall — a comfortable, sleep-focused flight rather than a “wow” luxury experience ✈ The big wins were the Qantas A380 business seat, mattress pad, quiet/smooth ride, and crew. He apparently slept about 9 hours, which is basically the holy grail on a 16h48m flight. The weak points were pretty clear: Food: dinner was decent, but snack/breakfast sounded poor — lots of commenters also thought the catering looked below business-class standard. Entertainment/tech: limited IFE and no Wi-Fi, so the product feels dated. Ground experience: denied Flagship Lounge access, then ended up in a crowded Admirals Club. So: great bed, great crew, mediocre food, outdated tech. For a 17-hour Dallas–Sydney flight, I’d call it a successful flight — just not a top-tier business class experience like Singapore, Emirates, Qatar, etc. 😄

yt_comments.author: @vijaymohaniyer
yt_comments.text: The emirates 380 business class feels more premium than this. Screen sizes are bigger and the meals look and taste better too. Sad that Qantas doesn't have wifi. They seem to be like the Air India of Australia 😂

yt_comments.author: @high-reshallucinations
yt_comments.text: Qantas chose Viasat, not Starlink, and its long-haul retrofit is moving slowly — especially on the A380. ✈ On that Dallas–Sydney QF8 A380, the main reasons are: 1. Qantas already committed to Viasat Qantas announced its international Wi-Fi rollout using Viasat’s next-generation satellite network, with A330, 787 and A380 aircraft to be progressively retrofitted. That means they are not simply installing Starlink like Qatar or United. 2. A380 retrofits are hard Qantas said older A380s are especially challenging because they were built before modern onboard internet infrastructure was common. Installing Wi-Fi means adding antennas/radomes and aircraft wiring — basically physical surgery on the aircraft roof. Qantas specifically said the A380 is the most challenging fleet to retrofit. 3. Qantas is doing it during maintenance, not all at once The first international Wi-Fi aircraft were A330s, mainly for Asia routes. Qantas said 787, A380 and A330-300 installations would follow later, so the A380 fleet is behind the smaller/easier aircraft. 4. Coverage over the Pacific is still a weak spot for Qantas Qantas’ own Wi-Fi page says international connectivity can vary, and it lists areas where coverage is not available, including the South Pacific Ocean — exactly the kind of region a Dallas–Sydney flight crosses. 5. Other airlines moved faster with Starlink Qatar Airways, for example, has already equipped nearly 120 widebody aircraft with Starlink and completed its A350 rollout. That is why Starlink feels “already here” on some airlines while Qantas still feels behind. So basically: Qantas bet on Viasat, the A380 is difficult to retrofit, and the Pacific coverage/rollout is lagging. Starlink may be faster, but switching providers is expensive and disruptive once an airline has contracts, hardware plans and maintenance schedules in place. Reuters also notes that changing satellite providers is costly because aircraft need provider-specific equipment and downtime for installation.

yt_comments.author: @high-reshallucinations
yt_comments.text: Other airlines moved faster with Starlink mainly because they had stronger urgency, easier rollout paths, and better timing than Qantas. 1. They picked Starlink early, while Qantas picked Viasat Qatar, United, Hawaiian and others committed to Starlink as their next big Wi-Fi upgrade. Qantas instead committed its international A330, 787 and A380 fleet to Viasat’s satellite network, so it is locked into a different hardware and provider path. 2. Starlink installations got faster after the first fleets Qatar is the best example. It said its Boeing 777 Starlink retrofit time dropped from three days to 9.5 hours per aircraft, letting it finish the 777 rollout in nine months, about 50% faster than planned. That kind of process improvement makes a rollout much faster once the airline, installer and regulator have the aircraft type figured out. 3. Some airlines made Wi-Fi a headline competitive feature United is using Starlink as a big customer-experience weapon. It completed Starlink installation on 300+ regional aircraft and said more than 25% of its daily departures had Starlink by February 2026, with plans for 500+ mainline aircraft by the end of 2026. 4. Regional/narrow-body aircraft are easier to roll out first United started with regional jets and then moved to mainline aircraft. That is easier than starting with huge long-haul widebodies. Qantas’ problem is the opposite: its most painful gap is on international widebodies, especially A380s. 5. Qantas’ A380s are especially difficult Qantas has said retrofitting older international aircraft is complex, and that the A380s are the most challenging aircraft in its fleet to retrofit. Even the first international A330-200 Wi-Fi retrofit took around three weeks in the hangar. 6. Starlink had momentum and hardware scale Reuters reported that Starlink now has contracts on more than 7,000 aircraft, and airlines are rushing to upgrade because fast/free Wi-Fi has become a premium-cabin expectation. Once many airlines choose the same supplier, certifications, installation know-how and supply chains improve quickly. So the simple version: Qatar and United treated Starlink like a strategic priority and scaled the retrofit fast. Qantas chose Viasat, has older hard-to-retrofit long-haul aircraft, and is moving more cautiously. 🛰✈

yt_comments.author: @high-reshallucinations
yt_comments.text: The weak points came from a few specific things: 1. Lounge issue: He was denied access to the American Airlines Flagship Lounge, likely because of the lounge’s alcohol access rules in the US. He had to use the Admirals Club instead, which was crowded. 2. Food inconsistency: Dinner was good, but the mid-flight snack and breakfast were weak. The waffles apparently tasted like a frozen meal, and commenters felt the food looked more like economy food served on nicer plates. 3. No Wi-Fi: On a nearly 17-hour flight, no Wi-Fi makes the product feel outdated, especially compared with other premium long-haul airlines. 4. Limited entertainment: The IFE selection was not strong enough for such a long flight. So the main cause was not the seat or crew — those were good. The weak points were mostly ground lounge rules, catering quality, and old tech/entertainment. ✈

article_text: Inflight entertainment system providers are going great guns to roll out 4K HDR 10+ screens onboard aircraft to deliver crystal clear and stunning pictures to passengers. But whether 4K OLED, QLED or miniLED LCD displays are in play, a key part of the 4K narrative is lagging behind: the delivery of 4K content to the aviation market.
“It’s slow,” Safran Passenger Innovations (SPI) vice president of products and strategy Ben Asmar told RGN.

“I would say we’ve had some requests from some of our customers for 4K content, but the supply chain just isn’t there to get it consistently across all titles. It still seems to be ‘point by point’ deals for specific titles.”
Nor too, it seems, is the demand all there. “So, whilst it’s increasing, we’re still not seeing huge demand for it,” said Asmar. “I think cost is prohibitive still for a lot of airlines.”
As previously reported, SPI has a clever answer to the problem. It has enough processing power in its latest RAVE IFE hardware to be able to upscale lower resolution content .

“Based on the technology we use here, we do upscale. So, my recommendation to most of my customers is go get 720p content and let our displays upscale,” Asmar said. In short, SPI will take the content through the final 4K mile. And in testing, most people don’t realize upscaling has taken place: “most people pick 720p as the 4K content.”

Panasonic Avionics has also developed an upscaling algorithm for its nextgen Astrova IFE system that automatically enhances the viewing experience on the seatback screens, transforming 480p, 720p, and 1080p to 4K with what it says is “little to no discernible impact to picture quality for passengers.”
Passengers simply can’t tell the difference, Panasonic explains in a blog post.

article_text: 9 October 2025 By Seth Miller Leave a Comment

Entertainment options on the ground have shifted rapidly in recent years. Inflight entertainment was caught flat-footed, with legacy solutions simply not designed for the pace of change and barely able to keep up with the new content structure and needs. At least one industry executive is now taking some responsibility for that situation. Ken Sain, CEO of Panasonic Avionics offered an impressively self-aware observation during a conversation at the World Aviation Festival in Lisbon:

Sain later continued along those same lines, noting that it was the job of IFE manufacturers to “make it easy for airlines to deploy” the solutions, both hardware and software. Until recently, however, the hardware was more of a one-and-done configuration and software changes could take years to percolate through the development, testing, and deployment process.
Dominic Green, Director of IFE at United Airlines , in a later conversation, confirmed this challenge and also the progress that has been made in addressing it.

We now have the ability to do stuff quickly, which historically was not a great feature of inflight entertainment systems. Two or three years ago we were doing software updates every couple of years, and it would take two years to roll that out across the whole fleet. So if you were rolling out a new feature, you tested the heck out of it to make sure you get perfect now. Now, with the support of Panasonic, we’re rolling out updates every quarter or so, which may not be as fast as people in the web and app space are, but we are in a state now where we can roll out new features really quickly.

We now have the ability to do stuff quickly, which historically was not a great feature of inflight entertainment systems. Two or three years ago we were doing software updates every couple of years, and it would take two years to roll that out across the whole fleet. So if you were rolling out a new feature, you tested the heck out of it to make sure you get perfect now.

Now, with the support of Panasonic, we’re rolling out updates every quarter or so, which may not be as fast as people in the web and app space are, but we are in a state now where we can roll out new features really quickly.

The change in pace allows the airlines to be more responsive to shifts in consumer trends. It also allows airlines to experiment more. Knowing that an update can be further tweaked (or rolled back) on this schedule allows the carrier to be more aggressive in its decisions.

Green further noted that the company pulls significantly more data off the aircraft now, and far more quickly than in the prior generations of the IFE platforms. That enables United to quickly learn how passengers are interacting with the systems and tweak the experience.

Sain also shared a vision where each IFE screen on board ties in to the on-board connectivity solution – likely LEO satellites – to deliver a personalized passenger experience. That could be as simple as a passenger saving their preferred configuration of the icons on the screen, and that following them from flight to flight. One of the best parts, Sain observed, is that these improvements are all software based. It doesn’t add weight [and associated costs] to the aircraft, and it can be reset and reconfigured for a new set of travelers on each subsequent flight.

It will also lead to different content being served to different passengers. One implementation of that is saving the favorites list of movies. Panasonic implemented something along these lines with its companion app a decade ago. That was a limited solution based on limited technology available at the time. It has evolved since then – and includes other airlines and suppliers – to passengers being able to set certain preferences and have them follow from flight to flight. JetBlue’s Blueprint solution, built in partnership with Thales , is another example.

Airlines (and their suppliers) must also address the competing demand of delivering solutions that improve their own value, not just that of the passenger. IFC “may create value for the passenger, which indirectly creates value for the airline,” Sain shared. “But that is very different from having an ecosystem that airlines can create loyalty from. And some will want to monetize it. That’s the fundamental reason why IFC is not a substitute for IFE.”

One version of that added value on the airline side comes in the form of targeted advertising. “Our previous model for customers was showing the same three or four pre-roll ads before every movie, every TV show,” Green observed. “It was not great for anyone. The only advertisers we got were major brand partnerships that were okay with just saturating the campaigns, but customers didn’t like it.”

With the updated platform, however, flight manifest data is uploaded to the aircraft as the gate agent closes out the flight, “so we know a lot of information about every customer at every seat. We’re able to start targeting. And it is not just ads, but promotions and messaging as well. We can tell a customer there’s an upgrade opportunity on your connecting flight and offer it to them in miles or dollars, giving them something valuable there and then.”

United, like the other US airlines, has a deep partnership with its co-brand credit card partner. In a recent update the carrier added a verification step – passengers confirm on the IFE screen who they are – which allows for a deeper level of targeting. The data includes whether the passenger is a MileagePlus member and which Chase credit card they might hold. Green shares that United uses that, plus the verification, to vary the offering. An existing cardholder will see a pitch to upgrade, for example, rather than one for an entry level new card.

This is arguably one of the easiest levels of customization, and also one with the most potential profit. But it has proven elusive to the industry until very, very recently (and even now not always perfect).

Impressively, United also shares that its shift towards this targeted ad platform is showing positive results. It can include more advertisers thanks to smaller, targeted campaigns. Engagement (i.e. click-throughs) is increasing because passengers are seeing more relevant content. Green also shared that “passenger satisfaction scores go up at the same time as we’re serving even more ads and messages and combining the high-margin revenue for that as well. It works together.”

And it all depends on the convergence of inflight entertainment and connectivity systems. Those relationships are now maturing at a much faster pace, enabling these sorts of solutions. And the IFE providers are no longer making it as difficult for the airlines to realize those goals.

yt_comments.text: 14:55 This may be true for economy, but it can't be said for premium economy and Upper Class. I've flown their 787s twice, once in economy and once in premium economy class. The state of the cabin in economy was fine, but the premium economy seats are really worn out. There were multiple issues with them, one being the hinge that attaches the seat to the floor literally broke off so our flight had to be delayed while a mechanic came onboard and fixed it, and the other being the touch screen remotes for the IFE was broken at just about every seat. It's also worth mentioning the Upper Class seats on the 787s are really old and outdated, and I think the premium economy and Upper class cabins should be refurbished, if not the whole cabin.

reviews.transcript_full:
Did you know that Emirates flies up to eight A380s 
per day from Dubai to London, making this by far   the busiest A380 route in the world? This is the 
money-maker for the airline - it’s pretty much the   route that makes them love the A380 and makes them 
desperate to keep it around as long as possible.   So, completely as an excuse to fly Emirates A380 
First Class again, I thought why not test out   their flagship route because I wonder - is this 
experience any different? Qatar Airways famously   has a vastly different soft product to London 
compared to most other cities in Europe - so is   it the same on Emirates? Come with me, Dan, a 
full-time airline reviewer who has flown over   160 airlines in the decade I’ve been reviewing 
airlines, on this seven-hour flight, to find out! Today’s flight starts at the least surprising 
place possible, Gothenburg International Airp…,   I mean Dubai Airport where it’s time to get 
our VIP on. To be fair, Emirates carries   thousands of first-class passengers every 
single day, so you’re one VIP among many,   except I suspect I paid a lot less 
without even using credit card points. Let’s start out in the Emirates 
First Class lounge A-gates. Now do you have a moment to look at 
the first-class lounge menu because   OMG this is incredible. I don’t think 
I’ve ever seen a bigger lounge menu.   What would you go for from this 
menu? Speaking of menus - do you   think it’s going to be any different 
on Emirates’ flagship route to London? There’s also naturally a huge buffet. 
I don’t usually go to any lounges early   to spend time there but given that 
you get a free 15-minute massage,   I’d say spending at least two 
hours here is a good idea. Boarding from the lounge is one of my favorite   features - it’s not available from 
a lot of gates so I’m lucky today. Seat map: The Emirates Airbus A380 
has a lovely 14 first-class seats,   meaning that your odds of finding an available 
seat are far higher than on airlines with smaller   4-8 seat cabins. This definitely isn’t the 
most spacious first class in the world,   but it’s certainly spacious enough. There 
are four rows along the window with rows 2   and 3 being slightly preferable in my 
opinion since they have three windows   rather than two. In the middle, there are 
three rows of two seats. I almost always opt   for the last row as loyal viewers know, but 
Emirates blocks it until close to departure,   so I’ve opted for row one in the center instead. 
Normally when I talk about the ratio of lavatories   to passengers, I’m not mentioning showers, but 
that’s what’s fun about Emirates A380 first   class because we have two bathrooms shared by 14 
people - 7 people to one shower, in other words.   Now let’s hop onboard and see just how fun 
we can have on Emirates’ flagship A380 route. Welcome onboard Emirates’ iconic 
A380 first class. This aircraft,   like the majority of their A380s, has not been 
refurbished with the new interior colors so the   seats look a little worn, but who cares - 
they are comfortable and private as heck. So cheers! One of my favorite things 
is the little snacks basket waiting at   your seat - not because you need 
it but because it feels opulent. A cheeky hot towel - don’t mind if I do. Next up Arabic coffee with Bateel dates 
that are worth their weight in gold. Finally, we start our pushback and 
blast off toward lovely London. The menu: This is the first sign that this 
route is different. Unlike most of their   Europe routes with 5 main course options, the 
London flights have six. Even their longest   flight to New Zealand only has five options, 
not six. I cannot understate how much I love   having access to menus beforehand like this. 
Emirates loads them many months in advance   so you can choose to fly Emirates first class 
when the menu looks especially appealing to you! On the A380, you can shower whenever you want,   but there needs to be a shower available, so 
usually at departure time the crew will come   around and schedule your shower. Knowing most 
people would want to shower before landing,   I offered to shower right after takeoff since I 
just want to shower but don’t really care when. Welcome to the beautiful bathroom/shower spa. 
Is this very unnecessary? Yes. Does it make me   only ever want to fly the Emirates A380 in first 
class? Also yes. They went so far as to even heat   the floors in here. In here you have all types of 
toiletries in addition to what’s in your Bvlgari   amenity kit. You get 5 minutes of continuous 
running water which you can start and stop. I   have never even come close to using all the water, 
so 5 minutes seems plenty to me. After the most   refreshing in-flight experience possible, it’s 
time to get into the Emirates first-class pajamas. We start out the first meal with my 
typical favorite olives, potato chips,   and today a mango juice because why not?   For some reason, the whole table setup looks 
even more incredible today than usual. Oskar   even opts for some Dom Perignon to celebrate 
his first Emirates A380 First Class experience. Maybe I need to take a course to 
understand champagne better. Anyway,   look at our beautiful amuse bouche! For the first meal, we opt to eat our 
specially loaded vegan meal and dine   from the menu before landing. That is 
why this Arabic mezze doesn’t look as   grandiose as the typical first-class mezze. 
Don’t worry because it tastes just as good. For the main course - biryani. To my 
surprise, this is spicy. I like spicy food,   but you get so used to never getting truly spicy 
food on a plane that it can take you off guard. Finally, a berry cake to 
round off meal number one. After the meal, I’m ready to get reeeeal cozy, so 
I order some popcorn and tea as I watch a movie.   Seriously, I will never take this for granted. 
If 15-year-old Dan could see this, he’d think   it was cool enough I was on an A380, let alone in 
first class, to which he’d probably start crying   tears of happiness. To be fair, I don’t think 
I knew much about first class at that point. After a while, I figure I might as well get 
even comfier, so I ask our fantastic crew to   help me prepare the bed - I mean seriously 
- how comfortable does this look? I think   this is a good time to discuss just how much I 
paid for this flight because as always with me,   I think of ways to save, even when the airline 
tries to make it impossible like Emirates. So yes, it’s time to eat again. 
These are my two meals for the day,   and I wouldn’t have it any other way. This meal starts with the heirloom tomato 
salad from the menu which looks straight   out of Ratatouille. As far as I’m concerned, 
Emirates has the tastiest salads in the sky.   I live for anything with Kalamata olives 
so I’d have a hard time not loving this. The main course of this meal is another 
star - miso-baked tofu with pumpkin and   pak choi. WOW. I don’t know why 
some people don’t like Emirates   catering. How can anyone eat this dish and not 
love it? It’s absolutely packed with flavor. Finally, the chocolate pecan cake for 
dessert. This video turned into a long   showcase of Emirates’ food but you 
know what, why not? I’m glad I get to   show you so many incredible dishes from the 
menu, especially since they are all tasty. I head back to the lavatory one more time before 
landing. The bar is set up outside and has the   most incredible display for drinks, including some 
very expensive alcohols. As I always say, this   airline is about fun, and the experience will be 
so much more fun if you enjoy it with a loved one. So there you have it. A Japanese 
toilet is all it would take to   make this product even more over the 
top and fun, as if it isn’t already. With that, we touch down at London Heathrow and 
the experience is over all too soon. Luckily,   we can do it again sooner rather than later 
without completely breaking the bank. So how   different is the London route from others? As 
far as I can tell, it’s the addition of one   more meal option. Besides that, the experience is 
exactly the same as other routes of this length.   I really appreciate that about Emirates since 
consistency is key for being a high-quality   airline - whether it’s the seat or the soft 
product - it’s always nice to know what to expect.

reviews.transcript_full: We have put together two calendars for 2025, one with our all-time best in-flight shots  and one with the most photogenic airplane meals, and this is your last chance to order  them so they still arrive in time for Christmas.  Go to SimpliViation.com and get yourself or a loved one, a Simpli Aviation Wall Calendar  for 2025.  In August of 2021, JetBlue commenced its first ever transatlantic route, connecting New  York and London.  A bold move jumping into the world's busiest long-haul route, where JetBlue's current  three daily A321 Nios are competing against eight daily British Airways flights, four daily  American Airlines flights, six on Virgin Atlantic, and two on Delta, plus another nine daily  flights from Newark and three flights from JFK to Gatwick.  JetBlue has since expanded its transatlantic offering, with its current summer 2025 schedule  seeing them offer flights from New York JFK and Boston to Dublin, London Heathrow, London  Gatwick, Amsterdam, Paris-Shalde-Gole, and the also flight of Edinburgh, albeit only from  JFK.  On every single one of those routes, except for Boston to London Gatwick, they have to  compete with at least one other airline.  Going up against so many larger, more established carriers, JetBlue needs to do things differently  to make it in those markets and give passengers a reason to choose them.  So in today's video, we'll take a flight across the pond aboard their Airbus A321  NOLR from Amsterdam to New York JFK and see for ourselves what they do differently,  where they made cuts to offer competitive fares and whether they are worth choosing at  all.  Glad you've decided to join us on this trip, so let's get going.  Aviation Geeks and Frequent Flyers, welcome to this new episode of our flight review series  Brutalianist, where we aim to showcase as many different airlines in flight products  in the most factual and detailed mannered possible.  We are just about to arrive into Amsterdam approaching parallel to this A320 of EZJET  coming in from London Luton.  JetBlue doesn't have a lot of co-chair partnerships in Europe, solely working with lot and  British airways, and there too in a very limited manner, meaning their European routes  are kind of dead ends.  Since I live in Vienna, I had no way to book a continuous ticket from Vienna to somewhere  else in Europe and continue from there across the ocean on JetBlue, so I took the risk  to fly in on a different airline.  Luckily, I was able to check in for my JetBlue flight online, so I did not have to exit  the secure area of Amsterdam Airport and was able to proceed directly to my gate.  Or well, I WILL be in like an hour.  The Dutch border police, or Koniklike Maritio Say, hasn't found any solution to deal  with a spike in border crossings before noon, so we'll have to wait until things come  down a bit.  After an hour and a half in the lounge, there was nobody left and we're able to head directly  to our gate.  Oh, by the way, look at how cool this shot is.  I'm trying my best to continuously improve the quality of our videos and I recently  got a special filter for my camera lens to allow me to capture these stunning time-lapse  shots with motion blur and I'll incorporate them into more videos in the future.  And since not just our equipment, but also the animations and the flights themselves are  pricey, we rely on various types of support to run this channel.  As you might know, we rarely promote other companies and products here at SimpliViation  because I simply won't lend my credibility to shady VPNs and risky investment products.  But there is a company we have been working with for almost two years of which product  I am a very satisfied user which is sponsoring today's video.  Holtzcan is a jewelry brand with a special focus on watches offering a wide variety of  products to both men and women, headquartered right here where we live in beautiful Vienna,  Austria.  Myself own three different Holtzcan watches and love each of them individually for their  unique designs.  All of Holtzcan's products are made from natural materials like wood, stone or even leaves  and peacock feathers.  If you can't make up your mind of what to gift to that special someone for Christmas  this year, Holtzcan has designs for everyone from elegant to business eve, to casual and  modern and with their free worldwide express shipping you can place orders until December  19th for the product to still arrive in time for Christmas.  If I could interest you with that, go to Holtzcan.com.com.  SimpliViation and use coupon code aviation for 15% off your order, using this specific link  will make it more likely for Holtzcan to help us put more effort into our videos in the  future too.  Before we board our aircraft, let me also briefly give you some information on booking this  flight.  On JetBlue's website you can easily see the features and amenities offered on each flight,  plus the different bundles they offer where I'm going with blue as it allows me to pick  a window seat in advance which is always a priority for me when recording these reviews.  There are options to pre-order special meals for free and when selecting the seat you  may also opt for extra legroom or emergency exodrome seats for an additional fee.  For my regular seats I always consult a website called erolopa.com which is also kind  enough to allow me to use their seat maps in our videos to better illustrate the layouts  of the planes we're flying on.  Lopa by the way means layout or location of passenger accommodations and is an industry  term for seating charts.  The flight itself wasn't expensive at all, but I paid even less than that thanks to  a friend of mine who still had a jet blue voucher left over.  So special thanks to Keishi for helping me out.  I know Keishi from being a nerd for aviation and Japan and he runs a fantastic English language  block and aviation and aviation related news in Japan called K&A where he also regularly  posts great in-depth flight and hotel reviews and I highly recommend you give him a follow  and check out his blog.  The first of Amsterdam's two daily jet blue flights is departing to Boston right now  with our rights to JFK coming in as we speak.  Today we will be traveling aboard November 4076 Juliet, a brand new 2023 build Airbus 8321  NOL.  Generally speaking the 8321 NOL is the same plane as the regular 8321 NOL, the capacity  limits for seats and fuel are a bit different but apart from that the planes are almost identical  which is why Airbus was able to bring it to market that quickly.  The new 8321 XLR on the other hand has structural differences that took years of work to get  right and certified by authorities which is why it is only now starting to get delivered  to airlines.  Jet Blue has ordered a bunch of these as well which will allow the airline to launch flights  further into Europe but due to their recent poor financial performance jet blue has decided  to defer the deliveries of their 8321 XLRs beyond 2030 so it will be a while until we potentially  see jet blue planes in places like Milan or Zurich.  Jet Blue currently operates 11 Airbus 8321 NOL which is quite hard to find out because  as I mentioned the LRs are so similar to the regular Nios there is no official separate  type code for the LR which means most websites list them all together.  However it is easy to spot that the two sets of 8321 Nios at Jet Blue carry slightly  different registrations.  The ones starting with N2 are the regular 8321 Nios and the ones with N4 are the LRs.  Keep that in mind that information will be relevant towards the end of the video again.  Since I did an air site transit I wasn't able to drop off my suitcase but they were looking  for volunteers to check their bags anyway which gave me another option to get rid of it  for the flight.  Jet Blue's Airbus 8321 NOL Rs are equipped with two classes.  Up front there is the Mint Cabin featuring 24 Thompson Vantage solo seats in a 11 herring  bone layout.  This is followed by the 8321's standard 333 layout and economy class where Jet Blue  offers additional leg room for the first 5 rows recognizable by an orange headrest outline  but we want to see what an average seat is like so we are back here in 20F.  Jet Blue installed Collins Aerospace Meridian seats in economy class which come with adjustable  headrests both vertically as well as on the sides.  And we've also got a blanket but unfortunately no pillow.  This is standard on Jet Blue Transatlantic flights and even during booking we got the  information that a blanket would be offered but no mention of a pillow.  Seeing a 180cm tall the leg room is very impressive and I love that the seat back pockets  come with these handy little extra pockets for things like your phone.  Beneath the seats you will find universal power ports as well as USB-C ports offering  fast charging which were even fast enough to power my laptop.  There are two of each per every 3 seats.  We've also got a standard tray table as well as a non-adjustable entertainment touch screen  with the audio port and a USB-A port at the bottom.  In the ceiling above you will find both non-adjustable personal reading lights as well as adjustable  private airweds.  Code hooks are not installed.  Now here's where the journey gets interesting.  Before departure you need to select what you want to eat using the entertainment screen.  You can choose between one of three different main courses, all of which sounding really  tasty and then you can pick two out of three side dishes.  But there are some changes coming to this unique kind of service structure soon so stick  around until the end when I talk a bit more about that.  You can also choose which drink you want to have with your meal and I really like this  in particular because it gives a much better overview of what's even an offer.  Often times when I'm asked what I want to drink I don't even think that they would  have things like ginger ale.  On transatlantic flights both hot and cold, non-alcoholic as well as alcoholic drinks are  offered at no extra charge.  While we're at it let's also take a closer look at the entertainment system as a whole.  JetBlue uses Tali's Avent in flight entertainment system and while you can connect your phone  through the Wi-Fi with the system to use it as a remote control it sucks that such a  modern system does not support Bluetooth headphones.  Earbuds are provided by JetBlue but given how modern this brain is it would have been  better to include Bluetooth instead of the phone as a remote control thingy which let's  be honest is mostly just a gimmick.  And entertainment wise JetBlue offers a solid selection of movies and TV shows to stream  on demand as well as a small number of live TV channels.  Within the US JetBlue is known for offering dozens of live TV channels and the reason why  they don't on transatlantic flights is likely that it's a licensing issue.  US TV channels license content to show it to US audiences so an airline flying outside  of the US is likely not able to show these channels.  JetBlue more than makes up for that by offering tons of content and multiple episodes of  popular TV shows in addition to games and audio and a high quality in flight map application.  With that it's finally time to head out.  Given that JetBlue has inflated entertainment screens on all of their planes it does  surprise me that they still do manual safety demos as opposed to having a fun safety  game.  After take off the crew immediately began with their first round of service consisting  of just beverages.  As on all JetBlue flights sweet and savory snacks were available for free throughout the  entire flight but for now I was just craving a coffee and some sparkling water.  As we're leaving Ireland behind it's finally time for that main meal service.  It served in these uniform reusable containers and the crew puts together the meal from a few  large boxes they have on their meal cart checking their tablet computer for what you have  ordered.  I went with meatballs with tomato fero, the kale quinoa salad and the cucumber with vegan  ranch dressing.  It was served alongside a bottle of water and a bit of sweet and sour sauce.  All in all this was superb.  It was beautifully presented and very tasty and I highly appreciate how inventive and  healthy these dishes appear to be.  That's not a standard chicken or pasta choice, this is a meal service somebody put thought  into and I love it.  I'll share some more thoughts about this towards the end of the video when I also have to inform  you that JetBlue is going to cut all of this from their service but there's more to  this story for now let's get on with our flight.  The meal chocolate ice cream was handed out by the crew.  T and coffee were offered too.  The cabin of this A321neo is absolutely stunning.  Airbus calls this set of innovations and designs in their newest cabin's airspace.  And as part of these airspace cabins the overhead bins are notably larger allowing for more  cabin sized suitcases to be stored in each of them.  It also comes with LED lighting and certain new materials and innovations beyond the passenger  site which help the airline operate more efficiently.  One downside to operating A321neos across the Atlantic is that they are quite bothersome  for crews.  The galleys are much smaller, there is less space for passengers to loiter meaning that  everybody is in closer proximity to each other than they normally would be on a widebody  aircraft.  Because of that crews also don't have regular crew rest areas which is what this curtain  is for.  Behind that are a few seats blocked for the crew for when they are on break.  And if the plane operates a flight where no crew rest is necessary the curtain just  stays open and the seats get sold.  Another unique thing to this plane but unique to JetBlue not to the A321neo is the pantry.  Aborted transcontinental and transatlantic flights JetBlue offers a snack bar where  you can serve yourself at any point during the flight.  We've got pop chips, plantain chips, pretzel sticks, bottled water and the crew will also  help you with any additional beverage needs.  The lavatories are quite small but I do love the New York style wallpaper and the  waistband and flush are touch free.  As you can see with my shoes I'm a person who wears a lot of brown tones and these wooden  harts can watches fit my style phenomenally.  And by the way while the company designs the outside the inner clockwork are still manufactured  by renowned companies like Japanese watchmaker Seiko ensuring they last.  I can genuinely vouch for Haltscan's quality and reliability and can guarantee their products  will make great Christmas presents.  I got myself some snacks and drinks to enjoy the rest of the flight.  This is my personal favorite beverage combo on US Airlines.  This cranberry apple juice mixed with sparkling water so refreshing.  Another really cool thing about JetBlue is that they offer free unlimited wifi on transatlantic  flights and a usably fast one at that.  Before landing another hot snack is offered.  This time a slice of cheese pizza and some more water always stay hydrated on long haul  flights.  After a long flight half of the drowsiness you feel is simply dehydration.  The drier cabin air combined with sitting for prolonged periods of times and not drinking  enough liquids it strains your body more than any time difference usually does.  As we're starting our descent into New York there are quite a few things we still need  to address.  First, let's recap the good things because there are a lot.  Free unlimited wifi is such a handy component to this flight especially with the speeds  it offers as I was able to get a decent amount of work done on this flight.  I also love the main meal service not just where the dish is inventive, healthy and  balanced.  I also found them to be delicious and in a world where plenty of airlines just try to  make the cheapest pasta with cheese they can I appreciate JetBlue putting so much thought  and effort into their economy class meals.  The beverage selection also left nothing to be desired and I'm a big fan of the pantry  being there as a standard feature not just a will they won't they have snacks in the  back which for many airlines you don't know until you check.  But there are all the things that bothered me mainly because I'm unable to understand  the reasonings behind them.  Front and center being that the ive system does not support Bluetooth headphones either  tollies does not offer this feature yet or JetBlue opted against it both not good for  a plane that will remain flying with this cabin for probably another decade.  Bluetooth headphones are ubiquitous already and will only increase in adoption further  down the road.  I also believe it would be in JetBlue's own interest to provide pillows.  If I think about this journey and which service elements gave me the least return in terms  of comfort compared to their price to the airline, a pillow simply wouldn't be the  first thing I would cut.  Since the main meal was so substantial and the pantry being offered on all transatlantic  flights, I would argue it's the cheap slice of pizza that brought the least additional  comfort relative to its price.  So I would say JetBlue should think about cutting that and instead give everyone pillows.  But JetBlue has put some additional thought into their transatlantic product and they  have made a decision regarding their main meal service.  Being right now they will cut the hot main dish meaning it'll be just a cold meal.  Now calm down.  I know there have been heated reactions to this and people calling JetBlue cheap skates  and whatnot but after researching these changes and even reaching out to JetBlue directly,  I believe the airline actually deserves to be cut some slack here.  First, the main meal service will still feature various high quality items.  They're not going down to doing cheap mass produced wraps and sandwiches but rather  still offer thoughtfully crafted dishes that I would argue sound still better cold than  what you might find on other airline served warm.  The current menus can be found on their website and while the selection got smaller, only  offering two main dishes as opposed to three and just two sides, the inventiveness seems  to still be there, although it is undeniably disappointing that the cool select your  sides and main dish is no more.  JetBlue gave us the following statement saying that this change is part of our effort  to ensure we can continue to provide a great experience at JetBlue's competitive fairs  on these routes.  In addition to our dig meals, our transatlantic flights offer fast and free fly-fi and  seatback entertainment at every seat.  Pre-landing light bites vary based on route and aircraft and have not changed with the  new menus, JetBlue continues to provide free unlimited snacks and drinks available during  the InFlight service and self-service from the JetBlue pantry.  Which raises the question, why?  Why would JetBlue do that?  They did mention their effort to provide competitive fairs which puts a financial reasoning behind  that, and while I'm sure that is the case with reducing the number of options, I don't  think that it is necessarily cheaper to provide a high quality cold dish as opposed to a  high quality hot dish.  There is something else a hot dish needs though, and that's galley space and ovens  to heat it up.  And that's where the different registration is for regular A321 Nios and LRs I mentioned  earlier in the video coming.  So my personal assumption as to why the meals are now served cold is that due to delivery  delays at Airbus as well as the persistent issues with preten Whitney Geert's Tourbuffin  engines, JetBlue was forced to send their regular A321 Nios across the Atlantic on selected  flights last season, replacing the originally scheduled A321 Nios LRs.  Now the A321 Nios can do those routes, likely somewhat weight restricted but they have the  same type of seats so it doesn't matter too much from the perspective of the passenger.  Or so it seems, you see if you look closely you'll see that the regular A321 Nios have  less galley space in the back than the A321 Nios LRs.  That's because JetBlue ordered their regular A321 Nios with fewer ovens because they  don't need them.  There are no hot meals on transcon flights, so when you substitute the LRs with regular  Nios you end up with too few ovens to offer hot meals to all passengers which is why I assume  they decided to just offer cold meals on all flights across the Atlantic.  JetBlue has said this change is not temporary but I do think they will keep their options  open.  If passenger satisfaction does not decline too much they might keep it this way.  If the A321 Nios LRs and later XLRs come into service maybe they'll go back to hot  meals.  All we know right now is that the free Wi-Fi, the snack bar, the beverage selection, the  pre-landing snack all that will stay the same.  Only the main meal will now have a cold main dish as opposed to a hot main dish which  I would argue in the grand scheme of things is much less of a quality decline that some  people made it out to be.  While I love the concept of the meal I had and it's disappointing to see it change I would  say that even with a cold main course, the overall experience flying transatlantic with  JetBlue is a good one.  Very good in fact.  They offer a superb value for money at the moment and their service is almost over  the top for the length of their flights.  After all JetBlue only connects the very northeast of North America with the very west of  Europe so their transatlantic flights are comparably short anyway ranging in the roughly  six hours eastbound and seven hours westbound.  So with everything we saw in experience then my endless monologues we had finally made  it to New York's John of Kennedy International Airport.  One underrated advantage of flying JetBlue into JFK is that you arrive in Terminal 5 which  at this time of day is a breeze to go through immigration at taking me less than 10 minutes  today.  I hope you enjoyed another one of our hopelessly long and egregiously detailed flight reviews.  If that's exactly what you're longing for make sure you are subscribed to our channel  as we have plenty more where that came from.  Special thanks to Kishi once again for letting me use his JetBlue credit to all of our fantastic  channel sponsors who through their financial contributions help us dedicate more time and  resources to this channel and every single one of you for watching InstaKillaround until  the end.  Of course thank you to Holtscam for sponsoring this video, go to Holtscam.com slash simply  and use coupon code aviation for 15% of your order.  I will see you again for a new video next week and until then, safe travels.  And go get yourself a calendar for 2025.

yt_comments.text: Flew with them recently. The food was amazing. The staff were bitchy as you can expect. I said to one flight attendant "can you please put my bag in the compartment I'm too short". There were 3 open seats, with 3 more open seats in front of them. Someone called it "reserve seats" whatever that is supposed to mean..this Australian flight attendant, for some weird reason, took a liking to this Indian couple. They asked about the 6 open seats. She told them "yeah you guys can sit there". She was all chatty and smiley with them. The husband then took 3 seats for himself, and the wife took 3 seats in front of him..I just thought the whole thing was really weird. Sorry, but where do you get off just roaming a plane looking for open seats? And the flight attendant just giggles and says "yeah sure guys!" Not fair to other passengers. We don't want to see that kind of favouritism. But the food was really amazing, there was free internet on the first flight ( starlink ) and I could charge my phone on the plane ❤

chapters.title: Why does Brisbane need a metro?

reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Brisbane! When we think of a metro, we often associate it with rapid transit train systems like the Sydney Metro, London Underground, or Singapore's MRT. Today, Brisbane is launching its own metro, though it's not what you might expect from the name. Let's go and take a closer look! Since September 2000, Brisbane has developed a Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) network, mainly through the construction of dedicated busways that run separately from regular traffic. These exclusive corridors have enhanced the efficiency and reliability of bus services, encouraging more residents to opt for public transportation. As a result, the city’s bus infrastructure quickly reached capacity in a number of areas and has led to congestion on some bus routes and at key interchanges. To address this, in 2016, the Brisbane City Council proposed the Brisbane Metro. Initially, the plan was to convert the busway from Woolloongabba to Herston into a track-based, rubber-tyred underground metro system similar to the Paris Metro. However, by March 2017, while keeping the same name, the project shifted to using high-capacity bi-articulated buses on the existing busway, reducing costs by $500 million. And this becomes the Brisbane Metro we see today! The first stage of the Metro consists of two routes covering 21 kilometres. Metro 1 will replace bus routes 111 and 160, connecting Eight Mile Plains to Roma Street with 11 stations. Metro 2 has 12 stops and will replace route 66, linking the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital to the University of Queensland. The system will utilise the existing busways and was initially designed to offer turn-up-and-go services with three-minute intervals during peak times, though this was later scaled back to every five minutes. Full services for Metro 1 and Metro 2 are expected to commence by the end of the year. Today, Brisbane Metro is having a soft launch, running between UQ Lakes and Eight Mile Plains, replacing some regular buses on route 169. The 60 buses ordered for Brisbane Metro are built by the Swiss manufacturer HESS and are similar to the models operating in Basel, Switzerland, and Nantes, France. Each bus has three large double doors for efficient boarding, including one automated on-request ramp access at the first passenger door. Before we hop on board, do you know what this is for? Brisbane Metro buses are battery-electric and rely on charging facilities to operate. This is one of the end-of-route flash charging locations on the network, where each bus uses a pantograph that autonomously connects to the charger, recharging the bus in just six minutes. At the Rochedale Metro depot, slower overnight chargers are used to enhance battery lifespan and optimise energy efficiency. At 24.7 metres long, each bus can carry 150 passengers in comfort mode or up to 170 in event mode. There are three accessible spaces at the front with next stop audio and hearing loops in all compartments. As you'd expect from a modern bus, there are WiFi and USB charging ports throughout, along with real-time travel information screens. Brisbane-born actress Melanie Zanetti provides the voice for Brisbane Metro. The expected cost to deliver Brisbane Metro is $1.4 billion. It will reduce around 125 buses from the CBD during the morning peak while maintaining passenger capacity. Route 169 serves nine stations. Thanks to the dedicated busway, what typically takes 28 minutes by car in regular traffic only took 20 minutes on the metro. Overall, I found the ride enjoyable. It's more flexible than a tram line while offering similar capacity, making it the next best alternative to the original rubber-tyred metro design. Given that most people associate "metro" with trains, I do believe names such as Brisbane Electric Rapid Transit (BERT) would be more fitting for this new public transport option. Thank you so much for watching! If you find this video interesting, please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more train and flight reviews. See you all in my next video!
