Additionally, Thales will install the AVANT Up IFE System on Air India’s 11 new Airbus and Boeing aircraft with deliveries to commence in 2025.
Thales’ AVANT Up features Optiq , 4K QLED HDR displays for high-quality outputs.

The Optiq system features in-screen USB-A and USB-C high-speed charging ports and is the only display with two Bluetooth connections and built-in Wi-Fi. With Optiq passengers can pair their wireless headphones or other devices to the display while also charging their phones and laptops so they can arrive at their destination recharged and relaxed.
This is paired with 3D mapping and Thales’ Select User Interface.
In Quotes
Yannick Assouad, Executive Vice-President Avionics, Thales said

“At Thales, we are very proud to deepen our long standing partnership with Air India. ​ We are committed to support the airline’s transformation by delivering state-of-the-art AVANT Up technologies that transcend the ordinary to offer Air India’s customers with world-class inflight experiences celebrating the vibrant culture and colours of India.”
Ashish Saraf, VP and Country Director for India, Thales.

“India is the fastest growing aviation market in the world, with huge potential for further growth. This sets the stage for airlines to elevate overall flying experience of passengers. We are pleased to support Air India in achieving the ambition of providing superior customer experience with our advanced AVANT Up inflight entertainment.”
Rajesh Dogra, Chief Customer Experience Officer, Air India.

“Air India is committed to providing a world-class travel experience to its passengers. Partnering with Thales for its top-of-the-class AVANT Up inflight entertainment systems is a step in the direction of our transformation programme. This latest inflight entertainment technology will allow us to stay at the forefront of aviation technology and will help us provide our passengers with a unique onboard entertainment system.”
AVANT Up and Optiq in real life
At Economy Class and beyond, we’ve used the AVANT Up IFE System with the Optiq screens at Aircraft Interiors Expo,

I used Optiq seatback, trying out some of the system’s features (not just the display technology), and it is pretty impressive, to put it mildly, with the displays capable of impressive resolution and delivery.

The dual-Bluetooth pairing is great for sharing content or hogging the two connections to yourself with a headset and game controller (and this was a standard Xbox controller being used in this demo).
It’s also impressively thin – reducing the weight of the system installed on the aircraft.
But the issue won’t be the technology – it will be with content.
Don’t forget the Content

We’ve all been on flights where the content is blocky or stretched, with IFE systems delivering DVD-quality content…on a good day (what could be called 480p content). On larger displays, there is some HD content – but it can be a struggle to have suppliers deliver content at the high resolutions needed to play this – as well as the storage servers on the aircraft to deliver this content.
It’ll be interesting to see how Air India addresses this with their suppliers to deliver HDR and 4K content to the seat – and what its requirements will be.
As well as the size of the storage server.
For Air India passengers, it’s going to be a giant leap forward in passenger experience in terms of visuals alone.

article_text: Air India, India’s leading global airline with the largest international network in the country and the most non-stop routes connecting India with global destinations, has selected Thales’ AVANT Up inflight entertainment (IFE) solution. With Thales’ AVANT Up, Air India will deliver engaging and memorable guest experiences.

Thales will upgrade and retrofit Air India’s current fleet of 40 Boeing 777’s and 787’s with its state-of-the-art AVANT Up system, starting in 2024 and continuing through 2025. Additionally, Thales will install AVANT Up IFE on Air India’s 11 new Airbus and Boeing aircraft with deliveries to commence in 2025. Thales is proud to build on the enduring relationship with Air India to support the airline’s transformation in redefining the passenger entertainment experience.

AVANT Up offers tremendous possibilities for integrating a wide range of services and applications, such as an interactive 3D map and immersive route-based programming. Thales’ Select User Interface (UI) enhances passenger engagement enabling guests to enjoy the most intuitive user experience to navigate across the rich catalog of entertainment.

Thales’ AVANT Up features Optiq, 4K QLED HDR displays designed to provide the best viewing experience in the air with unrivalled picture quality. Optiq features in-screen USB-A and USB-C high speed charging ports and is the only display with two Bluetooth connections and built-in Wi-Fi. With Optiq passengers can pair their wireless headphone or other devices to the display while also charging their phones and laptops so they can arrive at their destination recharged and relaxed.

“At Thales, we are very proud to deepen our long standing partnership with Air India. ​ We are committed to support the airline’s transformation by delivering state-of-the-art AVANT Up technologies that transcend the ordinary to offer Air India’s customers with world-class inflight experiences celebrating the vibrant culture and colours of India,” said Yannick Assouad, Executive Vice-President Avionics, Thales.

“India is the fastest growing aviation market in the world, with huge potential for further growth. This sets the stage for airlines to elevate overall flying experience of passengers. We are pleased to support Air India in achieving the ambition of providing superior customer experience with our advanced AVANT Up inflight entertainment,” said Ashish Saraf, VP and Country Director for India, Thales.

“Air India is committed to providing a world-class travel experience to its passengers. Partnering with Thales for its top-of-the-class AVANT Up inflight entertainment systems is a step in the direction of our transformation programme. This latest inflight entertainment technology will allow us to stay at the forefront of aviation technology and will help us provide our passengers with a unique onboard entertainment system,” added Rajesh Dogra, Chief Customer Experience Officer, Air India.

Present in India since 1953, Thales is headquartered in Noida and has other operational offices and sites spread across Delhi, Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Mumbai, among others. Over 2,000 employees are working with Thales and its joint ventures in India. Since the beginning, Thales has been playing an essential role in India’s growth story by sharing its technologies and expertise in Defence, Transport, Aerospace and Digital Identity and Security markets. Thales has two engineering competence centres in India – one in Noida focused on digital identity and security business, while the one in Bengaluru focuses on hardware, software and systems engineering capabilities for both the civil and defence sectors, serving global needs.

reviews.transcript_full: Vistara, or as it is officially known, Tata Sia Airlines.  That name consists of the two companies that came together to form the carrier in 2013.  India's Tata conglomerate and unfathomably large corporation involved in almost every  part of India's economy and Singapore Airlines.  Their goal was to finally establish a reliably high-quality Indian carrier, but after 10 years  its days are already numbered, as Tata has finally taken over India as well and will merge  the two under the Air India brand.  So before things change, and Vistara's brand will disappear from India's skies.  Let's take a flight with them, an economy class from Delhi to Frankfurt and see what  they're like, and especially look at weather and in what aspects they are better than  my Air India flight from Vienna to Delhi was the week before, the video of which is available  on our channel already too.  In Longhol Economy class and Vistara for the first time, and likely also the last, let's  jump into it.  Aviation geeks and frequent flyers welcome to the bustling streets of Old Delhi from  where we're taking a taxi to India Agandi International Airport.  We could have taken the Delhi Airport Metro Express, which leaves from nearby New Delhi  Railway Station and gets you to the airport in just 15 minutes.  But since there were three of us with plenty of luggage carrying it all through downtown  and across the entire New Delhi Railway Station seemed like too big of a trade-off to not  spend on the comfort of a taxi today.  A roughly 45 minute cab ride later, we arrived at Indira Gandhi Airport Terminal 3, from  which Air India, Vistara and most international carriers operate out of.  The name Vistara by the way comes from the Sanskrit word Vistar, meaning limitless expanse.  The 1250 pm flight to Frankfurt, that's ours.  It's one of just a handful of Longhol routes operated by Vistara.  As Delhi to Frankfurt, the carrier's Longhol network also boasts connections from Delhi  to Paris and London Heathrow, as well as Mumbai to London Heathrow and soon all the Frankfurt.  Check-in was quick and easy, and after a rather chaotic security check, as I'm used to in India,  we're off to our departure gate.  Vistara's white body fleet, as of September 2023, consists of six Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners,  which I'll feature the same interior, except for one which I'll get to in a second.  Vistara's chosen interior features a business class cabin, consisting of 30 staggered Stalia  symphony seats and a 1-2-1 configuration, thus offering direct aisle access to all passengers,  followed by three rows or 21 seats of premium economy class with a Recoro PL3530 seats installed  in a 232 pattern, and in the back a 333 configured economy class cabin with 248 Recoro CL3710 seats.  At Simpliviation, we pride ourselves in creating the most detailed and thorough airline reviews  possible, and in line with that I now have to inform you that the review you're watching  might be quite useless to you.  That's because we're flying on the one exception to that standard configuration,  the one Boeing 787 and Vistara's fleet that looks completely different inside.  You'll still get a close look at Vistara's soft product, meaning the catering and the amenities,  but the hard product, meaning the seats and the inflight and attainment, will only be like this  on this particular aircraft. So what is this plane and why is this one different?  We're flying aboard the 2018 build, VTTSQ, the oldest Boeing 787 and Vistara's fleet,  because this one was originally supposed to be delivered to China's Hainan Airlines,  which didn't take delivery of the aircraft due to financial difficulties.  And Vistara, wanting to expand quickly, simply took over that plane and left the original cabin,  chosen and put together by Hainan Airlines inside, simply changing the colors of the fabric.  And where can you find this plane? That's fairly straightforward too, because as of October 2023,  this plane almost exclusively serves the Delhi-Defrancford route.  Virtually all Delhi-Defrancford flights ever operated saw this particular aircraft,  and only on the weekdays where the Frankfurt route isn't flown, you might encounter it on a  random domestic or rare Paris flight. So what does it look like inside?  Just like Vistara's other five Dreamliners, VTTSQ has 30 business class seats.  However, this one featuring a reverse-herringbone configuration with a Suffron 0's three seats installed.  The biggest difference is in premium economy class, because VTTSQ didn't have a premium  economy cabin installed, so Vistara simply designated the first four rows of economy classes such  and increased the legroom a bit. You still get all the amenities that come with premium  economy class like the better pillows, meals, etc, but at the end of the day still featuring  the same seats as the rest of economy class. An economy class doesn't feature recarrow seats,  this one is equipped with Zafran Z300 seats. Overall, that's not a big issue, both seat models  are great and to the average passenger not many differences would become apparent.  Each seat comes with a headrest which is adjustable vertically as well as on the sides.  And waiting for us already is a little bottle of water, a pair of complimentary headphones,  and a blanket. Notably absent is a pillow, which even though this is a daytime flight,  would be nice given the flight time of 8.5 hours.  The legroom is okay, being a 180cm tall of seen considerably better in economy class,  but also worse. The seats also have a basic seat back pocket and a bifold tray table.  Behind that, a literature compartment, an up here and adjustable entertainment screen.  At the bottom of it you'll find a USB port to charge small electronic devices as well as an audio  port. Coat hooks are not installed, but for each row of three seats you might find two universal  power outlets down here. The windows are dimmable, like on all Boeing 787 Dreamliners, meaning there  are no window shades, and in the ceiling you may find personal reading lights but unfortunately  no adjustable air vents. The seats offer standard recline, and the armrests can be raised.  With that it's time to sit back, relax and get ready for departure.  After takeoff, the cabin remained very bright for quite a while since Vistara is fairly  illiberal in allowing passengers to decide over the dimming of their own windows,  having locked the controls for virtually the entire flight.  Now it's time for lunch, the main meal service on today's flight. Vistara offers two different  Indian dishes, either a vegetarian one or one with chicken. I went with a chicken dish,  which was a creamy curry with steamed white rice and beans. It was served alongside a bread roll  and butter, a cup of chana chad, a piece of coffee cake for dessert, a little pack of afterment,  as well as another small bottle of water and beverages of your choice where I went with a can of  Singaporean beer and some water. What impressed me was the size of Vistara's cups, fitting considerably  more liquid than these little shot glasses most other airlines use. All in all, a very tasty meal  service, although some airlines do offer a beverage service before lunch or dinner with drinks and  a little salty snack and such, which was absent on Vistara. The reason why I am mentioning this is  because Air India did this on my Vienna to Delhi flight the week before, and not just one beverage  and a pack of peanuts, every passenger who asked for a can of beer got two and plenty of crunchy  corn alongside it. But overall, Vistara's meal service was tasty and plentiful.  If you're not familiar with what afterment is, an Indian cuisine that's known as Mokwas,  a combination of seeds, nuts and oils, most often containing fennel, anise, coriander, peppermint  and the likes. It is supposed to help with digestion and smelly breath, and for me as a European who  isn't super used to spicy foods, I also felt like it helped me get that burning sensation out of my  mouth after eating spicy stuff here in India. After lunch, tea and coffee were offered.  Now let's have a look at what the flight offers entertainment-wise. The other five Boeing 787s of  Vistara are equipped with a state-of-the-art Panasonic X3 entertainment system. Our plane has a  different cabin and obviously also a Panasonic system but it seems to somehow be incompatible  with the system on their other planes resulting in some minor differences. The system itself  looks fairly bare-bone with just movies, TV shows and music on offer. The selection of content  within each one is totally okay with plenty of local and international content available on demand.  However, that's it. There is nothing else there, no games, no additional information,  not even an in-flight map. On their other 787s and A321 Neo's, Vistara offers the phenomenal  Panasonic Arc in-flight mapping application, which I praised in numerous recent videos including  on thin air and Iberia. Vistara was actually the launch customer of this fantastic mapping  application which I particularly love for it's straightforward display of where you are and the  cool flight recap at the end. However, possibly the system on this plane is just old enough to be  incompatible with this new program and Vistara seems to have been unwilling or unable to get a  license for a different program for this one plane leaving you with just this bar down here  telling you the approximate remaining flight time. Another symptom of this system being different  than the others is that this is the only 787 and Vistara's fleet not offering Wi-Fi.  However, at the end of the day that doesn't matter too much either since the content selection  is there, good headphones were provided and for most of the remaining flight the windows were  dimmed and locked anyway so why care about where we are when you can't see it anyway.  The lavatories also come with hand wash, hand sanitizer, mouthwash and little cups.  During the flight the crew regularly went through the cabin offering water but there were no  snacks or other beverages available in addition to the meals. Talking about meals, a second hot meal  service was offered before landing. This comes with a dish consisting of some type of bread of not  seen in India yet, somewhat reminding me of Arrepas I had in Colombia recently. The closest I  could find researching this video were corn meal breads simply called Maki Kiroti from Northern India  so if you know what this is let me know in the comments. Anyway it was served alongside a vegetable  stew with chicken. A piece of cake was provided too as well as a pack of orange juice, a bottle of  water and another pack of afterment. Peculearly, Vistara did not offer a full beverage selection  alongside the second meal service. Soft drinks, alcoholic beverages and such were unavailable  with only the drinks provided on the tray as well as water, tea and coffee being offered.  As our flight is coming to an end, looking back at it I'm not sure if I'd share the hype for  Vistara. If all I ever experienced was her India I'd surely be excited for an airline that is  at least normal too but that's really what flying Vistara came down to for me. It's a normal  airline. The cabin was modern, the meals were okay, the movie selection was nice,  there were a few things missing that just kept me from being overly thrilled with the experience,  the absent pillow was probably the most annoying, the legroom was okay but nothing to write  home about and the missing features on this particular plane were noticeable. And this is really  anecdotal but I also felt like the air India crew on my flight from Vienna to Delhi the week  prior was much more upbeat friendly in general while the Vistara crew today was a bit more neutral.  Again that's just my anecdotal input here. If you check out the video about the air India flight  you'll see that in turn the plane was in a truly shocking state. So if Tata is going to take the  best of both worlds when they merge the carriers they truly have a once in a generation chance of  establishing a reliably great Indian flag carrier. The risk remains though that they just  merge the negatives resulting in something merely better than India has now and it remains to be  seen where things go. But you can always rely on us to take you along any and all developments in  the future so make sure you are subscribed to our channel.  With that welcome to Frankfurt Airport I hope you've enjoyed this video and will join us again  on our quest to showcase as many different airlines and products as possible as detailed and  factual as we can. If you share our passion for airlines and their products please consider  joining us as a paid sponsor of our channel and get your name into this list of amazing people too.  Thanks to them we can continue to invest in our work and bring you all the facts you need to know  before choosing a flight. Thank you again for watching, have a great rest of your day and I'll see  you for a new video next week. And if you haven't seen it yet check out our recent Bertuliana  step-isode about flying long-haul in India and see what they did better and what they did considerably

yt_comments.text: Subang Airport was Kuala Lumpur’s primary airport until KLIA opened, so that’s something. I find Asiana to be one of the better value Asian airlines. I first flew with them last year and they charged half of what Singapore Airlines was charging for Singapore-Seoul flights. The experience was solid, nice enough crew, decent hot meals, just that their A330 economy IFE was very unresponsive to touch and ran very hot. The return journey on the A350 was more pleasant. I’m flying them again to Tokyo in 2 weeks time, first leg will be in the A350 again, so the upcoming video is really gonna pump me up for the trip. Even more exciting, my onward flight from Incheon to Tokyo will be on the A380! I have a goal of flying as many A380s as I can and this journey will kick start that endeavour. I hope to score a seat on the upper deck at check-in too. You were so lucky to get to fly their 747, I hope to do so before it retires 😊

reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Zurich Airport in Switzerland. Today, I'm flying with Etihad Airways to Abu Dhabi. I've flown with them several times in economy class, I'm excited to finally experience their business class product. In the future, I will also be reviewing Emirates and Qatar Airways, so let's go and see how good Etihad is first! Zurich Airport is the main gateway to Switzerland. I travelled with Air Serbia from Belgrade the night before and arrived here at 7:55 pm. Since it was relatively late, and I wanted to maximise my lounge use for my Etihad flight the next day, I stayed at the transit hotel. The hotel offers single, double, and triple rooms, as well as couches, and can be booked for periods ranging from 3 hours to overnight, depending on your budget and transit time. Switzerland is a notably expensive country. It cost me 120 Swiss francs for an overnight stay in this single room. In addition to the bed, the room is equipped with reading lights, charging ports, a desk, a TV, a sink, and a kettle. There’s no ensuite bathroom; they’re shared with other guests. Nevertheless, the place is well-maintained, and the shower water is warm with good pressure. As an avgeek, all of these inconveniences and high costs were forgiven when I opened the curtains. This is quite a unique view. The transit hotel is in Terminal D, and my flight to Abu Dhabi departs from Terminal E. To get there, I had to take a short ride on the Skymetro, a driverless automated people mover. Terminal E, also known as the midfield terminal, is exclusively dedicated to non-Schengen international flights. Being a standalone terminal, it is installed with floor-to-ceiling windows on all sides of the building, providing abundant natural light and impressive views of the apron. The bench chairs don’t have armrests, making them perfect for napping if you have an overnight layover and don’t want to pay for a hotel room. Zurich Airport is the hub for Swiss International Air Lines. As such, it operates three lounges at Terminal E. The Swiss First Lounge is open to Star Alliance first-class passengers and HON Circle members, the Senator Lounge is designated for Star Alliance Gold members, and the Business Lounge is accessible for Star Alliance business class passengers. Alongside the Swiss Air lounges, there are two third-party lounges and an Emirates Lounge. Anticipating that Etihad, not being a Star Alliance member, would direct me to either the Aspire or Primeclass lounges, I was surprised by a special arrangement Etihad made with Swiss, allowing me to use the Swiss Business Lounge instead. The Swiss Business and Senator Lounge share a common reception desk. The Senator Lounge is marginally superior. Therefore, I tried to enter using my Star Alliance Gold status. Unfortunately, I was still directed to the Business Lounge as Etihad isn’t a Star Alliance airline. I have to say, even the business lounge is quite amazing. Upon entering, you’ll find a map that helps first-time visitors navigate the available facilities. While lacking a whisky bar, there’s a self-serve mini bar offering a diverse selection of spirits, wines, beers, fizzy drinks, and water. Adjacent to the bar is a cold buffet station offering fruits, cold meats, salads, cheeses and also different condiments, and bread. I must note that the choices are not overly expansive; it’s similar to a Qantas Club in Australia. However, there’s a live chef station where you can order eggs cooked to your liking. In the middle of the lounge, there are wines, chocolates, more fruits, and coffee machines. Covering an area of 1200 square metres and a capacity of 200 seats, the business lounge has many seating options, including bar stools, dining tables, and couches, accommodating both business and leisure travellers. Additionally, there are a few semi-enclosed workstations, ideal for making phone calls and completing tasks before the flight. For those facing a long layover, towards the back of the lounge, there’s a quiet area with day beds. I ended up picking a seat next to the window. Zurich Airport’s busiest route is to London Heathrow; consequently, there are both European and UK-type power plugs next to my seat—an impressive attention to detail. Given the limited food options, I grabbed two Swiss chocolates, which were amazing, and ordered an omelette from the live cooking station, it tasted pretty ordinary. However, my eyes were quickly drawn to the outdoor terrace. In addition to offering some fresh air, the terrace presents spectacular views of the apron, takeoffs and landings on the runways, and the Swiss Alps in the distance. Moreover, there are even binoculars for scoping out planes on the far side of the airport. Lastly, private showers are available. Despite the limited food choices, this is still one of my all-time favourite business-class lounges. There’s so much natural light throughout the lounge, even in the toilets, and the outdoor terrace makes the views unbeatable. For those without lounge access, Zurich Airport has established two observation decks, one at Terminal B and the other is here in Terminal E. Positioned at the western end of the terminal and in the centre of Zurich Airport’s three runways,  this observation deck gives you a 270-degree view of the airport. There are free-to-use binoculars that provide close-up views of all airport activities, and various play areas add an element of fun for children. Zurich Airport is certainly a heaven for avgeeks and plane spotters. The aircraft that will be taking me to Abu Dhabi today is a Boeing 787-9. Currently, Etihad’s fleet comprises 30 787-9s, with some having first class and others with only business and economy class. Furthermore, the airline has three new aircraft with a fresh interior and cabin design on order and is expected to join the fleet soon. Boarding commenced 45 minutes before departure. This aircraft is in a 2-class layout. At the front are 28 Etihad Business Studios in a 1-2-1 configuration. Based on the Zodiac platform, these business class seats are arranged in an alternating forward/rearward staggered pattern. The best seats for solo travellers are the forward-facing window seats, providing more privacy as they are closer to the window and less exposed to the aisle. In the centre section, the forward-facing rows are ideal for couples travelling together, as the seats are positioned right next to one another. Each business class passenger has access to a large overhead bin. I chose seat 10K, a forward-facing seat in the second last row. Although these seats share a strikingly similar footprint with Qatar’s Q-suites, they lack the sliding door, making them feel less private. An Acqua di Parma amenity kit was already on my seat when I boarded, and the crew offered me a choice of water, orange juice, Champagne, or lemon mint juice as soon as I settled in. My seat wasn’t particularly clean. There were small flies crawling on the windows, fluff above the air vent, and around the control buttons. Once everyone was on board, the crew handed me a menu and a hot wet towel, which I found perfect for wiping the surfaces around my seat. Welcome aboard Etihad Airways flight EY74 bound to Abu Dhabi.  Our flight today will take us a flight time of 5h35m, initially we are expected to climb to 37,000ft, and a final cruising altitude of 39,000ft. Seats 9C and 9H are definitely the ones to avoid, as they are rear-facing and lack windows. The business class cabin is pretty full today, with around six empty seats toward the back. Now, let’s dive into the seat’s features. The seat has a width of 22 inches and plenty of legroom. A blanket is placed on the footwell, and there’s a small storage area below. Next to the TV, there’s a small reading light, a coat hook, and an exceptionally solid and sturdy tray table. Above this table, there are two USB ports for charging small devices, a remote for controlling the TV, and an all-in-one touch-sensitive control screen. Along the edge of the table is another seat-control strip, allowing one to easily control the essential functions while lying down. This screen is available in both Arabic and English. I can use it to control the electronic window shades, the massage function, the seat cushion firmness, the seat’s recline, the lights around me, and the ‘do not disturb’ button. In addition to the overhead reading light, there’s a lamp next to my seat, which, in my opinion, adds a luxurious elegance to Etihad’s business class product. Under the lamp, you can find a magazine holder, a universal power plug, and a hidden storage space where a bottle of water and headphones are placed. The plane is equipped with Wi-Fi, and there are two packages. The $2.99 text package only allows you to send text messages on social media, while the $9.99 package enables unlimited internet access for the entire flight. If you are an Etihad Guest member, which is free to join, you can get the text package for free. With this package, I couldn’t refresh my Instagram feed, but I successfully sent a message on Messenger. I later decided to purchase the full $9.99 plan. The speed was fast enough for me to upload instagram stories and watch a few videos on YouTube. While attempting to connect to the internet, the crew kindly offered me a drink and some warm nuts. As the 13th-best airline in the world, according to Skytrax rankings, Etihad has a massive range of beverages in business class. There are six choices of teas, various types of hot and iced coffee, four mocktails, some premium mixers, soft drinks, juice, and water. Printed on a separate piece of paper is a wine list featuring Bellini, Champagne, wines from all over the world, different spirits, liquors, and beers. The Butterfly Effect mocktail is such a beautiful drink—refreshing and fragrant without being too sweet. It’s definitely one of my favourite mocktails I’ve had in the sky. In the meantime, the crew also took my lunch order. Etihad allows its business class passengers to dine anytime they want, but the crew do try to encourage everyone to eat soon after takeoff. The menu features some all-day snack items and a full à la carte meal choices. The service was indeed on the slower side. The crew served from the front to the back. It took about an hour from taking my order to being served the entrée. I was starving. Each meal comes with a seasonal salad with olive oil, balsamic vinegar, and Etihad’s signature duo bread. For starters, I chose Cecina beef. Etihad partnered with Armani/Casa tableware in December 2022. The vibrant green, white, and black colours truly make the dishes stand out. The new cutleries also look stunning. This Spanish-cured, paper-thin beef tastes delectable, with a slight nuttiness, melt-in-the-mouth tenderness, and a hint of smoke. Accompanied with tomatoes and olives, it’s a well-balanced dish. Benefiting from Etihad’s partnership with Virgin Australia, I’ve had the chance to visit Etihad’s first lounge in Abu Dhabi, even when travelling in Economy. One dish I consistently enjoyed there was the beef tenderloin. So, on this occasion, I decided to try it on the plane. Considering the initial cooking is done in a central kitchen on the ground, serving a perfect reheated steak in-flight is not an easy feat. My steak was cooked to “well-done”, which isn’t typically how I like it, but thankfully, with the generous amount of mushroom sauce, the meat didn’t taste dry at all. Furthermore, I have never had poached apples in my steak before; surprisingly, the sweetness of the apple worked well with the sauce. To finish, I opted for the Häagen-Dazs ice cream; there were three flavours available: vanilla, strawberry, and chocolate. We are now already halfway through our journey. There are two lavatories for the 28 business class passengers, both at the front of the plane. There’s no cologne or body lotion here, as everyone was already given an amenity kit. “Acqua di Parma” is an Italian luxury lifestyle company that produces fragrances, skincare, and other scented products. In this beautiful faux leather bag, there’s cologne, hand cream, as well as sanitising wipes, hand sanitiser, a dental kit, socks, an eye mask, and earplugs. Let’s now take a look at the inflight entertainment system. The TV screen is 18 inches in size. As an airline that flies to over 70 destinations around the globe, I was surprised to find that the system only has two languages. The screen displays a comprehensive list of all available beverages on board. Although I couldn’t just order my drinks with a simple touch of a button, it was still nice to see what they have without having to refer to the paper menu. Regarding the movie selection, it may not be as extensive as that of Emirates, Cathay, or Turkish Airlines, there are still numerous choices available. There are also TV series, live TV, music, games, podcasts, radios, weather forecasts, and a live newsfeed. And of course, you can check out the flight path as well. If the main screen is too far to reach, you can use the touch-sensitive remote to make your selections. In addition, you can use the remote to check out the flight path while watching a movie on the main screen. There are still 2 hours left until landing. As expected, the seat can be converted into a fully flat bed. The rear-facing seats can extend into a 75.7-inch-long bed, yet my forward-facing seat is 80.5 inches long. I’m 6’1’, and my toes can’t reach the wall.  The narrow footwell limited the space for my legs, but I still find it comfortable. And the 22-inch seat width provides ample room for my arms and shoulders. If I have to say something negative, without a sliding door, I still feel quite exposed when lying down. Despite the lack of mattress pad on this daytime flight, a luxuriously soft and warm Armani/Casa duvet is still available. I couldn’t work out the brand of the headphones, but they did an excellent job of filtering out the aircraft noise. If you're flying with us in Business or First, you are welcome to refresh in our arrivals lounge. This is where you'll meet your pre-booked Etihad chauffeur. I had an uninterrupted 1-hour nap. For those starting or concluding their journey in Abu Dhabi, all first-class, The Residence, and certain eligible fare-class Business class passengers can enjoy a complimentary chauffeur service to and from the airport. If your fare qualifies, the booking option will appear on the app, and the chauffeur can transport you to any location within the UAE. In general, it was a pleasant flight. Other than the slightly dirty seat I discovered at boarding, I was thoroughly satisfied with everything else. I love all the fancy touchscreens. It truly adds a delightful touch to the conclusion of the Etihad business class journey. Thank you so much for watching! reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Belgrade, Serbia! Today, I’ll be flying with the nation’s flag carrier, Air Serbia to Zurich. Since this is an intra-Europe flight, I don’t expect much from the business-class seat, but I do hope to enjoy a delicious Serbian meal onboard. Let’s go and find out! Belgrade, the capital of Serbia, has a population of 1.6 million. The city is nestled along the banks of the Sava River and the Danube. It holds a unique position as the crossroads of central and southern Europe. Owing to its strategic significance, the city was the battleground in 115 wars and was razed 44 times. The Belgrade Fortress is one of the most iconic landmarks in the city. It served as a pivotal military stronghold and witnessed numerous battles and sieges. It is a testament to the strength and determination of the people who have called this city home throughout the ages. Today, Belgrade is known for its dynamic and vibrant nightlife. Many weekend visitors from neighbouring countries prefer Belgrade’s nightlife to that of their own capitals due to its welcoming atmosphere, numerous clubs and bars, and affordable drinks. During a casual stroll along Knez Mihailova Street, I even stumbled upon a live concert at Republic Square. And let’s not forget that Belgrade is the hometown of the world’s greatest tennis player, Novak Djokovic. In 2009, he and his family established a tennis centre, inspiring hundreds of young players in the nation. Belgrade has an extensive public transport system consisting of buses, trams, and urban train lines. The easiest way to get to the airport by public transport is by catching the A1 minivan. This express bus can take you from Slavija Square to the airport in 35 minutes at a cost of 400 Serbian dinars, payable directly to the driver in cash. There’s limited space to store large suitcases, the 19km journey is generally quite smooth. Belgrade Nikola Tesla Airport, named after the famous American-Serbian inventor and a pioneer of modern electricity, is the busiest airport in Serbia. It is currently undergoing an expansion project. Terminal 1, located on the right, is used mainly by low-cost airlines, whereas the new and much larger Terminal 2 accommodates all other airlines. Most of the expansion work has already been completed. They are now working on the finishing touches. Air Serbia is the country’s flag carrier and the airport’s largest operator. It is partially owned by Etihad Airways and adopts Etihad Guest as its frequent flyer program. There are three counters dedicated to business class passengers and Etihad Silver members or higher. Afternoons appear to be a particularly busy time for Air Serbia. The economy class lane is extremely long, with the queue starting at the terminal’s entry. If you are travelling in Economy, you can purchase the priority check-in service for a fee. In this situation, I think it would be a worthwhile investment. Once you’ve obtained your boarding pass, you can take the escalators to the international departures floor. Again, there’s a small queue. Once the expansion project is complete, the airport will be able to handle 15 million passengers per year, and hopefully, the queuing issues will be resolved. After passing through immigration and the new centralised security screening, you’ll be greeted by the new duty-free shop, selling everything from alcohol, clothes, and souvenirs to juice and water. The central part of the terminal is called Tesla Square. There’s limited seating space and several restaurants. It’s clear that this terminal is operating beyond its capacity. The airport has two lounges, they are situated near each other. The Business Club is a contract lounge used by most foreign airlines, certain credit card holders, and lounge members. The other one is the Air Serbia premium lounge, located opposite gate A5. It seems that passengers from selected airlines can use this lounge too. However, during busy periods like now, they only admit Air Serbia’s business class passengers. At quieter times, travellers on any airline can pay a fee to enter the lounge. The lounge is rather compact and basic, lacking any windows. It was pleasantly tranquil inside. The space is partitioned into two sections. To the left is the seating area, with many comfortable chairs and couches, all equipped with power plugs nearby. The other side is a dining area featuring a modest buffet spread. The hot food includes soup, mashed potatoes, creamy chicken, rice, and vegetables, and there’s salad, various pastries, and dessert. Interestingly, knives are not provided here, possibly for security reasons. For drinks, you can choose from a range of alcoholic beverages, water, juice, soft drinks, and coffee. I noticed that Serbian cuisine tends to be quite salty, not only here but in the city as well. The mashed potatoes and chicken were on the salty side. But, overall, I did enjoy the food. The rice had good flavours. Lastly, the lounge has its own toilets, along with a shower room. Considering that most flights from here are less than 3 hours long, I think the lounge serves its purpose well. If I were travelling in Economy, I would be happy to pay 25 euros for an hour here. The departure gates are configured in a large L-shaped structure, named Pier A and Pier C. There are ten aerobridged gates at Pier A. Before the expansion, Pier C had six gates, and now it has 14, significantly boosting the capacity of this terminal. The old building has a very low ceiling and appears quite dim. Luckily, my flight today departs from one of the new gates, giving me the opportunity to explore this area. The expanded space features floor-to-ceiling windows on both sides of the building, making it much brighter. In addition, travelators have been added to help passengers reach the gate more quickly. Air Serbia operates a fleet of 22 narrow-body aircraft primarily serving nearby European and Middle Eastern destinations. It also has 2 A330s dedicated to flights to Chicago, New York, and, surprisingly, a lesser-known city called Tianjin in China. The airline pays tribute to important and famous Serbs by naming several of its planes after them. The aircraft that will be taking me to Zurich is an A319, which was, in fact, the first plane Air Serbia received when it was established in 2013. It bears the name ‘Novak Djokovic.’ I felt extremely fortunate to be able to fly on this aircraft. Boarding commenced just 30 minutes before departure. If you aren’t already aware, business class seats on most European B737 and A320 flights are the same as Economy, except for the vacant middle seat and the separating curtain. This setup gives the airline the flexibility to adjust the number of seats sold as business class on each flight but also makes them subpar compared to the rest of the world. On this flight, there’s only one row of business class, comprising four seats. Shortly after I settled in, the cabin crew handed me a food menu and took my order a few minutes later. No pre-departure drink was offered. Business class passengers receive a complimentary main course and dessert for flights between 1.5 and 2.5 hours long. For flights exceeding 2.5 hours, there’s an additional salad served as an appetiser, and for flights less than 1.5 hours long, only a small snack is provided. The flight was almost full, with only several economy seats vacant, but boarding was completed in 25 minutes, and we pushed back on time. Belgrade has two runways that are parallel to each other. This afternoon, we took off from runway 30L. That’s a bit of a shame! I have to say that, despite being labelled as business class, Row 1 has the worst seats on this plane. This is due to the bulkhead ahead, which forced me to stow my bag in the overhead bin, and the severely restricted legroom. The tray table is stored inside the armrest, making my seat slightly narrower than the others. The seat is reclinable.  I didn’t see any USB charging ports or power plugs under my seat, so I suppose you’ll need to carry a power bank if you wish to charge your phone on board. There’s no Wi-Fi on this aircraft. In the seat pocket, you’ll find two in-flight magazines and a menu, mainly intended for economy class passengers. There are sandwiches, snacks, soft drinks, hot drinks, and alcoholic beverages. The prices are pretty reasonable. Payment can be made in cash, in either dinars or euros or by credit card. “Elevate” is a specialised in-flight magazine distributed monthly on all Air Serbia flights. It gives updates regarding tourist attractions, culture, sports, and recommendations for the next getaway spots. Furthermore, it provides information about Air Serbia’s network, flight schedules, fleet, and official merchandise. The other magazine, “Outstanding Serbia,” presents Serbia’s gastronomic and wine landscape, showcases destinations worth visiting, and takes readers from the best restaurants to nightclubs. Both magazines are worth reading, and I believe they provide ample material to help passengers pass the short flight time. The crew served us the meal shortly after the seat belt sign was turned off. Seated in 1A, I was served first. My first impression: the use of plastic cups instead of glasses and paper napkins instead of cloth napkins made the service look less premium. Alongside the main meal, there was a dessert and some bread. The bun was still warm. I ordered the only non-vegetarian hot dish option. The portion was quite generous. There was a plentiful amount of beef mince, it wasn’t overly salty, and the noodles weren’t dry. I really enjoyed it! The dessert, parfait, is essentially cream with ground hazelnuts. It was pretty rich. Overall, the meal was acceptable.  Although I don’t think any of the three main course choices represent Serbian cuisine, the spaghetti was still enjoyable. After clearing my tray, the crew offered me a choice of tea or coffee. We are now flying over the Alps. As someone who lives in Australia, where our highest mountain, Mount Kosciuszko, is only 2,228 metres high, I was amazed to see snow covering a large portion of the Alps even in summer! The actual flight time between Belgrade and Zurich today was just 1 hour and 29 minutes, which is about the same time as flying from Adelaide to Canberra. We began our descent just a few minutes after the service was finished. There’s one lavatory for the business class passengers, located just behind the cockpit. It’s quite ordinary and lacks additional amenities like body lotion or cologne. To summarise, it was a good flight by European standards. I knew what to expect, so I didn’t have high expectations to begin with. The lounge, the food, and the amenities were all basic but satisfactory. The seats are similar to the Jetstar seats in Australia, they don’t have headrests, and the seat-back is rather hard. On the positive side, the scenery was beautiful, just like the flight crew. A one-way economy class ticket on this route is roughly 50 euros, or 81 euros with checked luggage, while business class is 234 euros. These prices are slightly cheaper than its direct competitor, Swiss International Air Lines. This flight is part of my multi-city itinerary from Belgrade to Bangkok via Zurich and Abu Dhabi, booked with Etihad Airways. If I were only flying in this one sector, given the similarity with Economy, I don’t think I would spend the extra money to fly in business class. We hope you had a comfortable flight, on behalf of the captain and the entire crew, thank you for flying with Air Serbia. And we are looking forward to welcoming you on our flights again. For your next flight, please visit AirSerbia.com and follow us on social media. Thank you and goodbye. Thank you so much for watching! If you found this video interesting, please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more flight and train reviews. In my next two videos, I will be reviewing Etihad Airways’ Business Class product on the B787, and the newer A350-1000. See you again soon!

reviews.transcript_full: Hello and welcome to Singapore! Today, I finally have the chance to fly in Cathay Pacific’s business class to Hong Kong. I arrived in Singapore last night at 7:30 pm after flying on Finnair’s A350 from Helsinki. I had a 17-hour layover at Changi Airport, so I entered Singapore and stayed at the Crowne Plaza. Its king-bed standard Runway View room is 36 square metres in size and has a fantastic view of the apron, Terminal 3, and the airport’s western runway. This hotel offers the most convenient location at Changi Airport, one of its entrances is directly connected to Terminal 3. Moreover, Jewel Changi Airport Shopping Complex is just a 5-minute walk away via an undercover footbridge. Changi Airport consists of four main passenger terminals. Terminals 1 to 3 are interconnected and arranged in an elongated ‘U’ shape.  Travellers can use the automated Skytrain for easy movement between these terminals. Terminal 4, on the other hand, is isolated from the rest of the terminals. To get there, the airport provides complimentary shuttle services from both the land side and airside areas of terminals 1-3. The bus stop at land side Terminal 3 is situated outside departure door 8. The shuttle operates 24/7, but the frequency varies depending on the time of day. The ride takes approximately 10 minutes. Terminal 4 was initially designed for budget airlines. Its primary occupants are mostly low-cost carriers, such as Air Asia, Bamboo Airways, Cebu Pacific, Vietjet, and Jetstar. However, some full-service airlines, including Cathay Pacific, Hainan Airlines, Korean Air, and Vietnam Airlines, now use this terminal too. Check-in opens three hours before the scheduled departure time of each Cathay flight. Currently, they do not offer first-class service on flights to Singapore, but they have retained a first-class check-in lane for their Diamond and oneworld Emerald Frequent Flyers. Unlike terminals 1-3, at Terminal 4, security screening is conducted straight after immigration. Despite being a budget airline terminal, there’s a massive duty-free shop selling cosmetics, perfumes, and liquors, followed by stores from some well-known fashion brands on your way to the boarding gates. The terminal is home to over 340 species of plants. There’s also a few attractions, including the ‘Travelling Family’ aluminium sculpture and ‘Steel in Bloom’. When complemented by bright, multicoloured lights, this metallic structure is perfect for taking selfies.  Terminal 4 has two lounges. The Blossom Lounge is a contract lounge used by business class passengers on selected airlines, certain credit card holders, Priority Pass lounge members, and can also be accessed by paying a fee at the entrance. The other one is the Cathay Pacific Lounge, which opens to Cathay’s business class passengers, its silver, gold, and diamond members, and oneworld Sapphire and Emerald frequent flyers. The Cathay Lounge is divided into three sections with a seating capacity of around 200. The far-left section is the main seating area, the middle section houses the buffet, and on the right, you’ll find the iconic noodle bar, business centre, and toilets. The buffet is designed for those seeking a quick bite. Today, the Western choices include saffron rice, pasta, and grilled vegetables, and the local delights include chicken rendang, black pepper beef, and a vegetarian white radish soup. In addition, there’s a small salad and cheese station. In place of a traditional bar, this Cathay Lounge features a self-service drink station, offering an assortment of beverages such as spirits, wines, Moët champagne, and beer, as well as soft drinks, water, and juice. Normally, a lounge with such dining facilities would already receive a very good rating, but Cathay has taken it a step further with a made-to-order "Noodle Bar". It’s a fantastic way for travellers to savour some Hong Kong cuisine even before flying there. The seating comprises booths and communal tables, evoking the typical cafe seating found in Hong Kong. This morning, the noodle bar has three different noodles and three dim sum dishes, accompanied by several condiments. After placing your order, the staff provides a buzzer to alert you when your food is ready. I ordered the Dan Dan noodles, BBQ pork buns, and the siu mai. As an Asian, I eat these dishes frequently. While they taste authentic, I didn’t find them to be particularly special compared to other places. The main seating area is furnished with numerous cozy couches and chairs, most of which have power plugs and USB ports nearby. I particularly love the seats at the end. They provide an excellent vantage point for plane-spotting and people-watching. Given that all the other oneworld carriers operate from terminals 1-3, only Cathay Pacific passengers can access this lounge. Therefore, I appreciate the airline’s efforts in creating such a modern and comfortable lounge just for its five daily flights to Hong Kong. The toilet is clean and well-lit. However, the biggest drawback is the absence of showers. Considering how humid Singapore is throughout the year, I feel that showers are quite essential. I hope Cathay may consider adding them in the future. Cathay currently operates a mix of Boeing 777s and Airbus A350s on flights to and from Singapore. The aircraft that will be taking me to Hong Kong today is an A350-900, equipped with 38 business class, 28 premium economy, and 214 economy class seats. Boarding is well-organised with five boarding groups, and dedicated ground staff are stationed at the entrance of each lane to ensure passengers are in the correct queue. When boarding commences, those requiring assistance board first, followed by oneworld Emerald passengers, oneworld Sapphire and business class passengers, premium economy passengers, and finally, economy class passengers. The A350 family is the youngest aircraft type in Cathay’s long-haul fleet, with an average age of just five years. It features Cathay’s newest business-class product, Cirrus III. The seats are arranged in a reverse herringbone 1-2-1 configuration. Compared to the previous model installed on some of its B777s and A330s, these seats have more storage space, an expanded sleeping surface, and an enhanced entertainment system. I selected seat 19A, located in the last row of the front cabin. Beyond door 2, there are two more rows of business seats, followed by four rows of premium economy seats in a 2-3-2 configuration and economy class with a 3-3-3 layout.  A dining menu had already been placed on my seat, and not long after I settled in, the crew presented me with a choice of orange juice, champagne, and water, followed by a hot towel before departure. While the plane was taxiing, I received a special welcome from the cabin manager as a oneworld Emerald Frequent flyer. At the same time, other crew members took everyone’s lunch orders. Changi Airport currently has two operating runways, and this afternoon, we used runway 20L, which took about 15 minutes to taxi to. Let’s take a closer look at the Cirrus III business seat. At the front, there’s an 18.5-inch entertainment screen. The armrest next to the aisle is movable, it must be stowed during takeoff and landing. When raised, there’s a dedicated space for a water bottle. This new flip-out extension widens the seat slightly when fully reclined. While there’s no sliding door, the ‘wing’ offers eye-level privacy, ensuring passengers can’t see each other when seated. The seat has a pitch of 45 inches, providing ample legroom. I particularly appreciate this spacious storage compartment, which easily accommodates a laptop bag. The extendable tray table is stored here, and this surface doubles as a table. Next to the table is another compartment with a mirror and a netted pocket for placing valuable items. In addition, there’s a USB port and a universal power plug here.  Right next to the seat, you’ll find a remote, a reading light, and buttons to control the recline. The seat width is 20 inches, which is not the widest, especially after flying with Finnair. Thanks to the fully adjustable headrest and the massive, firm pillow, I still found it comfortable. My impression of this seat is that, after several adjustments from its older model, it’s nearly perfect. It has almost everything you’d expect. Shortly after takeoff, the crew served me some warm nuts and a drink. I asked for a Cathay Delight. It was fruity, zesty, and creamy. It had a delightful taste, and its pale green colour reflected the airline’s brand. It’s a brilliant mocktail. About 45 minutes after takeoff, lunch was served. There were three choices for the main course. Cathay allows passengers with a CX flight number to pre-select their meals online. Unfortunately, since my flight was booked as a codeshared Finnair flight, I couldn’t manage my booking on Cathay’s website, preventing me from choosing my meal in advance. Furthermore, as I was seated in the last row, the chicken option I desired had already run out when the crew reached me, so I picked the Thai halibut. As for drinks, there’s a modest selection of wines and champagne and a good range of cocktails, teas, and other non-alcoholic beverages. To start, everyone received a Parma ham appetiser, along with a side of artichoke salad. Additionally, the crew brought a bread basket, from which I chose a bun and a piece of garlic bread. To be honest, both dishes were rather ordinary, as they didn’t require much preparation and were easy for the crew to plate and serve. The red capsicum slices added a vibrant burst of colour to the dish and helped offset the saltiness of the ham. Here comes the main course, the Thai Red Halibut Curry. The plating is a bit disappointing. It looks more like a premium economy-class meal. I would be okay with this if I were flying with another carrier, but considering this is Cathay, one of the world’s highest-rated airlines, I expected a better presentation. I do love the coconut curry sauce. Its sweetness added flavour to the fish and complemented the rice. Sadly, there just wasn’t enough sauce. Halfway through my rice and I had already used up all the sauce. Regarding the vegetables, there were just three chunks of unseasoned boiled Kai Lan, or Chinese Kale. They tasted so bland. For dessert, I chose Häagen-Dazs ice cream, which is the same as in economy, except in business, I received a plate and had three flavours to choose from: Blueberry, Cookies and Cream, or Mango. The ice cream is still frozen and rock-hard.  While waiting for it to melt, let’s take a look at the in-flight entertainment system. The touchscreen is 18.5 inches in size and comes in several languages. There’s a ‘Do Not Disturb’ sign to inform the crew during meal service. The aircraft is equipped with Wi-Fi. If you wish to connect, you can follow these steps. It’s not free, even in business class. Given the short flight time, I didn’t bother buying a package. But from my past experiences, the speed is usually fast enough to send messages, refresh Facebook feeds, or stream videos. The screen is crystal clear, and Cathay claims to have the most extensive entertainment collection among airlines in the Asia Pacific. The flight map is easy to read, it displays essential information about the flight and the destinations. Cathay’s A350s are equipped with two exterior cameras that passengers can access at any time during the flight. If the screen is too far to reach, there’s a 4.3-inch handset that works as a remote for the main screen and can also function independently, allowing you to multi-task, check the flight map without interrupting your viewing on the main screen. With less than 90 minutes remaining, I decided to try out the lie-flat bed. Unlike many airline seats where I had to keep holding the button for it to go all the way down, here, one simple push and the seat goes flat automatically. Now, you can see that the flip-out extender has significantly widened the seat. The bed measures 75 inches or 190cm in length, there’s so much space for my feet to move around. The noise-cancelling headset doesn’t display the brand, but it works effectively. When lying down, the handset is still within easy reach, making it effortless to control the TV screen. There are four lavatories for the 38 business class passengers. They are clean and equipped with basic hand wash, hand gel, and body lotion. The actual flight time to Hong Kong usually takes just 3.5 hours, the plane has already begun its descent. The business class cabin was full on this flight. Although these seats do not have a sliding door, I still find them private. As I mentioned throughout the video, they are functional and carefully designed. The three-course meal was filling, and the ingredients, such as Parma ham and halibut, are quite premium. However, I think they should work on the presentation and flavours a bit more. The crew were very friendly and efficient, clearing up the dishes quickly. In general, I think Cathay has a decent soft and hard product on their A350s. I would fly with them again. On the other hand, I feel like Cathay needs a wow factor for it to succeed further. The company tends to play it safe and lacks innovation and imagination. Qatar’s Q-suite redefined business class, making sliding doors a standard feature, and airlines like Singapore, Emirates, and Etihad have wowed the world with game-changing first-class suites on their A380s upon their debut. Cathay’s current first-class product is outdated, and my flight today didn’t leave me with any particularly memorable experiences. I’m aware that Cathay is going to introduce a new first-class product on their new Boeing 777s in 2025,  I’m eagerly awaiting its unveiling. Welcome to Hong Kong International Airport. Just like Singapore, this airport is undergoing a massive expansion project. It took about 20 minutes to taxi from the runway to the gate. It has been a pleasure taking care of you today, on behalf of the captain and the entire team, thank you for flying Cathay Pacific, a member of the oneworld alliance. Have a good day! Thank you so much for watching! If you found this video interesting, please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more flight and train reviews. And, thank you for watching till the end. As a bonus, this is what the new Qantas lounge looks like in Hong Kong.  Reopened in May this year, I believe it’s the best International Business Lounge in Qantas’ lounge network. Well, that’s it for now, and I’ll see you all in my next video!
