But at that exact moment, the first problem is getting a heavily loaded airplane safely away from ground. So, personally, I don't see the gear up decision as the obvious mistake that some people online have made it out to be. Now, let's get into what we actually know. And before we continue, one very important distinction. Germany's BFU is the investigating authority. There is no final report yet. The detailed acceleration sequence I'm about to describe comes from preliminary material released by Vietnam Civil Aviation Authority, including the crew's initial account. It is not yet a BFU validated DFDR finding. So, throughout this video, I'm separating information into four categories. BFU confirmed, CAAV preliminary information, independent reconstruction, and theory. If I say something is a theory, I mean exactly that. We don't know yet. According to CAAV's preliminary information, roughly halfway down the runway the aircraft stopped accelerating for approximately 2 seconds. Its speed apparently stagnated. It wasn't gaining speed. Then, acceleration resumed. Again, this comes from CAAV preliminary material. We do not yet have BFU recorder analysis confirming the exact speed trace. But if that sequence is accurate, this is the first major anomaly in the takeoff. The aircraft continues towards V1. Now, V1 is a takeoff decision speed. In practical terms, the decision to reject normally needs to be made before V1. After V1, the normal expectation is to continue the takeoff unless the captain determines that the aircraft is incapable of flight. Because initiating a reject after V1 can take you beyond the available stopping distance. According to CAAV's preliminary account, around this point, the crew noticed another reduction in speed. So, now they have a very different problem. They are beyond the normal point at which you would reject, and runway is disappearing very quickly. According to the same preliminary information, the crew continued and applied maximum available thrust. Given the circumstances described, that wasn't simply keep going and hope the airplane flies. They were already beyond V1, and stopping distance was no longer available. Continuing was the rational option unless the aircraft was incapable of flight. According to CAAV's preliminary information, when the pilot flying finally began rotation, there were only around 300 ft of paved runway remaining, about 90 m. Watch. The nose comes up. The aircraft rotates, and the tail hits the ground. Germany's BFU has confirmed the tail contact during rotation, and the photographic reconstruction reported by Aviation Herald places the aircraft becoming fully airborne roughly 120 m or around 400 ft beyond the end of the paved runway. Flightradar24 also confirms that VN34 continued beyond the paved runway before becoming airborne. Once airborne, according to CAAV's preliminary information, the crew received indications relating to the tail strike and tire pressure. They informed ATC and the decision was made. They were not continuing 10 hours to Hanoi. They were coming back to Munich. This is the actual track flight path. VN34 climbed to approximately 9,000 ft. And after reaching 9,000 ft, it was vectored south of Munich. The total flight lasted roughly 2 hours. During that period, the crew held and jettisoned fuel to reduce the aircraft's landing weight. There you can see the fuel coming out of the wings, right at the tip of the wings over there. Now, that doesn't mean the 787 physically cannot perform an overweight landing. It can. But reducing weight gives you more landing margin. Reduces structural loads, reduces brake energy, and makes an already abnormal landing far more manageable. Before committing to the landing, they made two low passes over Munich. That allowed people on the ground and ATC to visually inspect the landing gear. Then they came back for runway 26 right. Touchdown. Now, watch the main gear. The tire rubber is shredding apart. According to CAAV's preliminary information, four of the eight main wheel well tires had lost pressure. Three on the left main gear, one on the right. Now, this airplane taxied clear of the runway under its own power. Personally, with tires shredded like that, I would have stopped it right there, on the runway. No emergency evacuation, which is good. No injuries. Eventually, all 287 people on board got off the aircraft safely. Now, let's look at this video. Let's look at the tire tracks. And this is where the case becomes genuinely unresolved. Germany's BFU has confirmed tire tracks attributable to VN34 near the runway end. Independent photographs [clears throat] and video analysis appear to show marks involving both the left and right main landing gear. But the photographs alone cannot tell us exactly what produced them. They don't prove pilot braking. They don't prove an electrical fault. And they don't prove a locked wheel. They simply show us that something unusual appears to have happened at the wheels during the final part of the takeoff roll. And this is where the theories begin. Theory number one is human factor. Could one pilot in sudden high-stress moment have instinctively applied the brakes? Possibly. Think about the sequence. You've already experienced one strange acceleration event, then you're approaching the point where you're committed to flight, then the speed appears to reduce again. One pilot may immediately be thinking, "We have to fly." And another pilot, even momentarily, could theoretically have an instinctive response associated with stopping. Startled reactions happen. But let me make this absolutely clear. There is currently no evidence that either pilot applied the brakes. None. This is pure conjecture. It's simply one possible explanation that the recorder data may eventually confirm or completely eliminate. The second theory is a fault somewhere inside the 787's electric brake system. Now, I'm not going to invent a specific failure mechanism because we don't have the evidence for one. But the 787's main wheel braking is electrically controlled. Between a brake command and what actually happens at the wheel, you have electrical brake actuators and electric brake actuator controllers or EBAX controlling the application of braking force. The Boeing 787 FCOM shows four EBAX controlling the eight main wheel well brakes with each EBAX controlling a fore and aft wheel pair. And this is the part that makes me curious. If you compare the apparent tire marks with the takeoff sequence, the braking on the main gear appears to begin around the point where the nose gear becomes airborne. Now, that timing does not prove that one caused the other. And I found nothing in the FCOM that says nose gear liftoff should normally command braking on the main wheels. But could some abnormal electrical event, an electric brake actuator controller fault, or something else inside the brake control chain have produced unwanted braking at around that moment? Possibly. But right now that's only a theory. We have no evidence yet that the EBAC failed. We have no evidence yet that the brake system commanded braking by itself. And we don't even know whether the timing we are seeing is casual or simply coincidence. The other possibility is the human factor theory we just discussed. Actual brake pedal input during the takeoff. Again, we have no evidence of that either. So right now we have two broad possibilities, a human input or something abnormal inside the brake control system. And we don't know which, if either, actually happened. That is exactly what the recorder data and the aircraft system data should help investigators establish. Until then, both remain theories. So for now, this is where we leave the A34. The most important thing is that all 287 people on board made it back safely with no injuries. And credit to the airport and emergency services at Munich for handling a very abnormal return. As soon as we get any fresh update from the investigation, I'll cover this incident again in detail. This is Cockpit Confession. Happy flying, folks.

reviews.title: Emirates Boeing777 From Bangkok to Da Nang | Flight Report
reviews.transcript_excerpt: This is a promotional video about Emirates' in-flight entertainment.…

captions.text: This is a promotional video about Emirates' in-flight entertainment.

reviews.transcript_full: I have just arrived at Suvarnabhumi Airport in Bangkok, Thailand. Here is the departure floor of the airport at around 2PM. Today, I will be flying from Bangkok, Thailand to Da Nang, Vietnam with Emirates. Emirates, which I will be on board today, is an airline based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Emirates operates five round trips a day on Dubai-Bangkok route. Of these five flights, one continues from Bangkok to Hong Kong, and another operates from Bangkok to either Da Nang, Vietnam or Siem Reap, Cambodia, as a fifth freedom flight. Whether the flight goes to Da Nang or Siem Reap depends on the day of the week, but today I will be on the Bangkok to Da Nang segment. Emirates check-in at the airport kiosks is available from 5 hours before departure. Online check-in on the Emirates official website is available from 48 hours before departure. The aircraft I will be boarding today will arrive in Bangkok from Dubai at 6:25 PM. Then, as a fifth freedom flight, it will depart Bangkok at 8:10 PM and head to Da Nang, Vietnam. Now, I'm going to go through immigration. I've completed immigration. It's always the same procedure at Suvarnabhumi Airport, and now I'm going to the lounge to eat something. This time I'm going to the Miracle Lounge near Gate D5. Incidentally, this lounge has the only place in the entire main terminal that has a smoking area. The courtyard inside the lounge is the smoking area. There is also an entrance to the Miracle Lounge near Gate D6. Although the room is spatially connected to the D5 area, passengers are not allowed to move between the two areas within the lounge. There is a halal and vegetarian food area that wasn't there the last time I came to this lounge. These are the halal and vegetarian foods. These are orange juice and guava juice. I brought gapao. Since it's halal food, I think they only use chicken and not pork. I'm currently here eating and editing YouTube videos. This is the regular food area, not the halal and vegetarian area. This is corn soup. This is the bevarage corner. They also have beer. Here is the cooking counter. When you order, the chef will cook the food for you. I ordered Khao Man Gai here. This is the Khao Man Gai I ordered earlier. This is the fruit corner. They have watermelon and dragon fruit. And there are ice cream in the freezer. I got vanilla icecream. Previously, there was food corner in this section as well, but in exchange for the halal food area, here has been replaced with a rest area with only chairs. Today I will be taking Emirates flight EK370 departing at 8:10 p.m.  I am leaving the lounge. Emirates always departs from the satellite terminal, not from the main terminal. So I will be moving to another terminal now. Only passengers boarding flights departing from the satellite terminal can go to this terminal. It takes about 3 minutes by train to get to the satellite terminal. Today I will be departing from Gate S116. Today's Emirates flight is EK370, running from Dubai to Da Nang via Bangkok. It is possible to board even if you only want to fly the Dubai to Bangkok leg. Passengers going from Dubai to Da Nang does not need to disembark in Bangkok and remain on board. Today's aircraft is a Boeing 777-300ER. Among the five flights on the Dubai-Bangkok route, the other four are operated by Airbus A380s. There seem to be quite a few passengers who only use the Bangkok-Da Nang fifth freedom leg. Today I will be seated in economy class. The business class area is at the front of the aircraft. The seat configuration is 2-3-2. My seat number today is 30H, an aisle seat. The economy class seat configuration is 3-4-3. This flight is scheduled to depart at 8:10 p.m. and arrive at 9:50 p.m. local time. The flight time is 1 hour and 40 minutes. The passenger sitting two seats away from me wanted to borrow my iPhone charger, so I lent it to him. He is using my charger and watching social media videos comfortably. The seat on the far right of this aircraft does not have a power outlet, so he is using the outlet at the seat to his left. This aircraft, which came from Dubai, landed in Bangkok at 6:25 p.m., so the passengers from Dubai will have to wait on board for 1 hour and 45 minutes before departing for Da Nang. This is a promotional video about Emirates' in-flight entertainment.  It is a video that showcases the abundance of in-flight entertainment (movies, games, etc.) offered by Emirates. This video is always shown before takeoff. Next is Emirates' "No-Nonsense" in-flight safety video, which has no singing or dancing. Takeoff is at 8:24 p.m. The flight time for this flight is 1 hour and 40 minutes, which is quite short for an international flight, so there is not much time to relax. The flight distance from Bangkok to Da Nang is approximately 1120 km. Here is inside a onboard restroom. In-flight meals are being served. Because it is a short-haul flight, the in-flight meal is a light meal, and there is only one menu option. The meal consisted of a sandwich, orange juice, fruit, and water. The sandwich has tomato and cheese between slices of bread. There was no drink service; the only beverage available was the 200ml bottle of water that came with the light meal. Emirates operates four flights a week on the Bangkok-Da Nang route. The other three flights a week are between Bangkok and Siem Reap, Cambodia. An announcement is being made before landing. Many Vietnamese people are sitting around me, and Vietnamese families are very lively and noisy throughout the flight. If this video gets good reviews, I’ll book an Emirates flight from Bangkok to Siem Reap, another fifth-freedom flight. At 9:23 PM, we landed at Da Nang International Airport. The actual flight time was about 1 hour and 10 minutes. Now, I will disembark the plane. Today, I will move to the terminal by bus. The first bus filled up just before I took on, so I let it go and will take the next one. The bus is as lively as ever with the voices of the passengers. This Emirates aircraft will wait in Da Nang for 1 hour and 40 minutes before returning to Bangkok at 11:30 PM. I arrived at the terminal. Now it's time for immigration. The immigration area is very crowded. The immigration line was so long that it took me an hour to get through. Da Nang is overflowing with many foreign tourists from all over the world. That's all for the video now, I'm going to call a taxi using the Grab ride-hailing app and head to my hotel. There wasn't the aggressive touting by taxi drivers as in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam.

reviews.transcript_full:
[music playing] NARRATOR: Black aviators,
they made history. But today, their were amazing
accomplishments are not well known. Risk takers and trailblazers. They push the envelope
of early aviation. They fought for America in
every war since World War I. And on the home front,
they have courageously battled against the prejudice
that tried to clip their wings. "Black Aviators: Flying Free." August 29th 1983
Dr. Guion Bluford becomes the first
African-American to journey into space. Bluford's flight was
a crowning achievement for African-Americans
in aviation. But reaching those
heights came only after individual
acts of great courage and difficult battles against
racism and segregation. VON HARDESTY: For
African-Americans, the birth of the Air Age also coincided
with a social climate in this country, a rather
grim one, the Jim Crow era. And this was an era when Blacks
were routinely segregated and barred from public access. NARRATOR: The history
of Black aviation begins with Eugene Bullard,
a young man who grew up in Columbus,
Georgia, then a place of frequent anti-Black violence. It was after he watched
his father's near lynching by a white mob that Eugene
decided his destiny lay elsewhere. Destitute, the teenager stowed
away on a steamer heading for Scotland. Bullard made his way to
Paris and earned his living for a time as a prize fighter. Once the Great
War began in 1914, the 19-year-old immediately
enlisted in the French Foreign Legion. Serving as a machine
gunner, he was seriously wounded during the Battle
of Verdun, which earned him France's highest
military honor-- the Croix de Guerre. In 1960, Bullard was accepted
into the French flight school. Something he wouldn't
have been in America. PHILIP HART: He was known as
The Black Swallow of Death. Eugene Bullard got that nickname
when he flew for the French. He was a flashy
dresser, and there are wonderful descriptions
of him in a red tunic. And he flew with a
monkey named Jimmy. NARRATOR: He became part of
the Lafayette Escadrille, a squadron of American pilots
flying fighter planes in combat under French command. On his first day in
battle, Bullard's squadron encountered four German
bombers and 16 fighters. In the fierce
dogfight that ensued, Bullard reportedly
down two planes. In all, Bullard flew at least 20
combat missions for the French, and he was a hero, until
America entered the war. VON HARDESTY: There was an
interesting encounter between this transplanted American
Black /French aviator, and then the Americans
that come over. And his reception within
the American military was very cool to say the least. There was a great deal
of hostility towards him. NARRATOR: Now under the
command of American officers who wouldn't fly
with a Black man, Bullard was denied
officer status, and abruptly taken
out of the sky. VON HARDESTY: His
brief flying career showed the enormous
difficulties for Blacks to become pilots,
particularly military pilots. And his encounter and experience
with the American military also showcased the
sort of hostile climate that would persist
for decades back home. NARRATOR: Yet by seeking
his destiny in France, Eugene Bullard had become
the first Black pilot in the world-- a true, if unsung American hero. And soon, there would be others
following in his footsteps. One of them-- Bessie
Coleman, faced discrimination not only against her
race, but against her sex. BETTY GUBERT: Bessie Coleman,
as Eugene Bullard was, was born in the South in Texas. She was the 10th or
12th of 13 children. She was born in 1892. Her mother didn't
know how to read, but Bessie was very, very smart. NARRATOR: At 18, having
squeezed all the knowledge she could from a one room
schoolhouse in Waxahachie, Texas, Bessie enrolled
in a colored University. But after one
term, lack of funds forced her to abandon her
hopes for a higher education. Like many African-Americans at
that time, she migrated North. VON HARDESTY: She
moved to Chicago, lived there with her family. And it's in this urban context
that she begins to demonstrate her ambitions, her native
intelligence, and this more elusive charisma that was
a part of her persona. And she became
interested in flying. PHILIP HART: And she decided
she wanted to become a pilot. And obviously, if
you're a Black woman, and you say you
want to be a pilot, most people look at you
like you're kind of crazy. NARRATOR: But Bessie
Coleman would not be denied. BETTY GUBERT: She was a
manicurist at the White Sox Barber Shop, where she
met influential men like Robert Abbott who was
the publisher of "The Chicago Defender." Now, Abbott wanted to help her. Partly because he was
interested in aviation, and partly because these
would be great stories in "The Chicago Defender." NARRATOR: But not surprisingly,
every flight school she applied to in America turned her down. So in 1920, like Eugene Bullard,
she sought liberty and justice in France. PHILIP HART: She went over
to France, her first time, and learned how to fly, came
back to the United States and went back a second time
and earned her license in 1921. So she is very motivated. BETTY GUBERT: When Bessie came
back to the United States, she wanted to open a school
for other African-Americans. And she's on record or saying,
I want to turn Uncle Tom's Cabin into a hangar. NARRATOR: Bessie had an
instinct for publicity. She began performing as a
stunt pilot to fund her dream. BETTY GUBERT: Bessie
Coleman was beautiful. She was vibrant. How many women were flying
at that time, white or Black? She was flamboyant. She had this kind of quasi
military uniform that she wore. She was an entrepreneur. She did a great deal of
self-promotion and boasting about her career. Air shows were going
on all over the country. There were a few Black pilots
that flew in the white air shows. But for the most part, the
air shows like the rest of the society were segregated. NARRATOR: Bessie
used her popularity to help other Black aviators. From 1922 on, she refused to
fly unless the air shows were integrated. But wherever they flew, Bessie
and the other Black pilots rarely had access to
quality airplanes. PHILIP HART: When
African-Americans were second class citizens,
so the equipment that they had available
to them was second class. In many instances, people were
building their own airplanes. VON HARDESTY: Bessie
Coleman, like so many of the early Black
aviators, always had a problem of generating
funds to buy the most modern equipment. And this became a perennial
problem for these people in the 20s and 30s. NARRATOR: In 1924,
flying an inferior plane, Bessie stalled in the air and
crashed just after take off. She suffered a broken leg
and three broken ribs. The accident kept Bessie
from flying for two years. But by 1926, she
was back in the air, still trying to raise money to
realize her dream of a flight school. Yet once again, lack of
funds had forced her to buy a less than perfect plane. On April 30th, 1926,
Bessie sat in the back seat as her co-pilot flew
over the terrain where she would perform
a daring parachute drop. Suddenly, the plane accelerated,
went into a tailspin, and flipped over. It's alleged that
a wrench or a tool got stuck in the prop area. And she didn't have
a parachute on. And for some reason, she
was not wearing her seatbelt. And when the plane
swerved, she fell out. NARRATOR: Bessie plunged
over 500 feet to her death. Her co-pilot died instantly
when the plane hit the ground and burst into flames. Substandard equipment
was blamed for the crash. Bessie Coleman's influence as
a pioneer of Black aviation is felt even to this day. Each year on the anniversary
of her death, pilots fly low over her grave in
Chicago, dropping flowers. In 1995, after 10 years of
intense lobbying by her niece, the United States honored
this almost forgotten hero by issuing a postage stamp
commemorating Bessie Coleman's extraordinary life as
the first Black woman to pilot an airplane. After World War I, aviation
entered a golden age, characterized by Charles
Lindbergh solo flight across the Atlantic in 1927. Yet for Black Americans,
it was still a world that was virtually closed. Although there had been
pioneering breakthroughs by Eugene Bullard
and Bessie Coleman, most Americans hadn't
heard about them. A lot of people didn't know
much about these Black aviators or their achievements. This was a function, I
guess, of just segregation. The white press routinely gave
them little, if any coverage. NARRATOR: But a few Blacks
were beginning to fly. After Bessie Coleman's
death, Black flying clubs appeared in Los
Angeles and Chicago. It was the era of
the barnstormers-- daredevil stunt pilots
flashing through the skies, performing hair raising
flying feats for the awestruck crowds below. The kind of stunts that
you know you would see would be spirals, you
know, dead motor landings. Then also, you would have
people who were wing walkers. And one plane would approach,
and you'd have a wing walker come out on the
wing, and then they would grab the wing of
the plane approaching and transfer from one
plane to another plane. NARRATOR: In the 1920s and 30s,
one of the most famous Black barnstormers was Hubert
Fauntleroy Julian. He would capture the headlines
with his outrageous adventures and flamboyant personality. Julian was known as The
Black Eagle of Harlem. What is your work? Aeronautics,
lecturing, to travel all over the country and-- VON HARDESTY: A very flamboyant
guy, really good looking guy dressed very sharply
and fit this mold-- heroic mold of an aviator. He did a lot of things that
got media attention, not only the Black press but
the mainstream press. He did things like
jump out of an airplane in the middle of Harlem in a
multicolored Cape and jumpsuit. VON HARDESTY: And Hubert Julian
quickly established himself as the Premier Black
Aviator in the 20s and 30s. NARRATOR: But like most
early Black aviators, Julian had been forced to
venture outside the United States to learn how
to pilot an airplane. PHILIP HART: He learned how to
fly in Canada from Billy Bishop who was a famous
World War I pilot. VON HARDESTY: He was
one of the first Blacks to obtain a license,
which was no small feat. And he had some manifest
skills as a pilot. However, to the chagrin of a
lot of other Black aviators in the 20s and 30s, he became
something of a disappointment. He was always
full of big plans, but he never could pull together
the resources to enable them to pull them off. NARRATOR: Like the time when
Julian announced three years before Lindbergh that he would
be the first man in history to make a transatlantic flight. On July 4th 1924, 25,000
fans flocked to the shores of the Harlem River
in New York to watch as The Black Eagle took off. Five minutes later,
he and his plane were fished out of Flushing Bay. Julian shook off the
embarrassing failure. And in 1930, he was back
in the news when he made a well-publicized
journey to Africa-- in an attempt to help
Ethiopian emperor Haile Selassie fight
the Italian army. ANNOUNCER: Officers of the
emperor direct mobilization, and among them is none other
than Colonel Hubert Julian-- Black Eagle of Harlem. ROSCOE BROWN: He
went to Ethiopia. He became the one man
Ethiopian Air Force, until he crashed the plane. PHILIP HART: Julian crashed
Haile Selassie's plane. He took it up without
the emperor's permission. And it was supposed to be
used in a big ceremony. Colonel, what happened to you
and the Ethiopian Air Force? There's no such thing as
existing as an Ethiopian Air Force. [laughter] REPORTER: What is your-- what
is your final opinion on-- VON HARDESTY: So Hubert Julian
is kind of a tragic figure when you think of what
he could have done. But his flamboyance and kind
of wild entrepreneurial style and self-promotion did
a lot to alienate him. NARRATOR: In an age when
few Blacks flew at all, The Black Eagle cut a bold
swath through the skies. And even if many of
his grandiose attempts ended in failure,
Hubert Fauntleroy Julian inspired a generation
of young Black Americans to become pilots. If Julian sometimes had
his head in the clouds, there were other Black aviators
whose dreams were firmly planted in reality. One of the most influential
was William Powell. Powell was born in
Chicago in 1897. A college educated engineer, he
understood that aviation would offer an important opportunity
for Black Americans. VON HARDESTY: He wanted to begin
to establish the credibility of Blacks as pilots,
mechanics, businessmen. And he felt that aviation
was so new that you might be able to get in on
the ground floor before all the tentacles of
this hydra-headed monster of segregation
would take it over, and then permanently explicitly
officially exclude Blacks. NARRATOR: In 1929, in
memory of Bessie Coleman, Powell organized the
Bessie Coleman Aero Club in Los Angeles. PHILIP HART: He had a vision
of having Bessie Coleman Aero Clubs in cities throughout
the United States. And the objective was to teach
young people aviation-- men and women, so that we
would be able to be owners, we'd be able to be pilots,
we'd be able to be involved in all aspects of aviation. NARRATOR: In 1931,
Powell organized the first all-Black air show. It's star would be
James Herman Banning. PHILIP HART: Banning
started actively learning how to fly in 1924,
received his license in 1926. 1926 was a year the US
Department of Commerce started licensing pilots
in the United States. So he was the first
African-American pilot to be licensed. And he became the most
experienced Black pilot. NARRATOR: Banning wanted
to be the first Black to make a cross-country flight. But first, he and his
co-pilot, Thomas Allen, would need an airplane. VON HARDESTY: They managed to
obtain a used Alexander Eagle Rock single engine biplane. And they had just a
small amount of money between them to purchase
gasoline and sustain them across the United States. NARRATOR: On
September 18th 1932, they took off with only $25
and some Sun-Maid Raisins. VON HARDESTY: Because they
had no money to speak of, and it was kind of hand-to-mouth
segment by segment flight, they called themselves
the flying hobos. They would stop a routinely
in a certain area, go to the local Black church,
and kind of preach the gospel of aviation, appeal for
some financial support, and then resume their journey. PHILIP HART: When Banning and
Allen landed in St. Louis, they were having engine
problems and primarily problems with the valves. And the valves were
basically shot, so they were kind
of commiserating. And there was a group
of people learning how to maintain engines. And the instructor told them
that the 1928 Nash had valves similar to the ones that
were in their engines. So they found in 1928 Nash, took
the valves out of that engine, and the students helped
them install those valves, and engine ran good. So they were able
to take it off. And then they landed October
9th 1932 in Long Island Valley Stream Airfield in Long
Island as the first Black as to fly coast to coast. And they took off
from LA as hobos, and they landed in
New York as heroes. NARRATOR: In New York, they
were given the key to the city by Mayor Jimmy Walker. The two aviators were celebrated
in Harlem at the Cotton Club by the likes of Duke
Ellington and Cab Calloway. One year later, on
February 5th 1933, a biplane in which
Banning was a passenger was performing in an air show. While hundreds
watched, the plane malfunctioned and crashed. Banning was only 32 years old. His death was a blow to the
world of Black aviation. And Banning's sponsor,
William Powell, was hit particularly hard. For Powell had hoped
his protege would help draw a future Black
aviators into the fold. But Powell continued to push
his dream of Black involvement in the world of aviation
through his book, "Black Wings" and his trade magazine. VON HARDESTY: In
his trade magazine, "Craftsman of Aero Wings,"
he would routinely publish this kind of utopian scheme
interconnected entities, Black owned hangars,
and aviation plans, and airlines and
training institutes. And this new technology might be
the thin edge of the wedge that would break down
this horrible pattern of racial discrimination
in the United States. Great vision. Sadly, he died in 1942 with the
great bulk of his dream never realized. In 1941, as America
entered World War II, the need for pilots was great. But Blacks who wanted to
serve their country in the air still faced barriers
of prejudice. Not only was the United States
Army totally segregated, but Blacks were also
excluded from the Air Force. The only jobs available were as
waiters in Air Force canteens. PHILIP HART: So you still
had that residue of doubt that Black men and women did
not have the aptitude to fly, did not have the skills
to learn how to fly. NARRATOR: But things
were about to change. To protest the lack
of Black pilots, the National Association for the
Advancement of Colored People and the Brotherhood of
Sleeping Car Porters, the largest Black
Union in the nation, threatened to hold a
massive March on Washington. The war office relented
and the Tuskegee Institute, a Black college in
Alabama, was commissioned to begin training Black
Americans as fighter pilots. But because officials
from the war department were skeptical about the
program's ultimate success, they called it the
Tuskegee experiment. VON HARDESTY: But it's set
up on a segregated basis. It's not racial integration,
it's desegregation of a sort. And this so-called
Tuskegee experiment could be described as almost
a separate Black Air Force. NARRATOR: As the program
began the army was concerned about the effect
all Black squadrons would have on the morale
of white pilots and troops, even though the men
training at Tuskegee were of the highest caliber. ROSCOE BROWN: To become
a Tuskegee airman, you had to be very bright, had
to be very well coordinated. You have to have good
physical fitness, and you had to
have a spirit that says nobody's going to break
you because of the segregation. We were trained by white pilots,
some of whom wanted to be there and some who didn't, some of
whom were very fair and some of whom weren't. But we were very fortunate that
the commander of our training base Colonel Noel Parrish
was a white southerner who did believe that
African-Americans have a chance. And he insisted that
we'd be treated fairly. As a result, we got
outstanding instruction. NARRATOR: But now, another
obstacle confronted the airmen. The Army Air Corps wouldn't
contribute the funds needed to help build a more
advanced runway. The Tuskegee
Institute was forced to approach the philanthropic
Rosenwald Foundation for a loan to save the program. ROSCOE BROWN: And just by
coincidence, Mrs. Roosevelt, who was on the board of
the Rosenwald foundation, went to Tuskegee for a meeting. And she heard that the
Blacks were flying, so she went to the
chief pilot, man by the name of Chief
Anderson, and said, I understand these
young men wanted to fly, I'd like to take a
ride with one of you. And when Chief Anderson
offered her a ride, she jumped at the chance,
although her secret service agents were aghast. ROSCOE BROWN: And she had
this ride all around Tuskegee. And said, that was
beautiful flight. I'm going to tell
my husband about it. NARRATOR: As a result
of her influence, Tuskegee was given
the needed money. And the President
and Mrs. Roosevelt would become staunch
supporters of the airmen. The training continued. ANNOUNCER: In July of
1941, five young Negroes made aviation history
at Tuskegee, Alabama. These five men were
the first of their race to graduate under the Army Air
Force's newly organized plan for training Negro pilots. NARRATOR: By March of 1942, 100
more had received their wings. MEN (SINGING): We are
the heroes of the night. To help get it back. Fight!
Fight! Fight! Fight! NARRATOR: The Tuskegee Airmen
formed the 99th Fighter Squadron which later became part
of the all Black 332nd fighter group. To lead them, the Army Air Corps
chose recent Tuskegee graduate, Benjamin O. Davis Jr. BETTY GUBERT: Benjamin O. Davis
Jr. Came from an army family. And he was the first
African-American West Point graduate in the 20th century. But Davis was given the silent
treatment for four years. During the four years,
he was at West Point, not a single social word
was spoken to him because of the prejudice. When they had dance classes,
he had a dance by himself. NARRATOR: The hardships Davis
endured at West Point only strengthened him. And by the time he
graduated from Tuskegee, he was ready to assume
the role of a leader. ROSCOE BROWN: The success of
the Tuskegee Airmen almost has to be attributed
to Ben Davis. He sought excellence. He lived excellence, and he was
a demanding commanding officer. And Ben Davis brought
that discipline to the Tuskegee Airmen. NARRATOR: Under Davis's
command, the Tuskegee Airmen would undergo extensive
combat training. And by June of 1943, they
were in battle over Italy, supporting allied ground troops
and harassing enemy supply lines. The air battle over Europe
was the ultimate test of a pilot's skill. ROSCOE BROWN: To be a successful
combat pilot, first of all, you have to be fearless, you
have to have great reflexes, and you have to have
excellent discipline. NARRATOR: On July 2nd 1943, the
airmen faced their first test in air to air combat. On a mission over Sicily,
a group of German fighters charged into battle
against them. As they approached,
Lieutenant Charles Hall turned inside the
enemy formation, firing a long burst which took a
German plane out of the air. Two other enemy planes were shot
down before the Germans broke combat. The Tuskegee Airmen had
passed their first battle in the air with flying colors. These guys, 19, 20 years old
were young alive, loved to fly, and had the same
sense of engagement with military aviation as
their white counterparts did. NARRATOR: But that wasn't enough
for those who wanted to see the Tuskegee Airmen fail. A biased report which
reflected the entrenched racism within the Air Force were
circulated in Washington. The report questioned the
airman's efficiency in battle. It suggested that the Tuskegee
experiment should be abandoned. And there was an attempt
made to send the 99th home. Bill Davis was called
back to the United States to explain why the 99th
shouldn't be taken out of combat. NARRATOR: Colonel Davis
returned to Washington. His arguments against the plan
triggered an investigation, which concluded that the
Tuskegee Airmen had performed as well as every other
squadron in the Air Force. The Tuskegee Airmen
would continue fighting. On January 27th 1944, the
Tuskegee fighter pilots were about to engage in one
of their biggest battles. Over the Anzio
beachhead in Sicily, a squadron of Tuskegee Airmen
spotted 15 German fighters dive bombing allied ships. The Americans attacked and
routed the enemy, shooting down five German planes. Later that day, they
scored three other kills. The next day, they would
bring down four more. The Tuskegee Airmen also
distinguished themselves in the dangerous job of
escorting America's bombers into enemy territory. ROSCOE BROWN: The bomber
pilots from my opinion were most courageous of
the Air Force pilots, because they had to sit
there flying straight and level up to
deliver their bombs or any aircraft was
exploding all around, and then the Germans were coming
down through the formation, sometimes ramming them,
shooting them down. And our task as Tuskegee
Airmen, the Red Tails, was to stay close
to the bombers, fly over the bombers
in such a way that they would be protected. NARRATOR: Also
called the Red Tails, because of the distinctive
marking on their planes, the Tuskegee Airmen gained a
reputation as the best bomber escorts of the war. In fact, they were the only
bomber escort group in World War II never to lose a bomber. ROSCOE BROWN: Because of our
success, at a certain point in time, the bomber pilots
would prefer to have the Red Tails escorting them. And even today, I run into
former bomber pilots, gunners, navigators who said, you
guys helped save our lives, because we felt really good
when we saw the Red Tails. NARRATOR: Between 1941 and 1946,
a total of 92 Tuskegee Airmen were trained. They flew 1,578 missions. In all, they destroyed
over 500 enemy aircraft. They received the
Distinguished Unit Citation for Outstanding Performance
and Extraordinary Heroism. And in the end, their courage
helped to change America. VON HARDESTY: So it's not
just a story of fliers. It's just not an episode in
the history of the US Army Air Forces in World War II. This carries with it a lot
of significance in terms of American social history
about race relations, about America's own
evolution as a society. Looking at it broadly,
the Tuskegee experiment led to Harry Truman's
executive order in 1948, desegregating the armed
forces, which is essentially the first order that
led to the desegregation of American society. NARRATOR: During
World War II, 66 Tuskegee Airmen were
killed in action. WILLIAM ELLIS: 66
of our comrades are scattered in the
fields and hills of Europe. 66. Five of them are my classmates. And they gave me the right to
stand and say and talk the way and feel the way
I feel about this, and they gave it to you, because
they died as Americans so that you can be free. ANNOUNCER: This convoy,
first to leave Europe since-- NARRATOR: The returning
Black veterans of World War II found a country
still mired in segregation. A country with a very freedoms
many had fought and died for were not accorded
to them at home. We came back on
the troop ship, and we came down
the gangplank, there was a sign that said
white troops this way, colored troops this way. And it was back to home,
back to segregated America. NARRATOR: When the
war ended in 1945, none of the 992
Tuskegee airmen was able to get a job in
commercial aviation. And I applied to Eastern
Airlines at the time, and went into the office
on Fifth Avenue, filled out the application. And then I left. But as I left, I remembered I
had left my "New York Times," I went back to pick it up, and
the secretary was crumbling up my application, thrown
in the wastebasket. NARRATOR: Although
Roscoe Brown would go on to become a leader in
American education, racism had put an end
to his dream of flight. Since piloting jobs
with commercial airlines were non-existent, many
young Black Americans who wanted to be pilots
joined the military. One of them was Frank Petersen. I was fortunate. I was at the right
place at the right time. And I say that in that the
Korean War started shortly after I joined the
military in 1950. Then in turn, created
a need for aviators. NARRATOR: But even in the 1950s,
becoming an aviator would not be easy for Black Americans. They still face prejudice
and the lingering traditions of segregation. The Truman edict
of 48 had essentially cleared the military base of
overt forms of discrimination. But there was still
vestiges of discrimination, especially amongst the civilian
workforce aboard the base. There was still the traditional
drinking fountains-- white and colored. There was essentially
segregated eating facilities for the civilian
population aboard the base. The buses aboard the base
had non-segregated seating. And this is a public
transportation system off base. As soon as you cleared the
front gate going into town, you were required
by state law then to move to the segregated
portion of the bus. NARRATOR: Petersen faced
discrimination at every turn even from his flight instructor. I felt that there was
always a barrier that had to be broken through. That in the early 1950s,
late 1950s, that obstacles were placed in your way to
preclude and prevent Blacks from achieving
certain objectives. In my case, to be an aviator. NARRATOR: One of Petersen's
first flying instructors tried to convince him that
he wouldn't make it. I was told, as an example,
just prior to my solo flight, I was given a
down, the only down or bad check mark in
my cadet flying career that I would never be able to
become an aviator that I just lacked the skills. NARRATOR: Petersen
was ready to give up, until a chance meeting
with another Black officer changed his mind. And it was not until
I was about halfway through my flight training that
I had the pleasure of meeting another Black pilot. And that was a Chappie James. NARRATOR: Daniel "Chappie"
James had been a Tuskegee Airman during World War II. He would steadily
rise in the military to become the first
Black four-star general. Now in 1950, he
had fought his way past racism and up
the chain of command to become a captain
in the Air Force. Seeing another Black pilot
caught Petersen by surprise. FRANK PETERSEN: And quite
frankly, I was in shock. I thought I was seeing a mirage. A chance meeting lasted
for over several hours and began the basis for
a friendship that lasted to Chappie's entire life. NARRATOR: Chappie encouraged
Petersen to stick it out. Petersen completed his training,
yet the prejudice continued. When he went to the officer's
canteen for the first time, Petersen was arrested for
impersonating an officer. The next day, the
charges were dropped. But Petersen was about to
go out of the frying pan and into the fire. At the age of 21, he became
the first Black American to fly for the Marine Corps
when he entered the conflict in Korea. Petersen found that
every move could be a matter of life and death. The top pilots were those who
had hair trigger coordination, very, very, very quick reflexes,
when to turn, when to climb and the dive, and possessing
a mental telepathy almost in the sense of being fully
aware of where your opponent is at all times. NARRATOR: Petersen went on
to fly more than 64 combat missions in Korea. For his heroism in battle, he
was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross and six air medals. After Korea, Petersen
continued in the Marines. By the time of Vietnam, he had
attained the rank of Lieutenant Colonel and was a squadron
commander flying the F-4 Phantom Jet. In these sophisticated
war machines, combat started before you
could even see the enemy. FRANK PETERSEN: In
an aerial battle, the war starts essentially
over the horizon. Whoever gets off the first
shot has a better advantage. Even if you don't have
a good fire perimeter, throw something out there
in front of you, that'll make him stop and think. NARRATOR: But no matter how good
you are in the air, everything changes if you're
shot out of the sky. It happened to Petersen
and his co-pilot during a bombing run
over North Vietnam. We had both engines on fire,
losing hydraulic pressure. We both knew that if we
punched out over North Vietnam, we were going to spend a long
time up in the Hanoi Hilton. And just as we crossed
over in the South Vietnam, the fire had burned through
all control surfaces, the stick froze. I pulled the bar back to get
within safer ejection seat parameters, and we parachuted. So total fear, not
being able to analyze what it is you're jumping into,
you're essentially unarmed, you're defenseless. NARRATOR: As he
dropped, Petersen saw the enemy running towards
the spot where he would land. FRANK PETERSEN: I landed in
a rice paddy, hunkered down, hoping that someone would answer
the emergency signals that we had sent and sure enough
there was a Marine helicopter that came in about-- oh, I guess 100 yards
from where I was hiding. NARRATOR: With the enemy
advancing and machine guns from the
helicopter covering him, Petersen ran for his life. FRANK PETERSEN: When I jumped
up, ran to the helicopter, picked up and
booted out of there. That was the day you
earned your flight pay. NARRATOR: Petersen returned
from Vietnam in 1969. He steadily rose up the ranks. In 1978, he received the
first of his three stars as a general. When he retired 10
years later, the man who had almost washed
out of military aviation had not only become the
Defense Department's senior ranking aviator, but
the only Black three star general in the Marine Corps. But to Frank Petersen, there
is an irony in his success. FRANK PETERSEN: This first
in Black, only in Black is a double edged
sword in the sense that it's something to
be proud of in the sense that you have achieved
a certain status. But it also has a negative
connotation in that if this is still important. We still have a long way to go. ignition and liftoff, liftoff. By the early 1960s,
the United States was taking its first
steps into outer space, yet America's astronaut program
remained exclusively white. VON HARDESTY: It took
a while for Blacks to be routinely part of the
astronaut training program. an ines to allow Blacks into
that sphere of activity. But these things changed
as the society changed. NARRATOR: It would take 15 years
until the first Black aviators would be given their chance. In 1978, Ron McNair, Guion
Bluford, and Frederick Gregory were among the 34 men and one
woman selected as astronauts. There were 10,000 people
who applied for 35 slots in the astronaut program. And I felt very fortunate to be
one of those that was selected. NARRATOR: Bluford was born
in Philadelphia, a scientist with an advanced degree
in aerospace engineering. He was also a veteran
combat pilot in Vietnam. Now, he and Vietnam
vet, Frederick Gregory, trained in simulators
in zero gravity as they followed their
dreams to become astronauts. We all work together
and socialize together. We all eventually flew together. But I think we
were all dedicated to helping the shuttle
fly for the first time. MAN: And lift off. NARRATOR: In 1981, the
first shuttle was launched. And two years later,
Guion Bluford's turn came. On August 30th, 1983 at 2:32
AM, he became the first Black American to journey into space. GUION BLUFORD: The
biggest thrill for me in flying in space for the first
time was just flying in space. And I still remember the
thrill of rocketing up, because it only takes 8 and 1/2
minutes to go from 0 to 18,000 miles an hour. NARRATOR: On February 3rd,
1984, Dr. Ronald McNair received his chance. Two years later, Dr. McNair was
on board the Challenger Space Shuttle as that mission
rocketed into space. MAN: Challenger
go at throttle up. GUION BLUFORD: Like the
nation, we were all shocked by the Challenger accident. And for me, it was the
loss of good friends. There were four
members of my class, including Ron McNair
there in the accident. MAN: Liftoff of the
space shuttle Discovery for its Thanksgiving
day mission. NARRATOR: The shuttle
did fly again. And in 1989, Frederick
Gregory became the first Black commander
of a shuttle mission. FREDERICK GREGORY: The
shuttle is a very, very, very complicated, very
complex vehicle. It is probably the most
technologically complex vehicle in the world. In the cockpit, there are
some 2000 switches, gauges, and circuit breakers. Each of which has a different
function in different phases of the flight. NARRATOR: From outer space,
the world looks harmonious. GUION BLUFORD: When
you're on orbit, you can't tell one country
from another with reference to boundaries and so forth. So you tend to look at the world
from a global point of view, and you recognize that we
all share this blue marble together. We all have to live
together, and we all need to learn to work together. NARRATOR: Yet back on Earth,
there is still a long way to go to reach equality. But while Black
aviators have been able to climb the ladder
of success in the military, in the world of
commercial aviation, the going has been tough. Today, of the more than 80,000
commercial airline pilots in the United States, about
750, less than 1% are Black. PHILIP HART: The
numbers of Black pilots in the commercial
aviation sector are nowhere near
what they should be. And nowhere close to what the
visionaries like Bessie Coleman and William Powell and
James Herman Banning hoped would be the case at this
point in our history. NARRATOR: In Washington DC,
the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum features an
exhibit recounting the extraordinary struggles
and successes of Black American aviators. It is called Black Wings. VON HARDESTY: African-Americans
were the only group that were singled out
for discrimination and excluded from aviation. They're the only group. So it answers the
question, why would you have a separate exhibit
on Blacks in aviation? Well, we have it, because
that's American history. NARRATOR: The struggle to open
the hangar doors to all Black Americans continues. It is a goal which began
when the first pioneers of Black aviation left
the runway to fly free. Their legacy has been handed
down to a new generation. As a group, we
are the old people. We are a grandfather, great
grandfathers in essence to these kids. The only thing we have is
our legacy, and our legacy we bring some way back. Persistence, struggle,
faith, and belief in our society as a place
where everybody can and should have the opportunity to achieve

reviews.transcript_full: Xin chào các bạn đã trở lại với kênh Sài Gòn Aviation. Một chiếc máy bay thân rộng thế hệ mới như Boeing 787 Dreamliner với cấu trúc chủ yếu từ sợi cacbon siêu bền sẽ chịu tổn hại ra sao nếu xảy ra va chạm trực tiếp phần đuôi xuống đường băng ở vận tốc lớn. Khi lớp vỏ composit phức tạp bị xé rách và các cấu trúc chịu lực bên trong bị tổn hại, nhà sản xuất và hãng hàng không sẽ phải đối mặt với những thách thức kỹ thuật như thế nào? Quy trình đánh giá thiệt hại bằng sóng siêu âm, chế tạo các tấm vá composit đặc biệt cho đến việc hút chân không và ra nhiệt nướng lại vỏ máy bay ngay tại Hanger sẽ diễn ra sao? Và câu hỏi quan trọng nhất dựa trên các dữ liệu lịch sử sẽ mất bao lâu để một chiếc máy bay sau sự cố trà đuôi nghiêm trọng hoàn tất việc đánh giá, sửa chữa, bay thử nghiệm và nhận lại chứng nhận đủ điều kiện khai thác để an toàn quay trở lại bầu trời? Mất 3 tháng, 6 tháng hay thậm chí là hơn 12 tháng đàm sân. Mời các bạn cùng Sài Gòn Aviation tìm hiểu chi tiết trong video ngày hôm nay. Trước khi đi vào các tìm hiểu kỹ thuật chuyên sâu, mời các bạn cùng theo dõi thức phim tư liệu của chiếc Boeing 7879 Dreamliner mang số đăng bạ VNA867 của Viet Nam Airlines. Đây là hình ảnh máy bay khi đang thực hiện một chuyến bay nội địa và hạ cánh an toàn xuống sân bay quốc tế Tân Sơn Nhất trước thời điểm xảy ra sự cố. Đây là một trong những dòng máy bay thân rộng hiện đại và tối tân nhất trong đội bay thân rộng thế hệ mới hiện nay. Vào ngày 15 tháng 8 năm 2026, một sự cố nghiêm trọng đã xảy ra với chính máy bay này tại sân bay quốc tế Munich Đức. Theo các báo cáo kỹ thuật ban đầu và hình ảnh ghi nhận tại hiện trường, chiếc Dreamliner 15 tuổi này đã chịu những thiệt hại cấu trúc đáng kể ở phần thân sau và hệ thống càng đáp chính sau quá trình cất cánh bất thường. Cú va chạm mạnh đến mức cơ quan chức năng tại sân bay Munich đã ghi nhận vết lốp máy bay in hằn kéo dài bên ngoài khu vực Đường Băng cất cánh. Đồng thời, một số đèn báo hiệu nền của Đường Băng cũng bị hư hại do máy bay cán qua. Ngay sau sự cố, cơ quan điều tra tai nạn hàng không liên bang Đức BFU đã chính thức vào cuộc để điều tra làm rõ nguyên nhân vụ việc. Phía cục hàng không Việt Nam cũng đang phối hợp chặt chẽ với nhà chức trách Đức để theo dõi sát sao tiến trình này. Cho đến thời điểm hiện tại, nguyên nhân chính xác dẫn đến góc ngẩng cất cánh bất thường của chuyến bay vẫn đang chờ kết luận chính thức từ BFU. Tuy nhiên, dưới góc độ kỹ thuật hàng không, vấn đề cốt lõi cần phân tích lúc này chính là mức độ tổn thương của lớp vỏ sợi cacbon và tiến trình khôi phục đầy gian nan phía trước. Trong thuật ngữ hàng không, hiện tượng trà đuôi hay còn gọi là shrine xảy ra khi phần đuôi phía dưới của thân máy bay va chạm hoặc cọ sát trực tiếp với bề mặt đường băng. Hiện tượng này có thể xảy ra trong hai giai đoạn. Khi máy bay chạy đà cất cánh hoặc khi máy bay tiếp đất hạ cánh. Khi cất cánh, nếu phi công kéo cần lái quá mạnh hoặc quá sớm trước khi máy bay đạt đủ vận tốc tối thiểu, góc ngẩng của mũi máy bay sẽ tăng lên quá nhanh. Do thân máy bay rất dài, đặc biệt là dòng Boeing 7879 dài tới gần 63 m, phần đuôi sẽ bị hạ thấp xuống và cọ sát vào đường băng trước khi hai càng đáp chính kịp nhất khỏi mặt đất. Mặc dù một số dòng máy bay được trang bị bộ phận giảm chấn đuôi để hấp thụ lực va chạm, nhưng với một cú trà sát mạnh ở tốc độ cao, lực tác động vượt quá giới hạn thiết kế sẽ truyền thẳng vào khung xương chịu lực của thân máy bay, gây ra nứt gãy cơ học, rách vỏ áp suất và tạo ra những tổn thất cực kỳ nghiêm trọng về mặt cấu trúc. Nhìn lại lịch sử hàng không, các sự cố tra đuôi gây rách vỏ trên dòng B in 787 của các hãng hàng không quốc tế thường mất từ 6 đến 12 tháng để hoàn tất toàn bộ chu trình từ đánh giá, sửa chữa, bay thử nghiệm cho đến khi nhận lại chứng nhận đủ điều kiện bay thương mại. reviews.transcript_full: For decades, two airlines have dominated the skies over Asia. Singapore Airlines became famous for its service, luxury, and attention to detail. Cathay Pacific built its reputation around Hong Kong, turning the city into one of the world's most important aviation gateways. And today, both are still fighting for the same passengers. Today, we're going to put Singapore Airlines and Cathay Pacific side by side in several different categories. But before we compare what they offer today, we need to go back to the beginning. Because the stories of these two airlines started very differently. The beginning. Cathay Pacific came first. The airline was founded in Hong Kong in September 1946 by American Roy Farrell and Australian Sydney de Kanzow. Its first aircraft was a Douglas DC-3 named Betsy, and the airline initially focused on connecting Hong Kong with cities across Asia. Within just a few years, Cathay had become closely associated with the Swire Group, which would play a major role in shaping the airline for decades. Cathay expanded through Asia, entered the jet age, and eventually began building a global long-haul network. Then came one of the most important aircraft in its history, the Boeing 747. The arrival of the 747 in the late 1970s gave Cathay the ability to connect Hong Kong with much longer range destinations. Europe and North America became increasingly important, and Hong Kong began developing into one of the world's great connecting hubs. Singapore Airlines followed a different path. Its story actually begins with Malayan Airways in 1947. The airline later became Malaysian Airways, and in 1966, it was renamed Malaysia-Singapore Airlines, or MSA. But there was a problem. Singapore and Malaysia increasingly had different ideas about what the airline should become. Singapore wanted a commercially focused international airline. Today we're travelling across Slovenia on 
the country's fastest and most iconic train! We'll be riding in First Class aboard 
this Pendolino, sweeping through the   stunning Slovenian landscapes from the 
capital, to the country's second city. But what is Slovenia's flagship train 
actually like... Let's find out,   on another epic Nonstop Eurotrip! This journey starts in Ljubljana. The Slovenian capital is home to 300,000 people 
and is a hidden gen within Europe, in my opinion. There is so much history and beauty here,   and I would really recommend adding 
it to your travel bucket list! OK, to the station! Ljubljana's main railway station 
is just 600m (2,000ft) north of   the city centre and is easily 
walkable in just over 5 minutes. The local bus and long-distance 
coach station is here too,   well it's just these parking bays 
out the from of the main building. Let's head inside now... The large, staffed ticket office 
is off to the left hand side here. Opposite this is a very posh McDonalds. And then heading through towards 
the platforms, and there is a   small convenience store on the left, and 
the station café and bar on the right. Out here are a few automatic ticket machines,   or you can also buy on the 
Slovenske železnice (SŽ) app. Our train today is the ICS20 service to Maribor, 
which departs at 3:15pm from Platform 6. Slovenian railways have invested 
heavily in recent years in new   rolling stock from Swiss company, 
Stadler, such as these FLIRT EMUs. They also have double-decker KISS 
EMUs which we will see shortly. The far platforms can be accessed 
by this central underground walkway. Renovations are currently underway, and 
not every platform has a proper lift yet,   but wheelchair stair lifts are 
available. Speak to station staff. Otherwise, you will need to ascend the stairs. Our train today is this 3-car 
SŽ Pendolino tilting EMU. These have a maximum speed of 200km/h (125mph), 
but only run in service at up to 160km/h (100mph) Let's check out today's route! We will depart Ljubljana and 
head east and then north,   making three intermediate stops 
before arriving in Maribor. Boarding is not level with the platform, 
but a ramp is available on request. We will be in First Class today, which 
takes up half of one of the three coaches. This is laid out in a 2+1 configuration. Departure is right on-time at 3.15pm. This services' name 'ICS',   stands for 'Intercity Slovenija' and it 
is the country's premium train service. The route from Ljubljana to Maribor 
covers 156km (97mi) in distance,   which is scheduled to take us 1 
hour and 52 minutes of travel time. Here we see one of the aforementioned 
Stadler KISS double decker trains. All onboard announcements 
are made in Slovenian only. An adult First Class ticket costs 
€23.60 (£20.19, $32.16), while in   Second Class it's €16.40 (£14.03, $19.11). All prices are fixed, and are not dynamic. However, there are special weekend 
tickets, which save 25% on the full-fare. The discounts available for children 
and youths can be seen on-screen now. SŽ has three of these Pendolino trainsets, 
which entered service in the year 2000. They are currently undergoing a mid-life 
refurbishment program, so these ICS services   are being periodically swapped out for the 
Stadler FLIRTs, until this has been completed. As we head out into the Slovenian countryside,   let me take a moment to tell you about 
today's video sponsor, Manta Sleep. When you are on the go as much as I am, it's 
sometimes difficult to get in a full night's   sleep, or it's been such a busy day filming, 
that I just need a quick 20 minute nap. That's why I've been using Manta Sleep and 
their excellent selection of high quality   sleep masks for the past few years now, and 
they are honestly a game-changer for me. They have a varied selection of different 
masks including the 'Cool Mask',   which calms your eyes and sinuses, 
the ultra soft and gentle 'Silk Mask',   which helps to protect your eyes, and 
prevents wrinkles, and the Sleep Mask Pro,   which gives unbeatable side-sleep 
comfort, ventilation and breathability. They all feature zero-pressure, 
100% blackout eye cups which have   quick and easy Velcro adjustments to fit everyone. I have been checking out the 'Sound 
Mask' recently which has built-in,   ultra-thin Bluetooth headphones ideal 
for side sleepers. This is perfect for   listening to music or a podcast when dozing off 
and the battery lasts 24 hours on a full charge. If you want to improve your sleep either at home, 
or while travelling, check out Manta Sleep using   the link in the description below, and get 
10% OFF all products using my code: NONSTOP. Now back to the video! About 20 minutes after departure,   the friendly conductor comes 
through the train to check tickets. OK, time to have a look the seats here in 
First Class, I must say they do look good! They are leather trimmed and have good 
padding on both the base and back,   along with a slightly winged 
headrest and soft head cushion. The arm rests are also adjustable and padded. They can be reclined a little bit by lifting 
this lever and sliding the base forwards. This old entertainment system is now defunct. The bay seats have a large, 
expandable table in-between them,   with a small litter bin next to the windows. There are standard 220v European 
power sockets located under the table. Coat hooks can be found on the wall, with reading 
lights on the underside of the luggage rack. The windows feature electronically operated 
sun blinds, which gives a very premium feel. Overall, I think this is a 
great First Class product. Super comfortable and with 
all the amenities you could   need for this 2 hour journey across Slovenia. Note there is no complimentary service included, 
it's just the seat upgrade that you are getting. Free WiFi is available for all passengers onboard. This was very easy to connect 
to, and while not fast,   it did the job for web browsing and messaging. OK, let's go and check out 
the rest of the train now! As mentioned, First Class take up half of one 
coach, with the other half being Second Class. This is laid out in a 2+2 configuration. The seats are similar to mine, but are 
cloth and have a reduced width and legroom. There are also some airline style pairs 
which have footrests and tray tables. Everything else is the same except there are   no power sockets. Hopefully the 
refurbishment will address this! Next we find the buffet counter. This was not in use in this service, but there 
were menus and a few items still lying around. Does anyone know if these 
are still regularly used? Just beyond this are the trains two wheelchair 
spaces with accompanying companion seats. The accessible toilet is 
in the adjacent vestibule. This was spacious, pretty 
clean and fully stocked up. The two other regular toilets were 
much smaller, as you'd expect. However, in this one, everything 
worked as intended, and the soap,   hand towels and toilet roll were all available. Again, it was pretty clean too! We are now running alongside the River 
Sava, in the gorge of the same name. This is the River Danube's longest tributary with   a total length of 990km (615mi). They 
eventually join in Belgrade, Serbia. This is also where you will find the 
best #TrainWindowViews on the trip. Did you know that Slovenia is the 
4th most forested country in Europe,   with 61% of its total land area covered by trees? Take a look here as we round the tight curves,   and you can see the Pendolino trainset tilting 
into the bends to improve passenger comfort. This also allows for quicker overall travel times,   with up to 35% faster cornering speeds, 
with a maximum tilt angle of 8 degrees. Our first intermediate stop 
today is at Zidani Most. This is in the small village of the same 
name, which mostly serves as an important   junction station where the line heads south 
east to the Croatian border and Zagreb,   and north to the Austrian border and Graz 
- the direction which we will be heading. It also lies at the confluence 
of the Sava and Savinja rivers   which we cross shortly after departure. This is a heavily used trunk line too for freight 
services between the three countries, and beyond. Despite their age, these Pendolino train sets are 
still very popular in Europe, with versions still   operating in Italy, Finland, Spain, Greece 
and the Czech Republic, among others... They have also been superseded by a 
'New Pendolino' model from 2008 onwards,   such as this Polish one seen here. These even operate as far away as China! We are now on the approach to Celje. This is Slovenia's third largest city, which has 
a population of 50,000 people in the municipality. I found the ride quality to be pretty 
good onboard these train, on the whole. In theory, they have a top 
sped of 200km/h (125mph),   however the maximum line speed anywhere 
in Slovenia is 160km/h (100mph). Most of the time today though, we 
travel at around 140km/h (87mph). We are now coming up to the final 
intermediate stop on the route,   this being the village of Pragersko. This is another important junction station,   where just after, another line diverges right to 
Slovenia's eastern border with northern Croatia. As we are now approaching the end of today's 
trip, let me summarise this journey with Slovenske   železnice onboard their flagship Pendolino 
trains, from Ljubljana to Maribor in First Class. Overall, I think these are great trains. Comfortable in both classes, and with good onboard   amenities for the sub 2-hour routes 
that they serve within Slovenia. The tickets are good value,   and for quarter century old trains 
they are in great condition still. I can't wait to come back and check out the 
refurbished versions once this has been completed! After crossing over the River Drava, we arrive 
in Maribor a couple of minutes early, at 5.05pm. Have you been on any trains in Slovenia 
before? If so, which ones and on which   routes? What was your experience like? 
Let me know in the comments below! I'm always open to new video ideas, so if you 
have something you'd like to see on the channel,   then drop me DM on Instagram, BlueSky or Twitter. Don't forget to subscribe, thanks for watching 
to the end, and I'll see you in the next video!

article_text: Will high-speed inflight connectivity disrupt the embedded inflight entertainment world, and ultimately sound the death knell for seatback IFE on board aircraft? This hoary chestnut of a question has been asked since broadband IFC first debuted in commercial aviation with Lufthansa’s 2004 introduction of the Connexion by Boeing Ku-band geostationary satcom service.

Over two decades later, the same question is still being asked in some circles but now it carries a bit more weight as Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and multi-orbit inflight connectivity systems demonstrate the art of the possible: passengers flying on equipped aircraft can consistently avail of an at-home Internet experience in the sky.

Among the carriers at the forefront of adopting LEO-based IFC, United Airlines is presently in the process of fitting its entire fleet with SpaceX’s Starlink service in a bid to power free Wi-Fi for members of its MileagePlus loyalty program.

But even as United moves with speed to bring Starlink to its fleet — it has equipped more than half of its regional jets and recently installed the system on its first Boeing 737-800 — the US major is also adding Panasonic Avionics seatback IFE systems to its narrowbodies and bringing larger screens to its new widebodies. Roughly 1,000 aircraft in United’s fleet are expected to carry seatback screens by the end of 2026 or early 2027.
NPS score boost
In a world where most people have smartphones and tablets, why would United bother to install Bluetooth-enabled seatback screens across its mainline fleet?

For the answer we turn to United Airlines EVP and CFO Mike Leskinen, who studies United’s business from a numbers’ perspective, and is fully aware that embedded IFE represents a significant upfront investment in the hardware, the installation, the testing and the certification, not to mention the weight it adds to planes which in turn increases fuel burn.
“[T]hose screens, along with the high bandwidth Wi-Fi, make our customer’s journey infinitely better,” Leskinen said on 3 September in a highly revelatory post on LinkedIn .

We offer a differentiated product in what has historically been a commoditized business, and that is driving brand loyal customers to choose United every time they fly. And that’s worth every penny. Leisure customers are rating their travel experience more highly and business travelers are more productive, proving the right investments in high-quality IFE drive stronger Net Promoter Scores, increased brand loyalty, and positive differentiation from competitors, which all translate into revenue growth and higher more sustainable profits.

Leisure customers are rating their travel experience more highly and business travelers are more productive, proving the right investments in high-quality IFE drive stronger Net Promoter Scores, increased brand loyalty, and positive differentiation from competitors, which all translate into revenue growth and higher more sustainable profits.

Seatback IFE, meanwhile, has long been a core feature of the passenger experience on Delta Air Lines’ mainline fleet, and the US major is now flying 165,000 seatback screens across over 930 aircraft — more than any other US-based airline.
Seemingly small tweak, big wellness impact

After sitting down with Delta’s general manager of customer research and advisor, Lizzy Martinez this spring, New York Times best-selling author and loyalty expert Fred Reichheld revealed what he learned in a LinkedIn post titled ‘Delta’s Ascent: How a Legacy Airline Earned a Leader’s Spot in Loyalty.’

Delta’s service philosophy is grounded in three brand beliefs: Make customers feel welcomed, elevated, and cared for. These aren’t just words — they’re operationalized through training and frontline behaviors. Using biometric data and customer sentiment analysis from volunteers, Delta mapped the emotional peaks and valleys across the travel journey. One surprising insight? Stress levels drop the moment customers sit down. To make that moment even sweeter, Delta turned on seatback entertainment as soon as passengers board — no need to wait to reach 30,000 feet. A small tweak, a big impact.

Using biometric data and customer sentiment analysis from volunteers, Delta mapped the emotional peaks and valleys across the travel journey. One surprising insight? Stress levels drop the moment customers sit down. To make that moment even sweeter, Delta turned on seatback entertainment as soon as passengers board — no need to wait to reach 30,000 feet. A small tweak, a big impact.

Of note: both United and Delta have bolstered their IFE content partnerships in recent months. The former is adding Spotify audiobooks and podcasts as well as select Apple TV+ hits to seatback screens and personal devices, and the latter is providing ad-free access to a selection of YouTube videos, podcasts and music playlists.

These types of collaborations are smart for several reasons: they deliver content created for the direct-to-consumer (D2C) market but not explicitly over a live inflight connectivity pipe which preserves costly bandwidth.

They also expose the brand and the D2C exclusive content to passengers, which can generate subscriptions. To wit, Delta says SkyMiles Members logged into Delta Sync Wi-Fi can unlock “a 14-day free preview of YouTube Premium on Delta Wi-Fi-enabled flights within the U.S”. No form of payment is required, though a Google account is needed (and set-up can be facilitated by the free Wi-Fi).

Additionally, such arrangements ensure that airlines are not falling afoul of content creators’ licensing rights, as there is some legal uncertainty right now around whether airlines should advertise streaming OTT to passengers.

“No major streaming service explicitly permits inflight access under standard terms and conditions. Inflight licensing is handled separately, via airline and content owner agreements, not through general streaming terms,” Airline Passenger Experience Association (APEX) CEO Dr. Joe Leader warned during the APEX Global EXPO in Long Beach. APEX and major studios will update industry on the state of play at the APEX TECH conference in Los Angeles in January.
Keeping pace with rapid change

The endurance of seatback IFE and its positive impact on both NPS scores and passenger wellbeing is no surprise to Panasonic Avionics, which is a key partner to both United and Delta, and counts United as a launch customer for its modular nextgen Astrova system.

“I’ve been in this industry since 1991 and my personal belief — and I’ve seen so many predictions of the death of IFE, you know, over and over again — is I don’t think this is the death of IFE because the business just keeps getting bigger,” Panasonic Avionics vice president of digital solutions Andrew Mohr said of the impact on embedded IFE of low-latency LEO connectivity.

During a sit-down interview at the offices of Malmö, Sweden-based Tactel, the digital interaction agency that Panasonic acquired in 2015, Mohr told Runway Girl Network: “You know, the iPad was supposed to kill it. Little personal video players were supposed to kill it.”

At the same time, Panasonic is fully aware it cannot rest on its laurels. LEO and multi-orbit IFC, for which Panasonic also supports with its own solutions , are “probably the most disruptive thing that’s going to happen” since overhead IFE displays transitioned to individual AVOD screens in the seat, Mohr said.

That’s why Panasonic is moving with the times, becoming more agile, offering new software suites — including tools that enable airlines to take full control of their digital experience — and supporting industry’s transition to a ‘connected seatback’ where personalization takes center stage.
“The potential for actually this being integrated and being very transformative is huge,” Mohr said.
A renewed focus on inflight wellness is also in the cards. “It’s a big untapped category actually for an IFE supplier because it’s the number one concern,” the Panasonic executive noted.
