article_text: Historically, inflight entertainment content processing has been notoriously slow, with new-run movie titles landing on board aircraft sometimes weeks after they’ve been made available to the consumer video-on-demand market.

But major airline content service provider (CSP) Anuvu is helping to change the game. The Lombard, Illinois-headquartered firm has built an AI pipeline that it says has cut IFE content processing time by 65% — turning a typical four-week manual delivery window “into something dramatically faster, without compromising compliance or quality.”

Given that the IFE market is steadily growing, and requirements are complex — a typical title needs roughly five dubbing languages and eight subtitle languages per airline — the decision is quite timely.

“Over 900 passenger airlines fly worldwide, with hundreds offering some form of IFE, each managing content standards route by route, market by market,” notes an Anuvu spokesperson. She suggests that the IFE content market is set to grow to $931 million by 2029.
Seeing the writing on the wall, Anuvu (formerly Global Eagle) several years ago created a cloud-based backbone for content delivery, and embedded rights management into the solution.

The so-called Open platform, which uses Amazon Web Services (AWS) as the core framework, ingests, selects, edits and delivers over 18,000 files per cycle and has allowed the company to support 4K HD and HDR delivery to new IFE systems.

What’s new is that Anuvu has now built AI into that same Open ecosystem, integrating two new tools — one for localization (dubbing and subtitling) and one for aviation-specific compliance checks — into how it processes and delivers content.

The result, it says, is faster turnaround on new titles and routes, without losing the human sign-off and audit trail compliance demands. This, in turn, is speeding up delivery and improving output quality.

But what does this development mean operationally for airlines, and indeed the passenger experience? We interviewed Anuvu vice president, global content and ops Kosh Hussain to learn more. Please enjoy our full Q&A.

RGN: On average, how much faster is Anuvu’s AWS-based Open platform able to process and deliver content with these two new AI tools, as opposed to in the past? Are we talking days or perhaps weeks’ worth of time savings? When were the AI tools first utilized by Anuvu?

Hussain: We have seen a 65% reduction in time needed for specific content processes since introducing these tools into our pipeline. Open has been able to encode a movie in only minutes for several years now, however, it’s not only about speed. The addition of AI tools are helping us become more efficient in traditionally manual tasks and processes.

To put that in real terms, a process that historically took around four weeks from content ingest to delivery-ready output can now be completed in a fraction of that time, without compromising compliance or quality. For example, we can screen a 120-minute movie in 20 minutes compared to three hours needed for a human screener. We began rolling these tools into production in 2024, and we have been continuously refining the workflow as we have scaled it across our operations.

RGN: It’s our understanding that agentic AI is now offered baseline as part of AWS. Would you describe these two AI tools as agentic AI, with Anuvu incorporating a human-in-the-loop approach once the actions are executed through the multi-step workflow?

Hussain: That’s a fair characterization. Both tools operate across multi-step workflows, one handling localization,(subtitling) and the other handling aviation-specific compliance checks, and they can sequence and execute those steps with a good degree of autonomy. But we have been very deliberate that this is an augmentation, not automation for automation’s sake. Every piece of content still passes through our human quality control teams before it goes out the door. The AI does the heavy lifting on the repetitive, time-intensive work; our people apply the judgment, context, and final sign-off that content, especially in aviation, absolutely requires.
RGN: Is closed captioning also facilitated by the AI tools?

Hussain: Yes, closed captioning sits within the same localization tool that handles subtitling for other languages. Broadly, our localization tool is built to handle the full text and language layer of a title, so it’s a natural extension of the subtitling workflow rather than a separate process. Closed captioning is becoming more in demand from our airline clients and we are in a great position to be able to deliver at scale and speed to ensure airlines are compliant with specific rules surrounding this.
RGN: Can Anuvu give us an idea of the volume of 4K content now being supplied to the aviation market (has it greatly increased over the last year)?

Hussain: 4K deliveries are up 20% year-on-year. What we can say directionally is that demand for higher-fidelity content in the cabin has grown quickly, driven by better screens, improved systems, and airlines wanting the inflight environment to feel more like what passengers experience at home. That’s part of the reason we have invested in a pipeline capable of handling that volume and complexity without extending delivery timelines. We have been delivering true 4K files in a live cabin environment since 2021.

RGN: Anuvu customer Cathay Pacific is introducing what it says is the “world’s first 4K HDR10+ inflight content”, paired with Panasonic Avionics’ Astrova screens (coming to new A321neos.) How will Open plus the new AI tools streamline delivery for Cathay?

Hussain: We’ve worked closely with Cathay Pacific for many years to help push the boundaries of the cabin experience, and this is very much the next chapter in that relationship. Our team has been supporting the vision for 4K in the cabin for a long time now, well before the infrastructure and screen technology existed to fully realize it, so seeing that ambition converge with Panasonic’s Astrova screens is genuinely exciting for us.

Higher-resolution, HDR-mastered content brings more complexity into the pipeline, larger files, more exacting technical specifications, etc. Our lab, paired with our AI localization and compliance tools, is what allows us to manage that complexity at scale without slowing delivery, so Cathay’s 4K HDR10+ titles can move through subtitling and compliance checks at the same pace as the rest of our catalog. We are looking forward to seeing this content onboard very soon.
RGN: To be clear, even as Anuvu embraces these new tools, there will be no headcount reduction at the firm?

Hussain: Correct. These tools were designed from the outset to empower our teams, not replace them. The change is in the nature of the work: our teams spend less time on repetitive, manual processing and more time on quality judgment, edge cases and the parts of the process that genuinely need a human eye.

In fact, the focus has shifted; we’re spending more time on quality control and curation, creating more jobs as technology evolves in line with the growing requirements for IFE and passenger experience.

RGN: If an airline wants to update its content more regularly (say, faster than a 30-day cycle), is Anuvu able to accommodate them more easily now that it’s using these AI tools? What’s the fastest turnaround that can be offered?

Hussain: Yes, an airline-led timeline is a meaningful shift the pipeline has enabled. A 30-day cycle was, in many cases, a result of lengthy, manual localization and compliance checks, which were necessary for the system OEM to conduct a full review of the content package. With processing time cut by 65%, we’re able to support more frequent refresh cycles, meaning more content with fewer restrictions.

We work with some of the world’s largest and most prestigious airlines. With the latest connectivity offerings and OEM systems, these airlines expect to move towards two different approaches: one for the traditional monthly content processing, and another for flexible content delivery . Content owners are playing a very important role in these discussions.

RGN: Anuvu offers airlines visibility into their content options via its Explore online entertainment library. This can be paired with Iris, Anuvu’s content subscription service. Are most of Anuvu’s airline customers utilizing these services? Does Anuvu see any opportunities for exploiting AI to transform Explore into a predictive recommendation engine? (Or perhaps that is already in play?)

Hussain: Explore is a key part of Anuvu’s digital supply chain and is used by the majority of our airline clients, regardless of the commercial model they have with us. It gives both our teams and airline teams visibility into their IFE lineup and enables them to work together on content curation. We see the continued digitalization of these workflows as an important part of the future of the industry, and will evolve based on feedback from our clients and teams.

The opportunity to use AI to make Explore a more predictive recommendation engine is absolutely a natural next step for us. We are already using AI to accelerate how content gets to the aircraft, and the logical extension is to use AI to help airlines decide what content to select in the first place: surfacing titles based on factors such as route, audience and viewing patterns, rather than relying solely on manual curation. Some of these capabilities are already in development, with launches expected toward the end of the year.
RGN: Does Anuvu ever take the reins on selecting the content for its airline customers, if requested? Are airline IFE managers still deeply involved in this part of the process?

Hussain: Yes, we offer both models depending on what our clients prefer. Some IFE teams want to be closely involved in every title selection, and we support that with the data and recommendations to make those decisions faster. Others prefer to lean on the expertise of our content teams and hand curation back to us for full direction, particularly airlines without a dedicated IFE content function. We treat every client as an individual, offering a flexible approach as requested.

reviews.transcript_full: Hey everyone and welcome back to my channel. Today I'm flying American Airlines  Economy class from Los Angeles to Chicago. I'm checking in the bag today and the  self-service baggage drop at LAX was quick and straightforward. Simply use the  kiosks to print your baggage tag and drop it off at the designated area.  Today's aircraft is an Airbus A321. For this flight I chose an ILC, seat  29D. The headrest is fully adjustable, it slides up and down and the sides fold  inwards. You'll find power outlets in front of your seat along with the  standard folding tray table that pulls out towards you. You also find a  compartment that holds the safety card in flight offer and a disposable bag.  There's also a device holder which can hold your phone or tablet while you watch  content from your device. Shortly after takeoff the crew started the snack  service. They passed out drinks, biscoff cookies and pretzels. I also tested out  the InFlight Wi-Fi. You can connect to their entertainment portal for free  content like movies, TV shows and live TV. If you're an American Airlines  Advantage member you can get free Wi-Fi browsing during the flight. While it  wasn't super fast it was noticeably faster than the Wi-Fi browsing I've  experienced on long-haul flights with international carriers like Starlux or  A&A. Since this was a red eye flight I spent the rest of the trip resting. The  seat recline was sufficient enough to catch a few hours of sleep before landing  into Chicago. Thank you for watching and I'll see you in the next video.

reviews.transcript_full: Come fly with me from Edinburgh to Shanghai with Highland Airlines.  I have never flown Highland Airlines before, so it was really exciting to experience this for the very first time.  First impressions, I was very impressed by the legroom and the freebies that they give you in the economy class.  You don't even get this with British Airways anymore.  Soon after taking off, I investigated the entertainment system which has some surprisingly interesting options,  like the European Perspective category, and then very soon after, we were served our first meet.  I went for the sweet and sour chicken with rice, whilst Fraser went for the braised beef.  It doesn't look like much, but I'll be honest, the food was pretty decent, especially for airplane food.  We even got chocolate moose for dessert, then I went for a toilet break and investigated the bathroom.  Nothing really to shout about, but I have to say it was very clean.  This was a nine hour flight, so we entertained ourselves with some anime and snacks,  before taking a few hours to rest with a very long nap, and then very quickly,  it was suddenly time for breakfast.  This was maybe my favorite meal on the plane.  It can conjure with chutake mushrooms, which I absolutely love.  The best meal so far.  After nine hours, we landed in Beijing, and this was probably the most annoying part of the trip.  We had to go through immigration, get our luggage, and then check back in to catch our flight to Shanghai.  Luckily, we had ample time during transit, and so we didn't really have to rush to our next flight.  We got onto a smaller plane, which also had incredible legroom.  I mean, Ryanair could never.  For this over one hour flight, we were given a lot of snacks.  I mean, I think this economy class is probably the most generous I've ever experienced.  I can't believe the amount of food that they gave us.  And the food wasn't bad, it is beef steam bun was actually delicious.  After the short travel, we finally arrived in Shanghai, ready to explore the city.  Would I travel in Haenan Airlines again?  Absolutely. reviews.transcript_excerpt: What changed is that Indigo no longer seems content to stay inside that box.…
reviews.transcript_full: I mentioned how big Indigo has become, but size is almost the less interesting part of  the story at this point.  For years they were very easy to understand.  Airbus narrow bodies, low fares, a huge domestic network, and a growing list of nearby international  routes, who is a very simple model, and it worked extraordinarily well.  What changed is that Indigo no longer seems content to stay inside that box.  The North 787s were probably the clearest early sign of that.  On paper it was a very strange setup.  In airline built around Airbus narrow bodies, suddenly leasing bowing wide bodies, just  to fly to Amsterdam and London.  But the 787s were only really meant to be temporary, giving Indigo a way to start stretching  further into Europe before the next generation of its own fleet arrived.  That experiment is now going to be ending on October 25th, though.  And notably, it's going to end before their A350s which are on order, show up.  After that point, the A321 XLRs will take over the Amsterdam service, and London will  be dropped for now at least.  I had a bit of time to kill, so I headed to the Miracle Lounge entering with priority  pass.  For most, the A350s on order are the obvious headline, but in many ways I'm way more interested  in the A321 XLRs.  Today, Athens is as far as Indigo's narrow body network stretches, and even that just  relies on the LRs.  The XLRs are going to be changing the equation quite a bit.  Suddenly, there are dozens of cities that become viable non-stop destinations without  needing to fill a much larger wide body.  It's the sort of aircraft that can really reshape an airline's entire route map, especially  when you're talking about a low-cost carrier with long-haul aspiration.

reviews.transcript_full: JetBlue has just made one of the biggest upgrades in its history, and it's something many travelers never thought they would see. The airline that once offered only all economy cabins and simple, no frrills service has now opened its first ever airport lounge. It's called Bluehouse, and it officially launches at New York's JFK Terminal 5. To understand why this is such a dramatic shift for JetBlue, you have to look back a decade. 4 years the airline focused on an egalitarian one-class experience with great legroom and seatback screens but nothing premium. Then things slowly began to change. JetBlue introduced its lifelat mint cabin. Then it launched longhaul flights to Europe. Now the airline is doubling down on the premium market and Blue House is its boldest move yet. Bluehouse spans 9,000 square ft across two floors near gate 527. It's designed to feel like a New York City apartment, not a generic airport lounge. JetBlue emphasized intimacy over size, limiting capacity to just 140 guests. The airline made this decision deliberately, aiming for a boutique, crowd-free atmosphere instead of the long lines seen at many lounges across the United States. As you enter the lounge, you'll notice the design immediately. The front desk resembles an old New York apartment mail room complete with vintage style mailboxes. A navy blue corridor leads you into the main space where you can take a nostalgic elevator up to the second level. JetBlue wanted the lounge to feel warm, artistic, and deeply connected to New York City, and it absolutely achieved that. The centerpiece of the first floor is the bar. It's inspired by New York's art deco design and features navy blue accents, gold trim, and a stunning ceiling that pays homage to the constellation mural inside Grand Central Terminal. The bar serves cocktails curated by the great of craft and espresso drinks from Joe Coffee, a well-known local roaster. Surrounding the bar are padded chairs, workspaces, and cozy booths. There's also a game room featuring JetBlue branded card and board games, and a large screen for entertainment. A library corner features books sourced from the Strand bookstore, adding to the local feel. And one of the lounge's most unique features is a photo booth that will soon include a retired Airbus A320 flight deck jump seat. Heading up the staircase to the second floor, you're met with curated artwork celebrating both New York and JetBlue. Upstairs, there is another bar offering beer and wine along with a self-s served kitchen area for coffee, soft drinks, and light bites. This floor is quieter and more relaxed with seating inspired by JetBlue's signature cabin mood lighting. Now, let's talk about food because this is where Blue House may surprise some people. For now, JetBlue is focusing on grab-and-go dining. That means no buffet and no restaurant service, at least for the moment. Instead, you'll find breakfast sandwiches, hot pastrami sandwiches, wraps, salads, and fresh snacks prepared daily. JetBlue partnered with Union Square Events to bring a local New York flavor to the menu. While the offerings are highquality, they are not meant to be the main attraction. JetBlue does plan to add a kitchen in 2026, which could elevate the dining experience significantly. The drinks, however, are already premium. The coffee program is strong, the cocktails are handcrafted, and the bar experience is clearly designed to be a highlight. But the question most travelers will ask is who actually gets access to Blue House. JetBlue has been very clear that access will be extremely limited. Entry is available only to holders of the JetBlue Premier World Elite Mastercard. Top tier Mosaic 4 Elite members and passengers flying in Mint to Europe. Mint customers traveling domestically do not get access. And even though JetBlue now has a partnership with United Airlines, United Elites and United Club members are not eligible either. Transatlantic Mint passengers can also bring one guest for $39. JetBlue will introduce day passes and annual memberships in 2026 along with paid access for more members of its loyalty program, but none of that will be available at launch. From a strategic point of view, this lounge signals that JetBlue wants to compete seriously for premium customers. The airline has struggled to return to profitability since the pandemic, and this is part of a broader push to strengthen loyalty and attract high-value travelers. JetBlue is also planning additional Blue House lounges. Boston Logan will get the second location in late 2026 and Fort Lauderdale is expected to follow. Blue House represents a new era for JetBlue. It's stylish, intimate, and designed to feel like a home away from home. It's also intentionally exclusive, which means many travelers may feel left out. But for JetBlue, this lounge is a statement. The airline is no longer just a budget-friendly carrier. It is evolving into a premium airline with premium ground services. reviews.transcript_full: Thinking about flying Singapore Airlines? Here's what you should know before booking an economy class trip.  Singapore Airlines is a popular option for long haul travel to Asia and Australia,  with convenient connections through Singapore Changi Airport.  For US travelers, the airline serves major gateways including New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Seattle.  Some routes operate non-stop to Singapore, and these can be seriously long flights.  New York to Singapore, for example, can take around 19 hours.  In economy class, passengers get personal entertainment through Chris Ward,  with movies, TV shows, music, and games to help pass the time.  Meals and beverages are included on long haul international flights,  and special meals can be requested in advance.  Another useful perk, Chris Flyer members can access complimentary,  unlimited Wi-Fi on most Singapore Airlines aircraft,  even in economy class. If Singapore isn't your final stop, Changi is a major hub for connections  across Asia and onward to Australia. And before booking, always check your fare's baggage allowance,  as what's included can vary. Overall, Singapore Airlines is worth considering if you're  planning a long journey to Asia or Australia, and want plenty of connection options.  For more airline reviews and helpful travel tips, stay tuned with ASAP Tickets.

From Dubai to Frankfurt, the experience starts with a massive business class lounge  and the convenience of boarding directly from it.  On board, the A380 uses a 1-2-1 staggered layout.  Each seat has its own non-chilled mini-bar.  While a thick mattress pad creates a comfortable bed for sleeping,  then there is the feature few airlines can match,  an onboard lounge where passengers can socialize.  Add Emirates' extensive entertainment system and high-quality breakfast and lunch,  including strong vegan options.  And the product feels genuinely premium.  Service was generally positive, though inconsistent and sometimes missing personal touches at  arrival. The flight was booked using 61,800 aeroplane points and approximately $750. reviews.transcript_full: My full comprehensive review of Lovetanza Airlines.  For this flight, I would be taking Lovetanza's LAX to Frankfurt Flight 451, a Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, and Munich to LAX, Flight 452 Airbus 38800.  Joining me on this journey would be Mom and my best bud Art.  So for the aircraft, I would have a spacious 3x3 or 3x4 or 3x3 row configuration.  I noticed the interior had a neutral yet orderly blue and gray upholstery on the seats,  that came with adjustable winged headrests for cranial support.  Noticably, there were no air nozzles, just reading lamps on the ceilings, but that's okay because the interior was temperature controlled.  Trails and floors were pretty clean, as were the bathrooms, although I must say they were pretty pedestrian and unassuming.  They just had what you needed.  Each flight gave you a standard pillow and blanket with headphones and sleep masks upon request.  The first flight to Frankfurt had no plug outlet on the USB and USB charger ports on the monitor screen,  which is pretty sufficient for most traveler devices.  Also, the monitor screens were bigger and wider on the aircraft,  whereas the A380 returning from Munich was an older aircraft that had smaller screens akin to the early 2010s,  with a USB and outdated Ethernet port, and it was hidden underneath the armrest, which was a strange place to put it.  And once plugged in, it was like the slowest charging ever, but on the plus side, both Mom and I had the entire rows to ourselves,  which was great, despite Mom kicking the back of my seat all the time.  I even ended up making my own little bed and office to get work done.  Why spend exponentially more on business class when you can get 83% of the exact same thing on an undersold flight with your own full row?  I love this hack.  Anyway, thankfully both screens offered that interactive 3D map thing, which I love, because you know me, geography guy.  It's kind of my thing.  Food came out for the first flight.  I requested the Hindu meal, because half the time standard meals suck, and they put more effort in the customized meals.  This one came with curry chicken and gulab jamun, which I love.  It was all syrupy and decadent.  Coming back, I got the standard meal, which was barbecue chicken and potatoes.  It was eh suboptimal.  Then I tried the quinoa salad and it was terrible.  Like, what the f***?  They put like weird vinegar stuff in it, and there was something slimy in the texture.  I hated it.  Please, Lufthansa, never make this f*** again.  Thankfully, Lufthansa has their own signature, a paratif cocktail, which I tried out of curiosity.  It was just the slight jovial recluse I needed from that horrendous quinoa fiasco.  One criticism, the seats lean back way too much, which I guess is comfortable, but it is kind of a hindrance when the person in front of you is all the way up in your face,  and you can't even fit your laptop for work.  And on the first flight, there wasn't much hangout space in the back, and it only had one bathroom on the side,  regardless I hung out there and chatted with art for like two hours.  Overall, the crew was nice.  The flight was decent, despite the second one having a few outdated features.  I'm gonna rate Lufthansa a 6.8 out of 10.  Not insanely exceptional, but noticeably above average, I guess.  It could have scored higher, but that quinoa salad ruined everything for me.  Never make that again, Lufthansa, please.

captions.text: The Inflight Wi-Fi on a Delta flight was hacked by something like this.

reviews.transcript_full: The Inflight Wi-Fi on a Delta flight was hacked by something like this.  So on August 10th, 2026, Delta Flight 591 from Las Vegas to Atlanta experienced disruptions to the Inflight Wi-Fi.  Passengers on the flight were disconnected from the Inflight Wi-Fi, and then this was followed by the appearance of a new Wi-Fi named Delta Wi-Fi Fast.  What was significant about this was that this flight was at the conclusion of DEF CON34 in Las Vegas.  This flight would have passengers who were attending that conference.  Based on the description of what happened, a Wi-Fi de-auth attack was launched against the Inflight Wi-Fi.  This is done by the attackers imitating a Wi-Fi access point and sending a special packet telling the clients to disconnect or drop from that Wi-Fi connection.  This was followed by a new Wi-Fi network, Delta Fast Wi-Fi appearing.  Passengers who connected to the new network were taken to a fishing portal requesting Google Login credentials.  This is an evil twin attack, which is an attack that presents a fake Wi-Fi network as a real one, combined with an evil portal attack, which is presenting a fake logon portal in an attempt to get users to provide their logon credentials to a legitimate website or service.  Google in this case.  The pilots of the flight sent a message through ACARS, a system for pilots to exchange messages with ground operations, that they were experiencing jamming of the Inflight Wi-Fi and that a bunch of passengers were at a cyber conference.  The pilots then sent a second message escalating to Delta Corporate Security.  The crew shut off the Inflight Wi-Fi for a period of about 30 minutes in order to clear the situation.  These attacks can be done with a device just like this, a Wi-Fi pineapple pager.  There are of course other devices in the Hack-Fi product line and by other manufacturers.  This device, though, the pineapple pager has its own battery and could be used in such a situation during a flight.  These tools are designed to be used by cybersecurity penetration testers or pen testers to find cybersecurity vulnerabilities with the goal for that organization.  Then to fix the vulnerabilities and become more secure.  These tools can also be used for educational purposes to demonstrate the need for a cybersecurity mindset in today's world.  Like any tool, these can be used for purposes both good and malicious.  And it is the responsibility of the user of the tool to use it for its intended purpose.  At the time of filming this, nothing has been reported regarding the individuals who did the attack.  It is also worth noting that Delta has reported the safety of the passengers and crew were not in danger.  However, in the United States, a federal law prohibits interfering with authorized wireless signals, including jamming wireless communications on an aircraft.  What are your thoughts on this situation? Was this harmless fun or a serious legal violation? Let me know in the comments.

reviews.transcript_full: Here's a quick light review of Condor Airlines in economy.  Condor is a German budget airline that flies medium and long haul flights between Germany  and different destinations around the world, so they were flying from Frankfurt, Germany  to LAX.  Our plane was in a 2-4-2 seat configuration, which does a couple of great because we got  our own road to ourselves.  The seat itself was surprisingly nice, especially compared to US domestic planes.  There were two tray tables that folded down, and the best part was this really large touch  screen TV that even angled out if you wanted it to and connected to our Bluetooth headphones.  We were served two meals in this flight.  The first was the main meal, which in our case was a vegetarian chili with carrots,  bread, and a dessert.  When you go online, it looks like they charge for meals, but actually on the plane, they  do give you a free meal, even in an economy.  The food itself was not the best, but for a budget airline, not too bad.  We ended up watching Zutopia 2 on this flight, and we've seen it, so our TVs played it  at the same time.  Fun fact, this movie is actually Zumania 2 in Germany.  There are a lot of different options on the screen, but the best part of course is watching  the airplane map to see where on the world you are.  They did have some snacks and drinks in the back galley of the plane.  We also ended up buying Pringles as well.  And then near the end of the flight, they brought around the final snack, which for us was  a cheese pizza.  Honestly, this pizza was really good. captions.text: Safran Unity seats offer high walls and excellent privacy.

reviews.transcript_full: Can Riyadh air compete with Emirates and Qatar airways from its very first passenger flight?  Follow flight points for daily award flight deal alerts.  On the short flight from Jeddah to Riyadh,  premium economy looks stunning with dark marble,  gold, and purple details.  But limited legroom, fixed headrests,  and a shared lavatory with economy weaken the experience.  For US BC ports and exceptional pre-departure service,  help recover it.  Business class is far more impressive.  Safran Unity seats offer high walls and excellent privacy.  While the front row business elite feels like first class in disguise,  the bed is surprisingly roomy and fabric-lined walls reduce cabin noise.  Even without alcohol, the meal service was exceptional for a 1.5-hour flight.  The verdict, world-class design, but its dense layout feels profit-driven.  Does Riyadh air have enough identity to challenge Emirates and Qatar?

reviews.transcript_full: American Airlines just found room for 26 more seats on its largest passenger jet, without  cutting economy. The airline is completely redesigning its Boeing 777-300ERs under Project  Olympus. The old layout carried 304 passengers and included just eight international first-class  seats. But first-class is now disappearing completely. Instead, American is expanding its premium  cabins while keeping all 216 economy seats. Business class is also getting brand new suites with  sliding privacy doors while premium economy grows significantly. The result? American can carry  330 passengers instead of 304 on the exact same aircraft. Passengers are also getting upgraded  entertainment screens, USB-C charging, and new VSAT Wi-Fi. The first remodeled 777 is already  flying and American plans to upgrade all 20 of its 777-300ERs by the end of 2027. So would you  trade traditional first-class for more premium seats? reviews.transcript_excerpt: I've sat through a lot of safety videos in my life.…

captions.text: I've sat through a lot of safety videos in my life.

reviews.transcript_full: I flew Starlux Airlines Premium Economy from Bangkok to Taipei to Los Angeles.  Boarding was quick, and the cabin looked brand new.  My seat was already made up with a pillow, a blanket, and an amenity kit waiting for me.  The screen lit up with a welcome message in five languages, and just look at this leg  room.  All the seat controls live on this glowing armrest panel, and the remote slides right  out of the side.  Then there's the leg rest, one button, and your feet are up.  Honestly, this is the part that sold me on Premium Economy.  Proper headphones too, which you'll want.  Because the safety video is an event.  Starlux made theirs with this little green alien, and it's genuinely funny.  Seat belts, oxygen masks, even a whole bit about taking off your high heels.  I've sat through a lot of safety videos in my life.  This is the first one I actually watched all the way through.  Ten out of ten, no notes.  After takeoff, they played a short film about the airline, Sea Turtles, a tea ceremony,  very calming before the food arrived.  Then dinner.  The art came down the aisle, and the trays looked better than some restaurants I've been  to.  Real metal cutlery, by the way.  Lasagna for the main, with shrimp to start, fresh fruit, a warm roll, and a little tarot  dessert, and a glass of red wine to go with it.  A few hours later, round two.  Beef with rice, salad, and tiramisu.  And breakfast before landing.  Crasant, yogurt, and congee.  The leg room, the food, the little touches.  One of the most comfortable long flights I've had.

reviews.transcript_excerpt: The entertainment wasn't working properly, and other passengers seemed frustrated too.…

captions.text: The entertainment wasn't working properly, and other passengers seemed frustrated too.

reviews.transcript_full: I flew Quantus from Singapore to Auckland on 2A330s.  Same airline, same journey, but somehow these flights felt like completely different airlines.  And I chose this route on purpose, Singapore to Brisbane, then Brisbane to Auckland, because  both flights were scheduled on the Airbus A330.  I liked the A330.  Apparently, that was only part of the story.  First up, QF-5-2, leaving Singapore on 13 September, 7.5 hours scheduled in economy.  The cabin felt really dated.  These tablets looked like first-generation iPads to me.  The entertainment wasn't working properly, and other passengers seemed frustrated too.  Honestly, I mainly wanted the flight map.  Even that wouldn't work for me.  After a while, I stopped bothering.  For someone my size, the economy seat felt extremely tight and uncomfortable.  Then the cabin manager came over because of how I was sitting.  Before speaking to me, he touched my arm and tried to push it inward.  There simply wasn't room for it to go any further.  If he just asked me to move, that would have been fine.  Being touched and pushed without first being spoken to felt invasive, uncomfortable, and  unprofessional to me.  The food didn't help.  Personally, I found the meals disappointing.  We reached Brisbane around 6 in the morning, with about 2 hours and 15 minutes scheduled  between flights.  After that, I wasn't exactly excited about another Qantas A330.  It's now exceeded.  With your seat belt bent like faster.  But QF-119 to Auckland was almost a complete turnaround.  The cabin felt much better.  The entertainment worked, and the crew were friendly and welcoming.  That made the whole flight much more pleasant.  The food still didn't impress me, and economy was still tight for me.  But that's what made this journey so strange.  Same airline.  Both booked for the A330.  A couple of hours apart.  Two completely different experiences.  Singapore to Brisbane?  Not one I'd want to repeat.  Brisbane to Auckland?  Much, much better.  That second crew showed how much the people on board can change a flight.  Have you ever had two completely different experiences with the same airline on one journey?

reviews.transcript_full: What is like flying business class for the first time?  In all honesty, I have one business class too other times, but they were all of not flying,  so I was just knocked out. But this is the first time I could to experience the whole thing as I  was flying to China, so let's see if it's really worth the money. There's business class and  there's first class. First class is people with real, funky money, which I would love to experience  one day. Any airlines want to collaborate. But me, I'm still using my credit card points and  getting the best discounts I can find for these flights, so we're not there just yet. When you have  business class though, you still feel pretty special. Immediately when you go to check in, you skip the  entire queue of people. Your check in luggage gets a priority tag made that it'll be the first to  come out at baggage claim, and you also get access to the business lounge of that flight. The business  lounges are clean, they're away from the crowd, so you can rest, do your work, take a comfortable  quit, and they're not so gross public toilet. And best of all, all the food and drinks are free.  And we haven't even gotten on the plane yet. And then when you finally get on the plane, you always  get a hot towel, a drink as soon as you sit down, and every single flight I've been on so far  give you a complimentary toilet tray bag that you get to keep with some bathroom amenities.  This flight was overnight first before I got any food, so I just washed up and slept.  And honestly, I think this is the best part of any business class flight. Being able to lay flat  for an overnight flight has made my flight experience so much more enjoyable. When I finally  woke up the next morning, I served as food, which it's still aeroplane food just served on a  plate if I'm being honest. I think the really extravagant looking food you always see on the internet  is mainly for first class, which is a bummer. And also, you can't actually ask for everything on the  menu. At least I've tried anyways and they've denied me every time. But apart from that, you can  ask for whatever snack or drink you want, including alcohol, which is all free. Is it really worth  on average like $5,000 per flight? Hell no. But my mama didn't raise me as a stingy agent for nothing.  Save your credit card and reward points and get business class for at least once a year. Or you can  wait for discounts on overnight flights, which are a bit cheaper as well, and at most you'd be paying  $2,000 max. I think. And for that, I would say for the free drink and food, for the comforts  of my old man needs, like, an agonizing pain. And so I can time travel when I sleep comfortably  on a plane. It is absolutely worth the money.

reviews.transcript_full: Bahrain's Crown Prince and Prime Minister Prince Salman bin Hamad al-Khalifa arrived in Malaysia on Friday for a special visit in conjunction with the Formula One F1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix at the Sepang International Circuit SIC.  The special aircraft carrying Prince Salman landed at the Bunga Raya Complex at Kuala Lumpur International Airport at 12 pm.  He was welcomed by Tungku, Temengong, Johor, Tungku, Idris Iskandar al-Haj Sultan Ibrahim, Tungku Panglima Johor, Tungku Abdul Rahman al-Haj Sultan Ibrahim and Tungku Putra Johor, Tungku Abu Bakar al-Haj Sultan Ibrahim.  Prince Salman then walked past a guard of honour, comprising 28 officers and personnel from the first battalion Royal Ranger Regiment.  The Sepang International Circuit was selected as the temporary venue for the 2026 Formula One Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix, which runs from October 2 to 4.  In July, Formula One confirmed Malaysia as the host following an agreement involving Formula One, the Federation International Deloitte Mobile, or FIA and the Governments of Malaysia and Bahrain.  The agreement allowed the Bahrain Grand Prix to remain on the 2026 F1 calendar after the race was cancelled earlier this season due to geopolitical tensions in West Asia.

reviews.title: Flying Qatar Airways Business Class was insane! Q-Suites from MIA-OH on their 777-300ER ✈️ #qsuites
reviews.transcript_excerpt: breakfast came, and then we landed in…
reviews.transcript_full: Here's what it's like to fly in the world's best business class with Qatar Airways. We boarded their 777-300 from Miami to Doha, where we would be flying in the award-winning Qsuites. After boarding, you're welcomed with a glass of champagne, and right away I was looking at that menu, which I was clearly very excited about. There was plenty of storage throughout the seat, and then before we knew it, we were taking off. We were handed our pajamas, which we changed into right after takeoff, and then started the dinner service. We started with an appetizer that consisted of caviar on top of lobster, followed by their famous mezze platter. Highly recommend this, as it was amazing. And after that, we had the beef short rib with some veggies and potatoes, and this was our favorite. One of the best parts about this seat is that they offer a turndown service, where your beds practically become one, and you can sleep side-by-side while 37,000 ft in the sky. Of course, Kat made us wear eye masks before we got some sleep. After waking up, I woke up hungry, and of course ordered off their dine-on-demand menu and got this incredible chicken sandwich. After a couple more movies and relaxing, breakfast came, and then we landed in Doha. So, do you think this seat is worth all of the hype? We certainly did.

reviews.title: Inside British Airways’ brand new Premium Economy (787-9 retrofit) 👀
reviews.transcript_excerpt: The TV is bigger and you get a little remote control as well which is attached to your seat so you can control it without having to lean forward.…

captions.text: The TV is bigger and you get a little remote control as well which is attached to your seat so you can control it without having to lean forward.

reviews.transcript_full: This is British Airways brand new Will Traveler Plus cabin or Premium Economy aboard their refurbished Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner.  My flight home from Vegas was oversold so at check-in the agent handed me a free upgrade to this Premium Economy cabin.  This cabin was so new that even the flight staff didn't know how to work the footrest.  The new standout feature is that the headrest no longer just has the smaller adjustable rest.  It now has these new privacy wings and they make you feel like you're actually sat in your own little pod  which was absolutely incredible for a Premium Economy seat.  You get 38 inches of pitch, a bifold tray table and a dedicated fold down footstool and their a client angle is also very deep.  Another really cool feature is that because it's a Dreamliner the windows don't have the pull-down shades.  They have electronic dimmers which I had never seen before.  You also got a little amenities kit which had socks and I mask pen dental kit.  You also get a blanket and a little pillow which is a nicer quality than an economy.  The TV is bigger and you get a little remote control as well which is attached to your seat so you can control it without having to lean forward.  You also get the nice big headphones which seem to be the same ones as in business which are much more comfortable than the ones you get in economy, the little earbud types.  For the food you get a welcome drink and then you also get a little menu so that you can pick exactly what you want from that.  Then that comes on proper china with metal cutlery which is a massive plus.  They obviously dim the lights for nighttime and then because you're in this sort of semi-private seat it was much easier to get a good night's sleep.  The seats are a climb really far and that's probably the only negative is obviously that when the person in front reclines it comes right into your space which means you have to recline as well.  But honestly on a night flight I really don't mind because I did want to get some sleep.  I've honestly never slept better on a long haul flight including in business.  Obviously not all the cabins are going to have been upgraded to this but this cabin honestly if I can get this again in premium I will definitely be upgrading.  Let me know if you've got any questions or if you've tried it let me know how your experience was because I honestly think this was absolute perfection.

reviews.transcript_full: Ever wondered what it's like at the front of the plane on a Contas flight?  I'm flying Premium Economy and I'm flying Business.  And here's what you get in each cabin on the 787 Dreamliner.  We're flying across the Tasman so it's only a short 3 hour trip.  In Premium Economy there are two seats on each side of the aisle and they are so comfy.  In Business you'll get a seat that reclines all the way into a bed.  Before take off we both got served bubbles.  Nice big headphones, comfy blankets and all the entertainment we could dream of.  And then there's the food.  In Premium I ordered the Ravioli which came with a Greek salad,  sourdough bread, cheese and crackers, a muffin and a lint chocolate.  In Business I ordered the pulled pork toasty with a smoked salmon salad for  cutcher and Maggie Bear ice cream.  The drinks menu is so good in both cabins.  You can order wine, beer, spritzes, you name it.  Don't miss the Avro Gin Spritz which is exclusive on Qantas International Flight.  It's not often you want a flight to keep on going but we could have definitely  spent more hours in these seats.  Have you flown Qantas Premium Economy or Business before? reviews.title: The Tomahawks Were Still in the Air When the Apaches Opened Fire #iraq #militaryhistory #pavelow
reviews.transcript_excerpt: The Tomahawks were still in flight to a Baghdad.…
reviews.transcript_full: The Tomahawks were still in flight to a Baghdad.  When US Army Apache's opened fire in the Iraqi desert, Navy warships had begun launching  Tomahawk cruise missiles toward Baghdad at about 1.30 a.m. on January 17, 1991.  The Defense Department calls it the first irretrevable hostile fire of Desert Storm.  Once launched, those missiles could not be called back.  The Apache's began firing in Western Iraq at 238.  Their targets were two early warning radar sites near the Saudi border.  Each hour, the moment the war was set to begin, was 3 a.m. Baghdad time.  Those radars had to go first, so that Iraq would not see the strike aircraft following  close behind.  Eight Apache's and four Air Force payload helicopters split into two teams, one for each site.  The first target was a dug-in power generator, then the command van and the radar dishes.  At both sites, the attack was over in four minutes, but according to the Gulf War Air  Power Survey, one site managed to get word out that it was under attack just before the  Hellfire struck.  The Defense Department describes the Apache attack as the opening blow of the conflict.  By then, two F-117s had already crossed the border and were on their way to Baghdad.  At 251, an F-117 stealth fighter bombed the Air Defense Center at New KB, the post those  radar sites reported to.  In the Pentagon's account, the helicopter and F-117 attacks together, opened gaps in  Iraq's radar coverage and its command network.  At 3 a.m., on schedule, two F-117s bombed targets in Baghdad, and through the gap the helicopters  had opened, American F-15E fighter bombers flew into western Iraq.  They were going after the fixed launchers for Iraq's scud missiles.  They released their bombs at 305, five minutes after H-hour.  According to an Air Force history by Richard Davis, the Air Planners assumed that once the  first bomb fell on Iraq, Saddam Hussein would order scud launches against Israel, and they  timed the strike to stop him.  Iraq's first scuds were fired at Israel about a day later, in the early hours of January  18th.  The Air Planners had hoped that heavy strikes on the fixed launchers in the first hours  would largely eliminate Iraq's ability to fire scuds.  The Gulf War Air Power Survey says that hope proved illusory.

reviews.title: The Flydubai Flight That Fell 14,000 Feet
reviews.transcript_excerpt: Tracking data shows it had lost more than 17,000 feet within about two minutes.…
reviews.transcript_full: Over northern Saudi Arabia, a fly Dubai Boeing 737 Max-8 lost more than 14,000 feet in  under 30 seconds, according to flight tracking data.  It was flight FZ1073, Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday 30 September 2026.  It left Dubai just after 7 in the morning, local time.  The UAE Attorney General puts the number on board at 172 passengers and crew.  Other reports say 174.  From about 34,000 feet, the aircraft kept falling.  Tracking data shows it had lost more than 17,000 feet within about two minutes.  The UAE Attorney General says the cause was inside the cockpit.  The co-pilot attacked the captain with the aircraft's crash-axe and tried to take control.  He called it an attempted terrorist act.  The captain was wounded.  Reports say he still managed to release the cockpit door from the inside.  Passengers and crew went in and overpowered the co-pilot.  About seven minutes after the first drop, the aircraft transmitted squawk 7700, a general  emergency.  A few minutes later it changed to 7500, the code for unlawful interference.  The cockpit tracking data has the aircraft level at about 15,000 feet roughly 12 minutes  after the first dip.  Two off-duty flydubi pilots traveling as passengers took the controls.  They flew the aircraft to Tabuk in northwest Saudi Arabia.  It landed at about 945 local time.  The UAE Attorney General later said the co-pilot meant to crash it into Tel Aviv's main airport.  Flydubi has suspended flights to Israel.  14,000 feet gone in half a minute.  And the aircraft still landed because of people who were already on board.  Next in the hijack files, why airlineers carry an axe in the cockpit.

reviews.title: Saudi Arabia’s airport was just struck by Houthis
reviews.channel_title: The Under Report by Eric Czuleger
reviews.transcript_excerpt: 12 people have lost their lives and 300 have been injured in a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia's main airport in Riyadh.…
reviews.transcript_full: 12 people have lost their lives and 300 have been injured in a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia's main airport in Riyadh.  It's very difficult to get information out of Saudi Arabia or Yemen for that matter, but this is a huge deal because of what it means.  I made this chart based off of the ranges of various missiles known to be used by the Houthis.  Their stronghold is here in Sadda in Western Yemen, so this would make sense as a launch point, but realistically it could be anywhere along this border.  The ability to land strikes on Saudi Arabia's main airport tells us a couple of things.  One in a high security environment like right now, they are either unable or unwilling to intercept incoming missiles.  Previous drone attacks have been shot down and missiles have also been intercepted with either Patriot 3 or 2 missiles.  Also I think that's, but if they're getting through that means that their defensive capabilities are much lower.  It also tells us a lot about the Houthis or Ansara laws offensive capabilities.  The airport is an unmoving target which is publicly known, so targeting is not that big of a deal.  We don't know for a certain if they were targeting directly the Saudi airline, but it's likely that the Saudi airline is the majority of that airport.  But the thing to think about here is the fact that they had operational control to make a successful launch.  Typically these missiles are hidden underground before they are taken out and fired.  They then move positions so they don't alert any ISR. This is known as shooting and scooting.  So we should assume that anything within this radius can be targeted.  Also this comes directly after a Saudi Arabian air strike, a series of air strikes.  So if Saudi Arabia's goal is to either suppress capabilities or take out leadership, it's clearly not working because they're able to fire back.  But there are some additional complicating factors that I want to get you guys caught up on.  So it looks like Pakistan and Turkey are going to honor the Mecca agreement.  This was a sort of pan-meda-leaster and collective defense treaty that was signed a couple months ago.  Anyway, Turkey's been very clear about what their role here is.  They will provide defensive troops, but in no way will they go into Yemen.  Same deal with Pakistan, but Pakistan has been sending troops to Saudi Arabia and training their Air Force for years now.  So essentially what they're saying is we'll add defensive depth through manpower to make sure that nobody comes into your borders.  But as far as dealing with the problem on the other side of the Yemen border, that's on you guys.  And remember the longer the Houthis or Ansar Allah holds this territory, the more that they are able to entrench, the more operational space they have, the more they can move their missiles around.  A harder it is going to be to fight them.  Saudi Arabia's inability to deal with this threat rapidly means that it is turning into a longer and longer conflict.  And it is important to remember this is existential for Saudi Arabia.  So that means one way or another they will have to go into direct conflict with the Houthis.  Hey while you're here make sure to subscribe to my newsletter.  That's where I give you guys a weekly intelligence brief as well as my predictions for the coming seven days.  Links are in the bio.

reviews.title: Etihad NEW First and Business Class🤩
reviews.transcript_excerpt: The finishes are luxurious, we have all the modern tech like USB-C, charging, OL position, power port and a large responsive TV.…

captions.text: The finishes are luxurious, we have all the modern tech like USB-C, charging, OL position, power port and a large responsive TV.

reviews.transcript_full: Etihad Airways just revealed their brand new first class and business class that will be featured on their upcoming Airbus E321LR deliveries.  These planes will fly everywhere from Chiang Mai and Krabi to Paris and Tunis.  I go to be one of the first people to check these seats out in person, so what are my first impressions?  The 14 business class seats are among the best single aisle seats in the world.  All offering direct aisle access and facing the windows unlike so many other E321 business class seats that unfortunately face the aisle.  The finishes are luxurious, we have all the modern tech like USB-C, charging, OL position, power port and a large responsive TV.  Etihad opted not to install a door unlike what even US carriers are doing these days, but only trying it in flight will tell if privacy is an issue or not.  They also have two first class seats in the front row of the cabin.  As you can tell, this seat is basically the same as business class except it has a door and you have a large,  Ottoman area. Of course you'll also get better in flight service with first class dining, bedding, amenities etc.  The bed in first, but even in business, seems super spacious, but I am a little confused about how they're planning to sell first class outright,  given that it lacks what people sort of expect in first class. A dedicated lavatory, a curtain separating it from business class,  a far more spacious seat than business etc. Don't get me wrong this seat is awesome, but I'm curious just how popular it ends up being.  But all in all, this is just about as good as narrow body flying gets.

reviews.transcript_excerpt: That's good news because it has Emirates latest cabins with a sleek economy class,…
reviews.transcript_full: Emirates just took delivery of its first new airplane type in 17 years and I got to be on the first flight.  This is the Emirates A350 and they're going to send this plane to second tier cities.  So if you, like me, grew up or lived somewhere people have to look up on a map,  this plane might be coming to your home city soon.  That's good news because it has Emirates latest cabins with a sleek economy class,  three rows of premium economy and finally 32 business class seats with direct i-likes as at the front.  What is it like taking the first flight of a brand new plane on Emirates?  To celebrate the launch, they have these sleek menus and give out flight certificates that you can bet I'll be framing.  The mood is so festive on board with people taking photos, comparing it to past experiences,  and even the crew geeking out over how cool it is to fly on the inaugural flight.

The world's biggest passenger airplane to A-threadie is the most spacious, quiet, and smooth ride in the world.  It makes flying economy class so nice and easy.  Two, they have some of the freshest and tastiest food of any airline and economy class on flights catered and Dubai,  and even from any outstations where they have better food than the airlines base there.
